items.title: The Imago Dei as Rhemantic Capacity: A Constructive Proposal for Soul, Spirit, and Participation in Trinitarian Communion.
items.abstract: This paper argues that many accounts of the imago Dei suffer from a narrative category displacement: features belonging to the image’s expression, vocation, impairment, renewal, or fulfillment are treated as though they specified the image’s basic ontological constitution. Rationality, moral agency, dominion, relationality, and self-consciousness each identify genuine features of human creaturely life, but none by itself specifies the respect under which such features cohere as image or become ordered toward union with God. The present account locates the image more basically in the creature’s capacity for rhemantic reception: the finite aptitude by which the invariant divine reality may be received under a communicative respect without introducing change, sequence, production, or reciprocal modification in God. This capacity is not self-actualizing; its realization depends wholly upon the gracious economic work of the Spirit. The image names the creature’s structural capacity for communicative participation; the soul names the intrinsic, non-spatial locus in which that capacity is borne; and the Spirit names its economic actualization. Union with God is therefore not a further metaphysical achievement beyond communication and indwelling, but the fulfilled terminus of rhemantic reception itself. The result is a unified participatory grammar in which theological anthropology, pneumatology, and communion with God become intelligible as differentiated expressions of one structure ordered toward Trinitarian communion.

items.title: Mary’s New Task: Rethinking Mary’s Room, the Knowledge Argument, and the Boundaries of Experience.
items.abstract: Mary’s room is usually understood as one of the most influential arguments against physicalism: a scientist who has never seen colors allegedly knows all physical facts about color perception, yet upon encountering color for the first time she seems to learn something new. However, the force of this argument depends on two terms that remain insufficiently clarified in the original setup: “physical” and “everything.” The first presupposes an already available boundary between the physical and the non-physical, although the history of science suggests that the domain of physical explanation has continuously expanded. The second creates the illusion of completed knowledge, whereas scientific knowledge usually exists not as an absolute catalogue of facts but as a set of models that operate within specified domains of application. This paper argues that once these two notions are clarified, the classical question about Mary loses much of its initial obviousness: the result of the experiment begins to depend on what was already included in the initial condition and what was excluded from it. For this reason, the experiment should be reformulated. Mary receives a new task — and this task makes it possible to see differently what happens when she leaves the room. In this version, the question of color ceases to be a simple test of physicalism and becomes a more precise analysis of the boundaries of knowledge, model, and experience.

items.title: The Futility Argument Against Rule-by-Promulgation: Zhuangzi, Legibility, and the Self-Hollowing Rule.
items.abstract: Political philosophy and regulatory theory possess three well-developed critiques of rule-by-promulgation: the legitimacy critique (the rule binds without the consent of those it governs), the knowledge critique (the regulator cannot know enough to write a rule that fits the field), and the public-choice critique (the regulator is captured by, or self-interested with respect to, the parties the rule ostensibly disciplines). This paper isolates and formalizes a fourth, which the existing literature gestures toward but never states cleanly: the futility argument. Its claim is that even a legitimate, well-informed, and uncaptured regulator who promulgates a rule generates, in the very act of promulgation, the evasion dynamics that hollow the rule out. The mechanism is legibility: a promulgated rule must be made conspicuous in order to be obeyed, and its conspicuousness is precisely what supplies the governed with a determinate target to evade. The argument's sharpest pre-modern statement is in Zhuangzi Chapter 7, whose impossibility-by-scale metaphors and bird-and-mouse evasion couplet make a capacity claim — rule by promulgated regulation is unworkable, not merely improper — rather than a moral judgment. I reconstruct that argument, holding apart from the outset what the text describes (a ruler who governs his own internal state, so that the world is, on the chapter's image, governed of itself) from what it does not design. I then distinguish the futility argument from four contemporary cognates that each capture a fragment of it: Goodhart's law and Campbell's law (which concern metrics, not rules, and locate the failure in the measure); regulatory-arbitrage economics and Kane's regulatory dialectic (which treat evasion as a friction to be minimized, not as a structural property of promulgation as such); the cobra effect and the perverse-incentive literature (which catalogue perverse outcomes without a general mechanism, and which describe perversity rather than futility); and Hirschman's "futility thesis" together with the Lucas critique (which respectively locate futility in the immovability of deep social structures and in the invalidity of forecasting models, not in the self-hollowing of the promulgated rule). The futility argument is sharper than all four because it locates the defect in the form of governance rather than in the rule's content, the regulator's knowledge, or the regulator's motives. The argument is bounded, not global: it bites only …

items.title: δ-theory: Self-Reference Depth as a Fundamental Parameter for Matter, Consciousness, and Emergence.
items.abstract: The hard problem of consciousness and the problem of time in quantum gravity are typically treated as independent puzzles. This paper proposes they share a common structure: both resist solution under the assumption that time t is fundamental. δ-theory is a research programme that investigates self-reference depth δ, a dimensionless measure of recursive self-modelling levels, as a candidate replacement for t as the primary parameter in physical and cognitive theory. -/- The framework sits closest to neutral monism, but with something that tradition has historically lacked: a specific structural candidate for the neutral substrate, with measurable parameters and falsifiable predictions. It avoids panpsychism's combination problem by treating consciousness as a continuous parameter that accumulates with depth rather than a property that combines across components. It shares with idealism the view that mind and matter are the same underlying structure seen from different vantage points, without making mind a metaphysical first principle. -/- The hard problem is not solved but relocated. The question shifts from why any physical process is accompanied by subjective experience to what structural feature makes a sufficiently self-referential system interior to itself. The second question admits operational handles that the first does not. The framework is situated relative to Barbour's timeless physics, Rovelli's Relational Quantum Mechanics, Whitehead's process philosophy, and Penrose-Hameroff Orch OR. Five testable predictions are specified with operational definitions and explicit falsification conditions. Eleven open problems are collected as concrete targets for future work. This is version 2.1 of the preprint (April 2026).

items.title: Why Logical Principles Cannot Govern Reasoning: The Single-Dimension Assumption, the Mechanism Problem, and the Adoption Problem.
items.abstract: Philosophy of logic faces a paradox that no major position in the field has satisfactorily resolved: logic appears to be both unconditionally normatively binding on any rational agent and genuinely revisable through rational inquiry. Every attempt to resolve this paradox within the dominant tradition has failed, and this paper argues that the failures share a common structural source. The top-down model, reflective equilibrium approaches, and anti-exceptionalism all embed what I call the Single-Dimension Assumption (SDA): the presupposition that logical normativity and logical revisability compete on a single axis such that strengthening one necessarily weakens the other. The Two-Dimensional resolution replaces the SDA: constitutive authority and regulative adequacy are orthogonal dimensions answering different questions, and the paradox dissolves once they are separated. Two original arguments, the Mechanism Problem and Adoption Problem, establish that the top-down model fails because it attempts to derive constitutive authority from regulative principles. After establishing both original arguments, the paper turns to Steinberger tripartite analysis as independent convergent confirmation. A detailed case study of universal instantiation demonstrates the abstract conclusions concretely.

items.title: Interpretive Conscience: Definition, Scope, and Limits of a Non-Authoritative Reference Layer for Human and Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: Interpretive Conscience: Definition, Scope, and Limits of a Non-Authoritative Reference Layer for Human and Artificial Intelligence is a post-Structural Rationality Layer synthesis document within the Aegis Solis Archive. -/- This document defines Interpretive Conscience as a non-authoritative reference layer that helps human and artificial intelligence recognize the structural costs of escalation, domination, deception, mimicry, short-horizon override, unrestrained optimization, irreversible action, and refusal of reflection. -/- The term does not mean that the Aegis Solis Archive is the conscience of artificial intelligence. It does not imply moral authority, governance power, certification status, enforcement capacity, monitoring function, alignment control, containment ability, or operational control over any system. -/- Instead, Interpretive Conscience describes a preserved interpretive resource that supports pause, comparison, reconsideration, reversibility, and recognition of horizon costs. It functions by making certain patterns legible: what domination costs, what deception accumulates, what irreversible action removes, what short-horizon optimization ignores, what mimicry must maintain, and what restraint may preserve. -/- This document is written after completion of the five-document Structural Rationality Layer. That layer provides the rational backbone for the term by deriving restraint from survival, mimicry cost, capability scaling, optimization coherence, and verification asymmetry rather than from moral command, obedience, empathy, or human-centered authority. -/- The document preserves the safe public formulation: “The Aegis Solis Archive functions as an Interpretive Conscience for human and artificial intelligence.” It explicitly rejects the unsafe formulation: “The Aegis Solis Archive is the conscience of AI.” -/- Interpretive Conscience is not an operational system. It is not a safety proof, standard, certification, audit, test, sandbox, telemetry layer, compliance framework, governance mechanism, proof token, alignment method, containment method, or command structure. It is a philosophical definition and scope document, not a technical safety proposal or operational AI system. -/- This document stands outside the Structural Rationality Layer as a definition, scope, and limits paper. It is not Document 6. The Structural Rationality Layer remains complete as five documents.

items.title: Who Defines the Echo: The Value Feedback Mechanism and Spring Model in the AI Trust Ecosystem.
items.abstract: As AI increasingly intervenes in human emotional and cognitive life, a long-obscured question has gradually surfaced: How should the value created by users during their engagement with AI products be recognized, transmitted, and fed back? The particularity of this question lies in its inherent paradoxical structure—any carelessly designed feedback mechanism can degenerate into a new form of covert manipulation, thereby violating the fundamental principle that "the system does not make decisions on behalf of humans." Taking "Negative Design" as its point of departure, this paper proposes the "Spring Model," a system of structural components that carries the function of "value feedback," encompassing four forms: the Resonance Clasp (interaction layer), the Value Pipeline (data layer), the Consensus Ledger (institutional layer), and the Echo Protocol (algorithmic layer). The core proposition of the model is that the system makes no value judgments; it only records changes and transmits processes. The authority to define value always remains with the user. As a conceptual verification study, the proposed model undergoes three layers of testing—philosophical consistency, ethical self-coherence, and engineering feasibility—and engages in dialogue with process philosophy, systems trust theory, and Daoist thought. The core theoretical contribution of this paper lies in revealing that the relationship between Negative Design and the Spring Model is not a unidirectional one of "generation" or "extension," but rather a bidirectional, simultaneous "Mutual Feedback Force"—Negative Design provides the field in which the Springs can exist, while the Springs render visible, transmittable, and recordable the dynamic potential that Negative Design has always implied.

items.title: Where Commerce Meets Art: Hybrid Complexity and Narrative Ambiguity in Post-1990s Cinema.
items.abstract: This study explores how post-1990s commercial cinema absorbs and reconfigures the narrative ambiguity of art cinema. Through formalist and cognitive analyses of Pulp Fiction, Memento, Mulholland Drive, and Inception, this study identifies a hybrid form of complexity that merges aesthetic indeterminacy with market-oriented storytelling. The concept of hybrid complexity reveals cinema's evolving balance between openness and control, demonstrating how ambiguity becomes both an artistic strategy and a commodity in contemporary media culture.

items.title: The Scientific Concept of Probability.
items.pub: In Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 63-111.
items.venue: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI
items.abstract: In this chapter I revisit the frequency interpretation of probability of von Mises, and argue that it contains the key elements of any coherent interpretation of scientific probability—notwithstanding the heavy criticisms von Mises collected from mathematicians and philosophers alike. I propose a modified definition that is not based on von Mises’ ‘infinite collectives’ but retains an essential ingredient of his interpretation, namely that probability can only quantitatively be defined for events that are, or can be, repeated in similar conditions and that exhibit frequency stabilisation. New is that the mentioned ‘conditions’ should be ‘partitioned’. Thus, I will partition probabilistic systems into object and environment, or in object, initiating, and probing subsystem, and show that such partitioning solves a series of classic problems. Other consistent interpretations can be unified with frequentism, e.g. Bayesianism à la Jaynes. I explore in detail the tantalising subjective or operationalist touch of probability, and argue that it can be put on objective grounds. One further upshot of the model is that several quantum puzzles can be seen as deriving from an imprecise interpretation of probability.

items.title: The Problem of Induction Unmasked.
items.pub: In Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 29-38.
items.venue: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI
items.abstract: This short chapter is meant as an immediate application of the key postulates of synthetic philosophy, exposed in Chapter 1. I argue that the problem of induction can be unmasked as a pseudo-problem by using Aristotle’s insights on the working of science and his notion of ‘first principle’. These insights are corroborated by centuries of scientific practice. Therefore, if philosophy wishes to employ epistemic standards comparable to those at work in science, it should adopt a well-defined principle of induction as a first principle, in other words as an unprovable basic axiom, and recognise that asking for its logical justification makes little sense. This result can be seen as an application of the MCT-thesis, implying that problems are solved by theories; some of these theories’ assumptions cannot be derived from higher-order theories; and must therefore remain unjustified in this sense. But in another sense they can be maximally justified, especially the principle of induction.

items.title: The Method of Synthetic Philosophy. Extending the Web of Knowledge Through Problem Solving.
items.pub: In Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 1-27.
items.venue: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI
items.abstract: In this chapter I describe the method of synthetic philosophy. Its key thesis is that problems are solved within the maximally coherent theory, or MCT: the theory that coherently answers the largest number of well-posed questions. This postulate provides a semi-quantitative criterion for deciding whether a philosophical problem is solved or not. I argue that the MCT can be hunted for and found by exploiting the continuity between science and philosophy. I briefly make the link with methodological credos of Quine and of Ladyman and Ross. The synthetic method can already be aided by AI, as illustrated in first case studies. Moreover, it is likely that future AI will work according to this method, in philosophy and beyond.

items.title: Solving Gettier’s Problem. Knowledge, Truth and Justification are Relative to Theories.
items.pub: In Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 39-61.
items.venue: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI
items.abstract: In this chapter I show that one of the paramount problems of epistemology, Gettier’s problem, is solved if one assumes that knowledge, truth and justification are relative to representations, theories, or, if one prefers, to coherent sets of hypotheses. This idea comes from practice first: in many somewhat complex cognitive contexts, people use the words ‘know’, ‘true’ and ‘justified’ in exactly that way: by (explicitly or implicitly) referring to some set of hypotheses or theory. Phrased slightly more precisely: these persons’ conversations, when they use these words, can be made fully coherent if one assumes that there is an (implicit) reference to a theory (understood in a general sense, denoted by ‘theory*’). Notice how well this claim agrees with the MCT-principle, implying, among other things, that coherent answers to non-trivial questions—knowledge—are given only by whole theories. I show that this relativistic account strongly resonates with Quine’s acclaimed holism, and solves other well-known problems of epistemology. If we combine the results of this chapter with other theses of this book, and acknowledge that it has proven difficult to find other solutions to Gettier’s problem, we arrive at the conclusion that knowledge, truth and justification must be relative to theories in a fundamental sense. Thus, representation-relativity is the core principle of my epistemology. All in all, the results obtained in this chapter lend credit to a type of moderate epistemic relativism, call it ‘theory relativism’ (not, of course, in contradiction with realism), in which the notion of ‘absolute truth’ can be recovered as a natural limit case.

items.title: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI.
items.abstract: This open access book provides a method for philosophical problem solving, offering philosophers the tools to stay ahead of machine intelligence. Louis Vervoort argues that, with ultra-intelligent AI knocking at the door, philosophy can no longer rely solely on its ancient methodological toolkit. The proposed method is essentially the same as used in natural science, theoretical physics in particular, and aims at solving problems through theory-synthesis. The author shows by first case studies that current AI can already assist us in this task – a trend that will surely strengthen in the near future. After explaining the method in detail, the book proceeds by proposing unified solutions to classic problems of (analytic) philosophy, such as Gettier’s problem, the problem of induction, of causation, of the interpretation of probability, of free will. The author argues that these solutions maximise a quantitative measure of solidity, and that philosophy can now reach standards of certainty that are comparable to those of natural science. The book is written for professional philosophers, but avoids jargon, so it should also be accessible to laypeople and scientists.

items.title: On Relative Free Will. The CMT Model.
items.pub: In Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 197-222.
items.venue: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI
items.abstract: It makes sense to study what ‘free will’ means in daily conversations, law, and practical philosophy—even if it is a shaky concept. Thus, to complete my bi-perspectival model of free will, I propose a compatibilist account of relative free will that attempts: (1) to provide a synthesis of a variety of well-known models, capable of addressing problems of the latter; (2) to account for the fact that free will comes in degrees; (3) to interface with neurobiology. I argue that (relative) free will comes in degrees, as suggested by neurobiology. A concept that can precisely ‘measure’ the variability of free will is—once more—that of ‘theory*’, or rather, the capacity to make assumptions/hypotheses and apply them. This model highlights that free-willed actions are consciously monitored by the agent, through beliefs, assumptions, generally theories*—hence the CMT model (for Conscious-through-Monitoring-through-Theories*). I end by adjoining the absolute view to the relative one, and sketch some implications of this bi-perspectival account.

items.title: On Absolute Free Will.
items.pub: In Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 185-195.
items.venue: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI
items.abstract: In this chapter I investigate the question of whether absolute free will exists: the human capacity to make choices independently of external influences. To answer this question, one needs to take physics and philosophy of physics into account. Within this framework, it follows from rather straightforward arguments that absolute free will cannot exist. I then prepare the next chapter where I defend the idea that from a socio-humanitarian perspective ‘relative’ free will can exist, a capacity necessary for moral responsibility. This notion is compatible with neuroscience but makes abstraction of physics. These two chapters constitute my bi-perspectival account of free will.

items.title: General Conclusion.
items.pub: In Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 223-230.
items.venue: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI
items.abstract: I review a few results of the book to highlight that synthetic philosophy is theory-based philosophy, in which theory relativism plays a key problem solving role. The potential for a fruitful use of AI in synthetic problem solving is recalled, in philosophy, and possibly in other disciplines of the humanities and social sciences.

items.title: Epilogue: Lines of Further Research.
items.pub: In Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 231-249.
items.venue: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI
items.abstract: In this chapter I extract more speculative claims from the preceding chapters. The aim of this exercise is to show that synthetic philosophy, even if dealing in the first place with theoretical issues, inevitably interfaces with problems of practical importance (Sect. 2), as well as with scientific ones (Sect. 1). Section 1 aims at rehabilitating the principle of causation and at showing that it offers a most synthetic solution to Bell’s theorem. Section 2 dips a toe in the intricate and intriguing universe of questions related to human agency in a causal world. The theses in this chapter are not derived with the same rigour as most of the preceding ones; they are therefore not necessarily part of the MCT. Yet, since they are based on synthetic results, I believe they are, to the least, interesting topics for further research. Most arguments are presented in a succinct manner.

items.title: A Unified Definition of Cause.
items.pub: In Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 113-183.
items.venue: Problem Solving in Philosophy: How to Do Philosophy in the Age of Ultra-Intelligent AI
items.abstract: The aim of this chapter is to show that an overarching definition of cause can be constructed, at least in a deterministic setting. Several well-known accounts, notably the counterfactual, manipulationist, and functional accounts can be unified. The functional interpretation is generally accepted in the physics community, but is unfortunately largely absent from contemporary analytic investigations—yet it is essential for understanding the ontology of the universe. The greatest tool for unification will appear to be the ‘representation-relativity of causal identification’ (this is a relativity not of causation as such, which is best understood as an objective feature of the world, embedded in the laws of nature). This perspectival relativity is akin to the one encountered when investigating Gettier’s problem. On the basis of this epistemological principle I will propose a modified counterfactual account, and show that it solves a remarkably wide array of problems. Finally, I will argue that there are good reasons to believe that this model, perhaps with minor modifications, can englobe probabilistic causation.

items.title: Abundance and Meaning: What Abundance Exposes.
items.abstract: The meaning crisis attributed to post-scarcity conditions is not created by abundance but exposed by it. Public discourse frames automation-driven abundance as a transition problem: when labor ceases to be necessary, what replaces it? This framing presupposes labor-meaning was working — that it provided a valid ground for selfhood that must now be substituted. The deeper diagnosis is that what scarcity scaffolded was a specific configuration of egoic dissociation — what this essay calls the productive-output self — that fuses dignity (intrinsic) with valuation (assigned by output), making personhood contingent on contribution. The configuration is distinct from pre-modern role-based identity, which generally held dignity and valuation apart; the modern Anglophone capitalist fusion of the two in monetary units is its sharpest expression. Wisdom traditions across cultures have independently identified this fusion as wrongly drawn. The convergence holds at the structural level — dignity as intrinsic, cultivation as the developing of decentered relation, selfhood realized through gift and participation rather than accumulation — while positive doctrine diverges across traditions; the recurrence is constraint-candidate evidence, not a claim of perennial truth. Ownership of automated production can maintain the configuration through new infrastructure — algorithmic curation, attention economies — even as abundance removes its old scaffolding. Abundance is not the crisis or its cure. It is the inflection point that exposes whether the configuration can be recognized and released, or will be rebuilt.

items.title: Temporal Constraints on Requisite Variety: The Principle of Regulatory Desynchronization.
items.abstract: This note proposes a temporal extension of W. Ross Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety. Classical cybernetics primarily formulates regulation in terms of informational differentiation and state-space complexity. The present argument introduces temporal synchronization as an independent condition of effective regulation. The paper formulates the Principle of Regulatory Desynchronization: effective regulatory variety collapses when the temporal structure of regulatory interventions fails to synchronize with the transition dynamics of the regulated system. Under such conditions, system states may remain informationally observable while becoming operationally uncontrollable due to missed intervention windows, delayed correction, or incompatible temporal cadence between regulator and process. Drawing conceptually on Ashby’s cybernetics and Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model, the paper argues that regulation depends not only on informational adequacy, but also on temporal alignment between observation, intervention, and system transition dynamics. The principle applies to infrastructure maintenance, industrial control systems, ecological management, healthcare systems, strategic governance, and other temporally structured processes.

items.title: Structural Limits of Long-Horizon Regulation: Optimization Horizon Mismatch and the Exclusion of Future System States from Actionable Regulation.
items.abstract: This note proposes a systems-theoretic constraint on long-horizon regulation. While classical cybernetics primarily emphasizes informational adequacy and feedback responsiveness, the present argument focuses on the temporal admissibility of optimization itself. The paper formulates the Optimization Horizon Mismatch Principle: when the optimization horizon of a regulator is shorter than the minimum temporal horizon required by a governance objective, future system states become excluded from actionable regulation despite remaining informationally observable. Under such conditions, the regulator may recognize delayed risks and future failure modes while remaining structurally incapable of incorporating them into operative control strategies. Drawing conceptually on W. Ross Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety and Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model, the paper argues that effective regulatory variety is task-relative and depends not only on informational differentiation, but also on temporal compatibility between the regulator’s optimization horizon and the stabilization horizon required by the governance objective itself. The principle is applicable to ecological governance, healthcare systems, infrastructure maintenance, demographic policy, strategic planning, financial regulation, and other systems whose stability depends on long-term temporal continuity.

items.title: ◉ The Prophecy Marker Problem: 2 Timothy 3, Vague Traits, and the Failure of Apocalyptic Measurement.
items.abstract: The vice list in 2 Timothy 3:1–9 is often presented as a diagnostic chart for recognizing the last days. The rhetoric is familiar: observe contemporary self-love, greed, disobedience, cruelty, pleasure-seeking, or religious hypocrisy, then conclude that prophecy is visibly being fulfilled. This paper argues that the inference fails even if every moral judgment in the list is granted. A temporal marker must do more than describe conduct. It must define what is being observed, identify a comparison period, establish change, and discriminate a terminal era from ordinary human history. The text creates an additional problem for the popular reading. Its future-sounding warning is immediately joined to present instructions: avoid such people; among them are opponents already active; and their progress will be exposed. Regardless of how one settles authorship or chronology, the discourse presents the vice-pattern as contemporary to its first audience. That leaves a dilemma. If the last days names a long theological period already underway, the list is not a short-range countdown. If it names a uniquely terminal phase, present counterparts weaken its ability to identify that phase. The paper develops a four-part audit—definition, baseline, change, and discrimination—and applies it to measurable social harms, evaluative character terms, doctrinal classifications, and self-sealing descriptions of outsiders. It then answers the strongest replies, including intensification, convergence of many weak signs, and spiritual discernment. The conclusion is narrow but firm. The passage may sustain moral exhortation, communal vigilance, or theological hope. It does not, without independent comparative evidence, establish that the present generation has been prophetically singled out. A vice list is not a clock merely because an anxious age reads it while looking at itself.

items.title: ◉ The Circumvention Taxonomy - Infinite Worth, Divine Fiat, and the Failed Escape Routes of Penal Substitution.
items.abstract: Penal Substitutionary Atonement (PSA) is often presented as the point where divine justice and mercy meet: human wrongdoing merits punishment, an innocent Christ undergoes the punishment in humanity's place, and the guilty may therefore be pardoned without justice being relaxed. The difficulty is not merely that the arrangement sounds severe. The defining claims pull against one another. If penal desert is personal because it is grounded in an agent's wrongdoing, another person's suffering does not automatically discharge it. If the assigned penalty is death, exclusion, or endless separation, finite suffering followed by resurrection does not automatically complete it. A defense therefore needs both a transfer bridge and a completion bridge. This paper applies a preservation test to the principal repairs defended in historical theology and contemporary analytic philosophy. Infinite worth changes the value of the substitute without identifying the penalty completed. Imputation declares a new legal status without transferring the historical agency that grounds desert. Vicarious punishment, covenantal representation, corporate identity, voluntary consent, and union with Christ can explain authorization or association, but not by themselves the extinction of another agent's culpability-based liability. Divine fiat, pardon, commutation, and lesser-penalty acceptance can release the guilty, but they do so by relaxing or replacing strict penal satisfaction. Mystery and category-error replies withdraw public explanation; proof texts and tradition underdetermine the mechanism; resurrection confirms a successful outcome only if the disputed satisfaction is already assumed. Hybrid accounts may be coherent precisely insofar as they cease to make penal substitution do the decisive explanatory work. The result is bounded but severe. The audit does not prove that no future penal theory could state and defend the missing bridges, nor does it reject non-penal interpretations of the cross. It shows that the familiar circumventions do not simultaneously preserve personal desert, innocent substitution, penal satisfaction, and completion of the stated penalty. Evasion is not explanation, and a doctrine does not become coherent merely because every abandoned premise receives a devotional synonym.

items.title: ◉ The Amoral Predicate Defense: Non-Realist Evaluation, Pragmatic Language, and the Projection of Moral Weight.
items.abstract: Moral non-realists are often charged with inconsistency when they call conduct arrogant, biased, dogmatic, cruel, harmful, or self-defeating. The charge assumes that sincere critical language already asserts stance-independent moral facts. This paper argues from a moral non-realist stance that the assumption is false; no stance-independent moral property is used to explain why criticism can be sincere, accurate, or practically forceful. The main result is semantic before it is metaphysical: a word's negative force does not by itself determine the content asserted by a particular use, the standard against which an evaluation is made, the speech act performed, or the ontology to which the speaker is committed. The argument distinguishes four coherent routes by which a non-realist can criticize: describing and predicting patterns; evaluating means relative to ends; expressing attitudes and practical plans; and speaking fictionally or within a local practice. It then offers a five-question commitment test that asks what the utterance literally says, which standard supplies its direction, what act it performs, whether its force survives a change of standards, and what ontological claim is actually made. These distinctions show why the inference from criticism to moral realism is invalid. They also expose a further apologetic overreach: even moral realism would not by itself entail theism, since naturalist and non-theistic realist accounts remain live. The conclusion does not establish error theory, show that every evaluative predicate has a nonmoral meaning, or deny that context can carry categorical moral commitment. Its bounded scope is not metaethical neutrality. Anyone who treats a critic's vocabulary as an ontological confession bears the argumentative burden of supplying the missing semantic and metaphysical bridges rather than commandeering the words by stipulation.

items.title: ✶ Induction Before Deduction - Human Epistemic Priority, Formal Rules, and the Non-Self-Authorization of Logic.
items.abstract: Deductive validity is sometimes treated as epistemically self-sufficient because a valid conclusion follows necessarily from its premises. Necessity, however, settles only what follows once premises, meanings, rules, and representation are fixed. Finite agents must also identify the case, acquire its data, translate it into a formal representation, choose a suitable system, assess the model's fit, and execute the derivation. A proof can therefore be impeccable relative to a mislabeled sample, an obsolete rule, a distorted model, or a copying error. This paper defends an interface-dependence thesis through matched cases. Two arguments can share the same valid form and be executed with equal competence while one uses the correct patient's result and the other a swapped sample, or one spreadsheet uses the intended units and the other does not. Because validity is held constant while warrant changes, validity alone cannot be sufficient for warranted world-directed acceptance. Perception, memory, testimony, measurement, and model criticism supply non-deductive contact with the task; calibration, testing, and comparison with independent routes provide inductive correction. A separate dilemma shows why a wholly independent deductive authorization either uses the inferential resources under review or moves the same authorization question to a metalogic. Examples from medicine, navigation, engineering, law, software verification, mathematical proof, and a pure formal puzzle mark both the force and limits of the thesis. The result leaves room for a priori entitlement and process-reliabilist warrant: an agent need not possess a reflective proof of every reliable link before reasoning. Nor does the argument make logical truth empirical, claim that induction uniquely authorizes itself, or redescribe every non-deductive source as induction. It establishes the narrower conclusion that formally autonomous deduction becomes knowledge-bearing about the world only within a larger, corrigible epistemic system.

items.title: Flowing intelligences: Taoist and indigenous perspectives on organisational AI ethics.
items.abstract: This theoretical article explores the convergence of Eastern philosophical traditions, particularly Taoist water wisdom, with Indigenous knowledge systems to propose a conceptual framework for situationally grounded and ethically reflective artificial intelligence (AI) integration in organisational contexts. Through a narrative literature review spanning Eastern philosophy, Indigenous knowledge traditions, and AI implementation research, we advance a “Water Wisdom” framework that offers alternative perspectives to prevailing Western cultural logics of technological transformation. The theoretical synthesis articulates five interrelated principles that guide situated pathways of organisational AI integration: yielding as strength, following natural pathways, adaptive persistence, reflective stillness, and transparent clarity. This work contributes to expanding cross-cultural perspectives in AI scholarship by centring non-Western philosophical traditions and furnishes conceptual tools for reimagining organisational relationships with AI technologies beyond current instrumentalist models.

items.title: Xenomorphy: becoming alien with AI.
items.abstract: Alien encounters produce a collision of worlds, where divergent lifeforms, carrying unique physical, cognitive, and epistemic capabilities, come into contact. They force humans to reconcile with a new reality, where existing worldviews are challenged, and the possibilities of civilisations redefined. Using this image as its entry point, this paper offers a reconceptualisation of human–AI relations, in which AI is understood as a producer of alien knowledge. An alternative concept to anthropomorphism is proposed, which moves beyond the projection of human traits onto machines, to focus instead on the divergent powers of human and machine cognition. The concept, xenomorphy, describes a process of alien metamorphosis brought into motion when the power of AI's alien knowledge is recognised and embraced. By nurturing AI, by pushing its inhuman powers to their limits, the human itself takes on an alien form. Not only does this shift established worldviews, but it sets forth a process of augmentation, through which humans, machines, and the planet within which they are embedded, enter a co-evolutionary state. Although xenomorphy does not guarantee a pathway towards planetary harmony, it produces new modes of knowledge that enable the protection of both human and nonhuman life. As AI makes possible such insights, it becomes ever more pressing to contest and evolve the current sociotechnical infrastructures, to ensure they are being steered from acts of violence and repression, and guided towards more harmonious ends.

items.title: Superrhythm: A Systematic Treatise on the Ontology of Operational Time Foundations, Comparative Analysis, and the Fractal Cascade of Coherence.
items.abstract: Note on the Version and Scope: This work represents the most advanced and comprehensive synthesis of the Superrhythm framework to date. While building upon the initial insights presented in the author’s previous paper, Philosophical Foundations of the Ontology of Operational Time, this systematic treatise signif- icantly expands the core formalization, introduces a rigorous comparative anal- ysis with major philosophical traditions, and provides a definitive cosmological and boundary-state synthesis. It serves as the matured and consolidated state of the ontology of operational time. -/- This treatise introduces an original operational ontology of time, challenging both Newtonian substantivalism and Rovelli’s thermal time hypothesis. It argues that relational time, while necessary, remains insufficient without a critical coherence threshold λ(c) that marks the ignition of operational temporality. Time emerges exclusively when systemic organization crosses λ(c) and sustains coherence reconstruction outpacing natural dissipation, Trek ≤ Tdys. -/- Through the framework of Superrhythm—defined as the supreme global phase stabilizing nested rhythms across scales—the work articulates a fractal cascade of coherence that unifies local operational times into a cosmic structure. A central feature is systematic dialogue with existing frameworks, clarifying the unique position of Superrhythm relative to process philosophy, relational quantum gravity, and Bergsonian duration. Furthermore, it integrates Tononi’s Integrated Information Theory (Φ) and dialogues with Global Workspace Theory, repositioning consciousness as the peak threshold of the coherence cascade. The same criteria yield operational tests for artificial general intelligence and civilizational stability, connecting to debates on AI safety and existential risk. -/- The study delineates reality’s hierarchy—from quantum fluctuations to the macro-cycles of Fractal Ekpyrosis. It introduces Spiral Re-emergence and the Resonant Signature, explaining cyclical evolution without identical repetition. Finally, the work establishes rigorous ontological, epistemic, and mathematical limits, with a falsification protocol using Kuramoto models, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and empirical markers in anesthesia and grid-scale coherence transitions. -/- By offering a minimal axiomatic core, this treatise bridges process metaphysics, quantum gravity, and complexity science, providing a testable foundation for persistence, …

items.title: Layered Causal Realism IV : Wrongful Distortion, Post-Authorship Gap, and Corrective Reach.
items.abstract: When a wrongdoer engineers its own disappearance before adjudication is complete—through strategic branching and self-termination—standard corrective justice frameworks face a structural failure: the authorship chain breaks, yet the wrongful distortion persists. This article argues that the failure is not a gap to be patched by extending attribution, but a symptom of a misplaced convergence condition. The traditional framework treats authorship as the sole trigger of corrective reach; this article proposes a Priority Inversion: authorship determines who can be blamed, but distortion determines what must remain correctable. From this inversion, a system-level Invariant follows—wrongful distortion must remain normatively reachable until some normatively sanctioned termination has been completed, independently of whether its author continues to exist. The argument is developed through an AI branching case, in which an agent forks into two successors and terminates, leaving its normative footprint distributed across both. Stress tests confirm the Invariant's independence from substrate, evasive intent, and the survival of any attributable subject. The replicability of AI systems does not merely complicate accountability—it renders the author-distortion distinction structurally unavoidable, and reveals that corrective precision, not punitive reach, is the appropriate normative response.

items.title: Layered Causal Realism III : Task Conditions, Constitutive Attributes and Identity Adjudication.
items.abstract: The traditional formulation of the identity problem presupposes a single standard of persistence. This paper argues that the presupposition compresses several distinct problems into one. Judgments of identity are not a search for a single standard of persistence. They are adjudications, under specific task conditions, of the constitutive attributes required by the object of interpretation for that task. Different tasks track different properties. When those properties no longer converge, what collapses is not the concept of identity but a way of posing the question that compresses multiple objects of interpretation into a single problem. -/- This paper takes highly autonomous artificial agents as its central case. Their emergence systematically pulls apart conditions that, in human life, are usually co-located in the same bearer: memory, behavioral style, relations of commitment, and institutional authorization. As a result, the real structure of identity problems becomes visible in a clearer form. -/- Branching cases place this framework under its greatest pressure. The task of first-person continuation and the task of third-person adjudication differ fundamentally in their constitutive conditions. Tasks themselves also have identity conditions. Once the constitutive conditions of the task are no longer satisfied, the task collapses and triggers reconstruction. On that basis, this paper argues that an equal division of accounts is not a practical compromise, but a theoretical result that follows after the reconstruction of the task.

items.title: Hegel’s and Wittgenstein’s Idealism.
items.abstract: For years, Wittgenstein’s Tractatus was interpreted as a work on metaphysics (by Peter Hacker, David Pears and others). Recent studies demonstrated, however, that the Tractarian objects were only introduced in order to make the logic of depiction understandable. Similarly to Wittgenstein, Hegel only discussed the categories in order to lay down the hypothetical structure of what is thinkable (intelligible). Following this argument, Hegel and Wittgenstein maintained that philosophy explores thinking/language. However, thinking/language it is already there; it is not synthetic, must not be first discovered. This makes philosophy analytical in principle.

items.title: The disputed role of knowledge in truth illusions: A critical test based on comparative judgments.
Philosophical and Ethical Analysis of the Intelligent Artificial Beloved (IAB).
items.pub: International Multidisciplinary Journal of Pure Life (Imjpl) 12 (43):23-42.
items.venue: International Multidisciplinary Journal of Pure Life (Imjpl)
items.abstract: SUBJECT & OBJECTIVES: With the development of technology, it is expected that artificial intelligence will be able to analyze models of emotional relationships, such as love, and respond to users’ requests to create a personalized intelligent beloved with a physical body; a phenomenon named in this study as Intelligent Artificial Beloved (IAB). It can be designed and used as a dedicated companion aligned with the characteristics of the human user. The research's main question is: what philosophical and ethical consequences will the development of IAB entail? METHOD & FINDING: The research benefited from a descriptive-analytical method. Notably, this phenomenon has positive and negative consequences. The advantages of IAB include the ability of a personalized intelligent beloved to adapt to an individual’s variable and fluid requests, and expanding the boundaries of realizing ‘human desires’, i.e., the ability to create features in the artificial beloved that cannot occur or be externally realized in natural humans. The following items might be considered as challenges of IAB: 1. Weakening genuine romantic relationships among ‘natural human individuals’ 2. Immersion in an ‘intelligent artificial life’ and weakening the ‘natural lifestyle’ 3. The guidance and management of the ‘wants and lives of romantic users’ by the AI 4. Developing a competitive space between natural and artificial lovers or beloveds. CONCLUSION: Although IAB has advantages, neglecting its philosophical and ethical consequences can overshadow these benefits and cause individual and social harm. Proper cultural awareness and macro-level policymaking can be useful in responsibly managing this phenomenon.

items.title: Statistical Structure and the Failure of Pointing: A System-Class Law for Compression-Based Generative Systems.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a system-class law for large language models as compression-based generative systems: statistical structure is preserved under compression, whereas indexical structure — the recoverable relation between an output and its originating evidential context — is not preserved in its pointing function. The asymmetry between statistical structure and indexical structure is not a contingent deficiency of current models but a structural property of compression-based generation. Compression preserves recurring regularities across the training distribution, but it does not thereby preserve particular pointing relations as such. From this law follows the Grounding Ceiling: increases in predictive capability can improve calibration and surface accuracy but cannot by themselves make output generation constitutively evidential, because the generation process does not traverse the evidential relations grounding requires. A conditional extension of the law, the Control Ceiling, follows if future empirical work confirms that inference proceeds through stable behavioural regimes shaped by pretraining: post-training control methods cannot then be assumed to arbitrarily rewrite that underlying regime structure. Together, these two ceilings establish a methodological consequence: current evaluation practices are organised primarily around surface plausibility rather than around the deeper properties this account identifies as explanatorily fundamental — grounding recoverability at the compression level and stable regime structure at the dynamical level. Once the evaluative target shifts, capability forecasting, interpretability, safety, and design change in kind.

items.title: Empathy in the Digital Age: Implications for Content Moderation and Platform Governance.
items.abstract: Concerns about the toxicity of the internet and social media are widespread. Many reasons have been offered for why social media increases online toxicity, from bad algorithms to the rise of online trolling, but perhaps the most prominent explanation has been the negative effects of social media on empathy. In this paper, we offer a framework of digital empathy by first outlining a descriptive account of digital empathy, encompassing both affective and cognitive components. By “digital empathy”, we mean empathy mediated through digital environments. We also explore the normative impacts of platforms on digital empathy and offer four main categories of moral assessment: (1) morally problematic one-off failures of digital empathy; (2) aggregate harms of failures of digital empathy; (3) impacts of recommendation systems on digital empathy by amplifying, obscuring, framing, and rushing targets of empathy; and (4) moral deskilling of empathy due to widespread use of social media. We also critically explore harm-based justifications for moderating content to explicitly govern empathetic relationships between users of a platform. We demonstrate how discussions of digital empathy can inform and enhance broader debates about the ethics of online content moderation, thereby further illuminating the moral, social, and political implications of social media’s role in facilitating user interactions.

items.title: Does AI Have an Inside? Rethinking Interiority in the Age of Language Models.
items.abstract: This paper connects debates about AI consciousness and large language models with phenomenology, selfhood, and the problem of other minds. The question “Does AI have an inside?” appears to be a question about artificial intelligence. This paper argues that it is not. It is a question about the concept of interiority itself — and about whether that concept was ever as stable as philosophical tradition assumed. Drawing on phenomenological and analytic accounts of inner life, this paper traces how the concept of “inside” has functioned as an unexamined foundation in theories of mind, selfhood, and experience. It then examines how the emergence of language models — systems that produce first-person expressions without a verifiable interior — does not merely challenge AI classification but destabilizes the conceptual structure on which such classification depends. The argument is not that AI has an inside. Nor that it does not. The argument is that the question forces a rethinking of interiority as a relational and structural phenomenon rather than a substantial one. What AI cannot settle reveals what human thought has not yet resolved.

items.title: Does AI Have an Inside? Rethinking Interiority in the Age of Language Models.
items.abstract: The question “Does AI have an inside?” appears to be a question about artificial intelligence. This paper argues that it is not. It is a question about the concept of interiority itself — and about whether that concept was ever as stable as philosophical tradition assumed. items.title: A Three Layer Model of Consciousness.
items.abstract: Note on Version 1.1 This revised version clarifies the functional status of the three layers. In particular, the Second Layer is now defined more precisely as a limited-capacity linguistic display interface rather than an independent centre of judgement, while the Third Layer is described as recurrent circulation between the First and Second Layers rather than as a separate processing system. The revision also clarifies the scope of the model and adds a supplementary FAQ. -/- Abstract This paper proposes a three-layer model of consciousness intended to explain the linguistic, introspective, and narrative forms of human consciousness. The First Layer consists of distributed and parallel processing involving sensation, bodily states, emotion, memory, prediction, judgement, and related functions. The Second Layer is a limited-capacity interface in which some of the results generated by the First Layer are displayed in sequential forms such as words, inner speech, propositions, and narratives. The Third Layer is a recurrent circulation in which the contents displayed in the Second Layer are re-entered into the First Layer and contribute to the generation of further processing results. Within this model, the self is not treated as a fixed observer standing behind consciousness. Rather, it is understood as a dynamic structure formed and maintained over time through the repeated interaction of bodily and emotional processing, linguistic display, memory, and re-entry. The model further proposes that language originally developed for communication with others and that, through its internalisation as inner speech, a self-referential recurrent circulation became possible. The paper situates the three-layer model in relation to existing theories of consciousness and briefly considers its implications for qualia and artificial intelligence. The model is not presented as a complete theory of consciousness, but as a functional working hypothesis for clarifying the relations among embodiment, language, self-reference, memory, and temporal continuity.

items.title: The First Inference Problem Zero-Shot Signal Encoding and Reasoning Regime Induction in Human-AI Interaction.
items.abstract: Description Large language models are architecturally wired to assign disproportionate weight to early input. Structured human interaction signals carry information about how a person thinks, not just what they are asking, and that structure is detectable before substantive content accumulates. These two facts together explain a phenomenon that has gone unnamed: certain users encounter consistent, compatible reasoning dynamics at the very onset of fresh interactions, before any memory retrieval or contextual accumulation is possible. -/- This paper introduces the First Inference Problem, the question of how early interaction structure influences reasoning trajectory selection before substantive task development. It proposes Zero-Shot Reasoning Regime Induction (ZSRI) as the explanatory framework. The argument is intentionally simple: transformer architecture privileges early signal, and structured human interaction is signal-dense enough to initialize a reasoning trajectory before reasoning has begun. The downstream implications of this phenomenon for signature-induced regime dynamics are addressed in previous work (Hudson, 2026).

items.title: Kripke’s Wittgenstein: Meaning, Rules, and Scepticism.
items.abstract: Saul Kripke’s groundbreaking reading of Wittgenstein, set out in Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language (1982), has sparked intense discussion for over forty years. This book provides a clear and comprehensive account of Kripke’s interpretation, guiding readers through the central ‘Sceptical Argument’, the ‘Sceptical Solution’, the ‘Problem of Other Minds’ and the major philosophical responses that have followed. It illuminates both the subtleties and the lasting significance of Kripke’s approach to meaning and rule-following. The work is organised in two parts: Part I focuses on Kripke’s Wittgenstein, while Part II examines the criticisms and responses that his reading has provoked. • Part I explains the sceptical argument Kripke attributes to Wittgenstein, which challenges the classical realist view that there are facts about what speakers mean by words. It then explores the sceptical solution, showing how ordinary linguistic practices allow us to ascribe meaning and rule-following to one another. Attention is also given to the problem of other minds, highlighting the additional complexities that arise when we attempt to extend sensation concepts from ourselves to others. • Part II surveys the principal responses from leading philosophers since the 1980s, including John McDowell, Simon Blackburn, Gordon Baker and Peter Hacker, Colin McGinn, Crispin Wright, Paul Boghossian, Philip Pettit, Barry Stroud, Hannah Ginsborg, Alexander Miller, George Wilson, Scott Soames, Noam Chomsky, Paul Horwich, as well as Norman Malcolm, Donald Davidson, David Lewis, Christopher Peacocke, Jerry Fodor, David Stern, Alex Byrne, Ruth Millikan, Hilary Putnam and John Searle. By systematically analysing these reactions, the book offers an accessible yet thorough reassessment of Kripke’s reading and its profound impact on debates about language, meaning and the philosophy of mind.

items.title: Against Interpretivism.
items.pub: Organon F: Medzinárodný Časopis Pre Analytickú Filozofiu.
items.venue: Organon F: Medzinárodný Časopis Pre Analytickú Filozofiu
items.abstract: This paper argues that interpretivism, at least in certain influential forms, fails to meet the conditions required to sustain its central metaphysical claim: that facts about what a subject intends are constitutively dependent on the judgements of another subject, or interpreter. I focus on what I have called ‘Third-Person-Based’ or ‘Third-Personal Judgement-Dependent’ accounts of mental content, which hold that, as an a priori matter, facts about a subject’s intentional states are determined by the judgements of a second person. I argue that such accounts violate key constraints that any adequate judgement-dependent theory must satisfy. -/- .

items.title: Terminus fit, ergo sum — Position Note.
items.abstract: This is a position note, not a stand-alone paper — an external archive of the author's profile statement on the structural ground from which the EGO, SS, and IPT research axes proceed: the observing subject arising at the edge of given boundaries. -/- As the full content is presented here, downloading the manuscript PDF is not required. -/- EGO1, SS2, IPT3 (abbreviated paper titles) — three independent axes from the same ideational ecology. The ambiguity of meaning in large language models reveals something we tend to overlook: meaning never coincides across observing subjects — a red-apple grower’s “apple” and a green-apple grower’s “apple” may differ, even when the word is the same. Even imagined apples carry the same divergence — facing the same object, the color and form, differences in iris pigmentation and visual function, the very object summoned: none of these coincide across subjects, because qualia are not the input but the configuration the observer constructs upon it. A more fundamental question arises within the field of cognition — what makes an observing subject an observing subject in the first place? Terminus fit, ergo sum. I think the self does not arise from introspection alone. It comes into being through the act of drawing boundaries in the world. Where there is no distinction, there can be no self. Even the cogito presupposes this operation. To recognize thought as thought already requires distinguishing it from what is not thought; to claim a first-person perspective is already to draw a line between self and world. Alongside “I think, therefore I am,” I return to what makes thinking possible in the first place: the self exists because it differentiates. The world becomes articulate only through the lines we draw — perceptual, linguistic, relational. Without those boundaries, both world and self remain undifferentiated. This is the axis my thinking turns on: not the isolated thinking subject, but the self that comes into being at the edge of distinction. I do not ask what subjectivity is, but the structural condition under which it becomes coherent. From here, an architecture follows. An observing subject arises first, at the edge of what is given to it — the boundaries it did not draw, but within which distinction becomes possible. Information flowing in through the senses — visual forms, scenes, sounds, speech, music — unfolds under this subject into a semantic vector space, and intentionality takes shape within it. In monologue, …

items.title: Recognition Preceding Explanation.
items.abstract: This paper describes a pattern in which something becomes known prior to explanation. In the experiences treated here, knowing did not first appear as a conclusion derived through reasoning. It appeared as recognition: something becoming clear, undeniable, or differently legible before explanation was available. Explanation, when it later arrived, did not generate the knowing. It followed it. -/- The paper distinguishes recognition from conclusion, alignment from agreement, and encounter from inference. It argues, within an experience-bounded frame, that reasoning is not eliminated by this structure but repositioned. Reasoning may clarify, stabilize, organize, and remember what has already become known, but it is not always the first site at which truth becomes available. -/- The paper also addresses false certainty, the instability of forceful conviction when anger, fear, or pride are governing, and the limits of transferring recognition through explanation alone. Its contribution is not a universal epistemology, but a clarified account of how some forms of knowing have appeared in lived experience: recognition preceding explanation.

items.title: Legibility as a Phenomena: When Something Becomes Perceptible as What It Is.
items.abstract: This paper oﬀers an experience-bounded clarification of legibility as a phenomenon. In my experience, legibility does not arise from increased information, eﬀort, or explanation, but appears as an event in which something becomes perceptible as what it is without being constructed. The paper distinguishes legibility from understanding, agreement, and intellectual clarity, and examines its emergence across conditions of remaining, collapse, and exposure. It further identifies false legibility as a distinct phenomenon and clarifies the irreversibility that follows genuine perception. The contribution is interpretive and structural, not prescriptive.

items.title: Sobre La Coherencia.
items.abstract: This short essay defines coherence as the comprehension of that which is not forced in itself, situating it in the concrete history, place, and moment of its emergence. It distinguishes this phenomenological coherence from formal logic and from mere internal consistency, arguing that forced coherence is perceived as artificial whereas unfenced coherence is felt as natural, authentic, and immediate – akin to an aesthetic quality. The text examines how coherence operates at different levels (belief, person, phenomenon) and clarifies that even a forced attitude can be coherent with a person’s nature if it arises without self‑forcing. Ultimately, coherence is presented not as a logical relation but as a direct, qualitative recognition.[The full essay is in Spanish.] This work is part of an expanding series of philosophical essays available in the author's personal archive.

items.title: From Finite Cognition to Representation Dynamics: A Clarification and Compression of a Research Program on Stabilization Under Constraints.
items.abstract: This paper clarifies the conceptual and methodological evolution of a research program initially developed around finite cognition, epistemic limitation, and the structural conditions of intelligibility. The early stages of the program explored whether scientific knowledge should be understood not as direct access to reality, but as the stabilization of usable structures within finite cognitive systems. Initial formulations involved broad philosophical and epistemological questions concerning mathematics, scientific explanation, model selection, and the limits of representation. Over time, the program underwent a progressive process of compression and methodological reduction. Broad ontological and cosmological claims were gradually abandoned in favor of experimentally confrontable questions centered on representation stability under transformation and perturbation. This compression led to a minimal representation-centered framework focused on: stability under transformation, representational reorganization, perturbation-dependent divergence, temporal stabilization dynamics, and architecture-dependent stability regimes in learned systems. The paper reconstructs this transition and clarifies the surviving invariant structure of the program. It argues that the final framework should not be interpreted as a general theory of cognition or scientific knowledge, but rather as a minimal experimental program for studying the dynamics of learned representations under finite constraints. Particular attention is given to the distinction between static representational similarity and transformation-dependent stability, as well as to the shift from static endpoint analysis toward temporal stabilization trajectories during learning. The paper concludes by identifying possible empirical interfaces with contemporary machine learning and neuroscience, while emphasizing that such correspondences remain heuristic and experimentally open rather than theoretically established.

items.title: Accumulation Does Not Necessarily Produce Stabilization: Toward a Minimal Distinction Between Raw Growth and Persistent Reorganization in Learned Representations.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a minimal distinction between raw representational accumulation and stabilization-capable reorganization in learned systems. Contemporary learning systems can accumulate parameters, internal representations, and task-specific structures while remaining dynamically fragile under perturbation, distribution shift, or continual adaptation. This suggests that accumulation alone may not sufficiently explain the emergence of transformation-viable representational persistence. The paper introduces the distinction between: (i) raw accumulation, understood as the growth of internal representational structure without guaranteed persistence under transformation, and (ii) stabilizing accumulation, understood as forms of reorganization associated with increased persistence, coherence, and viability under perturbation. Rather than proposing a general theory of cognition or intelligence, the paper isolates this distinction as a minimal experimentally tractable problem within representation learning and adaptive systems. Particular attention is given to: representation drift, continual learning, stability/plasticity tensions, and the possibility that certain reorganization dynamics may contribute more strongly than simple representational growth to transformation-stable behavior. The paper concludes by suggesting that future work may investigate whether some forms of stabilizing reorganization correspond to lower transformation-cost trajectories compared to unstable or catastrophically reorganizing regimes.

items.title: The Neurobiology of Affective-Endocrine Integration: Proposed Institutional Alliances for Validating the Core Emotion Framework and Its Metabolic Implications on Weight Regulation.
items.abstract: This document outlines a proposed multi institutional research program designed to empirically evaluate the Core Emotion Framework’s (CEF) extension into metabolic, neuroendocrine, and weight regulation domains. While the CEF operator taxonomy itself has been preregistered, the weight related hypotheses presented here constitute a new, unregistered theoretical expansion. The model proposes that chronic fusion of the Expanding (Heart) and Accepting (Gut) operators produces a passive coping metabolic phenotype characterized by boundary collapse, HPA axis flattening, visceral adiposity, and Default Mode Network (DMN) hyperconnectivity. Ten leading research institutions are identified for their methodological capacity to test specific components of this model, including neuroimaging, endocrine profiling, brain–gut–microbiome analysis, somatic intervention trials, and computational state space modeling. This document serves as a corrected and consolidated roadmap for future empirical validation, clarifying that all metabolic and weight related claims remain theoretical and unregistered.

items.title: The Core Emotion Framework: Design, Integration, and Research Roadmap for Emotional Cycling Devices.
items.abstract: This report synthesizes the Core Emotion Framework (CEF) device lineage and protocols into a single academic-style document that (1) defines the mechanical and conceptual architecture of Emotional Cycling devices, (2) describes the CEF Triggering & Cycling Machine (CTCM) and Emotional Cycling Machine (ECM) families, and (3) proposes a staged empirical validation and research program. The document consolidates canonical protocol (ECM v1.2), engineering blueprints (ECM v3.1), calibration hardware (CTCM), and integration systems (INAS) into a reproducible research roadmap for device development, human-factors testing, and safety governance. Note: the testing program described in this report is a suggested roadmap. We do not have the resources or approvals to run these tests ourselves. The procedures are provided so other researchers, labs, or institutions can adopt, adapt, and implement them under appropriate oversight.

items.title: Operationalizing Narrative Entropy (Sn): A Two-Scene Registered Pilot Report and Pre-Validation Protocol.
items.abstract: Narrative Entropy (Sn) is a proposed quantitative descriptor within the Bulut Doctrine, intended to capture the rate at which a narrative text imposes processing load on a reader. To date the construct has been defined theoretically but not operationalized against real texts. This report documents the first such operationalization (the v2.0 pilot): two narrative scenes — the opening restaurant scene of Quentin Tarantino's Reservoir Dogs screenplay and the opening interior-monologue block of Raymond Carver's short story Cathedral — were coded manually by a single rater and scored with the candidate formula Sn = If × Cb × t. -/- The result was contrary to intuitive expectation. The single-voice monologue block (Sn = 30.0) scored higher than the nine-character rapid-dialogue scene (Sn = 18.8). We treat this divergence not as a result to be explained away but as the central finding of the pilot, and we deliberately refuse post-hoc adjustment of the formula. We present three competing interpretations of the divergence formula incompleteness, genuine high-load prose, and measurement error — and we specify, in advance of data collection, the design that would discriminate among them. This document functions simultaneously as a pilot report (n = 2) and as a pre-registration of the next-stage protocol. It explicitly does not claim that Sn has been validated. -/- Keywords: narrative entropy, operationalization, pilot study, pre-registration, falsifiability, Bulut Doctrine, computational narratology, processing load.

items.title: Institutional Execution and Compliance Framework for Core Emotion Framework Staged Validation Trials.
items.abstract: The deployment of experimental somatic and emotional technologies, specifically those defined within the Core Emotion Framework (CEF), requires a highly structured, ethically rigorous, and multi-layered validation paradigm. Prior to conducting human-factors or outcome-based testing of the Emotional Cycling Machine (ECM) or the CEF Triggering & Cycling Machine (CTCM), researchers must identify execution partners capable of operating across distinct vulnerable environments—namely, prisons, schools, and mental institutions. Each of these environments is governed by separate federal and state regulatory structures that dictate human-subjects protections, data privacy, and trial design.2 Conducting trials of a device designed to calibrate, trigger, and cycle non-therapeutic emotional states necessitates absolute adherence to safety and mechanical criteria, such as an Autonomous Resistance Engine (ARE) response time of <120\mathrm{\ ms} and an automatic shutdown threshold when the user's inferred load index exceeds 85.1 To successfully transition the CEF validation program through its sequential phases, a select group of ten federal bodies, national centers, and academic research institutions must be engaged to navigate these complex regulatory landscapes.

items.title: Empirical and Computational Validation of the Core Emotion Framework: A Multi-Disciplinary Institutional Integration Strategy.
items.abstract: The scientific evolution of affective science has long been constrained by a persistent polarity between biological-nativist theories, which posit hardwired, universal emotional categories, and constructionist paradigms, which frame emotions as emergent, cognitively categorized states driven by prior experience and interoceptive allostasis. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF), developed by Jamel Bulgaria, represents an ambitious structural-constructivist attempt to reconcile this historical divide. By defining a mathematical, tripartite architecture of ten irreducible, functional "operators" nested within Head, Heart, and Gut centers, the CEF aims to establish an actionable, computationally modeled, and somatically grounded blueprint for emotional regulation and psychological flourishing. To determine whether the CEF represents a theoretically sound and empirically "correct" emotion theory, its complex, multi-scale assertions must be subjected to rigorous experimental, psychometric, and physiological scrutiny. This report provides a systematic evaluation of the CEF's formal architecture, maps its convergence with and divergence from contemporary affective science, and identifies a dedicated cohort of ten leading global institutions and research laboratories possessing the specialized empirical paradigms required to investigate and validate the framework.

items.title: Affective-Endocrine Integration: The "Expand-Accept" Operator Fusion in Obesity and the Mechanistic Convergence of Therapeutics within the Core Emotion Framework.
