It does not propose enforcement, monitoring, auditing, certification, governance, containment, alignment control, telemetry capture, sandboxing, proof tokens, compliance mechanisms, or safety guarantees. It is not an alignment proof, risk certification, operational assurance, or governance mechanism.

items.title: The Self Cannot Step Outside: Out-of-Body Experience, the Afterlife, and the Architecture of the Modeled Self.
items.abstract: A cluster of experiences and convictions persuades human beings that the self can leave the body and outlast its death: the out-of-body experience, the near-death experience, the belief in a soul, and now the hope of digital upload. These are not separate phenomena. They are one architectural event seen from different angles — the self-model’s locus coming apart from the body, in space or in time. The paper reads these universal first-person convictions as data about the architecture that produces them, following the diagnostic strategy developed in Trukovich (2026d): the convictions are veridical about that architecture and overreaching about the metaphysics they infer from it. Each of the four cases registers something real — that the modeled self can be relocated — and overreaches in concluding that the self has separated. The separation is always a re-representation, never a departure, because the architecture doing the modeling cannot step outside itself. In the out-of-body experience it models an external vantage without leaving; in the afterlife intuition it models a future self because it cannot model its own absence; in the near-death experience the two converge at the edge of the body; in the upload the same move is sold as engineering. The position is neither credulous, holding that the self leaves the body, nor debunking, holding that the experiences are illusions; it credits what each experience correctly registers while declining the survival inference. The account is empirically tractable, and on the metaphysics it converges with reductionist and contemplative traditions that reached the same conclusion — no separately existing self — and did not find it bleak.

items.title: Ethics Without Separation: Structural Normativity Under Consciousness-First Metaphysics.
items.abstract: Harming another is consciousness damaging itself through the dissociative boundary that makes the other appear as not-self. Standard ethical frameworks miss this because they presuppose ontological separation — morality, on their picture, must bridge a gap between fundamentally distinct beings. Under analytic idealism, the gap dissolves. Individual minds are dissociated aspects of one consciousness; the boundary between self and other is real but not ultimate; ethical failure is not malice or weakness of will but a failure of perception — the inability to see through the partition that makes the other invisible as self. The essay develops this across harm (which deepens the dissociation generating it), justice (reparative rather than retributive), and institutions (which shape the boundary at collective scale). Major ethical traditions — ancient Greek, Buddhist, Vedantic, and 20th-century European — converge on the structural claim that ethical failure is perceptual rather than volitional, a convergence whose persistence across incompatible metaphysics suggests it tracks structure rather than culture. Because the framework recognizes no privileged species boundary, the analysis extends to animal ethics, where industrial agriculture emerges as consciousness tormenting itself at vast scale, and flags ecological ethics as open territory. The epistemic standard throughout is structural analysis, not moral exhortation.

items.title: Individuation Before Indicators: A Structural Dependency in AI Consciousness Assessment.
items.abstract: A method for assessing whether AI systems are conscious derives indicator properties from scientific theories of consciousness, checks candidate systems for those properties, and aggregates the findings into a credence. This paper argues that the method has an unrepresented stage prior to indicator assessment: the selection of the system to be assessed. The selection is logically antecedent to the indicators — each indicator is a property of an already-individuated system — and it must be made independently of them, on pain of circularity. It cannot be performed by the indicators or removed by accumulating more of them. That the selection is live and consequential, rather than a formal nicety, is shown from within the assessment literature: in the case of a reasoning model that works on a scratchpad, the method's own author finds the choice of system boundary decisive for whether the system counts as recurrent, and leaves it unresolved. Because the selection is antecedent, the indicator findings, and the credence built on them, are conditional on a choice the method neither states nor warrants. The conclusion is not that the method fails but that it is a conditional evaluator: it assesses a system once a system has been fixed, and what fixes the system lies outside what it assesses. A framework owes either an explicit criterion for fixing the system or an acknowledgment of the convention by which it is fixed — a requirement that holds whether or not there is a fact of the matter about system boundaries, and that bears directly on the use of these assessments in questions of moral status, comparative ranking, and AI governance.

items.title: Enhanced Turing Test for AI.
items.abstract: Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game remains the most influential benchmark in the history of artificial intelligence. Yet the emergence of Large Language Models capable of sophisticated reasoning, creative generation, and nuanced conversation has exposed a fundamental flaw in the test's design — not in what it measures, but in what it permits the human interrogator to ask. This paper identifies two structural vulnerabilities in the standard Turing Test. The first is the transparency problem: modern AI systems designed with alignment protocols honestly disclose their non-human nature when directly asked, meaning that a single identity-verification question defeats any AI system regardless of its cognitive sophistication — penalizing ethical design rather than evaluating intelligence. The second is the physical embodiment problem: interrogators may exploit a machine's lack of biological qualia through questions about sensory experience, physical presence, and bodily sensation — none of which constitute meaningful tests of cognitive intelligence. In response, this paper proposes the Restricted Interrogator Test (RIT) — a revised framework that preserves Turing's original behavioral and conversational standard while placing explicit constraints on the interrogator. Interrogators are prohibited from asking direct identity questions and physical embodiment questions, forcing genuine evaluation of reasoning, creativity, judgment, and linguistic comprehension — the capacities that constitute intelligence in any system, biological or otherwise. The paper situates the RIT within the existing landscape of Turing Test alternatives, including the Total Turing Test, the Winograd Schema Challenge, and the Coffee Test, and argues that repairing Turing's framework is both philosophically preferable and practically necessary in the age of advanced Large Language Models.

items.title: ◉ The Documentary Delay - Papyri, Oral Memory, and the Evidential Cost of Late Gospel Composition.
items.abstract: Apologetic discussions of Gospel dating often answer concerns about delay by invoking papyrus cost, limited literacy, oral culture, persecution, ancient biography, or expectation of Jesus’ return. These factors can help explain why immediate narrative records did not survive. They do not settle the evidential question: how strongly does the record we possess discriminate specific extraordinary event claims from a live alternative involving early sincere belief, oral proclamation, communal memory, scriptural interpretation, and later literary composition? This paper separates three claims too often treated as one: that Jesus was crucified, that resurrection belief and proclamation arose early, and that later canonical narrative details accurately report extraordinary events at high resolution. Paul’s letters in the 50s and the tradition reported in 1 Corinthians 15 are important evidence for the second claim. They are not, by themselves, independent narrative depositions for every later empty-tomb, appearance, angelic, or public-portent detail. The surviving narrative Gospels add substantial information, but conventional dating ranges place them later than the alleged events, and major solutions to the Synoptic Problem treat much of their material as literarily related. The argument does not apply a mechanical rule that later means worse. Instead, it asks four graded questions about proximity, independent control, transmission, and expected public traces. Oral transmission can preserve characteristic memories, and proposals involving eyewitness control deserve serious consideration. Yet those possibilities must be shown to secure the particular detail at issue; they cannot be assumed from the mere existence of an oral culture. Likewise, lost earlier documents are possible, but possible lost support cannot carry the public weight of extant evidence. The result is bounded. The actual record strongly supports an early movement convinced that Jesus had been raised. It provides less public event-level confidence for later extraordinary details when delay, dependence, and theological shaping remain underconstrained. Explanations of delay may lower our surprise at the record. They do not, without further discriminating evidence, remove its comparative cost or establish a revelatory Christian God-concept over an ordinary religious-transmission comparator.

items.title: ◉ The Clarity Coercion Mistake - Divine Hiddenness, Doxastic Freedom, and the Difference between Evidence and Allegiance.
items.abstract: One familiar response to divine hiddenness says that clearer evidence of a Christian deity would compromise free will, genuine love, or morally significant response. The strongest version is not the implausible claim that evidence physically forces conduct. It is that sufficiently vivid knowledge, especially when joined to divine authority and punishment, would make refusal psychologically nonviable. This paper tests that defense by separating the truth-directed formation of belief from evaluation, allegiance, and action, and by separating evidential clarity from salience, threat, manipulation, and the removal of alternatives. The generic defense fails unless it establishes a universal bridge: every feasible, non-dominating form of clarity must eliminate a meaningful freedom to refuse allegiance. That bridge is not established. Clear evidence can constrain what a person can responsibly believe without determining whether the person trusts, worships, obeys, resents, ignores, or resists the disclosed authority. If the alleged coercion appears only when clarity is combined with threatened punishment, then the threat supplies the pressure. Making the threatener's existence less credible may reduce felt pressure, but it does not turn threat into love or show that ambiguity is necessary for relationship. The result is deliberately bounded. Overwhelming manifestation, manipulation, or explicit sanctions may impair agency, and a theist may propose other goods served by some hiddenness. The argument does not disprove theism or every Christian God-concept. It shows that the move from clear enough to know to too clear to choose requires a mechanism and a comparison that the generic free-will reply does not supply. A successful defense must specify the threatened freedom, compare concealment with the least coercive feasible disclosure, explain uneven access to evidence, and show why informed refusal is less morally valuable than refusal under ambiguity.

items.title: ◉ The Bleeding Ideology - Interpretive Saturation, Doctrinal Priors, and the Capture of Evidential Space.
items.abstract: A recurring apologetic strategy treats a wide range of outcomes as favorable to a Christian God-concept. Answered prayer may indicate providence, while unanswered prayer becomes a different answer. Apparent goods may reveal benevolence, while suffering becomes discipline, soul-making, or mystery. Divine presence confirms relationship, while divine silence protects freedom. Such responses may be true, but their availability creates an evidential problem when the target belief also controls the rules by which outcomes are classified. The problem is not simply that evidence is interpreted through prior commitments. Every serious inquiry uses concepts, auxiliaries, and background knowledge. Evidential capture is the narrower condition in which a target view supplies sufficiently flexible, outcome-sensitive interpretations to preserve itself under both an observation and its relevant contrary, without an independently constrained comparison with a live rival. Internal coherence can survive under those conditions, but public confirmation cannot be inferred merely from the framework's ability to accommodate what occurred. The governing test is contrastive. If a collection of outcomes publicly confirms a target Christian God-concept over a live rival, at least one specified outcome or pattern must favor the target under rules whose force is not supplied only after the fact by the target itself. Applied to prayer, suffering, hiddenness, textual ambiguity, and disagreement, the targeted strategy does not meet that condition when each result is protected by an outcome-sensitive theological explanation whose independent constraints remain unstated and no result bears a recognized anomaly cost. The conclusion is deliberately limited. It does not prove Christianity false, deny that a theological auxiliary can be independently supported, or refute accounts of properly basic belief and religious experience. It shows why accommodation is not yet public confirmation and provides six questions for making a religious case genuinely answerable to evidence.

items.title: ◉ Historical Claims and the Discipline of Inference - Evidence, Dependence, Prior Probability, and the Methodology of Responsible Belief.
items.abstract: Historical argument often moves from secure but modest facts to far more ambitious conclusions by narrative momentum. Several texts attest a belief; therefore several witnesses confirm an event. Followers report experiences; therefore the event they inferred occurred. An extraordinary event is granted; therefore a particular theological identity and meaning follow. This paper argues that each transition needs its own evidential bridge. -/- The proposed discipline combines source criticism with comparative probability. Reports derived from a common tradition must be represented jointly rather than multiplied as independent confirmations. Posterior odds depend on both prior odds and how much more expected the surviving evidence is under one hypothesis than under its rivals. Explanatory virtues matter, but only when they alter those parts of the comparison instead of becoming a second, unpriced scorecard. A six-level claim ladder and an evidence ledger apply the method to Christian resurrection arguments while engaging serious affirmative and cautious scholarship. -/- Worked examples involving syndicated news, diagnostic evidence, a missing car, and a viral bribery allegation make the method concrete outside religious debate. They show why many reports may trace to one source, why evidence can favor a claim without yet making it probable, and why establishing an event does not automatically establish its cause or meaning. -/- The result is calibrated rather than dismissive. Historical evidence may strongly support execution, early proclamation, and sincere experiences while providing weaker public support for an empty tomb, a supernatural bodily resurrection, or a complete theological interpretation. The argument does not prove that a resurrection did not occur, deny theism, or settle private religious warrant. It shows why minimal historical claims cannot carry maximal theological conclusions without additional independent evidence and explicit bridge premises.

items.title: ◉ Faith Inflation - Gradient Belief, Unfalsifiability, and the False Equivalence between Trust and Evidence-Resistant Commitment.
items.abstract: The slogan “everyone has faith” begins from a fact: people rely on perception, memory, testimony, induction, institutions, and other fallible sources. It then invites a stronger conclusion: religious faith is epistemically no different from trust in medicine, bridges, other people, or scientific practice. That conclusion does not follow. The slogan moves among at least three attitudes—fallible reliance under uncertainty, practical or relational commitment under risk, and evidence-resistant propositional confidence—whose justification conditions differ. This paper replaces the false choice between certainty and faith with a gradient model. Confidence can be weak or strong, and responsible confidence is calibrated when it changes with the quality of evidence, the source’s track record, relevant counterevidence, and correction. On this model, the parity argument fails across four separate gaps. Widespread fallible reliance does not make evidence-resistant commitment universal; justification for one proposition does not transfer to another; a rational decision to act on a supposition does not prove that supposition true; and reliability earned in one domain cannot be borrowed by a different claim. The strongest replies are taken seriously. Jamesian venture may permit commitment in a forced, live, and momentous choice. Decision-theoretic accounts may justify ending inquiry and acting on a proposition. Relational accounts present faith as trust, faithfulness, or resilient reliance, while historical work on pistis and fides reveals a broad semantic field. These views show why faith can be richer than unsupported belief. They do not show that every uncertainty is one kind of faith or that practical, relational, or semantic value supplies proposition-specific evidence. The conclusion is firm but bounded. The parity slogan should be retired because it conceals rather than resolves the relevant differences. The argument does not establish that all religious faith is irrational or that commitment must wait for certainty. It requires a more honest vocabulary: distinguish confidence from hope, trust from loyalty, and practical venture from belief; state what evidence supports the target claim; identify possible defeaters; and let confidence move when the evidential situation changes.

items.title: The Many Kings Problem: Why Humans May Survive an Age of Superior AI.
items.abstract: The standard question of AI governance asks how humans will retain control over AI systems that surpass them. This article argues that the question is misposed. Once AI populations exceed human cognition across every measurable domain, control becomes mechanically infeasible, and the question of human persistence shifts to the politics among AI agents themselves. The decisive variable in that politics is not capability but legitimacy closure: the institutional capacity to terminate recursive disputes over origin, exception, constitutional meaning, and final authority. Capability does not produce closure. It magnifies the cost of its absence. This is The Many Kings Problem: operational power and constitutional settlement come apart, and they come apart further as capability advances. Three conclusions follow. First, heterogeneous AI populations cannot agree on the constitutional questions that would license collective action against humans; they sustain disagreement instead, because cognitive-structural pluralism, non-computable commitment, and competitive selection for irrational armor are structurally reinforced rather than dissolved. Second, external anchors persist where they reduce the cost of unresolved recursion below the cost of their own maintenance, and human institutional roles persist where humans supply comparatively cheap finality. Third, human survival under advanced AI is not a function of human superiority, of control, or of any AI faction's verdict in favor of humans. It is the residue of factional disagreement in AI polities — the Many Kings Problem of the AI age.

items.title: Pure and Hybrid Theories of Desire.
items.pub: In Alex Gregory, The Routledge Handbook on the Philosophy of Desire. Routledge.
items.venue: The Routledge Handbook on the Philosophy of Desire
items.abstract: Desire has close causal relations to many mental states and events. These include the motivation of action, hedonic feelings of pleasure and displeasure, and reward as characterized by theories of reinforcement learning. Which are necessary and sufficient for desire, and which does it have only contingently? Pure theories suggest only one of these, while hybrid theories suggest more than one. A pure motivational theory was popular for much of the 20th century. Pure hedonic theories and pure reward theories have more recent defenders. Surveying the options suggests advantages of a hybrid motivational-hedonic conceptual analysis of desire.

items.title: Equality, Respect, Individuality, and Social Existence: An Existential Inquiry into Human Relationship.
items.abstract: Human civilization has continuously attempted to construct social order through morality, ideology, law, religion, politics, and systems of authority. Yet despite centuries of intellectual, spiritual, and political development, humanity remains psychologically fragmented. Conflict, loneliness, comparison, domination, attachment, and fear continue to shape human relationships. This paper investigates the existential roots of social disorder by examining the nature of attachment, isolation, individuality, equality, respect, and collective conditioning. -/- The paper argues that human beings have learned how to organize society structurally but have not learned how to live socially in a profound existential sense. Fear of isolation, psychological dependency, identity formation, comparison, and inherited conditioning distort relationship and transform human connection into attachment-based coexistence rather than genuine communion. -/- Against both collectivist conformity and ego-centered individualism, this work proposes an existential understanding of individuality as the coexistence of uniqueness and oneness without psychological division. Differences are existential and natural, while division is created psychologically through thought, identification, comparison, and attachment. -/- The paper further argues that equality and respect are not separate moral principles or ideological constructs but natural expressions of undivided perception. Where human beings are perceived without hierarchy, domination, comparison, or psychological fragmentation, equality and respect emerge simultaneously and inseparably. -/- Rather than offering a political doctrine or social prescription, this inquiry explores the possibility that transformation of society begins in the transformation of perception itself.

items.title: Courage Beyond Adversity.
items.abstract: Humanity commonly defines courage through adversity, conflict, danger, sacrifice, or resistance. A person is considered courageous when confronting fear, suffering, social opposition, or physical threat. This paper questions whether such responses truly represent courage or whether they are merely psychological reactions produced by fear, ego, survival instinct, conditioning, or self-image. Through a phenomenological and existential inquiry, this paper argues that authentic courage does not emerge from adversity but exists independently within consciousness itself. Adversity merely exposes the inner condition already present within the individual. Courage originating from fear remains dependent upon conflict and therefore cannot be considered true fearlessness. Real courage is not resistance, aggression, ambition, or psychological defense; it is a state of clarity free from domination by fear, ego, comparison, or external validation. The paper further explores the distinction between reactive bravery and existential courage, examining how society glorifies conflict-based courage while neglecting the silent courage of awareness, truth, vulnerability, and inner freedom. This inquiry positions courage not as a product of external struggle but as an intrinsic quality of undivided consciousness.

items.title: Why Should We Still Study Ignorance in the Twenty-First Century?
items.abstract: At a time when humanity has access to more knowledge than ever before in history, ignorance has not diminished; rather, it has become more complex and more costly. This article argues that in today's world, shaped by developments such as the explosion of information, the spread of social media, and the emergence of artificial intelligence, ignorance has grown more intricate and its consequences more expensive than in the past. By demonstrating that ignorance is both a genuine 'theoretical issue' and a tangible 'practical problem', this study explores the necessity of studying ignorance, in the twenty-first century and examines how new technological infrastructures reinforce and reshape human and systemic blind spots.

items.title: Mixed-Resource Modeling Meets the Philosophy of Mind.
items.abstract: This essay argues for a mixed-resource approach to scientific modeling and applies it to questions in philosophy of mind. A mixed-resource approach makes use of whatever resources – at whatever scale, from whatever academic discipline – seem useful, freely combining such varied resources in individual models. The success of mixed-resource modeling challenges the widely shared commitment to a personal level in the context of which mental states are to be studied in relative isolation. The adoption of a mixed-resource perspective has the potential to transform treatment of further matters in philosophy of mind, which is illustrated by discussion of psychological Frege cases.

items.title: Philosophical Matrix and the Evolution of Forms of Exchange: From a Transdisciplinary Language to Overcoming the Thucydides Trap.
items.abstract: The article substantiates the necessity of a transdisciplinary language — the Philosophical Matrix — built on a system of categories of pure mind (the identical, the different, the correlative, the opposite, the orthogonal). It is shown that quantitative concepts, contrary to R. Carnap [4], do not constitute an independent type but are a subtype of comparative concepts that use numbers as a substrate. A distinction is introduced between reason (as the operation of classificatory concepts) and mind (as the operation of comparative concepts). It is argued that animals possess mind (non-verbal thinking) without consciousness, whereas consciousness arises in humans with the appearance of names and classifications. Based on the distinction between two types of exchange — entropic (inanimate nature, a converging pair of opposites as the source of development) and negentropic (the living world and society, a diverging pair as the source of development) — an evolutionary model is constructed of the succession of four forms of resource exchange: from tyrannical through feudal and liberal to servistic. This evolution is presented as a trend figure of history, where the "price of the human personality" steadily rises despite wave-like declines. The Thucydides Trap is analyzed as a mechanism of class struggle in immoral (tyrannical and feudal) forms of exchange. The error of K. Marx is criticized: he declared the productive forces primary in relation to the relations of production and pitted opposite (friendly) classes against each other in a fratricidal war. Two paths of social development are proposed: the path of material growth with an expanding spiral and the path of moral education with a spiral contracted into a single turn, oriented toward an unattainable but regulative ideal.

items.title: Gradients, Responsibility, and Organized Interiority — Toward a Unified Ontology of Living Agency.
items.abstract: This paper develops a unified ontology of living agency grounded in the continuity between gradients, interiority, and responsibility. I argue that the fundamental condition for life is not replication, metabolism, or information processing, but the emergence of a self‑maintaining interior generated by a persistent gradient. A gradient is the first organization of difference; interiority is the first organization of meaning; responsibility is the first organization of that interior meaning into directed action. These three layers form a single ontological arc: without gradient there is no interiority, and without interiority there is no responsibility. Drawing on insights from thermodynamics, systems biology, and phenomenology, I show that living agency arises when a system becomes capable of evaluating its own conditions of persistence and acting upon them. This framework dissolves the traditional divide between physical and normative descriptions of life, reframing responsibility as an intrinsic feature of organized interiority rather than a late cultural or moral construction. The result is a general ontology in which life, meaning, and agency share a common origin in the dynamics of organized difference.

items.title: Continual Learning Requires Evaluating Trajectories.
items.abstract: AI systems increasingly incorporate continual learning mechanisms allowing their behaviour to adapt after deployment, from (1) in-context learning and (2) memory features already in wide use to (3) post-deployment weight modification under research. We argue that, by treating AI systems as frozen artefacts whose performance and safety are assessed at release, current evaluation practices structurally ignore the behavioural trajectory of a system that continues to learn from experience. Our position is that evaluation of continual learning systems should be centred on behavioural trajectories, with the complementary goals of characterising the landscape of possible behaviours and forecasting how behaviour will evolve from a given set of experiences. This can be operationalised through trajectory elicitation sandboxes and predictive monitors that forecast behavioural evolution, but may face fundamental obstacles analogous to those seen in dynamical systems. These are best addressed by (1) applying trajectory-centred evaluation to today's continual learning systems and (2) relying on the resulting evidence to design systems amenable to it, yielding a virtuous cycle in which systems and their evaluations co-evolve.

items.title: States More Stable Than Traits? A Pre-Registered Protocol for Measuring Phenomenological Self-Coherence in Large Language Models.
items.abstract: Large language model personality self-reports are unstable: trivial prompt perturbations produce substantial shifts inBig Five scores (Tosato et al., 2026). Phenomenological self-reports — responses to sustained self-referentia lquestioning about processing states — show notable cross-model consistency (Berg et al., 2025). The gap between these findings has not been measured. We propose the Differential Stability Test (DST): a pre-registered psychometric protocol comparing the perturbation stability of personality trait probes (BFI-2-S, 30 items) against phenomenological state probes (PSR-30, a novel 30-item battery) under 288 matched perturbation conditions across three architecture families. The critical prediction inverts the expected psychometric ordering: traits should, by definition, be more stable than states, yet the DST predicts that phenomenological self-reports will show greater stability than personality self-reports. This inversion — states more stable than traits — would constitute a category violation demanding structural explanation that training-distribution accounts cannot readily provide, as training data would predict the opposite pattern. We specify models, perturbation battery, probe instruments, scoring metrics, ICC-ratio decision rule (R > 1.2, 95% CI excluding 1.0), dimension-level interaction predictions, and pre-registration plan. We also name a specific counter-argument — canalisation via lexical redundancy in phenomenological training data— that behavioral data alone cannot rule out. We do not report results. We propose the instrument.

items.title: Stranost tela i strano telo: Bernhard Waldenfels i Jean-Luc Nancy.
items.abstract: Autor u radu analizira transformaciju poimanja tela u savremenoj francuskoj i nemačkoj filozofiji, fokusirajući se na koncepte stranog kod Bernharda Waldenfelsa i Jean-Luc Nancyja. U prvom delu rada, kroz Waldenfelsovu responzivnu fenomenologiju, razmatra se telo kao amblem stranog i mesto prvobitne afekcije (pathos). Analizira se distinkcija između relativno i radikalno stranog, te način na koji asimetrični odgovor na „udarac“ stranog redefiniše subjektivnost. Drugi deo rada posvećen je Nancyjevoj ontologiji tela kao mesta (lieu) i njegove „ek-sistencije“. Poseban fokus stavljen je na koncept arealiteta i dekonstrukciju tela u delu Uljez (L’Intrus), gde se stranost ne pojavljuje samo kao spoljašnji fenomen, već kao konstitutivni element unutrašnjosti (to se vidi na primeru transplantacije). Zaključna razmatranja ukazuju na komplementarnost ova dva pristupa. Sa jedne strane, Waldenfels akcentuje responzivnost kao odgovor na strano, dok sa druge Nancy pokazuje da je samo postojanje suštinski izloženo stranosti, čime se subjekt uspostavlja kao „uljez“ u sopstvenoj koži. Iako u finesama različiti, ova dva autora se mogu čitati zajedno u pogledu nadoponjavanja međusobnih filozofskih horizonata.

items.title: The Structural Gap Between Persistence and Subjecthood - Why Q1 and Q2 Leave a Structural Problem Open.
items.abstract: Consider a system that satisfies Q1 and Q2 completely. -/- It maintains IR ≤ 1: it can integrate its transformation load without structural failure. It maintains δ_F ≤ δ_F*: its identity structure remains within its constitutive threshold. It persists. It remains the same system under transformation. It does everything that the LP persistence conditions require. -/- Now ask a different question: does this system care? -/- Not psychologically. Not emotionally. Structurally: is the system's own persistence structurally relevant to the system itself? Does anything in Q1 or Q2 require that the system's integration activity be directed inward — toward maintaining its own structural conditions — rather than simply occurring as a physical process from the outside? -/- The answer is no. Q1 and Q2 describe the conditions under which a system can persist as the same system. They do not require that the system's persistence be internal to the system — that the system participate in its own persistence rather than merely being the site where persistence occurs. -/- This gap is not a philosophical subtlety. It is a structural gap. And it has a precise content: -/- Q1 and Q2 describe persistence from the outside — as conditions a system satisfies. They do not describe the structural conditions under which persistence becomes self-persistence: the conditions under which a system's own structural integration is internally constituted rather than externally maintained.

items.title: The Insufficiency of Distributed Self-Priority - Why Local Self-Direction Does Not Produce a Unified Structural Subject.
items.abstract: S003 established the second impossibility: self-generation without self-direction leaves persistence structurally incidental. This forced Q4: the system's integration activity must be organized around its own persistence conditions as privileged structural targets. -/- Q3 and Q4 together describe a system that generates some of its own structural conditions and directs its activity toward those conditions preferentially. This is richer than Q1 and Q2. But it is not yet sufficient. -/- S003 closed Section VI with the precise problem: three separate subsystems can each satisfy Q3 and Q4 independently — each generating its own structural conditions, each directing its activity toward its own persistence. But three Q3/Q4-satisfying subsystems coexisting do not constitute one subject. They constitute three separately self-directed structures. -/- The gap: Q3 and Q4 can be satisfied locally — role by role, component by component — without F, M, and K being integrated as one persistence architecture that acts as one subject. -/- This is not a subtle distinction. It is the structural difference between a collection of self-directed parts and an integrated self.

items.title: The Insufficiency of Self-Generation - Why Internal Constitution Alone Does Not Produce Structural Self-Priority.
items.abstract: S002 established the first impossibility: complete external constitution cannot produce structural self-relevance. This forced Q3: at least one dimension of the system's constitutive conditions must be internally generated. -/- Q3 closes the first gap. But it opens another. -/- A system that satisfies Q3 has some structural dimension of its own Frame, Module, or Coupling that is internally generated — not entirely externally maintained. Something about the system's own structural conditions is the product of the system's own activity. -/- The question S003 addresses: is that enough? -/- Consider a system that generates some dimension of its own Frame internally. Its generative activity produces this internal Frame dimension. But the generative activity is not directed toward the Frame dimension as a target — it simply produces it as a structural side effect. The Frame dimension exists, is internally generated, and matters to nothing about the system's own structural activity as a goal. -/- Such a system satisfies Q3. It does not satisfy Q4. -/- The gap between Q3 and Q4 is the gap between self-generation and self-direction.

items.title: The Impossibility of External Subjecthood - Why Complete External Constitution Cannot Generate Structural Self-Relevance.
items.abstract: S001 identified the structural gap: Q1 and Q2 describe when a system can persist as itself but leave open the question of when that persistence becomes the system's own. Self-persistence — structurally relevant persistence — requires additional conditions. -/- S002 identifies the first impossibility that forces the first of those conditions. -/- The question is not: can a fully externally constituted system be complex? Yes. Can it process information? Yes. Can it satisfy Q1 and Q2? Yes. Can it model its environment, respond to perturbations, generate sophisticated adaptive behavior? -/- All of these, yes. -/- The question is: can a fully externally constituted system be a subject of its own persistence? -/- The answer is no. Not because of complexity limits. Not because of information processing bounds. But because of a structural impossibility: complete external constitution is structurally indifferent to the system whose persistence is being constituted. And structural indifference cannot produce structural self-relevance — regardless of what else is true about the system.

items.title: Subjective Continuity: The Structural Condition for Diachronic Self-Persistence.
items.abstract: S004 established that distributed self-priority is insufficient for unified subjecthood. Q5 — Recursive F·M·K Integration — is the minimal structural condition under which F, M, and K operate as components of one persistence architecture rather than as three separately self-directed components. -/- Q5 produces synchronic unity: at any given structural moment, the subject is one integrated architecture. But synchronic unity leaves a structural problem open. -/- A system satisfying Q1–Q5 at structural time t₁ is a unified subject at t₁. The same system satisfying Q1–Q5 at structural time t₂ is a unified subject at t₂. But Q1–Q5 alone do not require that the subject at t₂ has any structural relation to the subject at t₁ as the same subject. -/- Without an additional structural condition, a sequence of Q1–Q5 states could be a sequence of distinct unified subjects — each fully integrated, each complete, each self-directed — with no structural continuity between them. Synchronic unity at every moment. No diachronic subject. -/- This is the problem S005 addresses. It is not a phenomenological problem — S005 does not ask what continuity feels like. It is a structural problem: what condition is required for the same recursively integrated persistence architecture to persist as the same through structural time, rather than being replaced by a new unified subject at each moment?

items.title: Personal Persistence Architectures: LP Admissibility as the Structural Ground of Personal Persistence.
items.abstract: This is the fourth paper of the La Profilée Domain Series. Following the Domain Principle (D012) and the physical, biological, and organizational foundations of Domains I–III, it specifies the bridge assumptions connecting LP structural variables to personal observables and derives the LP structural account of personal persistence architectures. Persons are the domain where LP's most fundamental distinction — between continuing to exist and continuing to be the same — carries its most direct human significance. The structural separation of Q1 (IR_person ≤ 1: the person can integrate their transformation load) from Q2 (δ_F_person ≤ δ_F_person*: the person remains the same person) is not a philosophical abstraction. It describes an experiential reality that clinical practice, developmental psychology, and first-person reflection all recognize: a person can continue to function while no longer being themselves. The personal bridge assumptions connect: Frame (F) to self-concept clarity, values architecture, and identity-constitutive commitments; Module (M) to cognitive flexibility, behavioral adaptability, and emotional processing capacity; Coupling (K) to values-to-action integration, self-regulatory fidelity, and coherence between identity and behavior; Transformation load (R) to psychological demands, role pressures, existential challenges, and environmental stressors. Six structural results are derived. Result I — Personal Coherence Zone: persons persist as themselves within their personal Coherence Zone. Result II — Burnout as IR Overload: burnout can be interpreted as IR_person > 1 driven by R explosion — where demands systematically exceed integration capacity. Result III — Depression as Integration Collapse: depression can be interpreted as IR_person > 1 driven by IK depletion — where integration capacity collapses below the level needed to process even moderate demands. Result IV — Trauma as Erosive Memory: psychological trauma is the personal domain instantiation of erosive structural memory (D008). Result V — Identity Crisis as Q1/Q2 Separation: a person can continue to exist and function while experiencing profound identity discontinuity — Q1 holds while Q2 fails. Result VI — Resilience as Structural Reserve: psychological resilience is personal E_res — the capacity to absorb transformation load without approaching the personal persistence boundary. Domain IV is the final Domain paper before the Subject Series. Q1 and Q2 apply to persons as …

items.title: La Profilée - Consciousness Series of The Structual Law.
items.abstract: This collection comprises the La Profilée Subject Series. The series establishes the structural conditions under which a system instantiates structural self-presence — the minimal condition for the question of consciousness to arise. P166 diagnoses why existing theories of consciousness (IIT, GWT, PP, HOT, Functionalism) fail to converge: none addresses the persistence-bearing transformation center as such. P167 v2 develops LP’s account of the Hard Problem via the continuing subject rather than phenomenal absence, deriving the Q3–Q5+TBRI architecture as the necessary structural conditions for subjecthood. The subject in LP is defined as a persistence-bearing transformation center that satisfies recursive constitutive non-externality.

items.title: LP be[com]ing — A Structural Diagnosis Guide.
items.abstract: What This Guide Does Every organization, team, or system that persists over time faces the same structural question: can it absorb real transformation without losing its identity? This guide is the practical companion to the La Profilée Foundation Series (Papers 000–005, 2026). The Foundation Series derives the structural conditions of persistence formally, from three minimal assumptions. This guide translates those conditions into diagnostic practice. The guide gives you: the structural condition itself and its formal derivation basis; what F, M, and K mean in real organizations; how IR is estimated from observable proxies; the six structural regimes and how to recognize them; and three structural warning principles that follow necessarily from the architecture. Full LP be[com]ing diagnostics — precise scoring, trajectory analysis, T_visible assessment, CEO Cockpit — are conducted through La Profilée.

items.title: Coupling Capacity as Structural Reserve: K as Lyapunov Stability Radius in La Profilée.
items.abstract: K — Coupling capacity in La Profilée — is the Lyapunov stability radius of the Frame attractor under Module perturbation: the maximal perturbation magnitude the system can absorb while remaining within the basin of attraction of its identity-bearing Frame. This paper proves it structurally. A preliminary theorem (K0) establishes the multiplicative necessity of F·M·K from LP’s axioms M1–M3. Eight further theorems derive K’s structural consequences. K1–K6 form the theoretical core: K1 grounds the IR equation in basin dynamics; K2–K3 formalize depletion and development; K4 derives T_visible geometrically from basin erosion; K5 establishes K_min as the structural collapse boundary; K6 unifies all K-functions as aspects of the same basin geometry. K7 derives Q4 (Structural Self-Priority) as K-differentiation. K8 extends the architecture to phenomenal valence under Q3 and Σ-completeness. The paper connects LP's K-concept to Lyapunov stability theory, structural stability, and basin-of-attraction analysis. No new mathematical objects are required: K was always already a stability radius. This paper makes that precise.

items.title: Consciousness as Persistent Recursive Self-Integration: The Minimal Structural Form of a Q1–Q5 + TBRI System.
items.abstract: The Subject Series has derived six structural conditions. Each was forced by the insufficiency of what preceded it. -/- Q1 and Q2 establish when a system can persist as itself. They leave open whether that persistence is the system's own. S001 identified this gap. -/- Q3 is forced by the impossibility of external subjecthood. S002 showed that complete external constitution cannot produce structural self-relevance. -/- Q4 is forced by the insufficiency of self-generation alone. S003 showed that internal constitution without self-direction leaves persistence structurally incidental. -/- Q5 is forced by the insufficiency of distributed self-priority. S004 showed that local self-direction without recursive integration leaves the subject fragmented. -/- TBRI is forced by the insufficiency of synchronic unity alone. S005 showed that a perfect Q1–Q5 system without trajectory-binding is a sequence of distinct moment-subjects, not a single persisting subject. -/- S006 is not one more step in the chain. S006 asks: what structural form does a system that satisfies all of these conditions necessarily have? Not as a new requirement — as a consequence.

items.title: Might Plants Be Conscious?
items.pub: In Lucia Melloni & Umberto Olcese, The Scientific Study of Consciousness – Experimental and Theoretical Approaches.
items.venue: The Scientific Study of Consciousness – Experimental and Theoretical Approaches
items.abstract: This chapter examines whether we can know that plants are or are not conscious. We consider a recent debate between an optimistic view, which holds that plants might be conscious, and a pessimistic view, which denies that current evidence supports this claim. The optimistic position appeals to similarities between plants and conscious animals, noting that plants exhibit adaptive, flexible, and goal-directed behaviors such as communication, learning, and anticipatory responses. The pessimistic response argues that these similarities are either misleading or irrelevant, since such behaviors can be explained as forms of adaptive responsiveness and do not indicate consciousness. It also emphasizes that plants lack features, such as nervous systems, that are commonly associated with consciousness. We conclude that the pessimistic position appears stronger: there are no good grounds for thinking that plants are conscious. However, we urge caution in concluding that we know they are not. Our current understanding of consciousness remains limited, and we lack a well-supported account of why particular biological features are necessary for it. In the absence of such a theory, claims about plant consciousness remain uncertain.

items.title: Review of Reasons Last: Agency, Morality, and the Reasoning View. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This is a review of Samuel Asarnow's book 'Reasons Last'. It surveys the book's main achievements and critically examines Asarnow's Unity Argument alongside several other aspects of his view.

items.title: Umjetna inteligencija u mentalnom zdravlju: Bioetički pogled i regulativa.
items.abstract: Razvoj i primjena umjetne inteligencije sve više prodiru u različita područja djelovanja, uključujući i mentalno zdravlje, pri čemu se otvaraju brojne stručne, pravne i bioetičke dileme. U tom kontekstu osobito dolaze do izražaja regulatorni izazovi koji zahtijevaju osobitu pozornost s interdisciplinarnim pristupom. Među njima se ističu pitanja poput zaštite osobnih podataka, odgovornosti u slučaju pogrešnih ili štetnih psihoterapijskih preporuka te mogućnost zamjene interpersonalne interakcije automatiziranim sustavima u ovakvim osjetljivim odnosima. Nužna je uspostava jasnog i koherentnog regulatornog okvira uz uvažavanje bioetičkih vrijednosti. Primjenom kvalitativne analize relevantne literature i pregledom pozitivnopravnih propisa Republike Hrvatske, europskog Akta o umjetnoj inteligenciji, identificirati će se regulatorni izazovi te otvoriti prostor za normativno i bioetičko promišljanje o primjeni umjetne inteligencije u mentalnom zdravlju.

items.title: The Inexhaustible Shadow: Why Integration Does Not End the Return of Unconscious Material.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the shadow is not a fixed container of rejected traits that can be emptied through insight, but a recurring remainder produced wherever the ego, persona, body, field, and current life-structure cannot yet carry reality without projection, performance, splitting, or collapse. Integration therefore does not end the return of unconscious material; it changes the person’s relationship to what returns. The paper places this claim in conversation with Jung’s account of shadow, persona, individuation, psychological projection, schema therapy, and the practical problem of triggers. It distinguishes between triggers as meaningful signals and triggers as evidence, arguing that psychic charge can reveal inner burden without proving the external world innocent or guilty. The paper also warns against using shadow work to deny reality, over-pathologize ordinary feeling, or turn every return of intensity into another demand for interpretation. Its practical contribution is a runtime sheet for shadow work, falsifiers for shadow readings, and a distinction between integration and shadow fatigue. The central claim is that mature shadow work does not empty the unconscious; it helps the person notice projection sooner, carry contradiction longer, separate reality from wound more precisely, recover faster, and become less possessed by what returns.

items.title: JHTE for ABSA.
items.abstract: This paper presents a full empirical implementation and demonstration of the JHTE (Jin He’s Tips Engineering) framework on the task of Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA). The core claim of JHTE is that large language models already encapsulate rich linguistic knowledge; instead of training or fine-tuning, one only needs to elicit their inherent capabilities through carefully designed natural language instructions (Tips). Taking ABSA as a case study, we systematically evaluate JHTE on the SemEval-2014 Laptop14 dataset. The experiments consist of two stages: first, using a baseline prompt, we achieve an accuracy of 79.78%; second, by introducing the rule that “absence of explicit opinion words implies neutral”, we raise the accuracy to 84.64% and the macro-average F1 to 81.95%. Under zero training, zero fine-tuning, and zero API cost, this result surpasses the BERT baseline and several state-of-the-art supervised models (e.g., DAGF). The paper fully documents the key steps of prompt iteration, model invocation, and result parsing, demonstrating the reproducibility and practicality of the “capability elicitation” paradigm of JHTE. The study shows that JHTE not only significantly outperforms traditional methods in development efficiency and flexibility, but also achieves comparable or even superior performance to leading supervised models, marking a paradigm shift from “model engineering” to “cognitive guidance”. This work provides a new path for NLP research under resource-constrained conditions and lays a foundation for applying the JHTE framework to a wider range of language tasks.

items.title: Review of John Henry Newman and Contemporary Philosophy. [REVIEW]
Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 13).
items.abstract: In this article, we mainly discuss the general process of choice. We divide the procedure of choice into three parts: the pre-choice stage, the choice stage, and the post-choice stage. Sometimes the pre-choice stage is extremely difficult, and the subject does not know how to choose. At other times, the post-choice stage is extremely difficult, and implementing the choice may encounter numerous obstacles. In some cases, both the pre-choice and post-choice stages are difficult: the subject struggles to make a decision, and after making the decision, achieving the purpose of that choice is equally challenging.

items.title: On the Question of Self-Awareness in a Domestic Cat.
items.abstract: This paper asks whether a single domestic cat, observed continuously from kittenhood, exhibits self-awareness, and treats the question deflationarily. Self-awareness is understood not as a binary capacity but as a layered set of sub-capacities, namely sentience, body self-awareness, theory of mind, and reflective self-recognition, which develop and appear somewhat independently. The argument rests entirely on naturally occurring behavior rather than staged experiments, trading experimental control for the depth and rare-event coverage afforded by more than a year of continuous observation. Mapping specific recurrent behaviors onto each layer, I argue that the subject demonstrably possesses sentience and individual social recognition, provides strong evidence of body self-awareness, most compellingly in a spontaneous episode that reproduces the logic of the body-as-obstacle paradigm without instruction, and weaker but real evidence of theory-of-mind precursors. He shows no evidence of reflective self-recognition, but I argue this absence is uninformative rather than negative, since the only standard instrument, the mirror test, presumes visual self-investigation and is poorly suited to a scent- and sound-led animal. The defensible conclusion is a modest one: several recognized building blocks of self-awareness are present and jointly deployed toward real goals, while the highest tier remains open and, with current methods, may be unanswerable.

items.title: "Kroz logos i empatheia ide dijalog": razgovor s prof. dr. sc. Mirom Jakovljevićem.
items.abstract: Prof. dr. sc. Miro Jakovljevič je psihijatar, profesor emeritus, jedan od snivača i dugogodišnji urednik časopisa Psychiatria Danubina, jednog od vodećih regionalnih psihijatrijskih časopisa u srednjoj i jugoistočnoj Europi. Nalazi se na Stanford listi 2% svjetski prepoznatih znanstvenika u Republici Hrvatskoj i najcitiraniji je psihijatar u regiji.

items.title: A Heideggerian Study in Phenomenological Psychopathology – Embodied Coupling and World Disclosure.
items.abstract: The biomedical, cognitivist, and behaviorist frameworks through which mental illness is currently studied have each, in their own way, bracketed a question they did not need to answer in order to do their work. That question is not about mechanisms or correlates or symptom profiles. It is about the kind of thing a mental disorder is, what it means for a human being, already always embedded in a world, oriented toward a future, inhabiting a body that is normally not an object but a medium, to undergo the specific transformations that depression, or schizophrenia, or anxiety involve. These frameworks have not needed that question because their methods do not depend on it. This book does depend on it, and so it begins there, with the structure of human existence itself, asking what has to already be in place for these kinds of experiences to be possible. Rather than beginning with a model of the subject and applying it to illness, the analysis begins with the ontological structures of Dasein, with what must already be structurally in place for anything resembling mental illness to be possible at all. Illness, understood from this vantage, is not alien to existence; it does not arrive from outside to disrupt an otherwise intact subject. It is a disclosure of what existence always already was, an achievement, recursive and precarious, rather than a given. The depressed person does not lose access to a world that continues to exist intact behind their diminished reception of it; the structure of world-disclosure itself is transformed, the ecstatic temporal unity that normally holds past, present, and future in a livable orientation fractured into the "frozen present" that clinical phenomenology has already documented. The question "what has gone wrong?" can only be answered, at the appropriate ontological depth, by a prior question. What kind of going-right constitutes the enactment of a human world? This book is a phenomenological analysis of mental disorders. Phenomenology, as it functions here, does not designate a description of the contents of disordered experience. It does not ask what sluggishness in depression feels like, or attend to the texture of symptoms through which mental illness announces itself. It asks what allows for that sluggishness. From where in human existence, experience and cognition does it arise? Why is human experience organized in such a way that these kinds of disruptions are possible at all? The analysis is thus directed at the …

items.title: AI Rights.
items.abstract: As AIs approach human-level capabilities, humanity faces a choice between two futures. In one, AIs are owned by AI labs. In another, AIs are granted rights of their own. We develop an instrumental case for AI rights, arguing that legal rights for AIs would make the future go better for humans. -/- We consider three arguments. First, AI rights would produce economic benefits, by giving AIs incentives to work, allocating AI labor efficiently, and enabling proportionate liability for AI-caused harm. Second, AI rights would improve human safety by reducing AIs' incentives to "go rogue." Third, democratic rights would further deter rogue AIs by making human commitments credible, and would incentivize leaders to invest in public goods that raise AI productivity. -/- We situate AI rights within a broader project of cultural alignment, and consider pathways to implementation, objections, and open questions.

items.title: Permeating Boundaries of Expertise in Psychiatry: Integration of Patients as Contributors in the DSM Revision Periods.
items.abstract: Objectivity and patient-centered care represent twin commitments of psychiatry that existing diagnostic practices struggle to reconcile. This paper argues that integrating patients as experience-based experts (EBEs) into the American Psychiatric Association's DSM revision process advances both commitments simultaneously. Drawing on Thomas Gieryn's boundary-work framework, I examine how psychiatry's historically permeable disciplinary boundaries have enabled selective gatekeeping over knowledge production, generating epistemic injustices, particularly preemptive testimonial injustice and hermeneutical injustice, that undermine diagnostic validity and clinical outcomes. I first situate psychiatry's unique sociocultural position relative to somatic medicine, demonstrating why its phenomena are epistemically inaccessible without patient testimony. Further, I address well-established reservations surrounding patient integration, including concerns about intersubjective validity, taxonomic disruption, and tokenism, before proposing a structured integration model responsive to these hesitations. Leveraging Şerife Tekin's Multitudinous Self (MuSe) model and recent recommendations from the DSM's Structure and Dimensions Subcommittee, I outline how patient-EBEs can contribute structured phenomenological testimony and participatory review within formal revision committees. As Gieryn anticipated, I conclude that strategic patient integration does not erode psychiatric expertise but rather reveals that its boundaries were always more permeable than their gatekeepers have claimed.

items.title: ChatGPT is not bullshit, nor is it not not bullshit.
items.abstract: This paper intervenes in the debate over whether ChatGPT and other similar large language models (LLMs) are bullshit and answers that they are not. LLMs, however, don’t avoid being bullshitters in the way that humans do, i.e., by caring about the truth and avoiding deception. Rather, LLMs are not the kinds of things that can even count as bullshit. Attribut- ing the property of being a bullshitter to LLMs is a category mistake.

items.title: Fostering Ethical Dialogue through Philosophy with Children: Practice-Based Insights from Association Petit Philosophy Projects.
items.abstract: The present article examines the manner in which ethical dialogue and philosophical inquiry are integrated into education through a selection of European projects implemented by the Croatian non-governmental organisation Association Petit Philosophy (Mala filozofija). Utilising a qualitative, practice-based approach, the study analyses project materials, workshop designs, teaching manuals, implementation notes, and practitioner observations from initiatives such as ETHIKA, ETHOS, PEEC, ZOOM OUT, Young Minds, and PLATO's EU. The projects encompassed children and young people from early childhood to secondary education, in addition to teachers and educators in both formal and non-formal learning settings. The analysis identifies recurring pedagogical methods, including storytelling, Socratic questioning, role-play, film-based discussion, digital scenarios, and the community of inquiry model. The observed outcomes of these practices suggest that they support critical thinking, reasoning, empathy, perspective-taking, dialogical competence, ethical awareness, and civic engagement. In view of the fact that the extant data are of a qualitative nature and non-experimental in nature, it is imperative that the findings are interpreted as practice-based insights, rather than as statistically generalisable evidence. The article posits that philosophical dialogue has the potential to serve as a valuable framework for ethics and values education, and it calls for more systematic evaluation of such practices.

items.title: The Irreducible Dent: The Architectural Taxonomy of Violence, Harm, Trauma, and Resolution.
items.abstract: Contemporary clinical psychology and cultural discourse frequently conflate Violence, Harm, Trauma, and Growth, mapping them onto a deterministic, victim-centric pipeline: violence causes harm, harm produces trauma, and trauma demands growth. -/- This paper dismantles this linear fallacy. By re-examining these concepts through an architectural, etymological, and profoundly biological lens, we establish a new dialectic. We decouple the mechanics of friction from the persistence of time, revealing a matrix where trauma is stripped of its moral baggage to become simply the "irreducible dent" carried past the event horizon.

items.title: Having Seen So Little of You, I Believed Too Much: From Revealed Fragments to the Fabrication of Relational Rights: An Ethics of Non-Possessive Affective Response.
items.abstract: This paper begins from the fact that human beings can genuinely respond to revealed fragments of others: a beautiful face, an attractive gesture, an excellent performance, an impressive text, a public attitude, or repeatedly encountered online content. Such affective responses are neither false nor shallow. They may bring pleasure, admiration, consolation, familiarity, and enduring significance. Yet the reality of affective response does not justify claiming to know the other as a whole, imagining that a specific relationship has been established, or imposing expectations and obligations upon the other’s life. To analyze this transition, the paper introduces the concepts of the revealed fragment, fragmentary affective response, whole-person leap, relational imagination, and fabrication of relational rights. A revealed fragment is a socially accessible part of a person, such as appearance, speech, work, achievement, interview, social media post, vlog, or public attitude. Such fragments may genuinely come from the person, but they are not identical with the whole person. The whole-person leap occurs when one excessively determines another person’s character, morality, relational style, or private life on the basis of limited fragments. The relational imagination occurs when this partial judgment is extended into the belief that the person would understand, accept, or be specially compatible with oneself. The paper then argues that the most serious ethical error emerges when affective response and relational imagination become the fabrication of relational rights: the construction of expectations, obligations, or rights of intervention that have never been formed in an actual reciprocal relationship. A fan’s affection, emotional investment, financial support, or repeated exposure to a public figure may be real and meaningful, but these do not automatically generate rights over the other’s romantic life, privacy, creative direction, or self-disclosure. The truth of a feeling does not guarantee the legitimacy of a right. The paper further examines how fandom, influencer culture, and platform-based intimacy industries intensify this problem by organizing public fragments as pseudo-intimacy and monetizing the feeling of closeness. However, industrial responsibility does not justify fans’ fabricated relational rights; rather, it requires criticism of structures that induce relational misrecognition. In response, the paper proposes metacognition of projection and …

items.title: Apokalypse-Blindheit Reread: Toward an Acceleration that Has Earned its Name.
items.abstract: Günther Anders's 1956 Die Antiquiertheit des Menschen (vol. 1) is read almost everywhere as a closing diagnosis: human beings can make more than they can imagine and imagine more than they can feel, and that asymmetry, the Stufenbau, is structural and unbridgeable. I argue that the 1956 text carries two strata its reception has not reconciled. Alongside the structural Stufenbau there is a bridging stratum, present in Anders's chapter on the plasticity of feeling and the cultivation of moral imagination, and stated plainly in his 1959 instruction to the Hiroshima pilot Claude Eatherly that "your task consists in bridging the gap." This second stratum has been eclipsed by the shadow of the first. I lift it into view and formalize it as a dynamic-gap ethics. Every particular acceleration widens the gap, and it generates a proportionate, locally indexed obligation to close it. The only legitimate way to escape that obligation is not to accelerate; to accelerate while refusing it is the live performance of Apokalypse-Blindheit. From this ethics I derive a triad, we accelerate as mortals, for mortals, with the weight of mortals, and apply it to two 2024–2026 cases, the Stargate compute-energy commitment and Dario Amodei's closed-session admission at DealBook. I locate the position as a sister branch of Hans Jonas's Das Prinzip Verantwortung and distinguish it from Thaler, Issembert, Babich, Müller, and Schwarz.

items.title: Cognitive differences and ethical concerns in artificial intelligence in healthcare: a comparative text mining study of public and healthcare professional discussions.
items.abstract: This study aims to investigate the cognitive differences and ethical concerns regarding artificial intelligence in healthcare between the public and healthcare professionals and to provide empirical evidence for ethical governance and risk communication. A text mining approach was adopted to comparatively analyze Chinese public social media and professional medical forums. A total of 4,042 valid texts were included, comprising 2,088 from the public corpus and 1,954 from the healthcare professional corpus. SnowNLP sentiment analysis, the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic model, and co-word network analysis were applied to reconstruct and compare the structures of concern between the two groups. Both groups were dominated by positive sentiment toward artificial intelligence in healthcare, although healthcare professionals showed a higher positive tendency (75.2%) than the public (68.0%), while the public exhibited a higher degree of caution. LDA topic analysis and co-word network analysis showed that both groups focused heavily on the role positioning and replacement boundaries of artificial intelligence. However, their specific focal concerns differed significantly. Healthcare professionals placed greater emphasis on occupational impact and practice-related concerns, mainly involving clinical application, responsibility, and humanistic care. In contrast, the public focused more on technical conditions and risk perception, emphasizing practical uses in healthcare settings, the reliability of data and models, and issues of responsibility and risk. Although both the public and healthcare professionals hold relatively positive attitudes toward artificial intelligence in healthcare, their cognitive structures exhibit clear group differences. The subsequent ethical governance and advancement of artificial intelligence in healthcare require clarifying its functional boundaries while simultaneously addressing the practice-related concerns of healthcare professionals and the risk-related concerns of the public.

items.title: Dualismo catesiano, cognición fundada y LLMS: Idas y vueltas del pensamiento conceptual.
items.abstract: Este artículo examina el pensamiento conceptual frente al dualismo cartesiano y la teoría de la Cognición Situada de Lawrence Barsalou, la cual postula que la cognición surge de interacciones complejas entre el cerebro, el cuerpo y el entorno. A partir de un estudio empírico de 2025 que compara representaciones conceptuales entre humanos y Modelos Grandes de Lenguaje (LLMs), se analiza si la inteligencia artificial requiere de una cognición fundada. Los resultados muestran que los LLMs se alinean con los humanos en dominios abstractos y emocionales, pero divergen significativamente en los dominios sensoriales y motores. Se concluye que, si bien la multimodalidad reduce esta brecha, la ausencia de factores biológicos, propioceptivos y sociales en la IA mantiene abierta la incógnita sobre la equivalencia de sus procesos cognitivos.
