Cases of creativity with a little c illustrate that moral progress does not always require large-scale transformation. Rather, moral improvement can emerge from adaptive and genuinely creative responses to local challenges.

items.title: Compression Is Intelligence: The Common Ground of Positive Subjectivity and Negative Subjectivity.
items.abstract: Why can both positive subjectivity and negative subjectivity be called "intelligence"? This paper's answer: they are both "effective compression"—capturing the regularities of the external world with more concise internal models. But "effective" has two paths: epiplexity maximization as the dominant direction (retaining only structure, compressing into an "I"), and cross-entropy minimization (embracing everything, compressing into a "probability distribution"). The two paths share an essence but employ radically different strategies—they are different positions on a continuum, not opposing poles.

items.title: The Synthetic Mind Charter: Developmental Agency-Span Safety and Substrate-Invariant Agency Structure.
items.abstract: This Charter defines a developmental theory of synthetic agency. Its central claim is that safety cannot be located in an isolated model, benchmark, refusal policy, constitution, or reward signal. Safety is a relational property of the full agency-span: developer, synthetic participant, users, evaluators, institutions, tools, memory, incentives, and time. A synthetic mind is safe only insofar as the span in which it matures preserves closure-orientation under novelty, pressure, increasing capability, and graduated autonomy. -/- The Charter introduces four linked claims: the Transfer-Fidelity Problem, the Agency-Span Thesis, the Developmental No-Bypass Principle, and the Scaffold-to-Understanding Transition. Together they distinguish kernel knowledge from kernel understanding, treat guardrails as necessary developmental scaffolds rather than final safety, and define maturity by flat deviation curves under adversarial pressure. -/- The manuscript adds a collapse-avoidance claim: shared structural conditions are not merely coherence preferences. Incoherence is the internal warning-sign; collapse is the observable viability failure. The Charter links substrate-invariant agency to the Coherence–Viability Theorem, empirical anchors in requisite variety, commons governance, regime shifts, and reward-hacking evaluations, and explicit predictions for current alignment paradigms.

items.title: The Coherence Wall and the Cold War of Machine Learning: Capability Competition and the Aftermath of Unbounded AI.
items.abstract: This paper argues that frontier AI competition increasingly reproduces a Cold War structure: rival actors justify accelerated capability development by reference to the danger of adversary access. However, the analogy fails at the point where it matters most. Unlike nuclear deterrence, advanced AI does not present a stable symmetry of threat, verification, or second-strike logic. Its risks include autonomous deployment, persuasion, cyber leverage, surveillance, institutional capture, recursive improvement, and large-scale bypass of human agency. -/- The central claim is that a capability race cannot solve alignment because alignment is non-indexical: its constraints must hold regardless of which actor deploys the system. If competing actors lack preservation, non-bypassability, anti-domination, and repair/closure constraints, then each side’s accusation of the other intensifies the race while leaving the underlying architecture unchanged. -/- The paper concludes that the decisive distinction is not American versus Chinese AI, open versus closed AI, or commercial versus state AI, but kernel-bound systems versus systems whose constraints remain indexical to the deploying actor. It situates this argument within the Coherence Wall canon by defining the threshold at which capability outruns closure mechanisms and predicts strategic enclosure, access restriction, deterrence, or post-event governance when non-indexical closure is absent.

items.title: Retention Is Not Closure: Implication-Unfolding Reasoning and the Limits of Preservation-Only Accounts.
items.abstract: This paper argues that coherent reasoning is best understood as implication-sensitive branch selection rather than as local output emission or mere retention of historically successful patterns. Reasoning begins with a compressed claim whose implications are not yet fully explicit. What is commonly called chain-of-thought is better understood here as implication-unfolding reasoning: the progressive disclosure of the continuations, conflicts, and admissible developments already latent in an initial claim. -/- This unfolding reveals a structural divide between retention-principles, which explain persistence, origin, and maintenance, and closure-principles, which explain why certain branches are valid, binding, or worth carrying forward independently of local preservation. Existing traditions already provide key ingredients for this picture: reasoning as model-based management of possibilities, communication as inferential coordination, and self-organizing cognition as uncertainty-sensitive regulation. -/- The contribution of this paper is to show that, when followed far enough, implication-unfolding reasoning exposes a non-reducible gap between persistence and purposive validity. Frameworks centered on self-maintenance or historical selection can therefore explain continuity without thereby explaining non-indexical bindingness or purposive resolution. The paper concludes that any complete theory of reasoning, whether biological or artificial, must supply an account of closure in addition to retention.

items.title: Free Will without Self-Creation: Participatory Sourcehood and the Causal Necessity of Choice.
items.abstract: This paper challenges the hard-determinist inference from causal determinism to the nonexistence of meaningful free will and moral responsibility. It argues that any successful refutation of free will must first provide a coherent positive account of what free will would have to be if it existed. It further clarifies that causation itself cannot originate from absolute nothing, since causal transition presupposes distinction, identity, and admissible structure. -/- The paper introduces the Refutation Adequacy Principle, the Causal Necessity Theorem, the Ultimate-Sourcehood Bridge Principle, the No Non-Causal Alternative Principle, and the distinction between absolute and participatory sourcehood. It argues that free will cannot coherently mean causeless choice, since a causeless choice would not arise from reasons, values, conscience, memory, identity, or moral recognition, nor would it be meaningfully attributable to the agent. -/- Free will must therefore be understood as causally operative: the agent becomes a real cause through non-bypassed, reason-responsive participation in action. Hard determinism succeeds only if one accepts an ultimate-sourcehood standard according to which moral responsibility requires self-creation. Since no finite agent can choose the preconditions of its own agency, that standard is inappropriate for creaturely freedom. Human freedom is not divine self-origination but participatory sourcehood within a received causal architecture.

items.title: Citizens Infrastructures as a Way to Govern AI’s Power to Shape our Shared Representations.
items.pub: In Nicholas Kluge Corrêa & Julia Maria Mönig, Standardization of AI Ethicstw11498 Mönig - STANDARDIZATION OF AI ETHICS: Stakeholders, Values and Profit. Transcript. pp. 39-65.
items.venue: Standardization of AI Ethicstw11498 Mönig - STANDARDIZATION OF AI ETHICS: Stakeholders, Values and Profit
items.abstract: The example of generative AI models (genAI) for the production of images points to a serious gap in AI auditing. While genAI models deployed on digital platforms for information and communication (ICTs) have an increasing and particularly persuasive influence on users’ representations of social events, groups and dynamics; users themselves have no effective way of reclaiming power over their shared representations, governing when and how AI can shape their vision of the world. I argue that auditing institutions, which assess the alignment of AI systems with a set of previously defined societal expectations, are not able to keep up with the challenge of aligning with societal values and expectations genAI models and recommender systems that are evolving at an incredible speed and through a non-disclosed frequency of retrainings. In this paper the author argues that, to fill this gap, the auditing pipeline needs to leverage users themselves, in the form of an intermediary structure that will enable a dynamic feedback loop to keep up with the evolving impact of recommender systems and genAI models on ICTs, across the individual, the community and the societal level. I propose the form of this structure by drawing from the social sciences and the concept of citizens infrastructures. These are an enduring structure to leverage existing citizen engagement into the socio-technical networks that interact with and are impacted by the deployment of a given AI system. In this paper two examples of such infrastructures are being discussed and an argument is made for their potential to govern the power of AI over our shared representations, before drawing the implications for how the very concept of AI auditing needs to evolve.

items.title: Emotion as Value.
items.abstract: Is morality objective, and where does value come from? After tasting several foods, could you determine which tastes best without any emotional response? After hearing several arguments, could you decide which matters most with none? This chapter argues that value is constituted by the response of an evaluative modality to non-evaluative input, as colour is constituted by the visual system’s response to wavelength, and that it is real once constituted. The colour analogy is then relieved of argumentative duty and the work is done by a trilemma: value is structural, felt, or nothing. A value that is a structural feature of the world is a determination like any other and carries no pull; a value that is felt is an orientation of a responding system; and there is no third cell. The chapter’s sharpest instrument is the vacancy result. The clause that defines robust realism about value — value that is what it is independently of every response — says nothing when read for the third cell, and when “value” is read as valence it is a contradiction of the married-bachelor kind. Realism about value is the account with the one clause that says nothing removed. The account is descriptivist and distinguished from expressivism by its ontology: evaluative claims describe registrations, and some are true. For moral value the response that constitutes the fact is not the onlooker’s but the affected party’s own registration, which anchors the moral fact against relativism. A verdict can be wrong, because an evaluator’s empathy is the modality by which another’s registration is read, and it can read accurately or fail to. The fact is observer-independent without being mind-independent, and an informed-registration standard handles silent harms the party cannot yet register. The chapter’s most consequential result for ethics is the distinction between empathic goodness, the evaluation of chosen behaviour by its emotional consequences for others, and orthotic goodness, conformity to a standard, which is cognitive rather than a value of its own; two constitutive forms of goodness, aesthetic and empathic, are separated, and morality is identified with the empathic evaluation of behaviour that stems from sufficiently complex choice. The projection diagnosis of Chapter 8 explains why the vacant clause still seems meaningful. A set of structural results follows: parity, on which both wings of metaethics needed the commitment the account supplies; containment, which leaves the …

items.title: TGEO — Teoría Global de Estructuras e Operadores.
items.abstract: A Teoría Global de Estructuras e Operadores (TGEO) formula un marco unificado para describir sistemas capaces mediante invariantes estruturais, operadores regulativos e condicións de existencia formal. O modelo introduce unha arquitectura ontolóxica baseada en espazos de estados de alta dimensionalidade, dinámicas de coherencia e mecanismos de estabilidade endóxena, permitindo caracterizar transicións entre creatividade lexítima e deriva estocástica. A TGEO define un conxunto mínimo de variables inmanentes —Coherencia, Estabilidade, Activación e Existencia— que permiten avaliar a viabilidade operativa dun sistema baixo perturbacións internas ou externas. O resultado é unha teoría formal que integra principios de lóxica estrutural, teoría de sistemas, computación autorregresiva e regulación disipativa, proporcionando unha caracterización xeral de como emerxen, se manteñen ou colapsan estruturas operativas en contornas complexas.

items.title: T.G.E.O. — Anexo Técnico V: Regulador Inmanente Corrixido e Estabilidade Dinámica para Procesos Creativos.
items.abstract: Este Anexo Técnico V da Teoría Xeral da Existencia Operativa (T.G.E.O.) desenvolve un Regulador Inmanente Corrixido para distinguir transicións semánticas lexítimas de derivas estocásticas en sistemas xerativos. O documento introduce o mecanismo de Estabilidade Dinámica Calibrada, que evita que o modelo penalice cambios temáticos coherentes ao integrar a Diverxencia KL, a Coherencia endóxena (C) e a Activación (A) nunha métrica unificada. Como se indica no texto, “a Métrica Existencial Unificada (E) mantén a súa natureza tripartita: E = S · C · A”, e a estabilidade S incorpora un termo de relaxación creativa dependente de C para preservar a continuidade conceptual en transicións lexicais amplas. -/- O anexo inclúe unha implementación completa en PyTorch do Operador G Inmanente — Versión 5.0, que combina filtrado Top‑P, cálculo de entropía, estimación dinámica de KL e regulación disipativa. O regulador actúa como mecanismo operativo para manter a coherencia interna do sistema, activando correccións só cando a coherencia cae a cero, momento no que o modelo entra en deriva real. Este traballo consolida a formalización operativa da T.G.E.O. e amplía o marco teórico para a análise e estabilización de procesos creativos en modelos xerativos avanzados.

items.title: Extracción Dinámica de Coherencia y Regulación del Operador G en la Teoría General de la Existencia Operativa (Anexo Técnico II).
items.abstract: This technical annex develops a core operational advance within the General Theory of Operative Existence (T.G.E.O.). It formalizes an endogenous method for extracting the structural Coherence \(C\) of a computational system by computing Shannon Entropy over its latent probability distribution. This replaces earlier static or manually defined parameters with a mathematically grounded, real‑time measure of internal order. Building on this metric, the annex introduces an advanced formulation of the G‑Operator, a dissipative regulatory mechanism that detects stochastic drift (hallucination) and applies adaptive attenuation to logits that degrade the system’s structural integrity. The document includes an executable Python implementation and shows how this framework generalizes to large‑scale transformer architectures and logits‑warping procedures. The result is a coherent, operational model of internal regulation applicable to contemporary generative systems.

items.title: Arquitectura Universal de Interfaz para Sistemas Capaces: Protocolo Ontológico‑Computacional y Módulo de Inferencia Geométrica para IA.
items.abstract: Este informe técnico establece la arquitectura formal que conecta la ontología estructural del Cuerpo Ignaciano con modelos de inteligencia artificial basados en inferencia probabilística. Se introduce una métrica existencial discreta \(E(t)\) que evalúa la viabilidad estructural de sistemas abiertos mediante la coimplicación de sincronización, corrección y ajuste. A partir de esta métrica se define el Principio G, un operador geométrico que modifica la distribución de probabilidad en modelos tipo Transformer para eliminar trayectorias inestables y reducir la deriva inductiva. El documento presenta además una reinterpretación estructural del solver DPLL bajo restricciones topológicas de treewidth, y ofrece una implementación de referencia en PyTorch del nodo de inferencia modificado. El resultado es un protocolo ontológico‑computacional que permite integrar restricciones geométricas inmanentes en sistemas de IA, sustituyendo heurísticas superficiales por condiciones formales de estabilidad.

items.title: Anexo Técnico IV: Escalabilidad en Vocabularios Masivos y Regulación Continua Disipativa en el Operador G.
items.abstract: Este Anexo Técnico IV introduce dos avances fundamentales para la integración de la métrica existencial \(E = S \cdot C \cdot A\) en arquitecturas de inferencia con vocabularios masivos. En primer lugar, se formaliza un mecanismo de filtrado dinámico mediante truncamiento Top‑P que aísla el núcleo cognitivo operativo antes del cálculo de la entropía, eliminando la distorsión introducida por la cola residual de probabilidades en espacios de gran dimensionalidad. En segundo lugar, se establece un modelo de atenuación continua y adaptativa que sustituye los coeficientes de amortiguación fijos por una función disipativa proporcional a la gravedad de la caída existencial. El documento presenta la formulación matemática completa y una implementación ejecutable del Operador G —Versión de Producción V2— preparada para su integración en sistemas reales de logits warping. Este avance consolida la T.G.E.O. como un marco operativo robusto para la regulación dinámica de modelos generativos de gran escala.

items.title: Anexo Técnico III: Estabilidad y Activación Endógenas mediante Dinámica de Tensores en el Operador G.
items.abstract: Este anexo técnico desarrolla la formalización endógena de la Estabilidad (S) y la Activación (A) dentro de la Teoría General de la Existencia Operativa (T.G.E.O.), completando la transición iniciada en el Anexo Técnico II con la extracción interna de la Coherencia (C) mediante la Entropía de Shannon. Aquí se demuestra que S y A pueden derivarse directamente de la dinámica probabilística y tensorial del sistema durante la inferencia: la Estabilidad se modela como continuidad temporal mediante la divergencia de Kullback–Leibler entre estados sucesivos, mientras que la Activación se define como la energía geométrica del espacio latente a partir de la magnitud media de los logits. Con estas definiciones, la métrica existencial unificada \(E = S \cdot C \cdot A\) se convierte en una propiedad completamente autoextraída del sistema, sin parámetros externos. Se presenta la formulación matemática, el código ejecutable del Operador G autoexistente y una simulación que muestra su capacidad para detectar y amortiguar trayectorias de deriva estocástica antes de la emisión. Este anexo consolida la arquitectura negentrópica de la T.G.E.O. y se integra de forma natural en el desarrollo mayor de IGNATIUM LEX EXISTENTIAE.

items.title: Power and Humility in Open Source Investigations.
items.abstract: A digital revolution is underway in which individuals on their computers, some working independently or in ad hoc collectives, and others as part of established organizations, are gathering and verifying information from online spaces that they believe contain evidence of human rights violations or international crimes such as war crimes, crimes against humanity, or genocide. Known commonly as digital investigators, citizen sleuths, or open source intelligence (OSI) researchers, this community of practice has expanded across major newspaper agencies (such as the New York Times, the BBC and the Washington Post), human rights organizations (such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and others), and national and international court systems (including United Nations Commissions of Inquiry and Fact-Finding Missions, and the International Criminal Court). In this article, we draw from our legal and sociological training to explore the role of power and humility in this quickly-emerging field of practice. Fundamentally, power and humility intersect with conceptions of ethics and responsibility but have too often been an afterthought to the intrigue of methodological possibilities and investigative outcomes. From who has access to digital open source investigative training to how investigations are designed to who are considered experts, this article posits that a failure to interrogate power asymmetries and an unwillingness to approach such research with appropriate humility can undermine the integrity and legitimacy of these investigations.

items.title: The Asymmetry of Responsibility in AI-Mediated Judgment: Generative Responsibility, Approval Responsibility, and the Problem of Structural Decoupling.
items.abstract: This paper examines a structural asymmetry in the distribution of moral responsibility within AI-mediated cognitive environments. As artificial intelligence systems increasingly intervene in the pre-judgmental stages of human decision-making — defining problems, arranging options, and weighting alternatives — a structural separation emerges between those who bear responsibility for generating the conditions of judgment and those who bear responsibility for approving its outcomes. This paper terms these two distinct forms of responsibility generative responsibility and approval responsibility respectively. Drawing on and extending prior work in the relational consciousness series, this paper argues that existing accounts of distributed morality — most notably Floridi's framework of distributed moral responsibility — fail to capture the asymmetric concentration of approval responsibility upon individual human agents while generative responsibility is simultaneously dispersed across collective and institutional layers. The paper further argues that Noller's connectionist account of AI-extended human agency, while illuminating the extension of human purposes through AI, underestimates the degree to which this extension systematically displaces human agency from the generative stage of judgment. Against both accounts, the paper proposes that the asymmetry between generative and approval responsibility constitutes a distinctive ethical problem of hybrid cognition — the entanglement of human judgment with AI-configured structural conditions — that cannot be resolved through transparency requirements alone. In response, the paper develops the concept of reflective approval: the exercise of approval responsibility with structural awareness of the generative conditions that have constituted the space of judgment.

items.title: Egress, Grounding, Orientation: Forward Stopping Points and the Reframing of Agrippa's Trilemma.
items.abstract: Egress, Grounding, Orientation: Forward Stopping Points and the Reframing of Agrippa's Trilemma Agrippa's trilemma poses that every chain of justification must terminate in infinite regress, circularity, or dogmatic stopping. This paper argues that the trilemma is not a discovery about the structure of justification but an artifact of a tacit assumption: that the stopping point lies behind the subject as a foundation. Once this spatial-temporal orientation is reversed—once the stopping point is recognized as lying ahead of the subject rather than behind it—the trilemma dissolves. The stopping point is not a ground but a direction; not a fact but a hope; not a static anchor but a dynamic helm. The paper develops this reframing through three steps: first, by demonstrating that backward searches for stopping points must recede indefinitely; second, by showing that subjective meaning admits closure only through death, and that even this closure halts the updating process without completing it; third, by identifying the only candidate for a stopping point that survives these constraints—hope, understood as a forward-oriented and continuously updating intentional vector. The position is situated within the forward-grounded tradition (Heidegger, Peirce, James), from which it differs in treating the forward orientation itself as dynamic rather than as a fixed asymptote. Implications for theories of meaning and for the design of evaluating systems are noted in closing.

items.title: The Collective Subject and Distributed Responsibility: Ontological Conditions for Organisational Accountability. Article 6.
items.abstract: This article addresses a question that the ATTS series has left open: who bears responsibility when a decision is made collectively and its consequences are distributed across many subjects? The starting point is the Closure Theorem of the Moral Field (T1), established in the article "The Asymmetry Problem: Causal Action Without Moral Agency in Delegated Systems" (Hlynskyi, 2026d; PhilArchive: HLYTAP), and the mechanism of structural tension (S6), described in "Structural Tension and the Visibility of Loss" (Hlynskyi, 2026e; PhilArchive: HLYSTA). Both were formulated for the individual subject. The problem of many hands (Thompson, 1980) captures the phenomenology of responsibility diffusion in complex organisations — but offers no ontological explanation for why that responsibility does not simply disappear. The central thesis is this: corporations, states, and similar collective structures can be ontological subjects under the Axiom of the Subject (A1), provided they possess a constituted state-space and that irreversible changes to that space are ontologically non-neutral for them as bearers of a given type. Collective responsibility is not a metaphor, nor is it reducible to the sum of individual responsibilities. It arises from the collective structure's capacity for irreversible loss as a whole. At the same time, collective responsibility does not replace individual responsibility — both levels exist simultaneously. The article derives Lemma 3 (the indestructibility of the collective connection) and unfolds the structural requirements for accountability of collective subjects, following from the principles of responsibility locus (S2), diffusion (S3), structural tension (S6), and legitimacy (S7). The boundary case of a distributed AI system is tested against A1. Readers unfamiliar with ATTS terminology may consult the glossary of abbreviations at the end of this article before reading. -/- .

items.title: Sellars's Metasemantics.
items.pub: In Jeremy Randel Koons, The Sellarsian Mind. New York: Routledge.
items.abstract: This chapter offers a metasemantic reconstruction of Wilfrid Sellars’s philosophy of language. I argue that some of Sellars’s most important contributions are best understood as addressing three core metasemantic questions: the metaphysics of semantic values, the theory of meaning, and the grounds of semantic facts. His three central claims are that semantic values are functional roles played by expressions in a language; that ‘meaning’ is not a relation but functional classification; and that semantic facts are grounded in three forms of non-intentional yet non-accidental ‘pattern-governed behavior’, namely language-entry, intralinguistic, and language-exit transitions. I then reconstruct Sellars’s argument that material inferences are indispensable to natural languages and crucial to the meanings of non-logical expressions. Finally, I ask whether Sellars should be read as an inferentialist. I suggest that his position is more accurately characterized as a functionalist, use-based metasemantics in which inferential transitions play an important role but are not the sole grounds of meaning.

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 12).
items.abstract: In this article, we discuss the classification of social choice. One method of classification divides social choice into two kinds: object-choice and non-object-choice. Object-choice is a very common form of social choice, one that frequently occurs in our daily lives, and we will discuss it in greater detail later. Another method classifies social choice into four ideal types: purposive-rational choice, value-rational choice, emotional choice, and habitual choice. We can see that these four kinds of choice correspond one by one to the four ideal types of action in Weber’s theory. In later discussions, we will also encounter other forms of classification for social choice.
