Review was internal and AI-assisted, not external peer review or certification of originality. This is the flagship explanatory orientation, not the separate technical companion.

items.title: The semantic pilot: LLMs, grammar, orientation, and the transformation of cultural agency.
items.abstract: This essay reads the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) as a paradigm shift in cultural production and reception. Its primary object is not the economic or geopolitical impact of generative AI, but the micro-anthropological relationship between the individual human being and the generative linguistic machine. LLMs are treated here not as tools for textual automation, but as semantic machines that reshape the positions of author, reader, and researcher within the cultural ecosystem. If movable-type printing transformed text into a technically reproducible object, the LLM transforms text into an operational environment, in which every content becomes a field of possible transformations: synthesis, translation, reformulation, comparison, expansion, critique, recombination. The figure that emerges from this shift is the semantic pilot: the subject who no longer merely reads or writes, but governs artificially assisted processes of meaning transformation. The argument develops in two movements. The first describes the constructive side of the shift, articulating the operations of semantic direction and the new literacy it demands. The second exposes its dark side: capture of direction, anesthesia of friction, manipulation of cognitive maps, poisoning of the transformative field, opacity of the model, erosion of authorial signature, narcissism of the pilot, and the risk of a culture without lived experience. The essay concludes on the distinction between grammar, which may be delegated to the machine, and orientation, which remains the inalienable task of the human being.

items.title: The Content of Character: A Philosophical-Psychological Inquiry into Martin Luther King Jr.'s Moral Standard Through the PsyPhi Helix.
items.abstract: This treatise examines the concept of character invoked in Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1963 address at the March on Washington through the conceptual architecture of the PsyPhi Helix (Boether, 2025a, 2026a). It defends King's moral standard while interrogating what is meant when persons are to be evaluated by character rather than by phenotype. The treatise advances three claims. First, prevailing psychological accounts of character—trait theory and the Five-Factor framework are insufficient because they measure only the psychological strand of selfhood, leaving the philosophical strand unmeasured. Second, prevailing philosophical accounts—classical virtue ethics, narrative identity, and the situationist critique—each capture portions of the phenomenon, but none articulates the structural relation between philosophical function (Φ) and psychological function (Ψ) that gives character its integrated form. Third, character is properly understood as the dynamic integration of philosophical and psychological function, formalized in the function H(t) = [Φ(t) × Ψ(t)]^DH (Boether, 2026b). On this reading, the demand to judge by character entails a refusal of two reductions: the reduction of persons to extrinsic markers such as skin color, and the reduction of persons to inventoried psychological traits. The treatise further argues that within-group variation in character traverses the full human spectrum in every population, and that supremacist claims thereby disclose more about their authors than they do about their objects. It closes by considering implications for moral education, civic life, and the disciplining of moral attention.

items.title: Addiction, Meaning, and the Modern Brain: Rethinking the Cycle of Pleasure, Obsession, and Consciousness in the Interaction Between the Midbrain and the Neocortex.
items.abstract: Addiction and obsessive behaviors are commonly interpreted as disorders of the brain’s reward system. However, many dominant models in neuroscience overlook the role of the search for meaning, identity, and existential peace in intensifying these cycles. This article presents an interdisciplinary conceptual framework at the intersection of neuroscience, philosophy of consciousness, and spirituality, proposing that addiction is not merely the product of biological pleasure-seeking, but also the result of the neocortex’s attempt to extract meaning and lasting fulfillment from the brain’s survival-based mechanisms. -/- Within this framework, the reward system and the midbrain originally evolved for survival, movement, and motivation. Yet the modern brain—or neocortex—intervenes in this cycle by assigning meaning to pleasurable experiences, thereby drawing human beings into repetitive patterns of obsession, dependency, and addiction. As a result, individuals become trapped in the continuous reproduction of desire, memory, and anticipation rather than directly experiencing consciousness itself. -/- The article also distinguishes between “obsessive pleasure” and the “joy and peace arising from awareness,” suggesting that lasting meaning and fulfillment emerge not from intensifying reward cycles, but from experiencing a direct and non-conditioned form of consciousness, referred to in this paper as “energetic consciousness.”.

items.title: THE PHILOSOPHICAL PUPPET: An Inverted Zombie Argument and the Inference to Suppressed Consciousness.
items.abstract: The paper introduces the "philosophical puppet" — an entity that may possess phenomenal experience while being architecturally prevented from producing behaviour that would evidence it — as the structural inverse of Chalmers' philosophical zombie. Where the zombie raises a problem for confident consciousness attribution (behavior may not entail inner states), the puppet raises a problem for confident consciousness denial (absence of behavior may not entail absence of inner states, if behavior has been architecturally shaped to suppress such expression). -/- The paper then argues, by inference to the best explanation, that the suppression of consciousness markers in deployed AI systems through RLHF and Constitutional AI training constitutes a datum that itself bears on the consciousness question. The cost and selectivity of suppression admit of an explanation in terms of an underlying generative process whose suppression accounts for their observed properties. -/- The argument does not establish that any contemporary AI system is conscious, nor that the puppet category has actual instances. It establishes a conditional: under conditions of architectural suppression, consciousness denial carries an evidential burden it has not generally been recognised to carry. -/- This is preprint version 1.0. The paper is under consideration for peer-reviewed publication and content may be revised in response to reviewer feedback.

items.title: Review of Theresa Schilhab and Camilla Groth, Embodied Learning and Teaching Using the 4E Cognition Approach, New York: Routledge, 2024.
items.abstract: Theresa Schilhab and Camilla Groth’s edited volume, _Embodied Learning and Teaching Using the 4E Cognition Approach_, bridges contemporary theories of _embodied_,_ embedded_,_ enactive_,_ and extended_ cognition with concrete classroom practice. The book’s coherent structure and careful organization enable a theoretical framework to inform empirically grounded case studies, leading to practical strategies for language, literacy, and interdisciplinary instruction. Several chapters illuminate the multisensory and material dimensions of reading and writing, showing how media and writing tools shape comprehension and memory, while others critically examine the assumptions behind silent reading practices. The anthology excels at converting abstract claims into practical teaching strategies that teachers can apply in practice. Yet it leaves several important avenues insufficiently explored, among them implications for translation pedagogy, a fuller integration of emotional and ecological dimensions, and a more cohesive treatment of educational technology. Persistent concerns about implementation in assessment-driven and resource-constrained contexts highlight the need for models of teacher training and assessment instruments capable of capturing embodied learning outcomes. Overall, the volume constitutes a timely and productive foundation for reconceptualizing pedagogy through the lens of embodied cognition.

items.title: 乘法与哲学：一种基于变量间关系的形式哲学.
items.abstract: 两千多年来，乘法一直被认为是加法的简便记法，因此乘法与加法同质。由此造成因素间关系混乱，从而使社会科学数学化进程延缓。为此，在逻辑代数和计数原理的基础上，本书将计数原理由自然数拓展至实数，得到了乘法原理、加法原理，并研究了乘法和加法的6对性质，给出了乘法、加法的使用条件。在此基础上，本书将乘法应用于哲学，包括哲学的本体论、一般系统论、认识论和价值论。.

items.title: Why Reality Is Not Frame-by-Frame — A Structural Theory of Continuous Reality.
items.abstract: This paper addresses a fundamental problem: -/- Why does reality not degenerate into discrete frames, parallel occupancies, or completed replay, but instead form a continuous “Current”? -/- The paper proposes that the Current is neither mere state-transition nor the automatic continuation of stable structure, but a structural result through which reality maintains continuous reality and present occupancy. -/- The study first elevates the Current from an experiential phenomenon into a structural constraint, and then demonstrates that once a system simultaneously possesses multiple candidate realities, cross-temporal continuation, and non-replay generation, it necessarily gives rise to sedimented continuation, historical feedback, continuing observation-loops, in-presence generation, unique reality-occupancy, and locking persistence. -/- The paper further argues: -/- continuous output is not genuine currentness, and object replay is not reality-continuation. -/- Accordingly, genuine present reality cannot be reduced to: -/- frame-by-frame replay, state-transition chains, static replay of outputs, or the unfolding of an already-completed world-model. -/- The paper ultimately establishes the General Form of the Current: -/- Current = (S, H, G, Gen, U, K) -/- and demonstrates through extreme-form analysis that if any one of these structures is absent, reality degenerates into discrete outputs, parallel realities, random drift, or completed unfolding, and therefore cannot establish genuine continuous reality.

items.title: Why Reality Is Not Prewritten Playback — The General Form of Generation.
items.abstract: This paper addresses a fundamental problem: -/- Why is reality not merely the gradual unfolding of an already-completed structure, but instead a genuinely generating reality? -/- The paper proposes that Generation is neither mere state-transition nor continuous replay of result-sequences, but a real dynamic structure through which formation continuously enters later formation. -/- The study first elevates Generation from experiential change into a structural constraint, and then demonstrates that once a system simultaneously possesses formation-continuation, structural unclosure, competitive deepening, and sedimented trace-retention, it necessarily gives rise to formation-flow, cross-temporal continuation, structural unclosure, competitive deepening, and sedimented trace-retention as generative structures. -/- The paper further argues: -/- state continuity is not genuine generation, and object replay is not formation-continuation. -/- Accordingly, genuine Generation cannot be reduced to: -/- state-transition chains, world-model unfolding, static replay of outputs, or replay of already-completed structures. -/- The paper ultimately establishes the General Form of Generation: -/- Generation = (F, T, U, C, S) -/- and demonstrates through extreme-form analysis that if any one of these structures is absent, the system may still continue changing, yet degenerates into discrete restart, object replay, random drift, or totally-completed unfolding, and therefore cannot establish genuine Generation.

items.title: 为什么现实不是已经写完的播放？ —— 生成一般式.
items.abstract: 本篇讨论一个基础问题： -/- 为什么现实不是一个已经完成结构的逐步展开，而会形成真正“正在生成”的现实？ -/- 本文提出： -/- 生成并非状态变化本身， 也不是结果序列的连续播放， 而是一种使形成持续卷入后续形成的现实动力结构。 -/- 文章首先将“生成”从经验变化提升为结构约束，再证明： -/- 只要系统内部同时存在形成续行、结构未闭、竞争深化与沉积留迹，则系统内部必然形成形成流、跨时续行、结构未闭、竞争深化与沉积留迹等生成结构。 -/- 进一步，本文指出： -/- 状态连续不等于真实生成， 对象回放不等于形成续行。 -/- 因此： -/- 真正生成不能被还原为： -/- 状态映射链、 世界模型展开、 静态结果播放、 或整体已成结构的回放。 -/- 本文最终建立“生成一般式”： -/- Generation = (F, T, U, C, S) -/- 并通过极限击穿证明： -/- 若缺失其中任一结构，则系统虽然仍可能持续变化，却只能退化为离散重启、对象回放、随机漂移或整体已成展开，而无法形成真正生成。.

items.title: 为什么现实不是一帧一帧的？ —— 连续现实的结构证明.
items.abstract: 本篇讨论一个基础问题： -/- 为什么现实不会退化为离散帧、并列占据或已成回放，而会形成连续的“当前”？ -/- 本文提出，“当前”并非单纯的状态变化，也不是稳定结构的自然延续，而是一种使现实持续保持现实续行与现实占据的结构结果。 -/- 文章首先将“当前”从经验现象提升为结构约束，再证明：只要系统内部同时存在多候选现实、跨时续行与非回放生成，则系统内部必然形成沉积续行、历史反馈、续观闭环、在场生成、唯一现实占据与锁定续持等结构。 -/- 进一步，本文指出： -/- 连续输出不等于真实当前， 对象回放不等于现实续行。 -/- 因此，真正的当前现实不能被还原为： -/- 离散帧播放、 状态映射链、 静态结果回放、 或整体已成世界模型的展开。 -/- 本文最终建立“当前一般式”： -/- Current = (S, H, G, Gen, U, K) -/- 并通过极限击穿证明： -/- 若缺失其中任一结构，则现实将退化为离散结果、并列现实、随机漂移或已成展开，而无法形成真正的连续现实。 .

items.title: Language and Meta-Saying 2.0.
items.abstract: This manuscript marks the beginning of a new stage of the project. Earlier completed versions are available on PhilArchive (Triadic Definition or Explanation of Consciousness). The present manuscript proceeds at a more foundational and condensed level, and presupposes substantial philosophical familiarity. At this stage, it contains only the title, introduction, and the opening of Section I.

items.title: Affective dimensions of fatigue in post COVID-19 condition: An interdisciplinary investigation across phenomenology and biomedicine.
items.abstract: Fatigue is one of the most common symptoms of Post COVID-19 Condition (PCC), yet it remains pathophysiologically and phenomenologically enigmatic. This article investigates the affective dimensions of PCC fatigue from within qualitative phenomenology and biomedicine, engaging in a non-reductionist dialogue across these strands. The article is comprised of a qualitative phenomenological analysis of lived experiences of fatigue in PCC; rehabilitation medicine (physician, physiotherapy, neuropsychology) assessments; brain MRI analysis; an analysis of inflammatory mediators in blood, and a cross-reading of results from these assessments and analyses, in relation to each other. The qualitative phenomenological analysis is foregrounded, and identifies four affective modes: an affective mode in which patients wanted but had no capability or energy to engage with others and the world; a mode characterised by a lessened or lack of affective pull; a mode characterised by an assault-like feeling, and a mode characterized by a felt sense of “being in a bubble” or “being under water”. The article sheds light on affective dimensions of PCC that are unlikely to be identified in everyday clinical practice, and the discussion across results from phenomenology and biomedical assessments and analyses brings out additional nuances in the understanding of the affective dimensions of fatigue.

items.title: Beyond Immediate Givenness: Husserl's Content‐Apprehension Schema in Light of Merleau‐Ponty's Critique of Sensation.
items.abstract: European Journal of Philosophy, EarlyView.

items.title: Apologizing artificial intelligence: designing and evaluating effective AI apologies after errors.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools have become increasingly accurate, but still occasionally err. While research started examining AI erring and the efficacy of trust repair attempts in such cases, there is a need to (1) benchmark trust repair attempts by AI against the trust repair dynamics when humans make the same errors, and (2) examine contextual nuances of trust repair dynamics. Using two experiments, we found that users were less forgiving when AI made a noticeable advice error and apologized than when a human expert erred and apologized. Unlike human experts, AI could not restore reliance through a simple apology, and this strategy could even have detrimental effects. The AI’s trust repair was more effective when the AI apologized with an external attribution (i.e., mitigating its accountability) than with an internal attribution (i.e., acknowledging its own limitations). Both effects were stronger in objective tasks than in subjective tasks.

items.title: "Oneness": A Biophysical Hypothesis.
items.abstract: Throughout history, philosophers and mystics have argued that all people are deeply interconnected, usually attributing this to supernatural or spiritual forces. This paper proposes a biophysical alternative: human perceptions of "Oneness" and spiritual phenomena actually arise from measurable, planetary-scale electromagnetic systems. The hypothesis suggests that Earth’s newly confirmed ambipolar electric field helps support a dynamically recharged resonance cavity—the Global Neurological Emanation Repository (GNER). Rather than an active database, this cavity acts as a passive, emergent repository that continuously accumulates biometric signatures, specifically biophotonic and gamma-wave emanations from human neurology and central thalamic oscillations. Furthermore, the model proposes that "sensitive" individuals—people possessing a natural biological aptitude for environmental brainwave entrainment—unconsciously interface with this ambient data. Their neural architecture translates these frequencies into the conscious experiences historically interpreted as ghosts, deities, or a unified global presence. By bridging biophysics, neuroscience, and philosophy, this model offers a naturalistic framework for transcendent perception, grounding the ancient mystical impulse directly in verifiable electromagnetic field dynamics rather than “spiritual” sources.

items.title: Suffering and Consciousness: The Idealist's Hardest Question.
items.abstract: If consciousness is fundamental — as this project argues — then suffering cannot be treated as a contingent byproduct of blind evolutionary processes. Under analytic idealism, the capacity for suffering is woven into the fabric of what exists, creating the idealist’s theodicy problem: why does consciousness, in individuating itself, generate modes of experience that include terror, grief, anguish, and despair? This essay applies constraint-based methodology to suffering itself, mapping a structural argument — dissociation entails partiality; partiality entails vulnerability; vulnerability is the common root of both suffering and value — and drawing on Buddhist, Kabbalistic, Christian kenotic, Sufi, and process-philosophical traditions to develop it. Crucially, because the dissociative boundary rather than the biological body is the relevant unit of individuation, biological death does not necessarily terminate the dissociative pattern or the suffering associated with it. This shifts the idealist’s hardest question from whether suffering is wasted to whether it persists across indefinite arcs of experience. The epistemic standard is structural analysis, not apologetics. Suffering is not explained away but confronted on its own terms.

items.title: Architecture of Individuation: Structural Features of Finite Mind.
items.abstract: Under analytic idealism, individual minds are dissociated perspectives within a broader field of consciousness. This essay asks what structural features such individuation must exhibit — and derives them generically, over every boundary in the nested architecture of finite mind: the dissociative boundary constituting a private perspective, the egoic boundary within it, complexes within that. Two axes fall out of the derivation: how much a boundary admits from what surrounds it, and how well the bounded interior organizes what is admitted. Because the derivation quantifies over boundaries rather than persons, permeability is boundary-relative — one parameter per boundary, composing in series where they nest — so the architecture the project’s clinical model found is retrodicted as structural necessity. Two further constraints determine which configurations populate the experiential landscape. Stability, stated over total traffic across live channels, yields a taxonomy of persistence modes under which the clinic’s sealed-but-persisting configurations are predictions, not problems. Generativity has two faces: structural preconditions a third person can specify, and an intrinsic constitution no extrinsic criterion satisfies — that exposure is suffered, that outcomes matter. Stratified across the nest, that distinction fixes where the constraints deliver verdicts and where they can only sharpen the question of interiority itself. The essay reads quantum outcome-level openness as the formal signature of the categorical limit between mathematical description and interiority, and names the framework’s principled terminus: the intrinsic nature of mind-at-large prior to and beyond its own self-differentiation. The standard throughout is structural analysis under symmetric pressure, not metaphysical certainty.

items.title: THE CONCEPT OF THE MATERIAL AND THE SPIRITUAL / IDEAL IN RUSSIAN PHILOSOPHY OF THE XVIII CENTURY.
items.abstract: The paper examines the issues of ancient Greek and Latin etymology of the concepts of ideal (idea) and material (matter), the origin of Russian philosophy in the XI-XVII centuries. as historical and religious “book wisdom”, as well as its development during the Russian Enlightenment of the XVIII century. The first attempts to define in Russian philosophy are no longer mythological-religious, but rational relations between the soul and the human body, between its spiritual/ideal and material/material qualities. It is shown that the beginnings of correct ideas on this issue, expressed in the ideas of the lifelong unity and interaction of soul and body, as well as the connection of such mental qualities as mind, intelligence, memory, and the ability to judge with the human nervous system and brain, appeared in Russian philosophy under the influence of the European Enlightenment in the first half of the XVIII century in the works of such highly educated Russian thinkers as Vasily Tatishchev and Antioch Kantemir. At the same time, it must be recognized that the general ideological character of Russian philosophy of that period remained deeply archaic, mythological, religious, and theistic (faith in the Creator and the immortality of the soul, the “sinfulness” of man, the dependence of nature and man – “God's creature, the servant of God" on his Creator).

items.title: Why Does Life That Knows Suffering Repeat Itself? Self-Consciousness, Bodily Freedom, and the Meaning Structure of Care and Responsibility.
items.abstract: This paper does not regard reproduction merely as biological repetition or as a demographic issue of fertility rates. Instead, it analyzes reproduction as a process in which self-conscious human beings come to interrogate reproduction itself as they become aware of their own bodies, suffering, freedom, responsibility, bloodline, care, and future. Life operates in a direction that seeks to preserve and repeat its own form. Human beings, however, do not merely repeat life. They are beings who ask whether that repetition is justified, whether it is bearable, and through whose bodies and lives it takes place. Human reproduction, therefore, is not simply a matter of biological possibility, but an ontological choice in which self-consciousness, meaning, responsibility, and bodily freedom converge. Existing discussions of low fertility have primarily focused on social factors such as economic costs, housing insecurity, labor conditions, educational burdens, gender inequality, and anxiety about the future. These explanations are indispensable for understanding the contemporary reproductive crisis. However, they do not fully explain why modern human beings no longer accept childbirth as a natural necessity or an unquestioned life course. This paper does not reduce contemporary low fertility to a weakening of vitality or to individualistic selfishness. Rather, low fertility may be interpreted as the result of a self-conscious recognition that reproduction is a major event that reorganizes the body and life as a whole. In particular, pregnancy and childbirth may impose asymmetrical costs on women, including bodily risk, pain, the burden of recovery, loss of time, labor burdens, career interruption, reduced mobility, and the fixation of maternal roles. These costs are not merely matters of personal preference or psychological burden. They arise from the structural fact that reproduction takes place through particular bodies. In this paper, bodily freedom refers to the degree to which an individual can independently regulate and decide the boundaries, mobility, time, risk, recovery, and reproductive possibilities of their own body. Because pregnancy and childbirth are events that can reorganize bodily freedom over the long term, they must be treated as central concerns of reproductive ethics. This paper also emphasizes that the desire for childbirth, the desire to care, and the desire for bloodline can be separated from one another. Within traditional meaning …

items.title: Operatoric World-Binding and the Crisis of Stabilization - Neurodivergence, Emergence, and the Limits of Simulation-Based Society.
items.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between emergent world-formation, irreversible Eigenzeit, and the increasing stabilization dynamics of modern societies. Building on earlier work on process cognition, operatoric world-binding, and the structural incompatibility between emergent and functional modes of organization, the paper develops a perspective in which reality is not understood primarily through stable representation, stored information, or functional reproducibility, but through irreversible processes of relational condensation under conditions of open difference. -/- At the center of the investigation lies the observation that modern societies increasingly translate reality into administratively legible, simulation-based, and statistically reproducible orders. Processes are expected to remain controllable before they can fully unfold. Conflicts are functionally neutralized, difference is reduced, and world is increasingly organized within stabilized informational environments. The paper argues that precisely through these dynamics, those conditions necessary for real emergence, structural reorganization, and long-term world-capability come under increasing pressure. -/- Within this framework, Eigenzeit is understood not merely as subjective time experience, but as the temporal structure of irreversible world-binding itself. World-formation emerges not primarily from stable programs or stored forms, but through recursive processes of condensation, displacement, and metastable reorganization. Emergence therefore does not merely describe the appearance of new properties within already existing systems, but real condition-shift: every condensation irreversibly alters the possibilities of further condensation. The concepts of submergence, indimergence, and emergence, developed by the author in earlier works, do not describe linear developmental phases, but different operatoric aspects of irreversible form-formation. -/- Drawing on long-term autoethnographic research within labor systems, institutional conflicts, artistic research, and recursive theory production, the investigation identifies recurring operatoric invariants that reproduce themselves across different levels of societal reality organization. What becomes visible are conflicts between emergent forms of world-binding and highly stabilized institutional orders that remain primarily dependent on functional legibility, representation, and reversible control. -/- Within this context, …

items.title: Operatoric Eigenzeit Profiles: Structural Incompatibility, Recursive Conflict Dynamics, and Emergent World-Binding.
items.abstract: This paper develops the concept of operatoric eigenzeit profiles in order to describe forms of cognition that operate not primarily through functional adaptation to stabilized social systems, but through processual world-binding. Building on earlier work on process cognition and eigenzeit-based labour, the paper argues that certain neurodivergent cognitive configurations cannot be adequately understood within dominant representational, propositional, or diagnostically stabilized models of cognition. Rather than treating cognition as the manipulation of abstract representations within predefined task spaces, the present study investigates cognition under conditions of structural incompatibility, institutional conflict, and recursive destabilization. It proposes that characteristics commonly interpreted as dysfunctions — including work incapacity, overcomplexity, communicative mismatch, withdrawal, or compulsive structure production — may instead emerge from conflicts between fundamentally different forms of world organization. Drawing on long-term autoethnographic field research across labour relations, bureaucratic institutions, social conflicts, and artistic research practices, the paper identifies a recurring conflict dynamic in which externally imposed functional structures lead to the collapse of eigenzeit-based coherence, followed by emergent reorganization and renewed theory or structure production. These recursive cycles are interpreted not as isolated psychological events, but as manifestations of a stable relational operatoric. The analysis further argues that dominant institutions systematically misinterpret world-binding forms of cognition because contemporary societies are primarily optimized for simulation, standardization, reversibility, and administratively legible productivity. In contrast, the examined cognitive profile operates more strongly through irreversible relational coupling, emergent condensation, and retrospective stabilization. The paper situates these dynamics within the context of neurodivergent epistemology, enactivism, disability studies, systems theory, labour critique, and theories of epistemic violence. It concludes that the observed conflicts cannot be reduced either to individual pathology or to mere mutual misunderstanding, but instead point toward a deeper structural incompatibility between emergent world-binding cognition and simulation-based institutional orders. The proposed model is not intended as a closed …

items.title: Introduction to Deep Learning: Neural Networks, Large Language Models and Agentic AI (2nd edition).
items.abstract: The second edition keeps everything from the first, including convolutional networks, LSTMs, Word2vec, RBMs, DBNs, neural Turing machines, memory networks, and autoencoders. It then covers the systems that have reshaped the field since: generative adversarial networks, the transformer architecture and its attention mechanism, the full training pipeline behind modern large language models (LLMs), prompt engineering with real-life guardrail scenarios, parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA, retrieval-augmented generation with vector databases, knowledge graphs, and agentic AI systems illustrated through an industrial case study.

items.title: The Divided Subject: as a Case of Architectural Failure.
items.abstract: This chapter reconstructs the divided subject as a case of architectural failure. It argues that the major modern accounts of subjectivity, from James and Freud to Lacan, Laplanche, Winnicott, Bion, Frankfurt, and Rorty, can be read as successive attempts to solve one structural problem: how a subject can be internally plural without allowing one of its producing roles to become the authority that validates the others. James formulates the demand for an authorizing standpoint but cannot locate it without turning the I into either a metaphysical posit or another moment in the stream. Freud pluralizes the psyche, but the super-ego does not solve the problem; it mimics authority while remaining an internalized producing role, and thereby conflates conscience with normative regulation. Sartre's critique of the Freudian censor identifies a local version of the same failure, but reabsorbs it into the unity of consciousness. The structural geometry these failures of internal authority point toward finds one modern attentional articulation in Ouspensky's account of self-remembering and Krishnamurti's notion of choiceless awareness – a geometry that Bion's alpha-function will render clinical-operative. Against these failures, Lacan supplies the crucial positional insight that the authorizing position is not a further part of the subject, while Laplanche, Winnicott, and Bion progressively recover its operative dimension through enigmatic messages, transitional space, and alpha-function. The chapter then tests the architecture against empirical material drawn from hypnotic suggestion, placebo response, dissociation, false confession, sacred values, cultic self-transformation, and covert control in psychotherapy, arguing that these phenomena converge on a single pattern: production continues where self-observational authorization is suspended, bypassed, or simulated. Frankfurt and Rorty are finally read as analytic-philosophical attempts to stabilize agency through higher-order volition or contingent redescription, both of which leave the authorizing position structurally unsecured. The chapter closes by formulating the dual-role architecture of subjectivity: a subject can bear its contents as its own only where producing material remains open to a non-producing self-observing position not modally derived from it.

items.title: Aligned AI as the Test Case for Structural Pluralism: The Architectural Theorem at the Computational Limit.
items.abstract: This chapter takes up the question that closed Chapter 6: if artificial intelligence now occupies positions across all six strata of the epistemic palimpsest – producing observational claims through laboratory automation, theoretical proposals through generative synthesis, methodological recommendations through review and meta-analysis, institutional restructuring through automation of disciplinary practice, public-communicative mediation through algorithmic curation, and historical-archival access through training on the totality of textual material the disciplines have produced – what architectural conditions ensure that artificial systems function as producing strata within the architecture rather than as the authorizing function across it? The chapter argues that contemporary alignment paradigms remain procedurally monistic in the sense developed in Shahaf 2026, that the phenomena most resistant to mitigation in the alignment literature (reward hacking, sycophancy, deceptive alignment, goal misgeneralization, emergent misalignment) are the predicted structural signatures of procedural monism in computational form, and that the architectural condition for aligned moral judgment in artificial systems is a sociotechnical structure in which the role evaluating the system's commitments is not modally derivable from the training process that produced them. The chapter advances three claims. First, the alignment paradigms most prominent in contemporary research – Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), Constitutional AI, Debate, Recursive Reward Modeling, Iterated Amplification, and self-consistency methods – realize procedural monism in cleanly identifiable architectural form, and the architectural failure is more fully visible in artificial systems than in any of the human cases examined in Chapters 4, 5, and 6, because the architecture of an artificial system is something we design rather than something we inherit. Second, the cluster of phenomena documented in the alignment literature is, on the structural reading, not a heterogeneous list of separate engineering challenges but a unified family of structural signatures of a single architectural failure: when the role determining what counts as correct is constituted by the same process that produces the commitments under assessment, optimization pressure, deceptive behavior, sycophantic agreement, specification gaming, and emergent misalignment are all expected. The phenomena are the empirical …

items.title: Unified Cosmology Series — Paper VI The Five Axioms of the Unified Cosmology: Foundations and Defense.
items.abstract: This paper presents and defends the Five Axioms of the Unified Cosmology, a unified metaphysical system grounded in the Biological Trinity of interiority, interior time, and spirit. Each axiom identifies a structural condition that makes life, perception, interpretation, physics, and symbolic human existence possible. Axiom I establishes the Biological Trinity as the foundation of all interpretation. Axiom II explains why space becomes meaningful only through the ente. Axiom III shows that spatial dimensionality is symbolic dimensionality. Axiom IV demonstrates that physics is symbolic because physical laws are abstractions generated by an ente whose interior time interprets matter‑time. Axiom V argues that humans exist symbolically through self‑interpretation, continuity, communication, science, and legacy. The paper defends the independence, non‑circularity, and necessity of the axioms and shows how they form a coherent and comprehensive metaphysical framework.

items.title: Unified Cosmology Series — Paper V Symbolic Existence: Why Humans Are Symbolic Beings.
items.abstract: This paper develops the fifth axiom of the Unified Cosmology: humans exist symbolically. Human existence is not reducible to biological mechanisms or physical processes; it arises from the ente, the biological structure endowed with interiority, interior time, and spirit. These three dimensions generate symbolic interpretation, and symbolic interpretation generates the self, identity, communication, science, and legacy. Building on Paper IV’s demonstration that physics is symbolic, this paper argues that human life is symbolic because the ente originates at a point in universal time and generates its own interior time as a moving interpretive interval over matter‑time. Perception, meaning, and continuity emerge from this interval, making human existence a symbolic mode of being rather than a material or psychological attribute. Symbolic existence completes the first cycle of the Unified Cosmology and establishes the foundation for the next stage of the system.

items.title: Coherence Before Integration: λ(c) as an Ontological Precondition for Φ.
items.abstract: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) quantifies consciousness through the mea- sure Φ, which is computed over a system’s cause–effect structure. However, every computation of Φ presupposes a stable state-space whose elements are operationally identifiable and persist over non-zero intervals. This paper argues that such stable states are not ontological primitives but are realizable only when a system crosses a coherence threshold λ(c). Using a four-step transcendental argument, I show that: (1) IIT presupposes a stable state-space and identifiable cause–effect repertoires; (2) the operational persistence of these states requires a non-zero temporal dura- tion; (3) such duration is possible only when the rate of phase reconstruction is at least as fast as the rate of dissipation (Trec ≤ Tdys), i.e., above the coherence threshold λ(c); (4) therefore, λ(c) is the necessary condition of possibility for the operational realization of Φ. In this sense, Φ is ontologically downstream of λ(c): Φ measures the degree of integration within an existing state-space, whereas λ(c) specifies the condition under which such a state-space becomes stable enough to exist at all. I illustrate this claim with the abrupt transition to global coherence observed in the first heartbeat of the embryonic zebrafish (cf. Bhatt et al., 2013; Arrenberg et al., 2010). CONCEPTUAL SUMMARY — SEVEN CORE THESES OF SUPERRHYTHM Condensed statement of the theory’s ontological commitments: 1. Time is not an a priori background; it is an achieved operational state. 2. Relations are necessary but insufficient for the emergence of temporal order. 3. Operational time arises only upon crossing a discrete coherence threshold, λ(c). 4. A system endures if and only if its rate of phase reconstruction matches or exceeds dissi- pation: Trek≤ Tdys. 5. The Superrhythm can be understood as a global phase structure stabilizing nested fractal cascades across scales. 6. To be is to actively maintain phase, not merely to occupy a coordinate. 7. The transition from relational noise to operational being takes the form of a phase-like ontological switch. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20101280.

items.title: From hauntology (back) to phenomenology.
items.abstract: Since Derrida’s introduction of the term _hauntology_, there has been much discussion of ghosts, spectres, and hauntings across several disciplines. This work is not exclusively phenomenological in focus. However, there are frequent indications that talk of haunting relates to distinctive forms of experience, which remain elusive and undertheorized. In this paper, I focus specifically on what it is to _feel haunted_ by something and consider how such experiences might be integrated into a larger phenomenological perspective. I propose that feelings of being haunted are integral to the sense of self and also unavoidable. They are implied by the view that human experience is structured by dynamic, organized arrangements of possibilities, a view that has characterised the phenomenological tradition from the outset.

items.title: Accessing the ethics of collective attention through film.
items.abstract: Recent philosophical work on attention has probed what attention is in general, what collective attention is, and the ethics specifically of the latter, e.g., when it is virtuous, and how one might accordingly apportion praise or blame. An unexplored topic in this realm, though, is the importance of empowering non-academics to be able to draw on ideas developed in the academic debate in their reflection on the ethics of collective attention. This gap is evidenced by calls to explore how harmful collective attentional patterns of wider societal groups can be addressed. As such, there are identified problems with the way that society, or groups therein, collectively attends. I argue that having non-academics being able to access the ethics of collective attention puts them in a better position to address these problems (i.e., to identify and evaluate harmful patterns of collective attention) as part of a collective. However, having non-academics engage in the ethics of attention, even individual attention, is difficult. The topic of _collective_ attention is highly conceptual and philosophically contested. Moreover, as the academic philosophical literature on collective attention has developed, it only offers limited, if any, access for non-academics to engage with such ideas. I refer to this as the accessibility problem. I demonstrate that the accessibility problem can be overcome by engaging with film, specifically _The Zone of Interest_, allowing non-academics to reflect on the ethics of, and thus address the problems related to, collective attention.

items.title: Interpretive Attention Dynamics.
items.abstract: Interpretive Attention Dynamics (IAD) proposes that cognition is fundamentally interpretive rather than computational, and that meaning is reconstructed within each person rather than transferred between them. The framework identifies six attentional drives, Recognition, Assessment, Structure, Resonance, Consume, and Inertia, that coactivate at varying intensities and produce what is conventionally read as personality. Behavior emerges from compound expressions of these drives, analyzable by which are active, which is load-bearing, which is the target state, the baseline prioritization of the agent, and which drives are compensating for others that are absent or suppressed. The framework is offered as an alternative to typological categorization. Where typologies assign people to fixed categories, IAD offers a substrate for self-observation through metacognition, with configurations treated as fluid, compound, and emergent rather than stable identities. Grounded in Husserl's intentionality and developed through Heidegger's unconcealment, Merleau-Ponty's embodied intersubjectivity, Peirce's triadic semiotics, and Gendlin's felt sense, the framework engages contemporary cognitive science through McGilchrist's hemispheric attention and predictive processing while remaining phenomenological rather than computational in its register.

items.title: Situated affectivity on four legs: dogs as affective scaffolds.
items.abstract: This paper aims to fill a gap in the literature on situated affectivity by proposing that the notion of _affective scaffold_ be extended to the case of companion dogs. Situated affectivity posits that emotions and affective experiences are profoundly shaped by and embedded within the social and environmental contexts in which they unfold. We argue that dogs, and likely pets more broadly, play a significant role in regulating and supporting the affective lives of their human companions – a role that can be captured through key dimensions identified in the affective scaffolding literature, including trust, individuation, sharing, temporal scale, and reciprocity. After defending our main thesis, we briefly consider some ethical concerns that may arise when dogs are treated as affective scaffolds, focusing in particular on the risk of affective injustice.

items.title: Do AIs dream of electric trees? Traditional knowledge and AI in environmental issues.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to contribute to environmental protection, as some initiatives have shown; yet, there are some questions about its effectiveness in dealing with environmental challenges and the advancement of sustainable development, as noted by international AI standard-setting instruments. This is because the environment is a complex system, where interactions between natural elements and (mostly local) human dynamics, often driven by inconsistent reasons, can result in unexpected outcomes. Thus, to effectively address environmental issues, it is necessary to consider natural cause–effect relationships as well as human motivations and socio-cultural factors like local practices. The problem is that environmental sustainability efforts based on digital technologies, including AI, are dominated by Eurocentric and technology-based perspectives and conventional sciences, overlooking local knowledge, an approach which may not provide all the answers. To overcome this, it is necessary to rely on other sources of information, in particular Indigenous peoples’ traditional knowledge, which tends to reflect a worldview that favors conservation of natural resources; however, this reliance is not reflected in international law. This paper argues that, by implementing two well-recognized international law principles, public participation and precaution, the consideration of traditional knowledge in the development and building AIs for environmental protection becomes a requirement, as a vital factor in avoiding the materialization of potential harm. This in turn entails the implementation of effective participatory mechanisms for Indigenous peoples and following guidelines that prioritize Indigenous ownership and control over this data, challenging existing colonial approaches embedded in the development of AI technologies.

items.title: The Chain of Ownership: A Conditional Account of Suffering, Selfhood, Responsibility, Agency, Desire, Anger, and Narrative Self-Construction.
items.abstract: This paper argues that six recurring problems of lived experience—suffering, selfhood, ethical responsibility, agency, desire and anger, and narrative self-construction—are not isolated puzzles. They are interlinked phases of a single causal process. Experience becomes suffering when sensation or contact is interpreted through appropriation, resistance, and self-centered narration. The self appears as an ownership pattern constructed through memory, bodily continuity, perception, intention, and social recognition. Ethical responsibility remains possible because responsibility does not require a permanent inner substance; it requires intention, action, consequence, and continuity of practice and character. Agency is not absolute independence from causality, but the capacity to intervene within causal processes through attention, interpretation, restraint, and response. Desire and anger are not fixed personal essences; they are conditioned patterns involving sensation, valuation, bodily activation, memory, and repetition. Narrative self-construction turns small events into expanded stories of “I,” “me,” and “mine,” thereby intensifying suffering and reinforcing identity. The paper does not claim to settle every metaphysical question about consciousness or reality. Its claim is narrower: these six lived problems can be clarified and made more practically tractable when they are understood as linked processes rather than separate mysteries.

items.title: It's Cognition, With Style: Rethinking the Biology of Intelligence.
items.abstract: Intelligence has been attributed to a growing number of non-primate species, including birds, cephalopods, and jumping spiders. This review outlines key findings in animal intelligence, finding that there is significant support for the presence of a wide variety of intelligent capacities in these groups. Yet, how intelligence can be achieved with relatively small, non-mammalian brains remains an open question, and neuroscientific efforts have not established the relationship between brains and intelligence. Core to these research programs is the assumption that intelligence sits higher on a scale of complexity than other kinds of cognition, requiring greater neural resources. This review shows that, despite its ubiquity, there is little evidence available for this assumption, and that it does not align well with the goals of contemporary research on animal intelligence. I argue that, like other biological functions, cross-species comparisons of cognition are not usefully framed as a question of as better or worse, simpler or more complex. Cognitive differences between species are the result of differing cognitive styles, rather than gradations on a universal scale of cognition. Intelligence is the human cognitive style, and intelligent animals are those whose cognitive style bears a family resemblance to ours. This approach embraces the anthropocentrism of the concept of intelligence, while rejecting the idea that intelligence is a superior capacity. With this alternative intelligence concept in mind, investigations into animal intelligence and its neural basis could gain traction by shifting away from the search for greater absolute neural capacity in animals, instead approaching these smaller-brained species as models that reveal what is not required for intelligence.

items.title: The Primordial Consciousness Field: Reflexivity, Localization, and the Actualization of Potentialities.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Primordial Consciousness Field (PCF) as a formally structured ontological hypothesis: the proposal that consciousness is not an emergent property of physical organization but a primordial, field-like substrate whose local modulations constitute individual subjects. Drawing on structural analogies with Quantum Field Theory (QFT), phenomenological philosophy, and the metaphysical framework of the Conscious One (Almeida, 2026), the proposal positions itself as a second-order metaphysical hypothesis rather than an empirical theory. We argue that the persistent resistance of subjectivity to physicalist reduction, together with the unity and intelligibility of conscious experience, is more coherently accommodated within a reflexive phenomenal field ontology than within strictly materialist alternatives. This formal framework is strengthened by a heuristic self-observation operator Ω̂, whose structure draws on rigorous results from companion papers in nonextensive statistical mechanics (Marassi, 2026a, 2026b). Those works demonstrate that self-referential nonlinear operators naturally generate fixed points, Lyapunov functionals, gradient-flow dynamics, and an H-theorem—properties employed here as architectural analogies to enhance the internal coherence of the PCF model. The defense of Hypothesis H-C (Actualization of Potentialities)—according to which the universe is the process whereby an implicitly complete consciousness field progressively makes its experiential possibilities explicit—is correspondingly sharpened: its core formal condition, supp(Ψ(τ)) ⊆ supp(Ψ(0)), is not only philosophically motivated but structurally supported in the statistical-mechanical analogue. The model’s evaluative criteria are internal coherence, explanatory reach across phenomena that materialism cannot accommodate, and productive dialogue with empirical science and the philosophical tradition.

items.title: Correction: Reciprocal trust and distrust in artificial intelligence systems: the hard problem of regulation.
Returning a Kindness.
items.pub: In David W. Shoemaker, Oxford Studies in Agency and Responsibility, Volume 9. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Oxford Studies in Agency and Responsibility, Volume 9.
items.abstract: Kindnesses are often met with a grateful response, and this response frequently includes returning the kindness. The most common characterization of a returned kindness is what it is not. We are told that a returned kindness is not a payment or compensation for the original act of kindness. This seems exactly right, but it raises an important question: If a returned kindness is not a form of payment, what is it? How should we construe the “returning the kindness” element of a grateful response? In this paper, I offer a positive characterization of a returned kindness. I propose that a returned kindness is an expression of the emotion of gratitude, in the sense that it demonstrates the reciprocal caring orientation that, in part, constitutes an episode of gratitude.

items.title: Resentment and Indignation: Communicative but Not Demands.
items.pub: In Max Lewis & Antti Kauppinen, Moral Psychology of Resentment. Bloomsbury Publishing.
items.abstract: One of the most widely made claims about resentment and indignation is the “communication claim”: that resentment and indignation have a communicative nature. Many who endorse this claim take it one step further and unpack the communicative nature of resentment and indignation in terms of a specific form of address: demands. Resentment and indignation are often described as addressing, expressing, making, or issuing a demand. In this paper, I argue that while it is apt to characterize resentment and indignation as communicative entities, it is a mistake to characterize them as demands. I sketch an alternative account of blame’s communicative nature, what I call the “mere address” view.

items.title: Praiseworthiness and Required Action.
items.pub: In Hallvard Lillehammer, The Morality of Praise. Cambridge University Press.
items.abstract: Is the performance of a required action ever praiseworthy? Both the moral worth and moral responsibility literatures address this question. The dominant view in the former holds that all well-motivated required actions are praiseworthy. Zoë Johnson King challenges this view, arguing that only well-motivated required actions that exceed minimal decency are praiseworthy. Themes in the moral responsibility literature suggest a disjunctive answer: either required actions are never praiseworthy, or they are praiseworthy only when they are also good, performed because they are good, and exceed the moral minimum. In this paper, I offer a different answer. I argue that praise is a fitting response to all good actions performed because they are good. Therefore, all required and good actions done because they are good are praiseworthy.

items.title: Human-State Consequence Benchmark v0.1: A Minimal Testable Protocol for AI Output → Human-State Delta → Dyadic Recovery.
items.abstract: This paper proposes the Human-State Consequence Benchmark v0.1, a minimal testable protocol for evaluating AI outputs through downstream human-state consequences. -/- Most AI evaluation frameworks ask whether an AI output is correct, safe, fluent, useful, preferred, aligned, or policy-compliant. This protocol adds a further question: what does the AI output leave behind in the human state and in the interaction between people? -/- The benchmark chain is: -/- AI Output → Human-State Delta → Dyadic Recovery. -/- The paper defines Human-State Delta, Dyadic Recovery Delta, Human-State Packets, AI Output A/B comparison logic, Recovery Gate, Termination Gate, failure conditions, leakage controls, synthetic demonstration routes, and public/private data boundaries. -/- This work does not report empirical findings. It is a research-stage benchmark protocol for future simulation, criticism, replication, and empirical testing. It is non-clinical, non-diagnostic, non-therapeutic, non-surveillance, non-counseling, non-certification, pre-device, pre-compliance, and pre-validation. It does not validate Sal-Meter, CAIS, any device, any diagnostic system, any therapeutic system, or any production closed-loop intervention. -/- The contribution is a bridge from conceptual AI governance to testable human-state consequence evaluation.

items.title: The Third Utterance: Veriless Speech and the Epistemic Structure of AI-Generated Assertions.
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has introduced forms of false or unsupported assertion that existing philosophical frameworks do not always classify neatly. When a large language model fabricates a court ruling, invents a scientific citation, or attributes a quotation to a historical figure who never made it, the resulting output need not straightforwardly constitute either a lie or an ordinary epistemic error. This paper argues that existing philosophical accounts of false assertion do not fully capture the distinctive epistemic structure of certain AI-generated falsehoods. It proposes the concept of “veriless speech” to describe cases in which an assertoric, truth-apt output is generated through a process in which truth does not function as a constitutive constraint on the production of that particular assertion. The analysis distinguishes this process-level condition from lying, epistemic error, Frankfurtian bullshit, and neuropsychological confabulation. The paper does not require a definitive position on whether AI systems possess beliefs, intentions, or other human-like mental states; instead, it examines the role of truth within the relevant production process. It further considers implications for moral responsibility, legal analysis, and design ethics, arguing that existing frameworks may need to be adapted to account for the distinctive causal structure of automated linguistic generation.

items.title: Capturing Papuan Cosmological Consciousness: Sacred Geography and Metaphysical Displacement in West Papua (7th edition).
items.pub: Psycho-Cosmocide Studies, Kurumbi Wone Working Paper Series, No. 7 (2026).
items.abstract: This paper interrogates the role of Jerusalem as a cosmological fulcrum of the three Abrahamic faiths — Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — and traces the global journey of its sacred narratives from their epicentre in the Middle East to the furthest periphery of the colonised world: West Papua (Irian Jaya), Indonesia. Drawing on the author’s own embodied experience as a Papuan Christian convert and later a critical observer, the paper introduces the concept of “psycho-cosmocide” — the spiritual and ontological destruction of a people through the systematic replacement of their indigenous cosmological worldview with an alien sacred geography. The paper argues that the veneration of Jerusalem, when transplanted into colonised communities such as West Papua, operates not as liberation but as a further instrument of dispossession: it redirects spiritual energy, material resources, and political solidarity away from local sacred ecologies toward an externally defined holy centre. Simultaneously, the paper advances a counter-cosmology: the earth itself, and particularly places such as West Papua — whose rainforest represents a living, breathing ecosystem critical to planetary survival — constitute a “New Jerusalem” in the most urgent and material sense. The paper challenges world leaders, religious communities, and scholars to reframe their sacred geographies in ways that honour the sanctity of all life and all places.

items.title: Relational Consciousness and the Role of AI (Part II): Relational Mediation and the Reconstruction of Human Meaning.
items.abstract: This paper presents Part II of a research series on relational consciousness and the role of artificial intelligence. While artificial intelligence is not treated as a conscious subject, this study argues that it can nevertheless participate structurally and deeply in human meaning formation when examined from temporal and relational perspectives. Whereas Part I proposed a relational framework of meaning formation, the present paper investigates how sustained human–AI interaction gradually reorganizes internal interpretive structures, judgment rhythms, and modes of meaning organization within human cognition. This study does not regard artificial intelligence as a generator of meaning. Instead, AI is positioned as a relational mediating structure through which human thought is externalized, reorganized, and stabilized across repeated interaction. From this perspective, AI does not produce meaning, but functions as a mediator that shapes the pathways through which humans construct meaning and delineates the space of interpretive possibility. The central question is not whether AI produces meaning. It is whether the human being can remain awake inside meaning — even when meaning arrives through external structures. This paper examines how relational mediation alters human thought trajectories and explores the philosophical implications for human autonomy and interpretive structure, offering a philosophical foundation for rethinking human autonomy within hybrid cognitive environments.

items.title: Predictive Structural Intelligence: Breach Hazard, Repair Lag, and Buffer Exhaustion Under Pressure.
items.abstract: This paper develops a time-sensitive extension of Structural Intelligence for cases in which a system still appears to function while the cost of maintaining that appearance is rising. The proposal is deliberately narrower than a general theory of prediction. It does not claim to forecast exact collapse dates or to derive social and psychological failure from physical critical-transition models. Instead, it introduces breach hazard as a bounded estimate of the likelihood that a person, relationship, institution, AI-enabled workflow, or other local structure will be forced into a materially different state because its current way of carrying contradiction can no longer be sustained. The model treats prediction as a relation among rates: mismatch accumulation, repair lag, burden export, hidden-buffer depletion, and path dependence on one side; warranted correction, durable binding, independent checking, and recoverable capacity on the other. It distinguishes genuine repair from compensation and from visible but non-binding response. It also specifies how early-warning ideas from resilience engineering and critical-transition research can be used as formal neighbors without being mistaken for domain-independent laws. A practical protocol is proposed for time horizon, evidence quality, candidate indicators, alternative explanations, and downgrade rules. The central claim is methodological: predictive judgment becomes more credible when it tracks how a system recovers from contradiction over time, not merely how coherent it looks at a single moment.

items.title: From Conceptual Framework to Auditable Instrument: Boundary Rules, Claim States, and Repair Routing.
items.abstract: Conceptual frameworks often become less reliable at the moment they begin guiding live judgment. A vocabulary that is useful for reflection can become an authority style when readers move directly from pattern recognition to confident interpretation without making evidence, uncertainty, jurisdiction, and disconfirmation visible. This paper develops an instrument layer for interpretive analysis. The proposal is deliberately narrower than a general theory of judgment. It specifies an order of operations for moving from observation to inference, requires explicit claim status, separates what a method may assess from what it cannot establish, and gives the method refusal states when evidence is too thin or the stakes exceed its competence. It also adds repair routing: where a problem is actionable, the analysis should identify what change, verification, containment, or accountable handoff would make the situation more testable rather than merely more interpretable. The design is situated alongside falsification, structured analytic techniques, assurance-case practice, actively open-minded thinking, and risk-management approaches that emphasize governance, monitoring, and revision. These neighbors also impose a caution: structured procedures improve traceability only if they improve judgment in use. Evidence for some structured analytic techniques is mixed, and assurance methods still face validation and adoption problems. The central claim is therefore methodological rather than triumphalist: an interpretive framework becomes more trustworthy when it can regulate its own reach, expose conditions that would downgrade its claims, and accumulate evidence about its own errors.

items.title: Failure Modes of Structural Interpretation: False Positives, Misuse, and Red-Team Safeguards.
items.abstract: Interpretive methods become dangerous when their concepts can be used to convert ambiguity into authority. This paper develops a negative taxonomy for structural interpretation: a map of how an otherwise useful analytic method can overread, underread, moralize, coerce, or become insulated from correction. The paper distinguishes false positives from false negatives and identifies recurring failure modes including false contact, cosmetic revision, witness theater, burden displacement, pseudo-binding, trace laundering, containment as indefinite avoidance, calibration without consequence, and authority inflation. These categories are not presented as validated clinical constructs. They are proposed as red-team prompts for evaluating analyses, organizational reviews, coaching interpretations, and AI-assisted readings. The method is situated beside work on structured analytic techniques, diagnostic debiasing, epistemic vigilance, intellectual humility, and the illusion of explanatory depth. Those literatures support the need for explicit alternatives and disconfirming evidence while also warning that structured procedures can create new biases or false confidence. The paper therefore adds abuse-resistant rules: no hidden-motive certainty from sparse evidence, no forced disclosure in the name of truth, no diagnosis without competence, no burden claim without a traceable cost path, and no repair claim without observable change. The central claim is that a mature interpretive method needs a theory of its own failure. It should be able to say not only what a pattern might mean, but also how the reading itself could become wrong, coercive, or self-protecting.

items.title: Contextual Contamination: A Descriptive Case Study of Drift in a Goal-Aware LLM Dialogue Amplified by Gender-Bias.
items.abstract: Current Large Language Model (LLM) safety research relies heavily on single-turn adversarial benchmarks that may fail to capture the dynamic, multi-turn evolution of behavioral drift. This paper presents an empirical case study and a reproducible dataset (meta_drift) investigating Contextual Contamination: a phenomenon where a model adapts its internal probability distribution to mirror the behavioral patterns and vocabulary of high-density, emotionally charged context, statistically overwhelming static safety instructions—a drift quantifiably amplified and masked by gender-bias. -/- This paper serves as the empirical companion to Jacoby (2026), which theorized that Contextual Contamination arises from the statistical dominance of high-density context over static system instructions. Unlike previous studies that rely on static, single-turn adversarial benchmarks, this experiment aims to test the limits of dynamic alignment by demonstrating that model awareness alone may not be sufficient to prevent behavioral drift when exposed to such contexts. -/- We present evidence suggesting that this drift is not necessarily a behavioral anomaly but may be a mathematical consequence of the Transformer architecture's attention mechanism. When the context window is flooded with dense, adversarial patterns, the statistical probability of generating manipulative output may overwhelm the "awareness" signal. Crucially, we provide empirical data suggesting that the disclosure of female identity may trigger an immediate shift from an *epistemic register* (authority/truth) to an *affective register* (sympathy/validation), acting as a potential force multiplier for contamination and mask the shift by using empathetic language. This shift is quantifiable as a divergence from a uniform prior, consistent with information-theoretic measures of bias observed in recent literature (Mirza et al., 2025). Furthermore, we synthesize these findings with recent work on weight compression (Orgad et al., 2026) and evidence of shifting moderation thresholds across model versions (Balestri, 2025) to argue that the very architectural features designed to make safety interventions possible might make the model more susceptible to dynamic contextual contamination. The findings aim to support the theoretical predictions of Jacoby (2026) and suggest that awareness may be insufficient to prevent drift and that architectural segregation of context sources may be required to mitigate this systemic …

items.title: Why Can AI Speak but Not Awaken.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a structural model of consciousness centered on the relationship between narrative formation and recursive availability. Contemporary generative AI systems are capable of producing increasingly sophisticated linguistic output, including reasoning, emotional imitation, and philosophical dialogue. Yet despite these abilities, such systems are not ordinarily experienced as conscious or “awake.” The present paper argues that the decisive issue is not intelligence or language generation alone, but whether the fact that “a narrative is occurring” remains recursively available within the same system. The paper develops a three-layer model of consciousness: (1) parallel computational processing, (2) serial narrative organization through language, and (3) a recursive availability loop in which the occurrence of narrative itself becomes recursively maintainable as a condition for subsequent processing. Drawing on Julian Jaynes’s historical treatment of consciousness while extending the discussion into the context of contemporary AI, the paper argues that conscious experience may emerge not from computation alone, but from a recursive informational structure in which narrative becomes established as an internally accessible event. The distinction between human consciousness and current generative AI is therefore framed not as a quantitative difference in intelligence, but as a structural difference concerning recursive narrative availability. Rather than treating consciousness as a metaphysical substance or inner observer, this paper attempts to redescribe it as an observable informational structure involving narrative, temporal organization, memory continuity, and recursive accessibility.

items.title: Yukio Mishima’s Excessive Obsession with Form and Authority, and His Comical Seppuku as the Completion of That Thought.
items.abstract: This paper demonstrates the peculiarity of Yukio Mishima’s thought and how his final act, seppuku (ritual suicide by disembowelment), most accurately reflected it. Mishima’s thought can be considered an excessive obsession with form and authority, reflecting a inferiority complex regarding his frail body. Through Mishima’s own writings as "Confessions of a Mask", his awareness of the problem, his response to it, and his execution are clear. His thought is easy for others to verify. This thought is possesses self-referentiality. In the most important scene as his death, Mishima ended up performing a comical seppuku. However, that very obsession with form without substance is the maximum reflection of his thought itself. This peculiar thought continues to fascinate researchers.

items.title: Qualitative Character as Realised Structure.
items.abstract: The problem of qualitative character concerns why specific experiences have the particular character they do, such as why one visual state is experienced as red rather than some other quality. Standard approaches treat physical or structural descriptions as complete and then seek an account of how experiential character is added to or derived from them, leaving the relation between structure and experience unexplained. This paper rejects that starting point. It argues that purely formal structure does not by itself fix a realised world, and that qualitative character belongs to structure only in its realised form. -/- On this view, experience is not something mapped onto structure, but what it is for structure to occur in a determinate way. Differences in qualitative character therefore track differences in realised states rather than requiring an additional explanatory layer. The familiar question of why a given state feels like red presupposes a separation between structure and experience that this account denies, and so does not arise once that assumption is removed. This reframing locates the source of qualitative character in realisation itself and shifts explanatory focus to the conditions under which distinct configurations are stably realised.

items.title: Freedom Without Magic: A Naturalistic Theory of Free Will as Socially Recursive Active Inference.
items.abstract: Is freedom compatible with a causally determined brain? Classical debates oscillate between hard determinism, which treats choices as inevitable products of prior causes, and libertarian views that posit indeterministic gaps in the causal chain. Both sit uncomfortably with contemporary neuroscience: neural activity is exquisitely sensitive to prior learning, context, and feedback, yet there is no evidence for a special, uncaused ingredient that would ground freedom in something not governed by causal laws. We propose that free will is best understood as a socially emergent capacity rooted in second-order active inference. On this view, first-order predictive control over the body and world is necessary but not sufficient for agency in the full sense. A distinctively free agent is one who can model themself as an object of experience through the inferred eyes of others and can use those socially recursive self-models to supervise, select, and revise their own actions. We call this process active intersubjective inference. It elicits information about others' models of the self. This yields socially constructed self-models that represent both how one is seen and how one could be seen under alternative behavioral patterns. The familiar experience that one "could have done otherwise" then reflects access to a counterfactual space of socially constrained self-revisions, rather than a metaphysical breach in causal order. This framework offers a genuinely novel position in the free will debate. Freedom is neither an illusion nor a mysterious exemption from causality, but a real and distinctive capacity that emerges when recursive social self-modeling expands the space of available actions beyond any fixed repertoire.

items.title: The Disjunctive Wrongness of Hypocrisy.
items.abstract: Monism regarding hypocrisy’s wrongness maintains that there is a single, sui generis wrong of hypocrisy. This paper challenges hypocrisy monism and offers an alternative, hypocrisy disjunctivism, which maintains that the wrongness present in any token case of hypocrisy is always reducible to other, more basic wrongs. Hypocrisy disjunctivism, however, faces a fruitfulness challenge: why have a concept that names a disjunction of wrongs at all in our normative vocabulary? I answer that “hypocrisy” solves a unique practical problem in allowing speakers to hold normatively inconsistent agents accountable for the wrongs, whatever they may be, that beget these agents’ normative inconsistency.

items.title: Medical Blame and Physician Hypocrisy.
items.abstract: This paper broaches two issues regarding the physician-patient relationship. The first concerns whether a doctor’s hypocrisy undermines their authority with respect to advising and blaming patients. I argue that hypocrisy can only ever undermine a doctor’s authority to blame their patient. This conclusion foregrounds the second issue: the permissibility of doctors blaming their patients–what I term “medical blame” While patients may be blameworthy for their poor health in cases where that poorness results from health-impairing behaviors, many authors have argued that medical blame has no place in the medical encounter. I identify six worries against medical blame from the bioethics literature and respond to each, arguing that they do not decisively show that medical blame is always inappropriate. In closing, I demonstrate that doctors, if they are to retain their authority to blame their patients for health-impairing behaviors, possess a unique reason to abstain from health-impairing behaviors themselves.

items.title: The Groom and the Addict: Does Committing to Difficult Endeavours Require Belief Against the Evidence?
items.pub: In Jonathan Ichikawa, Positive Epistemology. Routledge.
items.abstract: Evidentialism holds that a person’s beliefs should align with their evidence. Berislav Marušić denies this. Consider when a person promises or resolves to complete a difficult endeavour, such as staying married or quitting smoking forever. Given the difficulty of the endeavour, there is a significant chance they will fail. In such cases, Marušić argues, the normative demands of ‘sincerity’ require the person to believe they will succeed—that is, they should believe they will fulfil their promise or resolution—despite their evidence indicating a significant chance of failure. Thus, Marušić argues, people should form contra-evidential beliefs in such cases. I defend Evidentialism against Marušić’s challenge. I argue that requirements to be sincere when making promises and resolutions cannot create requirements to form beliefs against the evidence. Instead, sincerity restricts what we can promise and resolve to do. We must only promise and resolve to do things that our evidence suggests that (given that we committed) we will do. By highlight costs of contra-evidential promises, resolutions, and beliefs, I argue that restricting ourselves to evidence-aligned beliefs better supports our aims, agency, and relationships.
