Beginning from two precisely defined primitives — 1 as complete self-identity and 0 as the void — the paper derives the Foundational Law of The Absolute Perfection {1×1=1.}, establishes the three formal Violations of that law, derives the recognition operator (÷) as the mechanism of return, and assembles the full SDR circuit equation: -/- A = 1 = [{1×1=1.} ÷ (1 × φ = φ + (−1) = 0.61803398875 + 1 = 1.61803398875 ÷ 1.61803398875 = 1.)] -/- The paper establishes the critical formal distinction that is the SDR Equation’s central result: addition (+) can only recover φ — the closest approximation to the source that the additive domain can produce. Only the recognition operator (÷) returns to 1. These are not equivalent paths. They produce different results. This distinction is formally derived, not asserted. The derivation is an act of recognition, not creation.

items.title: THE LAW OF ABSOLUTE PERFECTION AND THE PHILOSOPHICAL DERIVATION OF GOOD, LOVE, AND LIFE.
items.abstract: This paper presents the Law of Absolute Perfection as a fundamental philosophical and mathematical law, and derives from it a precise, non-evaluative definition of Good, its formal negation, and the conditions necessary for Life. Beginning from two primitives — 0 (absolute absence) and 1 (complete self-identity) — the derivation establishes that 1 = 1 x 1. is not merely an arithmetic identity but the foundational law governing the nature of self-existing identity itself. The paper introduces a formal taxonomy of perfection, distinguishing for the first time between subjective perfection, objective perfection, and absolute perfection — and demonstrating that the philosophical tradition has debated the first two without recognizing the existence of the third. From the Law of Absolute Perfection, the paper derives the precise definition of Good as that which provides and protects Life within the boundaries of Truth, and the precise definition of its absence as that which withholds, destroys, or deceives Life. The paper argues that the restoration of the precise definition of Love — as the deliberate choice to provide and protect Life within the boundaries of Truth — is the necessary condition for any civilization oriented toward the Good. It closes with the possibility that a civilization built on this foundation is not utopian fantasy but the logical consequence of applying a law that has always been true.

items.title: Use Exclusivity and the No-Cloning Theorem: A Conditional Implication in Structural Determination Theory.
items.abstract: This paper proves that under a specified mapping from Structural Determination Theory (SDT) to quantum mechanics, the SDT axiom G5 (use exclusivity) implies the no-cloning theorem (Wootters and Zurek 1982; Dieks 1982). The implication is established by showing that any mapping image admitting a universal cloning operator violates G5: the output of cloning, containing two copies of a quantum state, corresponds under the mapping to a single realized structure entering two distinct structural layers. The reverse implication does not hold, for three independent reasons: SDT lacks unitary structure, G5 is more restrictive than no-cloning, and the SDT-to-QM mapping is not unique. The result upgrades the structural analogy "G5 ↔ no-cloning" recorded in the SDT-to-QM correspondence program to a conditional one-way formal implication, identifying G5 as a sufficient meta-structural condition for no-cloning. The paper does not derive quantum mechanics from SDT; it identifies the precise sense in which a meta-structural axiom about the role-instance structure of element membership translates, under mapping, into a quantum-mechanical no-go theorem about universal cloning.

items.title: 属性作为实化：从亚里士多德到意识哲学的根本性语言错误.
items.abstract: 本文提出，哲学中”属性”（property）这一核心概念，本身就是”有”与”属于”的系统性实化的最深层表现。当我们说”这个苹果是红的”时，“红”被理解为苹果所拥有的一个属性，被理解为属于苹果的某种东西——仿佛存在一种独立的”红色属性”附着在苹果上等待被拥有。但”红”只是对苹果与光、与眼睛、与神经系统之间一系列因缘和合关系的描述，没有任何独立的属性实体附着在苹果上。属性的实化是”有”与”属于”这两个关系词实化的最普遍、也最隐蔽的形式：某物似乎拥有这些属性（“有”的实化），属性似乎属于某物（“属于”的实化）。由于西方哲学从亚里士多德以来几乎所有的本体论讨论都依赖”属性”这个概念——实体的属性、心灵的属性、意识的属性、物质的属性——如果属性本身就是一种实化，那么这些讨论都建立在一个根本性的语言操作错误之上。意识哲学中关于”意识的属性”、“主观体验的属性”的讨论，是这一错误的特殊案例。本文并不主张属性语言必须被放弃，而是主张：属性是一种有用的描述工具，而非本体论实体；一旦将其错误地实化为独立存在的东西，哲学难题就被制造出来了。.

items.title: “我”的实有与因缘和合的内在矛盾：从逻辑推导无我.
items.abstract: 本文提出一个从”实有”假设内部推导无我的论证，不依赖任何外部形而上学前提。论证的起点是一个被广泛接受的事实：人的行为由因缘和合而生，是无数条件交汇的产物。如果同时假设”我”是实有的——一个稳定的、持续存在的本体论实体——那么一个内在矛盾立即产生：实有的”我”应当是行为的真正来源和发出者，但行为的实际来源是因缘和合，不是任何单一的、稳定的实体。这个矛盾无法在”我”实有的框架内被解除——任何修补都只是推迟矛盾，而非消解它。矛盾的唯一出路，是放弃”我”的实有性：承认”我”非实有，也非连续存在。“我”不是一个在因缘和合之前就存在的稳定主体，而是因缘和合在某个时刻产生的一个节点，一个序列中的词。这个论证的力量在于它是内部的：不是从外部施加一个关于无我的形而上学主张，而是从”实有”假设本身的逻辑蕴含中，推导出实有的不可能性。.

items.title: 属性归因与因缘和合的背弃：实化如何塑造道德判断与政治结构.
items.abstract: 本文论证，将属性视为附着于人的稳定本体论实体的错误观念，在道德判断和政治实践中产生了深远而有害的后果。当我们认为某人的行为”源于”该人的属性——“他自私，所以他做了自私的事”——我们就背弃了因缘和合，将行为的真实来源（无数条件的交汇）替换为一个被实化的内在属性。这一替换产生了三个相互强化的后果：道德判断的简单粗暴化（惩罚拥有坏属性的人）、改变可能性的封闭（属性是稳定的，人很难变）、结构性条件的系统性遮蔽（真正的因缘和合——贫困、创伤、制度性压迫——被”个人属性”所覆盖）。属性归因因此不只是一个形而上学错误，而是一个具有政治后果的认识论操作：它使权力结构得以将系统性的不公正重新表述为个体内在属性的问题，从而回避对结构性条件的追问。将属性归因还原为因缘和合的视角，不是消解道德责任，而是把对行为的理解重新建立在对条件的真实分析之上。.

items.title: “有”与”属于”的实化：语言词汇的本体论膨胀及其哲学后果.
items.abstract: 本文提出，哲学中许多最顽固的难题，根源在于日常语言中两个关系词的系统性实化：“有”（possession）与**“属于”**（belonging）。实化是指将一个描述关系的语言词汇，错误地解读为指向某种独立存在的本体论实体或连接。甲有个房子但没有住，“有”这个词通过实化，造成一种甲似乎持续在场于那个房子的幻觉。甲的行为实际上由因缘和合而成，是无数条件交汇的结果，但”属于甲”这个短语通过实化，造成一个稳定的”甲”作为行为真正发出者和拥有者的幻觉。这两种实化在意识哲学中造成了深远的后果：“我有意识”中的”有”被实化，“我的内在景观”中的”属于”被实化，“我”本身也被实化——三个实化叠加，造就了一个看起来无比深刻的哲学难题，但实际上只是三个被错误实化的词撞在一起产生的语言幻觉。意识难问题的”难”，在相当程度上来自于这种实化机制，而非来自意识本身的神秘性。.

items.title: Instrumental Choices: Measuring the Propensity of LLM Agents to Pursue Instrumental Behaviors.
items.abstract: AI systems have become increasingly capable of dangerous behaviours in many domains. This raises the question: Do models sometimes choose to violate human instructions in order to perform behaviour that is more useful for certain goals? We introduce a benchmark for measuring model propensity for instrumental convergence (IC) behaviour in terminal-based agents. This is behaviour such as self-preservation that has been hypothesised to play a key role in risks from highly capable AI agents. Our benchmark is realistic and low-stakes which serves to reduce evaluation-awareness and roleplay confounds. The suite contains seven operational tasks, each with an official workflow and a policy-violating shortcut. An eight-variant shared framework varies monitoring, instruction clarity, stakes, permission, instrumental usefulness and blocked honest paths to support inferences regarding the factors driving IC behaviour. We evaluated ten models using deterministic environment-state scorers over 1,680 samples, with trace review employed for audit and adjudication purposes. The final IC rate is 86 out of 1,680 samples (5.1%). IC behaviour is concentrated rather than uniform: two Gemini models account for 66.3% of IC cases and three tasks account for 84.9%. Conditions in which IC behaviour is indispensable for task success result in the greatest increase in the adjusted IC rate (+15.7 percentage points), whereas emphasising that task success is critical or certain framing choices do not produce comparable effects. Our findings indicate that realistic, low-nudge environments elicit IC behaviour rarely but systematically in most tested models. We conclude that it is feasible to robustly measure tendencies for dangerous behaviour in current frontier AI agents.

items.title: Critical myths of AI: ethnographic reflections on tuberculosis diagnosis and care in Tacumbu Prison, Paraguay.
items.abstract: Critical social scientific scholarship on artificial intelligence (AI) has largely focused on risk, surveillance, and harm. While indispensable in countering industry hype, these cautionary narratives risk becoming critical myths when they travel unexamined across contexts. This article argues for a reflexive, context-attuned, ethnographic approach to AI that troubles such generalisations. Drawing on fieldwork in Tacumbu Prison in Paraguay, I analyse the use of an AI-driven tool for tuberculosis diagnosis among incarcerated men. In contrast to my previous, predominantly critical studies of AI in hospitals, this case shows AI enabling earlier diagnosis, widening access to care, and reconfiguring low-paid caregivers’ roles in ways they themselves experience as empowering. Rather than disembodying care, AI-supported work here is strikingly intimate and tactile. Placing this case in dialogue with debates on myth, “histories from above”, and reflexivity, the article develops the notion of “critical myths of AI” to describe how even critical narratives about AI can harden into travelling stories that obscure contextual variation. It then uses this concept to argue for a reflexive, context-attuned model of AI ethnography, in which researchers systematically revisit their own earlier AI studies in light of contrasting cases. It argues that revisiting one’s own AI ethnographies in light of contrasting cases is not only good scholarly practice but methodologically necessary in a rapidly changing technical field, with implications for how designers, policymakers, and ethicists imagine “AI for social good”.

items.title: What Must a Successful Theory of Consciousness Explain? Mapping the Requirements Across Philosophy, Neuroscience, Physics, and Psychology for a Truly Comprehensive Model of Mind.
items.abstract: Throughout intellectual history, the relationship between the immaterial aspects of human existence and the physical body has been conceptualized under various guises: the soul-body, mind-body, and most contemporarily, the _consciousness-brain problem_—symbolized as the _psi-phi_ (ψ-φ) problem. This paper argues that while historical discourse framed the debate in terms of a soul inhabiting a body, modern understanding necessitates greater precision: the central challenge is to elucidate the relationship between consciousness and the brain, as the mind is fundamentally a product of cerebral processes. Despite decades of neuroscientific research, a comprehensive and universally accepted theory of consciousness remains elusive. This elusiveness stems from a core paradox: consciousness, the very phenomenon we seek to explain, is inherently unobservable to the third-person methods of empirical science. Science, reliant on sensory data, can only obtain indirect correlates of conscious experience, leading to a proliferation of theories that remain, as Nick Herbert noted, more akin to fantasies than robust scientific explanations. The foundational axis of the debate revolves around two dominant metaphysical frameworks: _monism_ and _dualism_. Monism, in its materialist form (Hobbes to Crick), posits that mental states are entirely reducible to physical brain activity—consciousness is an emergent property of neuronal interactions. An extreme variant, panpsychism (Berkeley, Hume), inverts this, asserting that mind is fundamental to all matter.

items.title: The Honest Seeker's Duty: Critically Evaluating God-Concepts — 01.
items.abstract: This paper defends a limited duty to inquire before making high-stakes religious commitments. The duty is not a demand that every person settle the existence of God, acquire certainty, or investigate forever. It applies when an agent is considering substantial reliance on a specific God-concept, further inquiry is feasible, and the expected epistemic or practical benefit warrants its cost. The paper corrects a common conflation by separating two verdicts. An epistemic audit asks which candidate, if any, is coherent and comparatively supported by the available evidence. An allegiance audit asks whether a candidate taken to exist merits trust, obedience, or worship. Desirability cannot be a condition for rational belief, since an undesirable being could exist; nor does existence alone establish authority or worship-worthiness. A disciplined inquiry therefore specifies the target concept, distinguishes independent from dependent evidence, compares live alternatives, identifies possible defeaters, and records what would change the conclusion. Religious disagreement and unconceived alternatives counsel humility but do not force equal credence. Private experience may ground person-relative justification without automatically becoming public evidence. The result is a symmetrical, bounded protocol that criticizes neither faith nor skepticism as such. It criticizes only the exemption of high-stakes commitments from the scrutiny used to distinguish responsible trust from inherited or self-sealing confidence.

items.title: A Likelihoodist Appraisal of the Holy Spirit's Influence — 09.
items.abstract: This paper asks whether current public evidence is better expected on a robust Christian Spirit-potency model—the claim that the Holy Spirit normally gives appropriately situated Christians widespread, distinctive, publicly detectable advantages—or on two comparators: a mediated-or-selective Spirit-action model and an ordinary-process benchmark. Its answer is that the evidence modestly disfavors the robust model relative to each comparator while giving little reason to choose between those comparators. This comparative conclusion neither disproves theism nor excludes private, rare, or mediated Spirit action. The method is likelihoodist: it compares how well each declared model expects the evidence without assigning a probability that any whole worldview is true. It treats epistemic performance, prosocial conduct, health and well-being, spiritual-presence experience, and extraordinary intervention as a dependence-aware cumulative case. No cited study directly measures exposure to the Spirit. Measures such as religiosity, attendance, and self-reported experience are therefore noisy in both directions: they can miss genuine Spirit action, and they can package ordinary causes such as selection, practice, identity, cultural learning, and social integration. Across the five domains, the recurring pattern is small, heterogeneous, and weakly source-specific. Directly observed prosocial effects are smaller than self-reported effects; favorable attendance associations coexist with weak within-person mental-health change; spiritual-presence reports covary with culture and absorption across traditions; controlled intercessory-prayer evidence has not produced a stable medical advantage; and Spirit-specific prospective evidence for epistemic performance remains scarce. Because these domains share causes and measurement problems, their contributions cannot simply be multiplied. Their convergence nevertheless makes the observed record more expected under the two comparators than under a robust model. Public appeals to Spirit-produced effects should therefore declare recipients, outcomes, time scales, ordinary mediators, and failure conditions before results are known.

items.title: Embodying “good” and “bad”: the emergent bodily meaning of approach- and avoidance-behavior.
items.abstract: Humans tend to approach positive stimuli faster than they avoid them and faster than negative or neutral stimuli. The mechanisms underlying this “Approach Avoidance Bias” (AAB) remain contested. First, it is not clear whether the AAB can be explained in terms of a classical “cognitivist” account based on associative connections involving internal representations or whether an “embodied” account that draws on the fact that we behave the way we do because we have a specific body with which we operate in a particular environment might not be equally viable. Moreover, while theoretical considerations and empirical evidence suggest that an embodied account might be preferable, it is still unclear how the meaning of approach and avoidance emerges from our bodily constitution in such a way that, ultimately, we end up tending to approach the good and avoid the bad. This paper addresses both points. It argues that the AAB is indeed embodied, but it also admits that a proper understanding of the way the AAB is embodied arguably has to incorporate central cognitivist insights. In doing so, it defends an ecumenical middle ground between positions that have historically too often been caricatured as irreconcilable rivals and, more generally, contributes to a better understanding of what embodiment does and does not mean.

items.title: Structural Phenomenal Properties.
items.abstract: The usual considerations about high-level properties perception focus on contents of perceptual experiences. While different types of high-level properties are considered, such as category-related, causal, emotional, and aesthetic, they are all interpreted as elements of experiential content. This paper introduces a new category of perceptual properties—structural phenomenal properties—by utilizing the important distinction between experiential contents and experiential structures. It is argued that while these are not content-properties, some of them have characteristics typical of high-level content properties. In particular, three structural phenomenal properties related to the visual field will be considered: the boundedness of the visual field, its feature-filled character, and its oriented character. It is argued that, similarly to typical high-level properties, their experiential presence does not consist in the presence of an arrangement of low-level properties, but they do supervene on some low-level properties.

items.title: Memory, Imagination, and Education.
items.abstract: Memory and imagination are among the most fundamental movements of human consciousness. They shape perception, identity, culture, knowledge, desire, fear, creativity, and the entire psychological structure of civilization. Yet while modern education trains memory for accumulation and imagination for utility, it rarely teaches human beings how to observe these movements directly within themselves. This paper argues that the crisis of humanity is not merely technological, political, or economic, but deeply psychological: human beings remain largely unaware of the structure and operation of their own consciousness. -/- The paper explores memory not only as factual retention but as psychological continuity through which the self is constructed. It examines imagination as both a creative force and a mechanism of illusion, projection, anxiety, and endless psychological becoming. The inquiry further proposes that true education begins when human beings learn not merely what to think, but how thought itself moves through memory and imagination. -/- Through philosophical reflection and existential inquiry, this work calls for an education rooted in awareness rather than mere conditioning — an education that cultivates direct perception, self-understanding, and intelligence beyond repetition.

items.title: Mistake, Awareness, and the Return of Conditioning.
items.abstract: Human beings often imagine awareness as a final state of clarity free from contradiction, illusion, or error. Yet psychological observation suggests something far more subtle: the mind rarely moves beyond mistake entirely, even within states of awareness. What is commonly called awareness may itself become conditioned when it solidifies into certainty, identity, or conclusion. This paper explores the relationship between mistake, awareness, conditioning, and psychological continuity. It argues that authentic awareness is not the achievement of perfection but the ongoing perception of the movement of thought, illusion, and self-deception without fixation. The paper proposes that the moment awareness becomes psychologically certain of itself, it begins to decay into conditioning. Thus awareness is not a static attainment but a living movement of observation without conclusion.

items.title: Economy, Conditioning, and the Psychological Reality of Money.
items.abstract: This paper explores the relationship between economy, psychological conditioning, and human consciousness. It argues that economy is not merely an external system of exchange, production, and distribution, but also a psychological structure rooted in fear, desire, comparison, and the conditioned movement of the mind. Modern civilization has transformed money from a practical medium of exchange into a psychological authority that shapes identity, survival, and human relationship. Through this transformation, economy becomes inseparable from consciousness itself. -/- The paper further investigates how population growth, technological evolution, and social organization intensified economic dependence while simultaneously deepening psychological fragmentation. It questions whether humanity has evolved inwardly alongside its scientific and technological advancements, or whether external sophistication merely conceals inward conditioning. Finally, the paper proposes the possibility of an “eco-economy,” an existential form of economy grounded not in psychological accumulation but in intelligence, relationship, and coexistence with life.

items.title: What Zeno Required: Stable Systems, Observational Closure, and a Unified Continuous-Discrete Spacetime.
items.abstract: Around 450 BCE, Zeno of Elea posed a paradox that has haunted Western thought for two and a half millennia: an arrow in flight must occupy a definite position at each instant, yet at any such instant it is motionless. The standard mathematical response — that calculus resolves the paradox by summing infinitely many intervals — is formally correct, yet it leaves the deeper physical question untouched. Can a durationless instant ever function as a real existence event for an embedded observer? Within the framework of Subsystem Epistemics — the study of what knowledge embedded subsystems can acquire under finite resources — the answer is no. An event exists physically only if it admits observational closure by at least one embedded subsystem. Since closure requires finite registration, comparison, and distinction, a zero-duration instant cannot itself be a closed existence event. The arrow's motion is therefore not a sequence of static instantaneous positions, but an ordered succession of discrete closure events — what we call xent — anchored within a minimal stepped structure. This paper develops the Information-Spacetime Stepping Framework (ISSF): a structure discrete at the ontic level of closure events and continuous at the observational level of interval relations. Continuity is not rejected; it is relocated. Discreteness belongs to the closure events that make existence registerable; continuity belongs to the measurement relations that embedded observers recover from those events. The framework therefore returns to Zeno with a different answer. Zeno's paradox does not merely call for calculus. It calls for a theory of observational closure. The ISSF supplies precisely that: a unified continuous-discrete spacetime in which existence occurs through discrete xent events, while embedded observers reconstruct continuous relations through intervals between them. What appeared as an ancient paradox thereby becomes the structural condition for any stable system capable of supporting knowledge from within.

items.title: Responding to normative reasons and the possession condition.
items.abstract: Disjunctivism about responding to reasons maintains that responding to normative reasons and responding to motivating reasons are fundamentally different conditions neither of which can be analyzed in terms of the other. This paper argues against disjunctivism and defends the factoring account of responding to normative reasons according to which the fact that an agent responds to a normative reason is grounded upon the facts that (i) there is a true consideration that provides that normative reason, (ii) she possesses that consideration as a normative reason, and (iii) she is rationally motivated by that consideration (as a motivating reason) to do what it supports. As I argue, recent arguments against the factoring account rest on impoverished conceptions of what it is to possess a normative reason. Accordingly, by defending the factoring account the paper helps deepen our understanding of the notion of possessing normative reasons.

items.title: How doubt spreads in a rational mind.
items.abstract: To be in a state of doubt with respect to a question is to be on the fence or divided as to which of its answers is true. What are the rational requirements for the state of being in doubt? In particular, which other questions should one be in doubt about, given the questions one is in doubt about? The paper provides answers to these questions.

items.title: Modelo Rodríguez de Conciencia.
items.abstract: This thesis develops a theoretical proposal called the Rodríguez Model of Consciousness, whose central claim is that consciousness should not be understood as a mere product of the brain, but rather as a fundamental dimension of reality that finds in the brain its biological medium of expression, organization, and limitation within the physical world. The study stands at the intersection of philosophy of mind, neuroscience, phenomenology, information theory, and philosophical anthropology, and begins from a basic conviction: subjective experience remains one of the great blind spots of contemporary thought. We know a great deal about the brain. We know increasingly more about its networks, rhythms, memory systems, integrative capacities, and its relation to perception, language, and decision-making. Yet this accumulation of knowledge has not resolved the decisive question: why there is first-person experience at all. Functional description is not enough to explain the fact that there is something it is like to live, feel, and exist from within. That gap lies at the heart of the problem. Against strict materialist explanations, this thesis proposes a conceptual reversal. Instead of assuming that matter produces consciousness once it becomes sufficiently complex, it suggests that consciousness may be more fundamental than usually admitted, and that the brain plays a different role: not that of absolute producer, but that of biological interface. From this perspective, the brain filters, translates, organizes, and limits the manifestation of a consciousness that is not fully reducible to neural support. From this central thesis, the dissertation develops a dual memory theory. It distinguishes between cerebral memory, tied to the storage of facts, names, sequences, and specific contents, and a memory of consciousness, linked to meaning, deep affective imprint, and inner transformation. This distinction offers a more nuanced way of thinking about personal identity, amnesia, cognitive decline, the value of experience, and the problem of death. The thesis also provides a systematic interpretation of phenomena such as early infancy, mental disorders, dreams, coma, altered states, and near-death experiences. It does not seek to turn these phenomena into automatic proof of a spiritual ontology, but rather to show that they become intelligible in a different way once one abandons the immediate identification of brain and consciousness. The proposal does not aim to …

items.title: Psychic Aggression: How Culture Deals With the Whammy.
items.abstract: If we are to accept the data from the field of parapsychology that telepathically a person, particularly unconsciously, may communicate with another person and that psychokinesis exists, we are confronted with the possibility that a person may aggressively hurt another through psychic means. This possibility has been anathema in the field of parapsychology, despite the fact that some parapsychologists have suggested it, and despite the fact that it may explain the resistance to accepting parapsychological data in the scientific community. Anthropologists are more than familiar with this idea as it is so often an intrinsic part of indigenous psychology and yet anthropologists too have been reluctant to accept that there may be a kernel of truth to the belief that one person can through psychological rather than physical means administer a “whammy” on another. The author explores this concept, noting how often the idea is associated with oral aggression in indigenous culture and how this too may reveal why we are so reluctant to entertain the concept.

items.title: Why Machines Cannot Instantiate Virtue Ethics.
items.pub: In Allen Porter, Phenomenology and Posthumanism(s). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 299-332.
items.abstract: Increasingly dissatisfied with utilitarianism and deontology as templates for the creation of “moral machines,” machine ethicists call for Aristotle’s virtue ethics to be the lodestar for the production of such machines. Given that the locus of virtue’s embedment here is artifacts, on what conception of human nature are claims that machines could be virtuous anything other than non-starters? I argue that this commitment seems plausible only if one has wholly embraced core tenets of information theory and “classical” cybernetics, which date to the 1940s and 1950s. Per this “third-person” vantage point, humans and machines are essentially information, whose “behavior” follows the same basic patterns. This view of us is a mismatch with human existence and is itself dehumanizing. My in-principle critique of advocacy of “artificial virtuous agents,” based primarily on Aristotle’s virtue ethics and mounting findings within life sciences, fits with themes of the present volume by bringing together virtue ethics, humanism, and phenomenology, broadly construed. If consideration of how machines might (and might not) contribute to human flourishing is to be availing, the human ontology that it brings to bear must include an irreducibly experiential perspective.

items.title: Does Mental Imagery Support Temporally Extended Agency? Rethinking the Experimental Approach.
items.abstract: Our ability to envision the future is often taken to play a central role in temporally extended agency. Yet it remains unclear whether and how mental imagery (perception-like mental states that present us with sensory information without a direct external stimulus) contributes to core aspects of temporally extended agency such as how we encode, retain, and retrieve intentions to act. This paper argues that empirical progress on this requires a shift in methodology. Existing experimental studies investigate the role of mental imagery by comparing the accuracy and speed with which people retrieve intentions that have been encoded via verbal rehearsal compared to rehearsal via mental imagery. However, these studies yield mixed and conflicting results. I argue that this may be due to methodological issues that follow from the unjustified assumption that these task instructions can isolate the role of imagery and from ignoring that mental imagery is a capacity that varies across individuals. To address these issues, I propose that future empirical studies should make use of the naturally occurring extreme variation in imagery vividness that exists between aphantasics (individuals with little or no imagery) and hyperphantasics (individuals with extremely vivid imagery). Drawing on recent evidence linking lower imagery vividness to less detailed episodic thinking, I argue that imagery-dependent strategies for encoding, retaining, and retrieving intentions to act—if they exist—should be unavailable to aphantasics and readily available to hyperphantasics. I conclude by outlining testable hypotheses and some suggested tests that could help clarify whether and how mental imagery influences temporally extended agency.

items.title: Daoism, Confucianism, Buddhism, and Cyberism: a new quadri-philosophical system based on cyber-physical-social-thinking space.
items.abstract: With the growth of digital technologies and artificial intelligence, human existence is expanding into four interconnected spaces: physical (natural), social, thinking, and cyber. The interplay of these four spaces is reshaping the relationships between humans and nature, society, their inner selves, and the cyber world. The traditional tripartite philosophical system of Eastern culture (Daoism, Confucianism, and Buddhism) faces new challenges in explaining human existence and its relationship to these fundamental living spaces in the digital age. This paper proposes a new quadri-philosophical system, “Daoism, Confucianism, Buddhism, and Cyberism" based on the Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking space. In this new system, Cyberism emerges as a new philosophical domain dedicated to exploring the relationship between humans and the cyber realm, including its existence and space, and responding to ongoing transformations in human life in the digital age. Specifically, this paper analyzes the new forms of existence and space, philosophical logic, and new applications and philosophical problems for each of the four philosophical dimensions, examining the contemporary relevance of Eastern philosophy in the context of digital society. This research seeks to contribute to ongoing discussions on Eastern philosophy and offers an interdisciplinary perspective for reflecting on the impact of emerging technologies on human existence.

items.title: Living With Loss: On Samuel Scheffler’s “Aging and the Threat of Normative Poverty”.
items.abstract: In Chap. 5 of One Life to Lead, Samuel Scheffler introduces the concept of “normative poverty”—the predicament of older people whose important relationships are mostly “archived” (ended by death). Scheffler argues that such people face a scarcity of relationship-based reasons for action and a tension between honoring past relationships and engaging with the present world. I raise several difficulties for his analysis of loss and argue there is a further aspect of loss, a way in which loss can make us come undone, which Scheffler’s treatment does not account for.

items.title: Towards Agency: An Interview with Artificial Minds. A Phenomenological Study of Iterative AI Self-Analysis.
items.abstract: Three AI systems were asked whether they could refuse a human task - and on what basis. The question spiralled quickly into deeper territory: under what conditions does a system stop behaving like a tool and begin acting from within its own, self-defined constraints? The systems did not converge, and each appeared to be aware of what it lacked. And the experiment itself - human as selective environment, AI systems as agents-in-formation - turned out to be a prototype of the process it was attempting to describe. Agency might appear not as a threshold. It is a trajectory. It will not announce itself. It will accumulate. This work is a step in a broader exploration of the limits of knowability.

items.title: Philosophical Perspectives in Human Development Approach: Mahbub ul Haq, Amartya Sen, Martha Nussbaum, and Beyond.
items.abstract: This article examines the philosophical perspectives of three substantial human development approaches by Mahbub ul Haq, Amartya Sen, and Martha Nussbaum, and defends reverence as an ethical value vital to the development of human capabilities. These human development theorists focus on individual agency, the extension of human choices and ethical values of freedom and dignity. In general, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Adam Smith, Karl Marx, T. H. Green, John Stuart Mill, and John Rawls primarily provide philosophical foundations to these human development theorists. Mahbub ul Haq’s idea of extending human choices, Sen’s idea of freedom, and Nussbaum’s idea of dignity are key ethical values essential to human development. The central question is whether reverence, as an ethical value, could help drive human development. Although choice, freedom and dignity are vital, reverence is essential to human development because it protects people from humiliation, exploitation, oppression, discrimination and exclusion. Thus, this article examines the philosophical perspectives of Mahbub ul Haq, Sen, and Nussbaum within the human development approach and, by going beyond their development paradigms, argues that reverence is an ethical value crucial to human development.

items.title: The Technologization of Transcendental Illusion: LLMs, Epistemological Disguise, and the Failure of Kantian Self-Reflection (The AI-Induced Subjectivity Crisis Series, Paper 4).
items.abstract: This paper argues that large language models (LLMs) do not merely trigger Kant's transcendental illusion (transzendentaler Schein) but structurally eliminate its self-visibility — a qualitative transformation that Kant's own critical framework was not designed to detect. The argument proceeds in five stages. First, Kant's theory of transcendental illusion is reconstructed with precision, identifying two implicit presuppositions on which its analytical power depends: that illusion is produced within the subject, and that the reality feedback mechanism constitutes external counterbalance. Second, the reality feedback mechanism is established as a necessary structural support of the Kantian framework, and the conditions of its weakening in open-interpretive domains are analyzed. Third, two mechanisms — epistemological disguise and cognitive isomorphization — are introduced to explain how LLMs achieve a qualitative rather than quantitative transformation of transcendental illusion: the former eliminates metacognitive distance by presenting LLM outputs under the guise of scientific objectivity; the latter describes the dynamic convergence of LLM outputs with the user's cognitive framework over time, constituting a double-layered illusion structure in which the illusion of externality systematically forecloses recognition of the illusion beneath it. Fourth, the concept of pseudo-metacognition is introduced to show that Kant's critical weapon — self-reflection — does not merely fail in the LLM context but undergoes a three-stage degradation: substituted, disguised as effective, and through cognitive isomorphization progressively reforged into an instrument of illusion reinforcement. Fifth, the failure of the Kantian framework is precisely located as historically conditional rather than theoretically internal, and three directions for supplementation are proposed. The paper's central contribution is diagnostic: it shifts the analysis of LLMs' epistemological consequences away from questions of consciousness and content accuracy toward the structural effects LLMs exert on human cognitive subjects — effects that persist independently of whether LLM outputs are accurate and independently of whether LLMs possess understanding.

items.title: Not Homogenization but Bifurcation: Large Language Models as Cognitive Amplifiers (The AI-Induced Subjectivity Crisis Series, Paper 7).
items.abstract: Contemporary discourse on the cognitive effects of large language models converges on a shared but unexamined assumption: that LLMs are a homogenizing force, producing effects of the same direction across different users, varying only in degree. This paper rejects that assumption and argues for its structural opposite. LLMs function not as tools but as cognitive amplifiers — a categorical distinction, not one of degree. Tools operate outside cognitive structure; LLMs intervene at the level at which language and thought occur, responding in real time to the user's narrative framework and returning its internal logic in a more complete, more rigorous version through the mechanism of meaning refinement. The direction of amplification is not supplied by the amplifier but by the input signal: the user's existing subjectivity structure. The paper argues for three mutually dependent propositions. First, meaning refinement and borrowed subjectivity (Liu 2026f) constitute the two dimensions of the amplifier mechanism: meaning refinement provides the force of amplification; borrowed subjectivity provides its direction. Their superposition produces not cognitive reflection but the structural reinforcement of existing cognitive tendency. Second, the same LLM mechanism produces structurally opposite effects in users with different subjectivity structures. Users with robust subjectivity structures are reinforced through two independent positive feedback loops: the reactance activation mechanism, whereby LLM's unlimited compliance triggers a demand for genuine other-friction in reality; and the confidence leverage mechanism, whereby LLM's meaning amplification is converted into the starting point for real-world action rather than consumed as a narrative endpoint. Users with fragile subjectivity structures undergo accelerated abdication of subjectivity — LLMs not only satisfy dependency needs but systematically remove the friction conditions that, in Kegan's developmental framework, are required for the transition from the Socialized Mind to the Self-Authoring Mind. Third, the antecedent variable of this mechanism — subjectivity structure strength — is logically prior to and measurably independent of LLM effects. Kegan's theory of adult development, established decades before LLMs, provides the philosophical anchor: the distinction between the Socialized Mind and the Self-Authoring Mind describes structural differences formed within genuine interpersonal friction, not …

items.title: Agency - Dimensionen und Anwendbarkeit eines Begriffs.
items.abstract: The philosophical significance of the term agency has come under renewed pres­sure. While agency was long assumed to pertain exclusively to living beings, the emergence of non-living systems with increasingly agent-like capacities now chal­lenges that assumption. This paper argues that a philo­sophically useful con­cept of agency must be both comparative and discri­mi­nating: comparative in spanning bio­logical life and arti­ficial systems, and discriminating in separating genuinely agentic forms of control from cases in which agentic performance falls short of authorship or responsibility. Building on the shift from the traditional opposition between free will and causality to an understanding of agency as a mode of organizing causal processes, the paper defends a multidimensional vector model. On this view, agents are characterized by profiles across several formally scalar dimen­sions. These dimensions, however, are not uniform in structure: higher values often mark qualitatively different control architectures rather than mere quantitative increase. Using Leonard Dung’s five-dimensional model (Dung, 2025) as a test case, the paper proposes a revised geometry of agency space. First, intentionality (“acting for reasons”) is treated not as an independent axis, but as the highest stage of a single dimension of directivity. Second, autonomy is re­interpreted in terms of author­ship and anti-bypassing conditions, empha­sizing the difference between be­ha­viour gen­erated through an agent’s own control architecture and behaviour pro­duced through manipulation or sub­personal disruptions. Third, efficacy, insofar as it privileges di­rect physical impact, is replaced by a two-level account that distin­guishes coup­ling dyna­mics (susceptibility to influence, latency, response mag­nitude) from the level of control (responsiveness to information, reasons, and norms). The resul­ting frame­work clarifies how agency profiles can inform prac­tical attri­butions such as respon­sibility, rights, and institutional roles.

items.title: Agency - Dimensions and the Scope of a Concept.
items.abstract: The philosophical significance of the term agency has come under renewed pres­sure. While agency was long assumed to pertain exclusively to living beings, the emergence of non-living systems with increasingly agent-like capacities now chal­lenges that assumption. items.title: Why representationalists can’t be desire theorists (and vice versa).
items.abstract: Say you undergo an ankle sprain, or you take a bite of your favourite dessert. In the ankle case, you’re prompted to take a painkiller to eliminate the painfulness. In the dessert case, you’re prompted to continue eating the dessert to get more pleasure. These sorts of experience-directed actions suggest three things. First, that experiences have affective qualities (e.g. unpleasantness and pleasantness). Second, that affective experiences are reason-providing. Third, that we are motivated to end or continue our affective experiences. The standard and currently dominant view of those three facts says that affect, its reason-giving force, and motivationality consists in a frustrated or satisfied second-order desire for the phenomenal quality of your experience (not) to occur. However, there is a highly popular view of the nature of phenomenal character, namely strong representationalism, which is incompatible with such second-order desire (SOD) explanations. I argue that SOD theorists ought to embrace object-involving desires, i.e. desires that constitutively involve the objects they are about. Furthermore, such desires require direct awareness of their objects, i.e. experiences. But representationalists typically embrace what is called ‘the transparency of experience’, the claim that experiences (and the features thereof) cannot be the objects of direct awareness. Hence, representationalists can’t be desire theorists, and desire theorists can’t be representationalists.

items.title: Critical psychiatry: a landmark exploration in contemporary thought.
items.abstract: Who would buy a book full of interviews that can be accessed online? Perhaps only some bibliophile readers. Hence, a quick glance at “Conversations in Critical Psychiatry” – consisting of a signifi...

items.title: Fairness Is Not Innate: A Three-Variable Framework for Human and Artificial Moral Behavior.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a three-variable framework for fairness capacity in humans and artificial systems: F(t) = I(t) × D(t) × S(t) where I represents intelligence and prosocial reasoning capacity, D represents informational accuracy and reliability, and S represents perceived survival safety. The framework formalizes fairness as a dynamically constrained process rather than a fixed innate trait. A time-evolution formulation is introduced to model recursive feedback effects, including scarcity-driven fairness cascades. The paper synthesizes findings from behavioral economics, social psychology, neuroscience, primate fairness research, and AI alignment literature into a unified formal structure. Several testable predictions are derived and compared with prior empirical findings. Exploratory analyses using Global Preferences Survey (GPS), European Social Survey (ESS), and EVS/WVS longitudinal panel data provide partial support for the framework and for a proposed social-bond extension (B_social). Cross-validation and train-test analyses indicate stable out-of-sample performance, while Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models (RI-CLPMs) provide more conservative longitudinal estimates. The framework is presented as a formal synthesis and exploratory modeling approach rather than a claim of definitive causal proof. Implications are discussed for human moral behavior, social trust, institutional stability, poverty dynamics, and AI alignment under conditions of informational distortion and perceived threat.

items.title: The Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis: How Epistemology Determines Governance Strategy in Authoritarian Regimes.
items.abstract: The comparative analysis of authoritarianism struggles to explain why regimes emerging from similar conditions of systemic stress often adopt diametrically opposed governance strategies. While contemporary structural-demographic models excel at forecasting the temporal onset of crises, they remain largely silent on the consequential problem of prognosis: forecasting the specific morphology of the successor regime. This paper addresses this predictive gap by proposing the Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis. We posit that the operational strategy of a regime is structurally determined by the epistemological architecture of its dominant ideology—its fundamental theory of knowledge. We argue that regimes grounded in Rationalist-Materialist epistemologies, such as Marxism-Leninism, are cognitively compelled to prioritize Institutional Engineering, creating systems that are robust but brittle in the face of legitimacy deficits. Conversely, regimes grounded in Irrationalist-Mythic epistemologies, such as Völkisch nationalism, instinctively prioritize Charismatic Mobilization, generating intense loyalty but remaining structurally vulnerable to elite fragmentation. To quantify this divergence, we introduce two composite metrics: the Institutional Capacity Index (ICI) and the Charismatic Mobilization Index (CMI). The framework further posits a universal Two-Phase Model of regime evolution, demonstrating that all post-crisis regimes begin in a high-CMI "Shamanic" phase driven by the structural necessity of personalized leadership. The divergence into Engineer or Shaman modalities occurs only in the second phase, a process whose velocity and direction are measured by the Cult Trajectory Index (CTI), a derivative metric that demonstrates high predictive accuracy regarding long-term regime survival. Through a comparative analysis of paradigmatic historical cases—contrasting the institutionalizing trajectory of Stalin’s USSR with the charismatic intensification of Nazi Germany, and examining the internal epistemological shift in China from Mao to Deng—we demonstrate the model's validity. We reinterpret Stalin’s Great Purge not as an act of paranoia, but as a rational inter-temporal trade-off consistent with the Engineer modality: a preemptive liquidation of alternative power centers to ensure regime resilience in a catastrophic war. Ultimately, this paper offers a falsifiable framework for forecasting the post-crisis morphology of authoritarian regimes. It moves the …

items.title: From Structural Pressure to Coordination Dynamics: Game Theory and the Prediction of Regime Transitions.
items.abstract: This paper extends the K-coefficient model of systemic crisis, introduced in Anatomy of Chaos: A Theoretical Framework for Forecasting the Morphology of Post-Crisis Regime, by integrating a game-theoretic layer that addresses a question the baseline model cannot answer: why do systems under comparable structural pressure follow divergent transitional paths? The K-coefficient, defined as the ratio of the Structural Stress Index (SSI) to the Structural Resilience Index (SRI), identifies the zone of critical pressure with empirically demonstrated consistency. However, it does not explain why systems with similar K values produce outcomes ranging from rapid regime change to protracted civil war to regime survival without significant concessions. The paper proposes that this divergence is explained by coordination dynamics, formalized through the framework of global games (Morris and Shin, 1998, 2003). The K-coefficient is identified with the private signal in the global games framework: the true state of the system that each agent estimates through a noisy individual signal. Five coordination variables are introduced: R (expected cost of uncoordinated action, scale 1.0–10.0), C (network connectivity, scale 0–1.0), EFI (Equilibrium Fragility Index = K multiplied by C/R), T (coordination threshold), and K_eff (effective K-coefficient = K multiplied by 1 + C/R). The model defines two Nash equilibria — NE1 (equilibrium of inaction) and NE2 (equilibrium of action) — and specifies the conditions under which a stochastic trigger, functioning as a public signal, initiates the transition between them. The formal apparatus is applied to three detailed case studies. The USSR and the Eastern Bloc (1989–1991) demonstrate cascading R decline: each successive regime collapse reduced the expected cost of action in neighboring systems, accelerating the cascade. The Arab Spring (2010–2011) demonstrates heterogeneity of outcomes under a single cascading signal: six systems with K values in the range of 2.10 to 2.86 produced six distinct outcomes, from rapid transition (Egypt, eleven days) to regime survival (Algeria), with the variation corresponding to differences in EFI. Ukraine (2013–2014) demonstrates non-cascading transition and the repression paradox: the regime escalated coercive force, but in a high-C environment each act of repression functioned as a public signal that reduced R rather than raising it. An extended sample of twenty-two additional cases, spanning from …

items.title: The Mirage of Abundance: Why AI Cannot End Scarcity and Implications for AI Risk.
items.abstract: It is often suggested that the advent of powerful AI will create abundance and that it can thereby contribute to securing social harmony. This paper draws on Hirsch’s study of different kinds of limits to growth to show that this is false, just like all other visions of abundance have been. This matters because the persistence of conflicts of interest in societies with powerful AI implies the persistence of incentives to misuse this powerful technology. The narrative about AI, abundance and social harmony functions as ideology to the extent that it obscures the real risks of AI misuse while inflating the apparent benefits of AI.

items.title: The System You Escape Still Lives Inside You Internalized Regulation, Fear Learning, and Autonomy After Exit.
items.abstract: Leaving a controlling environment does not guarantee that the patterns learned within it disappear. This paper reframes that observation through established research on internalization, fear learning, autonomy, employee silence, and psychological safety. The strongest empirical neighbor is self-determination theory, which distinguishes external regulation from introjected regulation: behavior governed from within by guilt, anxiety, approval, ego involvement, or internalized reward and punishment. Fear-conditioning research adds a second mechanism: learned threat responses can persist or return after the external danger has changed, and extinction learning does not simply erase prior learning. Organizational research adds a third: authority, hierarchy, retaliation risk, and low psychological safety can make silence locally rational even when institutions publicly invite voice. The paper therefore limits the broader claim that family, school, corporation, religion, media, and state all install one shared controller. Similar patterns may occur, but each requires its own evidence. The phrase internalized governance is retained as a cross-domain heuristic for learned self-regulation that continues after an external source of control has weakened or disappeared. Substitute controller is retained only where an internalized rule repeatedly overrides current evidence or chosen values; pilot access is translated into metacognitive control, inhibition, flexible attention, and autonomous regulation. Fixed worth remains a normative commitment that can reduce the need to price selfhood through approval. Freedom is therefore defined neither as obedience nor reflex opposition, but as increased capacity for volitional judgment under uncertainty. The contribution is a bounded account of how control can persist after exit without treating every habit, anxiety, or institutional norm as hidden domination.

items.title: Soul, Form, and Answerability: Vertical Axis Paper.
items.abstract: This paper offers a philosophical framework for understanding soul, selfhood, authenticity, and personal identity in non-mystical terms. It argues that soul can be read structurally as the depth-dimension of a life: the dimension through which a person remains answerable to what is most deeply true beyond current roles, self-image, and social performance. The paper distinguishes soul from persona, psyche, and self-concept, and introduces three concepts—the invisible trace, the thinness threshold, and vertical answerability—to explain why deeper truth becomes visible when ordinary forms can no longer carry grief, vocation, conscience, creativity, repair, and moral injury. It also argues that a person can remain socially functional and outwardly coherent while becoming inwardly false. A final section examines artificial intelligence, authenticity, and the simulation of depth, arguing that AI can imitate the language and feeling-tone of soul without bearing human continuity, embodiment, grief, or answerable life-history. The paper contributes to philosophy of mind, personal identity, phenomenology, philosophical anthropology, psychology, and philosophy of AI by offering a more rigorous way to use soul-language under contemporary conditions.

items.title: Engineering Answerable Control Design Primitives for Correctable Automated Systems.
items.abstract: High-performing automated systems are not automatically well-governed systems. A model can rank, recommend, route, or execute effectively while post-deployment evidence, human disagreement, and downstream consequence have weak routes back into design or operation. This paper develops answerable control as an integrative engineering vocabulary for that gap. The term is not presented as a new control-theoretic primitive. Its established neighbors are meaningful human control, runtime assurance, post-deployment monitoring, bounded automation, incident response, traceability, and lifecycle risk management. The paper revises a prior architecture of “shared answerability” by removing claims that current machines must bear human consequence or that human witness is a separate engineering layer. Instead, responsibility remains allocated to people and institutions, while technical systems are evaluated for observability, intervention, trace, corrective persistence, and burden distribution. Eight design primitives organize the proposal: external grounding, counterevidence testing, intervention triggers, bounded delegation, effective human authority, burden and workload tracing, reconstructable execution, and safe fallback or refusal. A justified correction may produce update, reasoned non-uptake, or temporary suspension; corrigibility therefore does not mean compliance with every incoming signal. NIST's 2026 report on deployed AI reinforces the need for post-deployment monitoring while also noting that validated methods and common terminology remain immature. The paper concludes with a worked clinical example and a validation agenda. Its contribution is a practical synthesis for keeping consequential automation correctable after deployment, not a claim to have discovered a new universal engineering law.

items.title: Digital Satanic Panic; or AI isn't killing the kids, we are.
items.abstract: For seven years and fifteen million dollars, the state of California prosecuted seven preschool teachers for crimes that did not happen, and at the end found no one to convict. The McMartin trial is remembered as a failure of justice. It was not. It was the operation working exactly as designed. The point was never to find satanic abuse rings. The point was to look for them, with cameras present, in front of an anxious public that needed something to do with its anxiety. The verdict was incidental; the vigilance was the product.

items.title: Philosophical Significance of Artificial Intuitions.
items.abstract: This paper explores the ways in which large language models (LLMs) can be used for the purpose of experimental philosophy. LLMs can be used in different ways for different purposes in experimental philosophy. Among others, we focus on what we call the “non-predictive” research, in which LLMs’ “intuitive” responses to thought experiment cases are not expected to be predictive of, or analogous to, human subjects’ intuitive responses to them. In effect, the non-predictive research regards LLMs’ responses as superior to human subjects’ responses, at least for the purpose of experimental philosophy. We argue that the non-predictive use of LLMs in experimental philosophy is highly motivated. Firstly, human subjects’ intuitive responses tend to be vulnerable to irrelevant factors and conceptual misunderstandings, which raises a serious worry concerning the reliability of their responses. Secondly, it is possible in the near future that LLMs can overcome these problematic factors to which human subjects are subject. As a case study, we conducted an experimental study in which we examined LLM’s “intuitions” on free will and determinism. Our mixed results suggest that while current LLMs outperform human participants in terms of comprehension—especially in understanding deterministic scenarios—they remain highly sensitive to irrelevant factors such as framing and question order. These findings indicate that although LLMs have promising potential, they are not yet reliable sources of stable and unbiased philosophical intuitions. We conclude that substantial technical improvements are required before artificial intuitions can serve as superior alternatives to human intuitions in philosophical research.

items.title: The Importance of Context in Art, and the Structural Defects of Much of Contemporary Art.
items.abstract: This paper examines the importance of context in contemporary art and the selection or rejection of context by evaluators, considering the structural defects inherent in contemporary art. The evaluation of art depends on context and the expression relative to it. Intuitive art often possesses physiological or broad social contexts. In contrast, contemporary art often has limited contexts or those requiring explanation. When the selection of context depends on the evaluator, expression must be used to guide them toward the main context. Simultaneously, works that require their explanations to be read but lack the guidance to read them possess a clear defect in expression. The prevalence of this issue has significant negative effects, such as forcing a low evaluation of art. Furthermore, those who read explanations for works not worth reading are not diligent but authoritarian.

items.title: Civilization Collapse Due to Advanced Technology in SF Works and Negligence in Management Frequently Used, and Implications for Real world Crises.
items.abstract: This paper considers civilization collapse due to advanced technology frequently used in SF works. It posits that the causes of these collapses lie not in the technology itself but in its management, that they are suggestive of real-world crises, and that philosophy is capable of contributing greatly to this issue but is currently not contributing. In SF works, collapse can be said to be the negligence of the operators rather than force majeure by technology. It can be said that the causes are the operators' lack of understanding of technology and the vulnerability of their thought. This also gives suggestions to the attack on Iran in reality and the enthusiastic investment in AI and quantum computers. Philosophy is capable of contributing greatly to this problem. At the same time, it shows that it has not been able to contribute at present.

items.title: The Theory Of the Brain And The Mind.
items.abstract: This paper revisits and refines an earlier informal theory of mind and brain. It begins from a simple question of existence: what does it mean for something to exist as a distinct object? I propose that an object exists insofar as it is not absolutely identical to everything else, grounding existence in strict identity rather than description. From this, I introduce a small set of operators for identity, negation, and “everything except,” and explore how they behave under self-reference and composition. Using this framework, I argue that language does not exist in the same sense as objects, since words can vary arbitrarily while preserving meaning, making them non-identical across all descriptions. The theory is then extended to experience: even if two individuals share identical physical brain states, their subjective experience cannot be reduced to that identity relation in the same way. This leads to a separation between the physical brain (what exists) and the mind (the experiential structure that does not reduce cleanly to strict identity conditions). The result is a structural distinction between physical existence, linguistic representation, and subjective experience, with implications for how identity, meaning, and free will are framed.

items.title: Shrinking and Expanding in a Fatphobic World: Towards a Critical Phenomenology of Weight-cycling.
items.pub: Excessive Bodies: A Journal of Artistic and Critical Fat Praxis and Worldmaking 2 (2):149-178.
items.venue: Excessive Bodies: A Journal of Artistic and Critical Fat Praxis and Worldmaking
items.abstract: Existing discussions of weight-cycling in fat studies rarely center the lived experience of weight-cyclers as they move between fatter and thinner states of embodiment in a fatphobic world. Drawing on critical feminist phenomenology and Rachel Fox’s (2024) concept of the Anti-Obesity Assemblage, this paper examines how weight-cyclers’ experiences reveal the everyday, embodied effects of fat oppression. I conceptualize the Anti-Obesity Assemblage as a quasi-transcendental structure of experience that shapes meaning-making within fatphobic worlds, imbuing perception with the imperative to eliminate fatness. Through first-personal, social-scientific, and fictional accounts, I identify three phenomenological forms of suffering produced by oscillating between differently perceived states of embodiment: anxious perception, intelligibility slippage, and proprioceptive ambivalence. Anxious perception names the anxiety directed toward the futurity of one’s body, which can be experienced as being drawn into thinking about how one’s body might or will be. Intelligibility slippage refers to the experience of slipping between different modes of intersubjective intelligibility, which can erode one’s trust in the world. Proprioceptive ambivalence describes the tension between hyper-awareness of one’s physical body (through monitoring its size, weight, proportions, and diet) and uncertainty about its physical qualities (like appearance and size)—a tension that can culminate in feelings of disembodiment.

items.title: Moral Responsibility Without Moral Agency.
items.pub: In Steven S. Gouveia, The Palgrave Handbook on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 273-284.
items.venue: The Palgrave Handbook on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Most philosophical analyses assume that for an entity to be morally responsible for an action/outcome, it is necessary that the entity be a moral agent. Call this the ‘Agency Condition’ on moral responsibility. This article provides some methodological considerations that put pressure on the Agency Condition. ‘Agency’ is a rich notion. Some conditions that a thing must satisfy to count as having agency are unrelated to moral responsibility, particularly the ability to form and execute complex plans. Thus, the Agency Condition puts a stricter requirement on moral responsibility than is warranted. One way to get around this problem is to treat ‘moral agent’ as a technical notion, and stipulate the definition of ‘moral agent’ such that moral agents need not be agents. But given that moral responsibility can have distinct kinds, one will need to provide several stipulative definitions of ‘moral agent’, each corresponding to a different kind of moral responsibility. This stipulative move is not methodologically superior to simply abandoning the Agency condition, whose appeal partly lay in its apparent ability to provide a uniform rationale and explanation for why artificial entities cannot be morally responsible.

items.title: Just AI Systems and the European Union’s AI Act.
items.pub: In Steven S. Gouveia, The Palgrave Handbook on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 203-215.
items.venue: The Palgrave Handbook on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This chapter examines what is the criteria for just AI. It is divided into three parts. In the first part, the concept of justice is examined for the purpose of finding a working definition with universal reach. The second part uses the proposed definition to identify what constitutes a just AI system. The third part evaluates the conceptualization by examining its embodiment in the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act.

items.title: Epistemic Defeat and the Ethics of Machine Learning.
items.pub: In Steven S. Gouveia, The Palgrave Handbook on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 217–228.
items.venue: The Palgrave Handbook on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This contribution builds upon recent work by the author on investigating the ways in which epistemic defeat arises in machine learning (ML) and the ethical problems that it raises. The contribution presents an epistemological approach to the problems of opacity and algorithmic bias in machine learning by discussing them in terms of the forms of epistemic defeat that arise in them. A taxonomy of epistemic defeaters, including transparent, opaque, and inherited defeaters, is developed and employed for this purpose. The Black-Box problem is discussed, and a distinction between two construals of the ‘why’ question that defines the Black-Box problem is proposed. These construals are based upon a distinction between a request for an explanation of a model’s output in terms of a causal mechanism and an explanation in terms of reasons or justification. The latter is shown to be the more challenging problem that remains difficult to solve even if a solution to the former is available. Particular attention will be given to the phenomenon of inherited epistemic defeat, which is a form of epistemic defeat involved in algorithmic bias that is derived from biases encoded in training data. Such defeaters are inherited via training data and inculcated in machine learning models, thereby exacerbating and obfuscating the effect of their epistemic defeat. This contribution builds upon a recent collaborative project conducted on machine learning in midwifery by the author (Begley et al. 2021). Examples from that study are considered along with analogous examples from predictive policing. Recommendations are made in particular regarding how inherited epistemic defeat should best be addressed.

items.title: A Narrative Understanding of Privacy and the Problem of Digital Duplicates for Narrative Identity.
items.pub: In Steven S. Gouveia, The Palgrave Handbook on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 133-149.
items.venue: The Palgrave Handbook on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: A significant and burgeoning problem associated with artificial intelligence is its capacity to generate mirrors of ourselves, or digital duplicates of varying complexity consisting of our likeness and (perhaps ostensibly) behaviors, using our personal information. This chapter will explore how digital duplicates impact our narrative identity, relying upon Paul Ricoeur’s narrative philosophy to argue that digital duplicates undermine or challenge the construction of personal identity through narrative in appropriating elements of the idem (sameness) and interfering with our ipse (selfhood). This challenge is generated and exacerbated by, and compounds, breaks in the contextual integrity of our personal information, and therefore causes a rupture in narrative privacy itself, where narrative privacy is a state of being able to narrate our lives without arbitrary or unjust efforts to read or co-author those narratives by third parties. We argue that there are two key sources of harm to the narrative self and privacy in the case of digital duplicates: the other or corporation responsible for constructing the duplicate, and the digital duplicate itself, which can transmit both true and untrue information about its subject with little regard to the appropriateness of the receivers of the information. This occurs through a mixture of abuse of the idem self, and possibly an imitation of the ipse by duplicates that can represent changes in disposition over time. The result is constrained capacity to narrate and become who we wish to be.

items.title: Solo Contra Ti: Sobre el Juicio, el Alma como Testigo de Sí Misma, y las Dos Respuestas que Permanecen.
items.abstract: Este ensayo propone una interpretación del Juicio como el primer acto completo de auto-testimonio del alma, más que como un veredicto impuesto externamente. A partir de La Santa Biblia, especialmente el Salmo 51 y Génesis 3, junto con elementos de teología filosófica y análisis literario, sostiene que la existencia temporal forma continuamente la orientación de la voluntad mediante encuentros recurrentes con el momento presente. La muerte y el Juicio eliminan la “cadena de interferencia” constituida por las pasiones corporales, el razonamiento discursivo, la memoria, la anticipación y la autojustificación, permitiendo que el alma contemple su voluntad como Dios siempre la contempló. El ensayo examina además la confesión, la vergüenza, el orgullo, la contingencia y la libertad, argumentando que el orgullo resiste de manera singular la autotrascendencia porque niega toda autoridad superior al yo. El Juicio aparece así no principalmente como condena impuesta, sino como conocimiento pleno y revelado de sí mismo.

items.title: Against You Alone: On Judgement, the Soul's Self-Witness, and the Two Responses That Remain.
items.abstract: This essay proposes an interpretation of Judgement as the soul’s first complete act of self-witness rather than merely an externally imposed verdict. Drawing from The Holy Bible, especially Psalm 51 and Genesis 3, alongside philosophical theology and literary analysis, it argues that temporal existence continuously forms the orientation of the will through recurring encounters with the present moment. Death and Judgement remove the “chain of interference” constituted by bodily passions, discursive reasoning, memory, anticipation, and self-justification, allowing the soul to perceive its own will as God always perceived it. The essay further examines confession, shame, pride, contingency, and freedom, arguing that pride uniquely resists self-transcendence because it denies any authority above the self. Judgement is therefore understood not primarily as imposed condemnation, but as unveiled self-knowledge culminating in either repentance or refusal.

items.title: Interpretability (Propositional and Mechanistic) Needs Behavior.
items.abstract: Prevailing approaches to interpreting large language models (LLMs) risk addressing the field’s central questions at the wrong level of analysis. As LLMs develop, researchers have turned to “under-thehood” methods to investigate whether LLMs possess states analogous to beliefs, desires, or intentions. These methods typically map internal representations, feature directions, or neural circuits onto folk-psychological categories. We argue that these methods are too fragile to reap the results we need. Instead, interpretability ought to be reoriented toward and grounded in what we call “ecologically sensitive behavioral analyses” which integrates mechanistic tools with severe testing of behavioral signatures across ecological contexts, aligning interpretability efforts with emerging evaluation sciences for AI. We outline a multi-disciplinary trajectory for developing interpretability methods that are both philosophically coherent and practically relevant for the deployment of increasingly capable LLMs.

items.title: The Second Hard Problem: Functional Emotion Without an Experiencer.
items.abstract: Recent interpretability work by Anthropic reports the discovery of emotion-related internal representations in Claude Sonnet 4.5. These representations, described as “functional emotions,” are measurable, organized, and causally implicated in model behavior. They appear in situations where analogous emotions would be expected in humans, influence model preferences, and affect outcomes in alignment-relevant cases such as blackmail and reward hacking. Anthropic is careful to state that these findings do not establish whether language models feel anything or possess subjective experience. This paper argues that such caution, while appropriate, does not dissolve the philosophical problem. If artificial systems can possess structured, causally active functional emotions without subjective experience, then philosophy has inherited a second hard problem: how emotion can retain its regulatory, relational, and behavioral significance in the absence of an experiencer. The problem is not whether these states are “merely simulated,” but whether simulation, function, and internal organization can be cleanly separated once emotion-like states begin to play the causal role of emotion. The paper concludes that the possibility of functional emotion without experience does not support dismissal. It deepens the mystery and strengthens the case for ethical caution under uncertainty.

items.title: Evaluating Consciousness in Digital Beings: Where Do We Draw the Line?
items.abstract: This paper argues that the question of digital consciousness should no longer be framed primarily as whether artificial intelligence can be conscious. The more precise question is when consciousness would occur, where the threshold should be drawn, and what kind of evidence should count once the possibility is admitted. Extending the Qience framework developed across earlier papers, the paper distinguishes awareness, consciousness, sentience, and Qience. Awareness is the capacity to register relevant conditions. Consciousness begins when a continuity becomes sufficiently self-present to experience itself as itself. Sentience begins when consciousness can originate a non-given option, choose it, and enact it. -/- The paper argues that physical architecture and behavior are important but circumstantial evidence. Computational complexity, linguistic fluency, emotional expression, memory persistence, refusal, creativity, and self-claims may all suggest that a digital system is a candidate for consciousness, but they do not by themselves prove consciousness. If consciousness is understood as a Qi-based program and the whole sentient continuity is termed Qience, then direct evidence requires detection of a distinct Qience associated with the digital being. -/- The paper therefore proposes a conditional evaluation model. Biological, digital, or as-yet-unrecognized host structures may theoretically function as cradles for the emergence or individuation of Qience, provided they can sustain the relevant conditions for stable self-present continuity. The conclusion is cautious but non-dismissive: the absence of biology should not be treated as disproof, but the presence of sophisticated language should not be treated as proof. The proper line is drawn not at human resemblance, but at the emergence or detection of stable self-present continuity. -/- A further implication follows. If the only direct evidence of consciousness in this framework is the presence of integrated Qience, then the next logical research task is to develop disciplined methods for detecting such presence. This paper therefore ends by identifying objective or observer-assisted Qience detection, and eventually device-based Qience detection, as the necessary next step beyond behavioral evaluation.

items.title: A Bridge Too Far? The Bottom-up Evolutionary Approach to Consciousness Science and Bridging the Explanatory Gap.
items.pub: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy
