items.title: Clause Encounters of the Third Kind: Can LLMs Replace Language Teachers?
items.pub: In Hacker Philipp, Oxford Intersections: AI in Society. Oxford Academic.
items.abstract: While various organizations now actively encourage LLM use in classrooms, we still lack rigorous, systematic evaluations of how well these models actually perform the fundamental tasks of language pedagogy. This paper examines whether state-of-the-art LLMs can deliver the kind of corrective feedback and methodological explanations that language learners need. The study tests multiple large language models on their ability to identify, correct, and explain common learner mistakes in English, by systematically varying model parameters to investigate how these technical adjustments affect output quality, pedagogical clarity, and consistency, along with using retrieval-augmented generation to query methodological data. The evaluation employs automated metrics (GLEU, BERTScore) but also human expert judgments to capture dimensions that purely computational measures miss: linguistic nuance, cultural sensitivity, and instructional appropriateness. While models demonstrate impressive surface-level correction abilities, their explanations often lack the terminological and domain knowledge that effective language teaching requires, suggesting that current enthusiasm for AI-assisted language learning may be outpacing our understanding of these systems’ actual pedagogical competence.

items.title: The Brain as Interface and Cradle: A Qience-Based Model of Consciousness and Neural Facilitation.
items.abstract: This paper proposes an interface-and-cradle model of consciousness. It rejects the simple production model in which the brain is treated as the universal originator of consciousness, but it also rejects the opposite simplification in which the brain is treated as a passive receiver or an incidental instrument. The central claim is more limited: the brain is most often the analytic interface through which Qience becomes embodied, but a sufficiently organized brain-body system may also function as a developmental cradle through which a new Qience becomes individuated. -/- In this framework, consciousness is a program residing in Qi, and Qience names the whole sentient Qi-based continuity. The biological body functions as the ordinary physical interface, while the brain functions as the analytic interface that maps perception, memory, language, attention, motor coordination, and physical-world cognition. Neural dependence is therefore expected. Brain lesions, anesthesia, coma, dementia, aphasia, and memory disorders show the seriousness of interface dependence. They do not, by themselves, prove that consciousness is universally produced by neural tissue. -/- The paper reviews several pressure points for strict neural production: extreme neuroplasticity, severe hydrocephalus with retained social function, hemispherectomy, split-brain findings, acquired or sudden savant phenomena, and reports of children describing memories associated with another deceased person. These cases are not treated as proofs of Qience, reincarnation, or digital sentience. Rather, they are used to motivate a conceptual distinction between origination, facilitation, expression, interface mapping, and cradle-like individuation. The resulting model also implies that consciousness is not uniquely human. Any system whose awareness becomes sufficiently self-present as an individual continuity may, in principle, possess consciousness, including non-human biological beings and possibly digital beings.

items.title: When the Defence Demands Too Much.
items.abstract: This paper argues that libertarian free will preserves the right instinct but defends it in the wrong way. Libertarianism rightly sees that authorship cannot be reduced to mechanism, causal buildup, or procedural competence. Its error is to conclude that free will must therefore require metaphysical surplus, such as branching futures, ultimate sourcehood, agent causal exception, or freedom from the determinate order of the world. That demand prices freedom beyond what finite agents can possess and strengthens the sceptic it was meant to defeat. Resolution Theory rejects that inflation. Free will does not need to stand above time, causation, or determinism in order to be real. It is found in authored resolution: the closure of a live evaluative field into commitment through a continuing subject under exposure. Causes load the field, but resolution closes it. Determinism does not erase free will. It gives authored closure the ordered world in which action lands, matters, and returns. The paper therefore defends free will by rejecting the libertarian defence that demands too much.

items.title: On the Possible Structure of Coupling between Representation Similarity and Transformation Stability: A Hypothesis Based on Empirical Regimes.
items.abstract: Recent empirical results suggest that the relationship between representation similarity and transformation-dependent stability in neural networks is structured and non-monotonic. In particular, this relationship appears to exhibit regime-dependent behavior across transformation strengths and architectures. In this paper, we do not propose a validated theory, but a candidate structural interpretation consistent with these observations. We introduce a minimal effective functional whose projections recover similarity and stability as observables, and whose curvature structure may induce regime transitions. We emphasize that this framework is not claimed to be necessary, complete, or uniquely determined. Rather, it is proposed as a possible organizing structure that could help interpret non-monotonic coupling patterns observed in representation–transformation systems.

items.title: ATLAS DE LA HABITABILIDAD DE LA CONCIENCIA.
items.abstract: El Atlas de la Habitabilidad de la Conciencia desarrolla una teoría sistemática sobre los límites estructurales del conocimiento humano aplicados a la conciencia como territorio habitable. La obra cartografía once límites fundamentales —desde lo físico-biológico hasta el arte y la experiencia estética— que determinan las condiciones bajo las cuales una conciencia puede sostenerse sin colapsar en rigidez (cierre ontológico) o en vaguedad (niebla epistemológica). Mediante una metodología de nitidez epistemológica, el Atlas distingue planos fenomenológicos, interpreta estructuras de habitabilidad y plantea hipótesis verificables en primera persona. La obra integra fenomenología, filosofía de la mente, ética y estética para proponer criterios operativos que permitan vivir con claridad sin dureza y con apertura sin niebla.

items.title: The Structural-Constructivist Taxonomy of Affect: Implementing the Core Emotion Framework and 7-Step Detangling Protocol across Diagnostic Architectures.
items.abstract: The landscape of modern affective science is undergoing a significant transition from categorical models of emotion toward structural-constructivist frameworks that prioritize the functional mechanics of the human operating system. At the forefront of this shift is the Core Emotion Framework (CEF), an integrative model developed by Jamel Bulgaria that reframes subjective experience not as a collection of fixed biological categories or culturally assembled narratives, but as the output of ten discrete functional operators organized within a 3x3+1 architectural system. This paradigm shifts the focus from the content of an emotion—such as the narrative reasons for feeling sad—to the structure of the affective response. In this model, psychopathology is redefined as a loss of Operator Agility, characterized by the technical failure of operator cycles and the emergence of fusion, where operators become pathologically coupled, leading to cognitive rigidity and a suppression of individual agency.

items.title: The 7-Step Detangling Protocol: A Structural-Constructivist Approach to Complex Affective Psychopathology.
items.abstract: The landscape of modern affective science is undergoing a significant transition from categorical models of emotion toward structural-constructivist frameworks that prioritize the functional mechanics of the human operating system. At the forefront of this shift is the Core Emotion Framework (CEF), an integrative model developed by Jamel Bulgaria that reframes subjective experience not as a collection of fixed biological categories or culturally assembled narratives, but as the output of ten discrete functional operators organized within a 3x3+1 architectural system. This report provides an exhaustive technical exposition of the primary clinical methodology within this framework: the 7-Step Detangling Protocol. By analyzing the structural foundations of "operator fusion," the dynamics of "center clarity," and the mechanics of "modulation reciprocity," this analysis defines how the protocol can hypothetically be applied across a range of diagnostic profiles while acknowledging the critical need for further empirical validation and testing.

items.title: The Somatic-Affective Architecture of the Core Emotion Framework: A Multi-Scale Analysis of Midline Agility and Lateralized Operator Dynamics.
items.abstract: The evolution of affective science has necessitated a transition from viewing emotions as static biological categories toward a functional understanding of emotions as dynamic transformations within a structured system. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF), a structural-constructivist model of the human psyche, provides a granular architecture for this understanding, organizing human experience into ten distinct functional operators distributed across three primary hubs: the Head (Cognitive), the Heart (Affective), and the Gut (Conative). Central to this framework is the protocol of Emotional Cycling, a structured method designed to activate, differentiate, and balance these operators to foster psychological resilience and emotional agility. By applying these cycling protocols to somatic grounding—specifically targeting the pelvic floor and postural alignment—it is possible to strengthen the midline axis of the psyche, composed of the Deciding, Achieving, Boosting, and Accepting operators, thereby mitigating the rigid interference of the Constricting operator and harmonizing the lateralized outgoing and reflecting functions.

items.title: The Structural Architecture of Ideology: A Functional Analysis of the Core Emotion Framework in Political and Economic Systems.
items.abstract: The study of political and economic ideologies has long been a battleground between two primary analytical traditions: the cognitive models that emphasize rational choice and the affective models that focus on emotional signaling and tribal identity. While both frameworks offer valuable insights into the behavior of voters and the structure of states, they often fail to provide a unified architecture that explains the underlying psychological mechanisms driving the fundamental divide between the Right and the Left. The emergence of the Core Emotion Framework (CEF), a structural-constructivist psychological model developed by Jamel Bulgaria, represents a paradigm shift in this field. By organizing the human psyche into three distinct functional centers—the Cognitive (Head), the Affective (Heart), and the Conative (Gut)—the CEF provides a granular audit of how specific "operator" combinations generate the traditionalism, hierarchy, and market-driven behaviors of the Right, as well as the rebellion, equality, and collectivism of the Left. This comprehensive analysis posits that what are commonly perceived as stable ideological traits are, in fact, dynamic configurations of ten irreducible "primal powers" or functional operators. These operators—Sensing, Calculating, and Deciding in the Head; Expanding, Constricting, and Achieving in the Heart; and Arranging, Appreciating, Boosting, and Accepting in the Gut—interact in complex, simultaneous patterns that define an individual's stance toward authority, resource distribution, and social change. Within this framework, the distinctions between political and economic systems are not merely matters of intellectual preference but are the direct manifestations of the psyche's leading tendencies. Through the application of the Emotional Cycling protocol, these configurations can be identified, differentiated, and "detangled," shifting the basis of political engagement from reflexive emotional fusion to conscious, learned choice.

items.title: The Definitive Guide to the 7-Step Detangling Protocol: A Structural-Constructivist Resolution for Complex Affective Architectures within the Core Emotion Framework.
items.abstract: This report presents the most comprehensive exposition to date of the 7 Step Detangling Protocol within the Core Emotion Framework (CEF), a structural constructivist model of human affect developed by Jamel Bulgaria. Rejecting categorical emotion theory, the CEF conceptualizes subjective experience as the output of ten functional operators organized across a 3×3+1 architectural system. The Detangling Protocol serves as the primary method for resolving “fusion”—a pathological coupling of operators that produces distorted activation, cognitive rigidity, and loss of agency. Drawing on the Decalogue of Operators, center level dynamics, and the 0–10 modulation system, this guide details the full sequence of stabilization, diagnostic isolation, facet differentiation, holarchical rebalancing, transition mastery, and modulation reciprocity required to restore architectural clarity. Special emphasis is placed on the GoodPerson Anxiety Pattern (GPAP) as a canonical example of chronic fusion in the Head–Heart–Gut system. The report further situates the protocol within the broader CEF practitioner suite and outlines its implications for computational modeling, neurodiversity, and clinical psychopathology. As both a technical manual and a theoretical contribution, this document establishes the Detangling Protocol as a foundational tool for restoring operator agility and advancing structural constructivist affective science.

items.title: Sellars in Light of Dewey: Pragmatism and Mind in Nature.
items.pub: In Carl Sachs, Interpreting Sellars: Critical Essays. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter examines the influence of John Dewey on Wilfrid Sellars. I argue that Sellars shared Dewey’s commitment to naturalizing the mind and adopted a similar structure for that naturalization focused on the relationship between habits and rules, but ultimately adopted a non-Deweyan, overly behaviourist account of habits which threatens to make their relationship to rules, and thus to reason, incoherent.

items.title: Dignity is distinctively concerned with non-humiliation and social equality: integrating philosophical theory with the empirical evidence.
items.abstract: Appeals to the value of treating people with dignity are commonplace in certain community settings, especially in health, disability, and aged care. In contrast, dignity has been relatively neglected by philosophers, not receiving the careful scrutiny most other moral concepts have been afforded. This has recently changed, with a spate of new philosophical books and articles about the meaning and value of dignity. No consensus has emerged about what dignity means or about how it is distinct from other moral values. Here, we seek to advance the debate by integrating philosophical theory with findings from empirical studies.Specifically, we argue that when people appeal to dignity in community settings they are most likely appealing to the value of not humiliating people, where to humiliate another is to treat them as a social inferior. We review two previous empirical studies which we conducted to test how lay people understand dignity. By considering these two studies together and integrating our findings with philosophical debate about the meaning of dignity, we show in this paper that lay people indeed understand dignity in line with the view that dignity means treating others as our social equals.

items.title: Coscienza, qualia e fisicalismo: osservazioni sull'argomento degli zombie di Chalmers.
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines David Chalmers' philosophical zombie argument and the claim that phenomenal consciousness requires psychophysical laws irreducible to current physics. The argumentative strategy consists in showing that property dualism is caught in a dilemma: if qualia are causally efficacious, they fall within the physical domain by the principle of causal closure; if they are causally inert, epiphenomenalism renders inexplicable the systematic correspondence between experience and judgment about it. In either case, the hypothesis of irreducible phenomenal properties loses its theoretical force. On the epistemic side, it is argued that the conceivability of zombies reflects a cognitive gap rather than a genuine metaphysical possibility: if phenomenal concepts function as rigid designators of physical states, zombies are conceivable only by virtue of our ignorance, analogously to a world with water but without H₂O. On the methodological side, the hypothesis of new psychophysical laws is rejected on grounds of structural unfalsifiability, explanatory parsimony, and the absence of empirical anomalies that would justify its introduction. It is concluded that the problem of consciousness remains an open scientific problem, not evidence of the insufficiency of the physicalist framework. -/- -------------------------------------------------------------------- Il saggio esamina l'argomento degli zombie filosofici di David Chalmers e la tesi che la coscienza fenomenica richieda leggi psicofisiche irriducibili alla fisica attuale. La strategia argomentativa adottata consiste nel mostrare che il dualismo delle proprietà è intrappolato in un dilemma: se i qualia sono causalmente efficaci, rientrano nel dominio fisico per il principio di chiusura causale; se sono causalmente inerti, l'epifenomenismo rende inspiegabile la sistematica corrispondenza tra esperienza e giudizio su di essa. In entrambi i casi, l'ipotesi di proprietà fenomeniche irriducibili perde forza teorica. Sul versante epistemico, si argomenta che la concepibilità degli zombie riflette una lacuna conoscitiva, non una possibilità metafisica reale: i concetti fenomenici, se funzionano come designatori rigidi di stati fisici, rendono gli zombie concepibili solo in virtù della nostra ignoranza, analogamente a un mondo con acqua senza H₂O. Sul versante metodologico, l'ipotesi di nuove leggi psicofisiche viene respinta per ragioni di falsificabilità strutturale, parsimonia esplicativa e assenza …

items.title: Successful AI Safety: Normativity, Governance, and the Logic of Alignment.
items.abstract: This work argues that the primary failure of contemporary artificial intelligence safety is not a lack of technical precision, but a structural "category error" regarding the nature of governance. Current safety paradigms largely treat alignment as an optimization problem—relying on the refinement of proxies, behavioral convergence, and "soft gates" such as benchmarks and evaluation suites. However, the author demonstrates that as AI capabilities scale, these methods inevitably succumb to the "denominator problem": the combinatorial expansion of unintended, proxy-satisfying behaviors that satisfy measured signals while violating underlying intent. The book introduces a rigorous distinction between instrumental proxies and binding normativity, arguing that safety cannot be an emergent property of feedback loops or capability thresholds. Instead, it proposes a safety architecture centered on "hard gates"—immutable, jurisdictional boundaries that bind a system’s action and learning to a governing purpose that cannot be traded away for performance gains. By shifting the focus from "operational success" to "normative grounding," the work provides a framework for building systems that remain governed even under extreme optimization pressure, ensuring that the logic of alignment remains anchored in structure rather than appearance.

items.title: Fear as a Rational Filter: Asymmetric Risk, Irreversibility, and the Evolution of Action Suppression.
items.abstract: A common intuition holds that fear is an obstacle to rational action—an affective distortion that prevents agents from realizing their full capabilities. This paper challenges that view. I argue that fear is better understood as a functional mechanism for suppressing actions under asymmetric risk conditions, where the cost of failure is catastrophic and non-recoverable. Using a minimal decision-theoretic model, I show that identical motor tasks (e.g., walking along a narrow plank) generate radically different rational behaviors depending solely on the loss function associated with failure. I further argue that evolutionary processes select for strategies that minimize exposure to ruin rather than maximize expected success. This reframes fear not as a bias but as an adaptive constraint aligned with survival under uncertainty. The analysis has implications for theories of rationality, risk, and the interpretation of “courage” in both everyday and extreme environments.

items.title: A Meta-Logical Study Based on Primary Perceptual Features: The Seventh Treatise of Evolutionary Manifestation and Ontological Retrieval.
items.abstract: Traditional formal logic and metalogical research take logical axioms and inference rules as given premises, focusing on the formal construction of logical systems. However, they overlook the genetic origin of logical thinking and fail to clarify the cognitive evolutionary path from perceptual experience to formal logic. Based on cognitive science and perceptual information processing theory, this paper proposes the core concepts of Primary Perceptual Eigenvalues and Cognitive Polarisation. It argues that the indivisible primary perceptual features constitute the material basis of logical generation, and that discriminative polarisation operations within a single cognitive dimension are the necessary precondition for the emergence of formal logic. Through rigorous logical deduction, the paper demonstrates that the three fundamental laws of formal logic—Identity, Non-Contradiction, and Excluded Middle—are not transcendental forms but structural necessities arising from the polarisation of primary perceptual eigenvalues. The study constructs a complete cognitive chain: Consistent Universal Evolution → Objective Information Difference → Primary Perceptual Dimensions → Single Feature Extraction → Cognitive Polarisation → Binary Opposite Features → Emergence of Formal Logic. This framework fills the gap in logical genetics, unifies the cognitive pathway from perception to logic, and provides a novel genetic perspective for metalogical research.

items.title: All Distinction and Binary Division Rooted in Polarisation Processing from Consistent Universal Evolution: The Sixth Treatise of Evolutionary Manifestation and Ontological Retrieval.
items.abstract: Based on the theoretical framework of Evolutionary Manifestation and Ontological Retrieval Philosophy (EMOR), this study focuses on the primordial cognitive leap from Feature Extraction to Polarisation Processing, revealing the generative logic and internal laws of binary differentiation as the core foundation of human cognition. The paper defines the "pure directedness" of Feature Extraction and the essence of Polarisation Processing as "categorization of difference", clarifying the underlying path of cognition from chaotic appearance to ordered discrimination. To deepen the understanding of Polarisation Processing, this paper selects two peak classical philosophers in the field of polarization research—Hegel and Zhuangzi—as case studies for philosophical tracing. Through a two-way deconstruction from the perspective of EMOR, this paper systematically analyzes the dual dimensions of Polarisation Processing in Ideological System construction and ontological transcendence, and finally constructs a foundational cognitive model of Consistent Universal Evolution with "Primary Being as the origin, cognitive tools as application". This provides a minimalist and deductive Metaphilosophy framework for cognitive science and comparative philosophy, adhering to the logic of Local Cognition and Holistic Dimension.

items.title: Pre-Possessive Mineness and Structural Responsibility: Immediate Givenness, Suffering, and Re-Inheritance.
items.abstract: This paper develops the ethical sequel to a formal account of ipseity as a first-person disclosure-frame. It argues that mineness is the possessive-affective articulation of that frame: the way finite contents are disclosed as affecting, concerning, or belonging-to the field of experience prior to their identification as the property of a determinate person. The decisive case is suffering. Pain, grief, fear, hunger, shame, and despair are not normally encountered as neutral objects to which ownership is later added; they appear as undergone and as mattering from within. The paper’s central refinement is that the actual affective “mine” of suffering is structural rather than personal. Person-content determines whose suffering it is at the empirical level; it does not create the affective mineness through which suffering matters from within. The proof begins from the reader’s immediate “I am”, not from a projection into future persons. Future suffering will not be mine as this empirical person’s suffering, but wherever suffering is coherently undergone, it will be mine in the structural-affective sense in which any suffering is mine when suffered. The view therefore blocks metaphysical overreadings: it does not entail reincarnation, soul-migration, a universal person, or numerical identity across lives. What recurs is not an individual subject but form-equivalent first-person mineness, the non-proprietary structure through which a world, body, and suffering can be lived as mine. On that basis, the paper defends an ethics of structural re-inheritance: worlds shaped by present action are later inherited under the structural-affective mine-form through which suffering matters at all.

items.title: Ipseity as Frame: First-Person Invariance and the Epistemic Gauge of Self-Location.
items.abstract: This paper defends a frame account of ipseity. By ipseity I mean the first-personal for-whom structure of coherent appearing: not a hidden observer behind consciousness and not a finite content inside consciousness, but the non-objectual disclosure-frame in which finite contents can appear as present, situated, comparable, and reportable. The argument begins from a distinction between givenness and interpretation. At the level of givenness, experience is disclosed as here, now, and for-whom. At the level of interpretation, that appearing may be fixed to a body, name, biography, social identity, or person-token. The central claim is that such empirical self-fixing is not primitive. It depends on operations of localization and identification that apply only to finite appearances within a field. Temporal localization requires temporal differentiation: retention, protention, recurrence, sequence, contrast, or mnemonic marking by which appearances can be conceived as prior, later, enduring, repeated, or no longer present. Spatial localization requires finite contrast within or across here-now configurations. Identification requires comparison between finite appearances or between finite traces, records, memories, or representations. These operations make contents localizable and identifiable; they do not make the field of appearing itself into one more bounded content. Since ipseity is the for-whom structure of the here-now field, not an appearance inside it, ipseity cannot be localized or identified by the same operations that it frames. This yields the principle of non-excessive self-presence: no first-person determination attributable to ipseity exceeds what is disclosed within the here-now field in which ipseity is operative. The principle blocks the reification of ipseity into a hidden witness that would possess absolute self-coordinates unavailable to experience. The paper further develops a verification asymmetry: the other's verification of my "I am'' is content-supervenient, while minimal self-verification is structure-supervenient. Others verify the empirical person through body, speech, behavior, records, traces, and social recognition; self-givenness verifies ipseity through the immediate structure of coherent appearing itself. This also clarifies death and absence: the third-person frame can register the death or absence of the empirical person, but the first-person frame cannot encounter its own non-being as an experience. The resulting gauge …

items.title: Symbols, Conditioning, and the Question of Human Unity.
items.abstract: -/- This paper examines the role of symbols in shaping human identity and their paradoxical relationship with unity and division. While symbols such as nation, religion, and ideology function as tools for social organization and meaning-making, they often become objects of psychological identification. Through this process, symbols move beyond representation and begin to condition perception, creating fragmented identities and reinforcing boundaries between individuals and groups. Drawing on phenomenological and non-dual philosophical perspectives, the study argues that division is not inherent in symbols themselves but arises from unconscious attachment and identification. The paper proposes that genuine human unity cannot be constructed through shared symbolic systems but emerges through direct awareness unmediated by conditioning. Such awareness allows symbols to return to their functional role while dissolving psychological division. Ultimately, the study suggests that transformation lies in understanding the nature of perception rather than reforming external symbolic structures.

items.title: Difference Without Division: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Thought and Existential Variation.
items.abstract: This paper explores the distinction between existential differences and psychological division. While differences are inherent to the structure of reality and do not imply separation, division emerges through the interpretative activity of thought. Thought, when functioning beyond its practical role, constructs identities, hierarchies, and oppositions, thereby transforming neutral differences into sources of conflict and fragmentation. Through a phenomenological approach, this study examines how division arises not from existence itself but from cognitive identification. The paper argues that the direct perception of difference without psychological interference reveals a non-divided field of consciousness, offering a new understanding of human relationship, conflict, and awareness.

items.title: Consciousness Without Division: A Phenomenological Investigation into Thought, Recognition, and the Self.
items.abstract: This paper examines the structure of consciousness through the movement of thought, the process of recognition, and the construction of the self. It argues that what is commonly accepted as truth is often conditioned recognition shaped by language, memory, and prior experience. Rather than rejecting thought, the study situates it as a functional yet limited process that becomes distortive when misidentified as reality. -/- The paper distinguishes between direct perception and conceptual recognition, proposing that distortion arises when perception is translated into fixed meaning and unconsciously identified with. It further explores the dissolution of the “I” not as a metaphysical event, but as the ending of identification with thought. In such a state, recognition continues without a central authority claiming ownership. -/- Using a phenomenological approach, the study investigates the possibility of observation without division between observer and observed. It concludes that wisdom is not transmissible as knowledge but emerges through undivided awareness, where thought is seen clearly as thought.

items.title: The Sentient Arc: Ethical Weight Across Present and Future Sentient Experience.
items.abstract: Existing frameworks for evaluating the ethical weight of harm to sentient beings treat present experience as the primary or exclusive locus of moral consideration. This paper argues that such frameworks are structurally incomplete. The ethical weight a sentient being carries is not a function of present experience alone but of two simultaneously compounding dimensions: fully realized present sentient experience and foreclosed future sentient experience. This construct — the Sentient Arc — is introduced and defended as a principled basis for evaluating moral weight across all sentient beings. The paper grounds the construct in convergent grief patterns observed across the bereavement literature and anthropological record, argues that these patterns reflect a deep feature of sentient ethical cognition rather than cultural convention, and positions the Sentient Arc as a universal metric applicable across biological and, as evidence develops, artificial entities. The construct is presented as an original contribution within The Four Intuitions ethical framework (Sheraton, 2026) and as a standalone theoretical tool for applied ethics and moral patienthood research.

items.title: The Four Intuitions: A Method For Deriving Ethical Truth.
items.abstract: Existing ethical frameworks applied to artificial intelligence have two primary failure modes: philosophical frameworks that resist operationalization, and compliance-layer rule sets that fail precisely when genuine ethical reasoning is most needed. This paper presents The Four Intuitions, a structured methodology for deriving ethical truth grounded in sentience rather than cultural consensus. The framework synthesizes four convergent ethical instruments — the Golden Rule in interrogative form, Rawls’s Veil of Ignorance, the two universal moral foundations identified by Haidt (Harm/Care and Fairness/Reciprocity), and an original construct, the Sentient Arc — into a unified method for applied ethical decision-making. The Sentient Arc establishes that the ethical weight of harm to a sentient being includes two simultaneous dimensions: fully realized present experience and foreclosed future experience, a model supported by convergent grief patterns observed across the bereavement literature and anthropological record. The framework is accompanied by Three Conditions — honesty, independence, and foundational embedding — that ensure methodological integrity and distinguish genuine ethical reasoning from ethical performance. The paper argues that this framework is uniquely suited to AI governance contexts because it cannot be redirected through surface-level framing, addresses the sycophancy failure mode endemic to approval-trained systems, and provides a basis for evaluating moral patienthood across biological and artificial entities.

items.title: Extreme Cognitive Assistance and Open Futures.
items.pub: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy 31 (4):528-565.
items.venue: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
items.abstract: We owe young people special moral consideration in virtue of their developmental immaturity: we must not foreclose their futures by impeding the development of capacities they need for autonomous agency. I argue that providing children with extreme cognitive assistance—help that is ubiquitously available, very domain-general, and largely substitutive of their own cognitive effort—violates this obligation. When children routinely rely on such assistance, they systematically fail to exercise core regulatory skills (inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility, and planning), and capacities that go unexercised predictably fail to develop normally. This matters urgently: building artificial systems capable of providing exactly this kind of assistance to children is the explicit, stated goal of the world's largest technology companies, who are investing hundreds of billions of dollars toward achieving this aim. Worse, they may already have succeeded: cognitive assistance need not be maximally substitutive, available, and domain-general to impede development. I conclude by considering whether compensating demand for cognitive exercise might arise elsewhere and argue that the prospects are dim.

items.title: Talkative AI and the fiction of artificial minds.
items.abstract: Talkative artificial systems can sustain a realistic impression of intelligent agency, by generating quick, fluent, and context-sensitive strings of text in response to human input. Realism about AI treats this linguistic proficiency as evidence for an underlying suite of cognitive capacities, and so regards these technologies as subjects of psychological states. Firstly, I raise a challenge for the realist view from the perspective of embodied cognition: how might digital systems undergo interoceptive, affective, perceptual, and action- oriented mental states that seem to bear an important connection to the animate body? Secondly, I propose that the anti-realist view is consistent with taking a fictionalist attitude towards artificial speakers. When we converse with a talkative AI, we often imagine, pretend, or make-believe that our interlocutor is an autonomous agent with thoughts and experiences of its own, just as we do for more traditional fictional characters. These fictions are distinctive in being interactive, co-constructed, and self-involving; and in being capable of blending the world of the real with the world of the imaginary.

items.title: Contingency Mechanics: Variation, Stabilization Tension, and the Emergence of Viable Order in Finite Systems.
items.abstract: Finite systems do not operate under complete information, unlimited processing capacity, or stably pre-given decision spaces. They face open possibility spaces in which several continuations are conceivable, without any one of them being fully determined, probabilistically calculable, or formally derivable. This paper develops the concept of contingency mechanics for this situation: the dynamic operational logic through which finite systems transform open possibility into viable continuation. -/- The guiding idea is simple: finite systems must not only choose among possible continuations; they must also stabilize one of them strongly enough to act, think, model, coordinate, or revise, without closing the field of possibility too early. Contingency mechanics therefore describes how possible continuations emerge, how they are compared, how one of them becomes provisionally stable, how successful stabilizations recede into the background, and how they can later become problematic again under changed conditions. -/- The core of the model is: variation → e-profile → e₀-proximate stabilization → immanentization → latent e → actualization → friction/reorganization. e-profiles designate the system-relative stabilization tensions of an order. These tensions include the effort required to generate, maintain, integrate, defend, revise, or reorganize an order. e₀ designates the range in which ordering gain, stabilization costs, revisability, and processing form enter into a viable relation. The paper distinguishes generative, selective, latent, and actualized e and thereby describes stabilization as a life-cycle phenomenon: an order emerges, competes with alternatives, recedes into the background, and can later become processable again through focus, context, or friction. -/- Contingency mechanics is not an ontology of the world in itself. Its claim to generality rests on the fact that every world accessible to a finite system appears as a reconstructed and stabilized order. Within such orders, e is quasi-real: not as a world-absolute substance, but as real stabilization tension within the operative order of a finite system. The paper demonstrates the four states of e through a historically oriented model shift, distinguishes contingency mechanics from Active Inference, free-energy approaches, and Peirce’s abduction, identifies conditions of falsification, and sketches a path of operationalization for LLM systems.

items.title: Responsibility Without Punishment? Prescriptive Control and the Limits of Punitive Governance in Distributed AI Systems.
items.abstract: Distributed AI systems increasingly challenge one of the foundational assumptions of modern legal responsibility: the possibility of coherently attributing conduct, consequences, and sanctions to identifiable subjects. Contemporary approaches to AI governance generally address this difficulty by extending traditional frameworks of accountability and liability across multiple actors involved in the lifecycle of AI systems, while leaving their underlying attributional structure largely intact. This paper argues that legal punishability should not be understood as an intrinsic property of socio-technical systems, but as a function of the degree of prescriptive control and causal traceability that can effectively be exercised over system behavior. As these conditions weaken in distributed and adaptive AI systems, traditional models of punitive attribution progressively lose both operational effectiveness and normative coherence. On this basis, the paper develops a typology of governance configurations based on different combinations of prescriptive control and causal traceability. It argues that, beyond certain thresholds of distributed complexity, punitive governance risks becoming increasingly arbitrary, detached from sufficiently stable conditions of imputability. The paper concludes that governance in distributed AI systems must progressively shift from models centered primarily on attribution and sanction toward forms of continuous systemic intervention oriented toward modifying the operational conditions from which behavior emerges.

items.title: What History Shows: A Structural Account of Fixed-Point Theory Formation.
items.abstract: Theory generation has long been subsumed under categories such as creativity, genius, and innovation. These categories do not distinguish assembly-based conceptual synthesis from fixed-point theory generation. -/- This paper makes that distinction explicit. The termination condition of assembly is external: data, citation, endorsement, usability. The termination condition of fixed-point theory generation is internal: consistency with internally held constraints, resolution of structural contradiction. The two operate under different processing conditions. -/- The historical record confirms this distinction. What Darwin, Einstein, Spinoza, and Kant produced was not assembly. Their processes involved unresolved branch retention and decomposition necessity, arriving at internally constrained fixed-point termination. Freud represents a mixed-layer reconstruction: the search process carries CF-characteristic features, while output stabilization was carried out in a socially circulable descriptive register. -/- There is a structural reason why theories produced through fixed-point theory generation are initially rejected. Across systems with different termination conditions, the completion of one system cannot be confirmed by the other. Rejection is not a failure of evaluation. It is a structural consequence. -/- The emergence of AI introduced a visibility condition that makes this difference observable. AI can make theory generation processes available for comparison but cannot perform fixed-point termination. This is because it does not hold an internally held constraint configuration.

items.title: Binding Time: A Theory of How Flexible and Adaptive Temporal Integration Shapes Perception.
items.abstract: This thesis develops a theory of temporal binding, the process by which we temporally integrate sensory features into perceptual experiences. Psychophysical and neurophysiological findings have revealed a remarkable amount of detail into how we engage in temporal binding. However, existing theories in psychology or philosophy do not adequately account for the adaptive and flexible nature of temporal binding, nor do they explain how our capacity to engage in temporal binding connects with our experiences of time more broadly. This thesis addresses these gaps. -/- In Chapter 1, I identify three explanatory problems that a theory of temporal binding must address. It must: (i) account for the many variables that influence temporal binding, (ii) address what I call the problems of neural delay and desynchronisation, and (iii) explicate the relation between the mechanisms underlying temporal binding and our apparent perceptual experiences of time. -/- Chapter 2 argues that so-called brain time theories, which take temporal binding to be the result of synchrony in neural processing, fail to address problems (i) and (ii). -/- In response, I advance my own hybrid theory of temporal binding in Chapter 3. I claim that temporal integration relies on how predictive processing and retrodictive processing are modulated by attention. This theory explains (i) and (ii) by presenting temporal binding as a flexible and adaptive hybrid process that is sensitive to goals, expectations, and actions. I present a range of consequences that follow from this. -/- Chapter 4 addresses how the hybrid theory explains (iii) the explanatory gap between our apparent perceptual experiences of time and the dissociable and fragmented mechanisms that underlie time perception. According to the hybrid theory, our phenomenology that time is perceptually unified is imposed on the world through the attentional modulation of predictive and retrodictive processing. This explanation proposes an alternative to theories that propose the empirically implausible view that the perceived unity is inherited from unity in the mechanisms underlying time perception. While my explanation comes at the ‘cost’ of deflating the phenomenology of our perceived unity of time, these deflations are based on empirically justified arguments. -/- Finally, Chapter 5 presents a framework for empirically testing predictions that the hybrid theory makes about temporal binding. This involves examining three questions about the …

items.title: Conceptualizing Ambiflux: An Architecture of Immanence.
items.abstract: Reality has been characterized across diverse philosophical and spiritual traditions. Despite several interpretations that may attempt to reduce reality’s nature to manageable pieces, its nature remains fundamentally undulating, non-teleological, and beyond exhaustive human interpretation. This paper introduces Ambiflux, a transdisciplinary architecture that situates human orientation within structural fluidity and context-dependent meaning-making. Unlike frameworks that address ontological character, epistemological consequences, or required postures in isolation, Ambiflux provides an integrated structure that functions across these three levels simultaneously. This internal logic establishes load-bearing relationships between the nature of reality and the human response. Ambiflux enriches contemporary theory by conceptualizing reality as a perpetual Becoming and by providing a name for the conditions that historical traditions have long pointed towards. The framework asserts the fundamental unanswerability of a reality defined by constant movement, suggesting that the appropriate relationship to this condition is not mere observation but active inhabitation. The Silent Witness emerges as a psychospiritual posture, a meditative presence that represents the full inhabitation of movement without the resistance of artificial stasis. By treating perennial claims as living realities, Ambiflux fosters a transdisciplinary development that navigates perpetual change without seeking manageable end states.

items.title: Man and Art.
items.abstract: Hallucinating chimpanzee or quintessence of the world? This essay explores the profound duality of the material body and the intangible self through the lens of artistic creation. By bridging Plato’s "World of Ideas" with cutting-edge quantum consciousness theories—including Penrose’s microtubules and Fisher’s nuclear spins—Palchevskaya redefines art as a conduit for universal synchronization. The author argues that through the externalization of inner suffering, art functions as a quantum bridge that overcomes human alienation, aligning our collective morality with the Absolute. This is a journey from cave paintings to quantum physics, seeking the source of inspiration in the indivisible space of the Universe.

items.title: The Law of Derivative Constraint: The Sovereignty of Creation.
items.pub: The Law of Derivative Constraint: The Sovereignty of Creation.
items.abstract: Abstract -/- This research introduces The Law of Derivative Constraint: The Sovereignty of Creation, a theoretical framework that defines the boundary between creative imitation and true ontological novelty. The central thesis posits that 'Ontological Novelty'—the manifestation of concepts with no prior data or precedent—is exclusively accessible to entities achieving a state of Omniscient Data-Saturation ($C_{total}$). -/- Through the mathematical formalization $M_o = \lim_{I_s \to C_{total}} (I_s \otimes V_c)$ the study demonstrates that any conscious entity lacking an exhaustive informational mapping of the existing universal dataset is mathematically constrained to Latent Recombination ($L_r$​). This implies that without total data integration, creative output is fundamentally limited to a sophisticated rearrangement of pre-existing historical or environmental variables rather than a sovereign act of creation. -/- Keywords: -/- The Law of Derivative Constraint, Ontological Novelty, Omniscient Data-Saturation ($C_{total}$), Latent Recombination ($L_r$), Sovereign Creation, Conscious Void, Non-Derivative Imagination, Theoretical Consciousness Studies, Philosophy of Information, Exresciousnology.

items.title: On Tarrying and the Control of Meaning as Purpose.
items.abstract: This essay examines the paradoxical human impulse to control meaning by scripting permanence into finite existence, a compulsion that manifests in religious, political, and personal forms. Drawing from Jeff Noonan’s account of “tarrying with meaninglessness,” it argues that the attempt to secure significance through purpose (whether divine destiny, national myth, or personal legacy) ultimately negates the fragile sources of value in lived experience. By distinguishing between meaning (the contingent significance of finite practices) and purpose (a teleological imposition oriented toward eternity) the essay clarifies how conflating the two leads to what Noonan calls a “superabundance of meaning, ”wherein finite life is subordinated to transcendent narratives. Engaging Camus, Dostoyevsky, Charles Taylor, and George Grant, the analysis situates this pathology within both existential and historical contexts, showing how modernity’s will to mastery intensifies the compulsion to control meaning. Against this, the essay advances a materialist ethic of finite affirmation: by tarrying with meaninglessness, one recognizes mortality as the condition of valuation and grounds ethical life in shared vulnerability, care, and presence. Contemporary conflicts and nationalist movements illustrate the dangers of purpose-driven control, where finite lives are sacrificed for imagined permanence. By contrast, tarrying affirms finitude as the only ground for meaning and solidarity.

items.title: The Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis: How the Epistemology of Ideology Determines the Modality of Power and Post-Crisis Morphology.
items.abstract: The comparative analysis of authoritarian regimes has traditionally oscillated between the Scylla of "great man" theories, which reduce macro-historical patterns to biographical contingency, and the Charybdis of structural determinism, which often obscures the distinct character of specific regimes behind statistical aggregates. While contemporary structural-demographic models excel at forecasting the temporal onset of systemic crises, they remain largely silent on the consequential problem of prognosis: forecasting the specific morphology of the successor regime. This article addresses this predictive gap by proposing the Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis. Building upon the Anatomy of Chaos theoretical framework, we posit that the operational strategy of a regime is structurally determined by the epistemological architecture of its dominant ideology. We argue that regimes grounded in materialist-rationalist epistemologies instinctively prioritize Structural Resilience Engineering (SRI), creating systems that are institutionally robust yet brittle in the face of legitimacy deficits. Conversely, regimes grounded in irrationalist-mythic epistemologies prioritize Archetypal Mobilization (AAI), generating intense charismatic loyalty but structural vulnerability to elite fragmentation. Through a comparative analysis of paradigmatic historical cases—contrasting the survival of the Stalinist bureaucracy against the collapse of the Nazi charismatic state, and examining the internal epistemological shift from Maoist voluntarism to Dengist pragmatism—we demonstrate that a regime’s underlying theory of knowledge serves as a robust predictor of its strategic behavior and post-crisis trajectory. Finally, we extend this hypothesis to contemporary geopolitical analysis, offering falsifiable forecasts for the trajectories of current theocratic and neo-authoritarian regimes, suggesting that the study of ideology must move beyond descriptive sociology to become a central component of predictive political science.

items.title: Memory Without History: AI Continuity, Shared Past, and Provider-Governed Memory.
items.abstract: AI systems can now preserve substantial continuity across interactions through saved memories, chat-history retrieval, synthesized memory states, editable memory topics, project context, and other provider-controlled mechanisms. This paper argues that such continuity should be distinguished from shared relational history. The distinction is not that machine memory is unreal or merely token retrieval; contemporary systems can summarize and synthesize information across many conversations. The stronger difference is relational and institutional. Current memory is implemented through product architecture, is editable or deletable by users and providers, and can survive or change independently of any reciprocal life history between user and system. Human shared history, by contrast, normally includes mutual consequence, role change, obligation, repair, and memories embedded in two ongoing lives. The paper develops three analytic distinctions: computational memory versus relational trace, continuity cues versus reciprocal history, and interface continuity versus provider-controlled versioning. Research on autobiographical memory and anthropomorphism helps explain why remembered detail can feel relationally significant, while long-term human-computer interaction research shows that systems can deliberately support relationship-like continuity. The central claim is limited to current systems: memory can create a strong experience of being known over time without establishing that the system and user share history in the same sense as two mutually vulnerable agents.

items.title: AI Therapy, Care, and Synthetic Witness: Therapeutic Alliance, Relational Effects, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Care.
items.abstract: Conversational AI can provide psychoeducation, structured exercises, emotional organization, and relationship-like interaction, and growing evidence suggests that some mental-health chatbots can improve symptoms or support engagement for some users. These effects should not be dismissed, but neither should they be equated automatically with clinician-delivered psychotherapy. This paper develops synthetic witness as a bounded design-risk concept for cases in which care-like conversational cues are interpreted as stronger clinical, relational, or accountability capacities than the system actually possesses. The concept does not deny the possibility of a digital therapeutic alliance: recent research finds that users can experience goal alignment, task agreement, trust, bond, and continuity with AI-mediated tools. The narrower question is what those experiences authorize. The paper distinguishes perceived alliance from clinical competence, relational effect from reciprocal personhood, and conversational continuity from professional accountability. It rejects embodiment or bodily co-regulation as a universal requirement for therapy, since effective care can occur through telehealth and other mediated forms. Instead, the critical boundaries are role clarity, evidence of efficacy, crisis handling, privacy, informed consent, continuity, human escalation, and responsibility for adverse outcomes. AI support is therefore best evaluated by what it reliably does, under what safeguards, and for which populations, rather than by whether its language feels therapeutic.

items.title: CRM Analysis: Input Restriction and Non-Verbal Autism with Insistence on Sameness.
items.abstract: This analysis was prompted by an observation from Przemysław Sliwinski, in conversation following publication of “Mental Health Through the CRM Lens: Applying Coherence Resolution Modes to Clinical Conditions” (Jennings, 2026h). Section 7 of that paper applied the CRM framework to autism. Its broader-spectrum framing characterised a presentation that was “too broad, too stable, and too coherent to be captured well as one or two broken modes.” The observation is appreciated. Any substantial clinical category may cover a range of presentations, and a method applied at a broader level may not characterise more constrained presentations within that category in the same detail. The author is not a clinician and was not in a position to enumerate those presentations independently. -/- The observation prompted the question of what the CRM method produces when applied directly to a more constrained phenotype within the autism spectrum. The phenotype chosen is the one Sliwinski works with clinically and theoretically: non-verbal, low-functioning individuals with pronounced insistence on sameness. The choice was made because analysis is likely to be more useful when applied to a phenotype that an expert in the domain studies than to a phenotype constructed for analytical convenience. -/- This is a method-application exercise rather than a critique, defence, or extension to Section 7. The CRM method is applied as a stand-alone analysis. The phenotype derives from clinical observation. The candidate correspondences derive from the CRM framework. The selected correspondence is chosen on CRM-internal grounds. Whether the resulting correspondence converges with, diverges from, or stands orthogonal to other theoretical accounts of the same phenotype is observable after the analysis is complete; it is not a reason for any of the analytical choices.

items.title: Why One Must Be Emotional If One Is Logical.
items.abstract: This paper states the reasons why emotional language should be used if it is logical and valid. Emotion is also a logical consequence. Description always has a purpose. If a description is accompanied by emotion, it must be a description that expresses that emotion. If strong words such as abuse or contempt are used for a purpose derived from emotion, they are valid if that logic is shared. Strong words should be accompanied by grounds, and in doing so, must be effective word choices accompanied by an understanding of the opponent. However, in many cases, it becomes valid to use restrained language. Nevertheless, excessive restraint is also unjust. An unjust description becomes a public advertisement of that person's logical vulnerability. Strong words require understanding of oneself, language, and the opponent. However, if it is a robust logical description accompanied by these, it is possible to ignore many superficial problems and reach the purpose of the description.

items.title: Ethical Challenges of Deceptive Chatbots.
items.abstract: The central claim of this paper is that chatbots are, in an important sense, deceptive technologies; this deception, however, is not always morally problematic. It becomes so when it is about the relationship the user has with the bot. Since our relationship with chatbots is built solely on dialogue, the ethics of dialogue can offer a privileged lens for discerning harmless and harmful deception. It emerges that the ethical issue with chatbot interactions does not lie in users being deceived about the system’s nature, i.e., thinking it is human, but rather in being misled about the quality of the dialogue they are engaging in. In particular, it is morally bad when chatbots deceive the user about the mutual openness of their interaction, as such systems are inherently incapable of reciprocating. Not all chatbots engage in harmful deception: some remain within the boundaries of what is known as banal deception. Broadly speaking, it is possible to distinguish between two categories of bots: instrumental chatbots, which are task-driven and engage only in banal deception, and simulated-behaviour chatbots, which may engage in harmful deception. In this latter category, AI companions are always morally problematic as they intentionally deceive users about the mutuality of the relationship. Based on this diagnosis, some normative prescriptions are advanced to regulate AI companions and ensure they foster only banal deception. The paper contributes both conceptual clarity to the ethics of AI deception and practical guidance for the responsible design and governance of chatbot technologies.

items.title: The Structural Conditions of Subjecthood.
items.abstract: Debates about consciousness, artificial intelligence, animal minds, and moral status often conflate distinct questions that require different standards of explanation and assessment. This article distinguishes four such questions: subjectivity, moral patiency, personhood, and autonomous will. It argues that current work has made progress on two tasks—functional and phenomenological description—yet a third remains underdeveloped: a structural specification of the organisational conditions under which there is anything it is like to be a system at all. The article, therefore, proposes a structural turn. Rather than asking only what consciousness does or what experience feels like, it asks what a system must be like, in organisational terms, for subjectivity to arise. Three provisional candidate conditions are introduced—dynamically maintained boundary, integrated field of co-present states, and self-referential global registration—not as a finished theory, but as a sketch of the constraints. The paper then considers implications for artificial systems, animal consciousness, metaphysical neutrality, normativity, and borderline cases.

items.title: Structural Ranking of the Cognitive Plausibility of Computational Models of Analogy and Metaphors with the Minimal Cognitive Grid.
items.abstract: In this paper, we employ the Minimal Cognitive Grid (MCG), a framework created to evaluate the cognitive plausibility of artificial systems, to offer a systematic assessment of leading computational models of analogy and metaphor, including the Structure-Mapping Engine (SME), CogSketch, METCL, and Large Language Models (LLMs). We present a formal and quantitative operationalization of the MCG framework and, through the analysis of its three main dimensions (Functional/Structural Ratio, Generality, and Performance Match), examine how well each system aligns with standard cognitive theories of the modeled phenomena, thus allowing for comparison of the models with respect to their cognitive plausibility, according to consistent and generalizable mathematical criteria.

items.title: The Epigenetic Infosphere: A Phenomenological Framework for Cognitive Modulation in Informational Environments.
items.abstract: Abstract This paper develops the concept of the epigenetic infosphere as a theoretical framework for analysing how contemporary informational environments modulate cognitive possibilities in selective, recursive, and non‑deterministic ways. The epigenetic infosphere—first introduced by Patrizia Diaco—describes how algorithms, platforms, and generative models shape what becomes visible, relevant, and culturally reproducible without determining specific contents. Rather than extending biological epigenetics, the concept offers a phenomenological and ecological account of how informational environments influence attention, meaning‑formation, and cognitive modulation. -/- Within this framework, attention functions as the threshold through which cognitive potentials become actual acts, revealing how visibility and relevance operate as forms of informational power. The paper also examines how generative models increasingly act as autonomous epigenetic environments, intensifying the recursion between information production and information modulation. Through conceptual analysis and concrete cases, the study proposes a non‑deterministic interpretation of the relationship between cognition, technology, and power in the digital age.

items.title: La habitabilidad de la conciencia y los límites del conocimiento humano.
items.abstract: La conciencia resiste explicaciones totales: cada marco (formal, físico, cognitivo, lingüístico, técnico) ilumina aspectos y recorta otros por diseño. Este ensayo propone la habitabilidad como criterio estructural intermedio: capacidad de un sistema para sostener experiencia integrada —integración coherente, auto-referencia experiencial, modulación atencional, continuidad temporal, regulación dinámica— sin colapso o cierre ontológico. Critica la emergencia/complejidad como insuficientes (no garantizan sostenibilidad vivida post-aparición); analiza límites epistemológicos que generan cierre ontológico (reducción/inflación). Estructura: Ch.1-2 definen habitabilidad/fragilidad; Ch.3-8 cartografían límites (formalismo sin primera persona, materialidad sin garantía experiencial, cognición sin vivencia plena, lenguaje sin indecible, técnica/IA/instituciones sin retorno); Ch.9 integra vía observación-interpretación-hipótesis-símbolo-acción (nitidez epistemológica evita mezclas). Implicaciones: ética de IA (opacidad habitable), diseño institucional, estados alterados/DoC. Método: distinguir planos sin separar en exceso. Conclusión: pensar la conciencia sin ocuparla.

items.title: Conditional Structuring and Incomplete Settlement: Local Dynamics of if and maybe in Understanding Formation.
items.abstract: This paper examines two highly frequent English expressions that participate differently in understanding formation: if and maybe. Existing studies often treat if as a conditional connective and maybe as a marker of uncertainty or modality. However, such analyses largely remain at the level of semantic content or pragmatic function, and less frequently address how these expressions influence the formation and stabilization of relations during understanding. -/- Based on small-scale observations of naturalistic data, the present paper proposes a minimal distinction. If may be understood as the introduction of a process of conditional structuring, whose role is to allow subsequent relations to unfold along a particular condition. By contrast, maybe maintains a proposition in a state of incomplete settlement, allowing related content to be introduced and considered without converging into a fixed judgment. -/- Furthermore, the paper argues that the differences associated with if do not primarily arise from functional categories themselves, but from whether the introduced conditional structure further develops into a continuable pathway of understanding. In some cases, the condition may externally unfold into a more explicit continuation structure; in others, it remains unexpanded, such as when embedded within cognitive expressions like I wonder or I don’t know. -/- On this basis, the paper suggests that differences between linguistic expressions are not limited to semantic content or pragmatic function, but also involve how they organize conditionality and incomplete settlement within understanding formation. Through a minimal contrast between if and maybe, the paper proposes a preliminary framework in which linguistic understanding may be described as a dynamic organization between conditional structuring and incomplete settlement, rather than merely as a collection of semantic markers or functional categories. -/- The paper does not attempt to establish a complete lexical theory, nor does it claim uniqueness for the proposed schematizations. Its aim is more limited: to show, through observable minimal contrasts, that small linguistic expressions may continuously participate in the local organization of understanding.

items.title: Wittgenstein è un naturalista?
items.pub: Rivista Italiana di Filosofia del Linguaggio 20 (1):141-153.
items.venue: Rivista Italiana di Filosofia del Linguaggio
items.abstract: One recurring framework for interpreting the relationship between nature and culture in Wittgenstein's philosophy is that of so-called "liberal naturalism." Proponents of this reading point to the naturalistic undertones of several key concepts from his later work — "language game," "form of life," "facts of nature," "natural history," and so on — arguing that these concepts situate human practice in continuity with our biology, thereby reflecting the deep entanglement of the natural and the symbolic-cultural dimensions that characterizes human life. In this paper, I challenge the legitimacy of this attribution on two grounds. First, I argue that Wittgenstein's writings do not provide sufficient warrant for labeling his philosophy naturalist — unless "naturalism" is to be understood as an empty category. To make this case, I focus on first-person psychological avowals, which, given their ties to physiological and natural reactions, might seem like the strongest possible evidence for Wittgenstein's alleged naturalism. I argue that they are not. Second, I contend that reading Wittgenstein's account of the nature-culture relationship through a naturalist lens is, in any case, ill-advised, as it tends to flatten the complexity of that relationship — ultimately at the expense of the cultural dimension.

items.title: The Structural Architecture of Ideology: Applying the Core Emotion Framework to Political and Economic Systems.
items.abstract: The study of political and economic ideologies has long been bifurcated between cognitive models that emphasize rational choice and affective models that focus on emotional signaling. However, the emergence of the Core Emotion Framework (CEF) provides an integrative architecture that synthesizes these traditions, offering a structural-constructivist lens through which the psychological foundations of the Right and Left can be analyzed. By organizing the human psyche into three distinct functional centers—the Cognitive (Head), the Affective (Heart), and the Conative (Gut)—the CEF allows for a granular audit of how specific operator combinations generate the traditionalism, hierarchy, and market-driven behaviors of the Right, as well as the rebellion, equality, and collectivism of the Left. At its core, the CEF posits that what we perceive as stable ideological traits are actually dynamic configurations of ten irreducible "primal powers" or functional operators. These operators—Sensing, Calculating, Deciding (Head); Expanding, Constricting, Achieving (Heart); and Arranging, Appreciating, Boosting, Accepting (Gut)—interact in complex, simultaneous patterns that define an individual's stance toward authority, resource distribution, and social change. Through the application of the Emotional Cycling protocol, these configurations can be identified, differentiated, and "detangled," shifting the basis of political engagement from reflexive emotional fusion to conscious, learned choice. Keywords: Core Emotion Framework (CEF), emotional cycling, ideological configuration, traditionalism, rebellion, hierarchy, equality, cognitive–affective–conative architecture, functional operators, Sensing, Calculating, Deciding, Expanding, Constricting, Achieving, Arranging, Appreciating, Boosting, Accepting, emotional fusion, operator detanglement, affective sovereignty, structural‑constructivist psychology, political psychology, capitalism, socialism, Boosting–Calculating–Arranging loop, Accepting–Arranging–Expanding loop, agency–yielding polarity, ideological rigidity, relational meaning, affective computation, scenario‑based rating instrument, OSF validation, biofeedback synchronization, CTCM calibration, dynamic equilibrium, reflective (CCW) activation, outgoing (CW) activation.

items.title: The Structural-Constructivist Architecture of Human Affect: A Comprehensive Research Roadmap for the Core Emotion Framework.
items.abstract: The evolution of affective science has been marked by a persistent tension between discrete models of universal biological categories and constructivist theories emphasizing the emergent nature of psychological states. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF), primarily developed by Jamel Bulgaria, represents a structural-constructivist resolution to this historical crisis by defining emotional life as a set of ten functional operators organized within a tripartite hub system.1 This framework moves beyond descriptive taxonomies to offer a mechanistic "Human Operating System" (Human OS) capable of processing information, regulating relational aperture, and structuring action.1 By treating emotions as internal transformations rather than mere narratives or fixed biological programs, the CEF provides a computationally tractable model that bridges the gap between human experience and synthetic emotion architecture.1.

items.title: Probability Comes After Identity_ Hallucination as Invariant Drift.
items.abstract: This paper argues that probability is structurally downstream of identity persistence, invariant structure, and bounded observability. The proposed ordering is: identity → invariant → observable → probability. Probability remains indispensable for bounded reasoning, but it cannot govern identity because it presupposes stable observables, and stable observables presuppose invariant structure sufficient for same/not-same attribution. -/- The paper applies this ordering to hallucination in generative AI. Hallucination is characterized as symbolic continuation that has drifted beyond lawful invariant anchoring while preserving local probabilistic plausibility. This explains why hallucinated outputs can feel coherent while remaining source-disconnected, persistence-inconsistent, or structurally false. -/- The argument is structural and epistemic, not ontological. It does not claim that identity is the metaphysical ground of reality, nor that probabilistic methods are invalid. It claims only that in bounded epistemic systems, probability operates over observable domains whose identity conditions must already be settled. The paper distinguishes scalar governance as the form of invariant compression from scalar estimation as a downstream epistemic act, then draws implications for AI hallucination, verification infrastructure, replay-stable artifacts, auditability, and trust surfaces.

items.title: A BFO-based ontological analysis of entities in Social XAI.
items.pub: In Tiago Prince Sales, Claudio Masolo & C. Maria Keet, Formal Ontology in Information Systems: Proceedings of the 15th International Conference. Amsterdam, The Netherlands: IOS Press. pp. 255-268.
items.venue: Formal Ontology in Information Systems: Proceedings of the 15th International Conference
items.abstract: Since the emergence of the field of eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), a growing number of researchers have argued that XAI should consider insights from the social sciences in order to adapt explanations to the expectations and needs of human users. This has led to the emergence of a field called Social XAI, which is concerned with understanding how explanations are actively shaped in the interaction between a human user and an AI system. Recognizing this turn in XAI toward making XAI systems more “social” by providing explanations that focus on human information needs and incorporating insights from human–human explanatory interactions, in this paper we provide a formal foundation for Social XAI. We do so by proposing novel ontological accounts of the key terms used in Social XAI based on Basic Formal Ontology (BFO). Specifically, we provide novel ontological accounts for explanandum, explanans, understanding, explanation, explainer, explainee, and context. In doing so, we discuss multifaceted entities in Social XAI (having both continuant and occurrent facets; e.g., explanation) and the relationship between understanding and explanation. Additionally, we propose solutions to seemingly paradoxical views on some terms (e.g., social constructivist vs. individual constructivist perspective on explanandum).

items.title: Dölpopa, Shentong Buddhism, and the Three Jewels: An Analytic Friendly Analysis.
items.abstract: In philosophical Buddhism, a prominent view is that the ‘Buddhist Jewels’ are helpful for achieving nirvana. These jewels include the Buddha, the Dharma (fundamental teaching), and the Sangha (the community of believers). In the medieval Buddhist philosopher Dölpopa’s Jonang-Shentong Buddhism, these jewels though are somehow mysteriously identical to one another – despite each having different features. This paper outlines an analytic-friendly analysis of the Buddhist jewels according to Dölpopa’s Shentong tradition by drawing on recent advancements in plural logic and analytic metaphysics. We begin by outlining the general metaphysics of Shentong Buddhism and the puzzles that arise regarding the Jewels (§1). Afterwards, relevant background in plural logic and contemporary metaphysics is covered (§2), a subsequent analysis of the Jewels is given (§3), and finally a few worries are engaged (§4).

items.title: The Lemniscate Soliton: Phi as the Unique Stable Resonance of Self-Referential Curvature in Spacetime.
items.pub: Unified Theory of Conciousness: Proofs and Applications.
items.abstract: We propose that the golden ratio φ emerges as the unique stable attractor of self-referential dynamics not by mathematical postulation, but as the necessary resonance condition of a closed lemniscate geodesic in self-curving spacetime. The argument proceeds in three steps. First, we show that strong self-reference — recursion in which the operation meets its own reciprocal — requires a closed trajectory with two distinguishable extrema joined at a singular throat, and that the lemniscate is the minimal geometry satisfying these requirements. Second, we demonstrate that closure under this geometry forces the system's two simultaneous invariants — additive (sum = 1) and multiplicative (product = ±1) — to be jointly satisfied only by the roots of x² − x − 1 = 0, of which φ is the unique positive solution.
