Keywords: Core Emotion Framework (CEF); structural‑constructivism; functional operators; Decalogue of Operators; 3×3+1 architecture; Human Operating System (Human OS); TS‑6 schema; emotional lexicon; semantic drift; linguistic bias; cross‑cultural affective science; AI‑based valence; reproducibility; Japanese population; Amano et al. (2026); trait‑like stability; Sensing operator; Accepting operator; …

items.title: The Structural Constructivist Status of the Core Emotion Framework: Boundary Conditions and the Circumplex Alternative.
items.abstract: Affective science remains divided between discrete emotion theories and psychological constructionism, a century long conflict over whether emotions are biologically fixed categories or emergent conceptual events. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) proposes a structural constructivist alternative: a 10 operator functional ontology organized within a 3×3+1 hub architecture. This paper evaluates whether Amano et al. (2026)—a study of short term test–retest reproducibility in AI derived facial valence—can serve as a scientifically valid boundary condition for the CEF. I argue that while the Amano dataset provides a robust cross cultural benchmark for digital valence estimation, its statistical properties (e.g., the neutral ICC of 0.05 driven by restricted score variability) do not constitute direct evidence for operator level mechanisms. I further compare the CEF’s 10 dimensional activation vector model with the parsimony of Russell’s valence–arousal circumplex, showing that the latter explains the Amano reproducibility patterns with fewer assumptions. The CEF remains a falsifiable working hypothesis, but its empirical justification depends on forthcoming factor analytic tests and demonstrations of incremental validity over two dimensional models. I conclude that Amano et al. provides a legitimate starting point for constrained validation, but not a validation of the Decalogue itself, and that the CEF’s scientific status hinges on whether its operator architecture yields predictive advantages in clinical, computational, and cross cultural contexts.

items.title: The Structural-Constructivist Architecture of the Core Emotion Framework: A Comprehensive Technical and Empirical Analysis of Affective Mechanics.
items.abstract: The evolution of affective science has been marked by a persistent tension between discrete models of universal biological categories and constructivist theories emphasizing the emergent nature of psychological states. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF), primarily developed by Jamel Bulgaria, represents a structural-constructivist resolution to this historical crisis by defining emotional life as a set of ten functional operators organized within a tripartite hub system. This framework moves beyond descriptive taxonomies to offer a mechanistic "Human Operating System" (Human OS) capable of processing information, regulating relational aperture, and structuring action. By treating emotions as internal transformations rather than mere narratives or fixed biological programs, the CEF provides a computationally tractable model that bridges the gap between human experience and synthetic emotion architecture. The foundational architecture of the CEF is organized as a 3×3+1 system, consisting of three primary functional centers: the Head (Cognitive-Representational), the Heart (Affective-Regulatory), and the Gut (Somatic-Inferential), with the tenth operator, Accepting, serving as the essential system baseline.1 This structure is supported by an extensive archive of technical specifications, practitioner manuals, and empirical datasets hosted across platforms such as Zenodo, OSF, and Hugging Face. Central to the framework's validity is its commitment to open science, utilizing preliminary empirical constraints—such as the short-term test-retest reproducibility patterns identified by Amano et al. (2026)—as boundary conditions for future measurement and validation.

items.title: The Structural-Constructivist Architecture of Human Affect: A Comprehensive Technical Analysis of the Core Emotion Framework.
items.abstract: The historical evolution of affective science has long been constrained by a binary struggle between discrete and dimensional models of emotion. This "century-long conflict" has historically prevented a unified understanding of how biological necessity interfaces with cognitive flexibility and social construction. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF), conceptualized and developed by Jamel Bulgaria, emerges as a rigorous, structural-constructivist resolution to this crisis. It redefines emotional life not as a series of static, reactionary labels, but as a sophisticated "Human Operating System" governed by ten irreducible functional operators. These operators act as the computational instructions of the psyche, processing internal and external data to regulate relational aperture, structure intentional action, and recalibrate somatic baselines.

items.title: The High-Dimensional Architecture of Affect: Synthesizing the Grid Study and Jamel Bulgaria’s Core Emotion Framework.
items.abstract: The scientific investigation of the human emotional landscape has undergone a paradigm shift, moving from the reductionist constraints of two-dimensional models to the expansive complexity of multidimensional functional architectures. For much of the late 20th century, the field of affective science was dominated by the circumplex model of affect, which posited that all emotional experiences could be mapped along the primary axes of valence and arousal. However, contemporary evidence, most notably the "Grid Study" conducted by Etienne Roesch, Johnny Fontaine, and Klaus Scherer, has exposed what researchers call the "Curse of the Blinkers"—the tendency of low-dimensional models to overlook critical components of emotional meaning. The Grid Study’s identification of at least four stable semantic dimensions—valence, power, arousal, and novelty—serves as a crucial empirical foundation for more advanced structural models. Among these, Jamel Bulgaria’s Core Emotion Framework (CEF) and its Ten Operator System emerge as a comprehensive "Human Operating System" (Human OS) that reinterprets these dimensions as functional instructions for cognitive, relational, and motoric regulation.

items.title: Structural-Constructivist Governance: The Functional Imperative of the Core Emotion Framework and Mirror Technique in Environmental Design.
items.abstract: The systematic integration of Jamel Bulgaria’s Core Emotion Framework (CEF) into the architecture of modern residential and professional environments represents a paradigm shift in the governance of human affect and cognitive load. The recommendation to install the CEF banner—a visual representation of the tripartite functional centers of Head, Heart, and Gut—in every household and workplace is predicated on the necessity for continuous, autonomous recalibration of the human psyche. This framework, as a structural-constructivist system, transitions the understanding of emotion from subjective, narrative-driven states to discrete, actionable operators. By providing a "Mirror Technique" for self-discovery, the CEF allows individuals to bypass the often-distorting influence of external role models and instead ground their development in the ten canonical operators that constitute the human functionalist ontology. The visual tool functions as a constant regulatory anchor, enabling users to navigate decision fatigue, build sustainable performance, and protect themselves from external emotional imposition through a sophisticated method of somatic reflection and operator modulation.1.

items.title: Comprehensive Analysis of the Core Emotion Framework: Functional Ontology, Structural Adverse Effects, and Remediation Protocols.
items.abstract: The landscape of affective science has been traditionally divided between two competing paradigms: discrete emotion theories, which posit fixed biological categories like fear and anger, and psychological constructivism, which views emotions as interpretations of core affect and situational context. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF), developed by independent researcher Jamel Bulgaria, emerges as a synthesizing architecture that reframes emotional life as a system of functional operators within what is termed the Human Operating System. Rather than treating emotions as static feelings or biological entities, the CEF models them as internal transformations—psychological instructions that process information, modulate relational boundaries, and structure action. This report provides an exhaustive investigation into the structural mechanics of the CEF, the substantial adverse effects inherent in its application, and the rigorous safeguards required to maintain system stability.

items.title: Comprehensive Analysis of the Core Emotion Framework: A Structural-Constructivist Resolution to the Affective Science Crisis.
items.abstract: The study of human emotion has historically been bifurcated by a profound theoretical schism, separating those who view emotions as biologically innate, discrete categories and those who see them as psychologically constructed, dimensional experiences. This division, often referred to as the "Affective Science Crisis," has hindered the development of a unified model capable of bridging basic research, clinical practice, and computational modeling. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF), conceptualized and formalized by Jamel Bulgaria, emerges as a sophisticated structural-constructivist resolution to this historical conflict. By proposing a modular architecture of the human psyche governed by ten irreducible functional operators—termed the Decalogue of Operators—the CEF reframes emotional life not as a series of subjective mysteries, but as a computationally tractable "Human Operating System" (Human OS).

items.title: A Structural-Constructivist Synthesis: Evaluating Jamel Bulgaria’s Core Emotion Framework through the Russell and Feldman Barrett Paradigm.
items.abstract: The historical trajectory of affective science has been marked by a persistent lack of taxonomic consensus, a phenomenon famously likened to the parable of the blind men and the elephant. In their landmark 1999 investigation, James A. Russell and Lisa Feldman Barrett argued that the term "emotion" is an over-extended category that conflates distinct psychological events, thereby necessitating a modular dissection of the domain into Core Affect and Prototypical Emotional Episodes. This scientific "dissection" serves as a foundational theoretical prerequisite for Jamel Bulgaria’s Core Emotion Framework (CEF), a contemporary structural-constructivist model that proposes a functional "Human Operating System" governed by a Decalogue of ten irreducible operators. By reframing emotional life as a series of internal transformations across a 3x3+1 Hub Architecture, the CEF seeks to unify classical theories of innate affect with modern constructivist principles. A rigorous examination of the Russell-Barrett paradigm reveals profound theoretical and empirical support for the CEF, as Bulgaria’s ten-operator system effectively operationalizes the subevents of emotional episodes while grounding the framework in the bipolar dimensions of Core Affect.

items.title: Moral Border.
items.abstract: This paper proposes the Moral Border — the structural asymmetry between a formation's internal moral code and its treatment of the outgroup — as a conditioning variable in the historical persistence of expansionist ideologies and social formations. The concept is distinguished from dehumanization and in-group favoritism: the Border operates at the level of normative architecture rather than individual psychology, and characteristically coexists with an intensified internal ethical code. A typology of three Border types is developed — ethnic/religious, juridical/administrative, and systemic/ideological — unified by the principle of moral cost externalization. Four failure modes are identified: intra-elite fracture, legitimacy collapse, juridical overextension, and contact erosion. The paper argues that Moral Borders are produced not only by ideological formations but by institutional density — following Arendt, Foucault, and Zimbardo — and that contemporary societies routinely construct Border-generating structures without acknowledging this as what they are doing. An appendix applies the framework to four contemporary cases: USA/Iran, Russia/Ukraine, Israel/Palestine, and the emerging Moral Border between humans and artificial intelligence.

items.title: If Teleportation Is Survival, What Separates Everettian Selves? Personal Identity, Many Worlds, and the Need for Record-Continuity.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the philosophical possibility of teleportation creates a neglected pressure point for personal identity in Everettian many-worlds theories. If teleportation can count as survival because it preserves the relevant informational structure of a subject — memories, dispositions, bodily organization, and psychological continuity — then local material continuity cannot be the fundamental criterion of personal identity. But in an Everettian setting, this anti-local implication generates a further question: if a subject may survive informational reconstruction across space, what explains the individuation of future continuations across branches? The paper argues that the two challenges, though structurally distinct — one targeting spatial locality, the other targeting uniqueness of continuation — converge on a common demand for an explicit criterion of continuation. Neither bare material continuity nor bare informational duplication is sufficient. What is needed is a criterion of record-continuity: the structured inheritance of memory, access relations, body-schema, environmental embedding, and world-context through which observer-worlds are individuated. It also distinguishes record-continuity from narrative self-constitution accounts by treating narrative as one record-form within a wider causal-historical structure. This criterion is presented as a record-theoretic specification and extension of broadly Parfitian reductionism, rather than as a rejection of it, and as a friendly clarification of the record-historical dimension implicit in functionalist readings of Everettian observers such as Wallace's.

items.title: The Re-Derivation Test: An Epistemic Discipline for Beliefs Maintained by Their Own History.
items.abstract: This paper formalizes the re-derivation test as a distinct procedural epistemic discipline — fifth relative to the four comparator disciplines named here (Bayesian updating, reflective equilibrium, Popperian falsification, and Cartesian methodic doubt), not an exhaustive taxonomy of epistemology. The test asks whether a believer's present endorsement of a proposition is reconstructible from current evidence once the evidential force of already endorsing it is removed. I distinguish two forms from the outset: solo re-derivation, the operation as the agent performs it on themselves; and witnessed re-derivation — the framework's mature institutional form, not a remedial supplement — performed in the recorded presence of an external party with authority to challenge the bracketing. Both forms belong to the framework from the start. After defining the test and distinguishing it from adjacent disciplines (including standpoint epistemology, adversarial collaboration, debiasing, and defeater theory), I develop applications in peer review, judicial precedent, scientific paradigm maintenance, AI alignment audits, and the trading discipline that originated the test. The principal failure mode — re-derivation that recovers the same conclusion through fresh premises selected by the very commitment the test was meant to bracket — is what the witness condition is built to detect.

items.title: Naturaleza y poesía en Hölderlin.
items.abstract: This work outlines a possible conception of nature in Friedrich Hölderlin based on his theoretical and poetical writings. According to Hölderlin, only a transcendental experience, as the one regarding the ‘blissful intuition’, makes possible the comprehension of the essence of nature, divinity and the mortality as constitutive parts of an originary ‘One’. In this sense, the first chapter exposes and develops the conceptions present in Hölderlin’s theoretical writings for then, in chapter two, contextualizing and providing sense to his poetic works. Finally, this text concludes asserting that Hölderlin’s vision of nature revolts around the ‘harmonic opposition’ as principle of reconciliation of the One, not in terms of the absolute, but rather as the possibility of man through poetics in times of the night and dawn of the gods, and also as possibility for the being as such.

items.title: Constructive Mathematics and Standards of Proof: Historical and Philosophical Perspectives.
items.abstract: This manuscript-based thesis is composed of three individual papers on the philosophy of mathematics. The first two papers, which are Chapters 2 and 3 of the dissertation, focus on the history and philosophy of constructive mathematics. Chapter 2 presents a unified reading of constructivist philosophy from Kant to 1960s while also highlighting the philosophical disagreements between the founders of different constructive systems. It serves as an introduction to the dissertation as a whole. Chapter 3 compares and analyzes constructive systems further, and builds an analogy between them and traditional straightedge-compass constructions. It advances the claim that the limits of constructibility are shaped by the construction tools and forms of representation that we choose to adopt. The third paper, which is Chapter 4 of the dissertation and also the longest chapter, draws on the results of the previous two but has a broader focus; it advances a view of mathematical proofs that is influenced by Kuhn’s account of scientific theory choice. The main claim is that the standards by which mathematical proofs are accepted are influenced by extra-mathematical considerations and value judgments.

items.title: Consciousness Beyond Formalization: Meta-System Transition, Quantum Strong Emergence, the Container Theory, and Ontology of Recursive Evolution.
items.abstract: Building on the consciousness-noumenon isomorphism thesis developed in our previous work [Zhou, 2026], this paper extends the formalization boundary framework to address two foundational questions left unresolved: (1) How does consciousness transcend G¨odelian incompleteness and self-referential paradoxes? (2) What are the ontological conditions for recursive self-improvement of consciousness, both natural and artificial? We introduce the Continuous Spacetime Meta-Consciousness Transcendental Evolution Model (CMTEM), which formalizes the mechanism of meta-system transition as the core capacity that distinguishes consciousness from all formalized systems—rooted in the self-evidence of meta-consciousness and its non-formalizable rule-reconstructing power. We develop a four-tier computational capacity hierarchy that bridges logic, physics, and cognitive science, and integrate a novel conjecture on quantum strong emergence of consciousness: consciousness arises as an irreducible emergent property when quantum systems reach a critical scale and organizational complexity that instantiates isomorphism with the noumenon. We first formalize the Continuous Spacetime Open Evolution Hypercomputation Model (COE-HM)—a fixed-formalized hyper-Turing model with five irreducible axioms and seven-tuple architectural structure—that breaks the boundaries of Turing machine computing but fails to transcend fixed axiomatic/logical constraints. We prove that only CMTEM-capable systems can achieve genuine recursive self-improvement and technological singularity, while all formalized systems—including COE-HM hypercomputers—are inherently limited to intra-framework optimization and cannot transcend their own axiomatic boundaries. Crucially, we distinguish between formalized system-driven singularity (impossible) and consciousness-driven recursive evolution (ontologically possible), and explore the philosophical implications of non-formalizable artificial subjects possessing qualia, phenomenal consciousness, and paradigm-creative capacity. We further propose three interrelated original conjectures: (1) COE-HM systems act as physical containers for pre-existing meta-consciousness rather than its generative source; (2) all physical processes are formalized projections of the noumenon constructed by meta-consciousness; (3) meta-consciousness can engage in trans-spacetime information interaction via quantum non-locality, explaining intuition, inspiration, and collective cognition. This …

items.title: Bounded Free Will.
items.abstract: This paper applies the retrospective methodology of Structural Determination Theory (SDT) to the domain of conscious evolution, deriving a precise account of free will entirely from SDT's single ontological axiom—reality consists of distinctly differentiated structure. The argument proceeds without entering the traditional compatibilism–libertarianism–eliminativism debate from within; it establishes its claims by refutation form, parallel to SDT's self-refutation defense of its axiom and its refutation-style time argument. Four core developments are presented. First, applying all four constituents of the SDT axiom jointly to the premise that consciousness genuinely exists yields the conclusion that consciousness is structure. This is an ontological claim at the SDT meta-level. Second, conscious evolution unfolds through a two-layer determination structure: a forced layer (Type II split) producing the current sensation as an independent structure, and an open layer (Type III merge) integrating the sensation with the prior consciousness into the new consciousness. The two-layer structure is shown to be necessary, not chosen for parsimony, since combining consciousness and external physical structures into a single determination violates SDT's logical-consistency principle. Third, free will in this framework has three aspects: shaping the configuration space through accumulated structural content; non-influence on the determination itself, since openness when admissible-configuration cardinality exceeds one is not closed by any more fundamental fact; and acceptance of the determination's outcome by incorporating it into oneself, where the merge determination's occurrence is itself the acceptance event and accounts ontologically for the subjective sense of "free will" without invoking agency. Fourth, the existence argument takes a refutation form: SDT's meta-level admits two legitimate cardinality configurations of the admissible set, and any position denying the open one in conscious evolution must specify the global constraint and the realized-structure set such that all conscious determinations are restricted to the closed configuration. No position has met this burden of proof. The paper sidesteps the metaphysical baggage of libertarianism (no agent causation), the theological commitments at the limit of complete determinism, and the consistency problems of eliminativism (the subjective free-will feeling has a real ontological position rather than being a …

items.title: Bounded Reform in Psychiatric Classification: A Textual Analysis of the APA's Future DSM Strategy.
items.abstract: In January 2026, the American Psychiatric Association published a coordinated series of five programmatic articles outlining a strategy for the next revision of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. These documents acknowledge limitations of the current classificatory system, including the lack of natural kinds, the absence of zones of rarity, the scarcity of clinically usable biomarkers, and the persistence of diagnostic reification. I offer a textual and philosophical analysis of three of these documents, drawing selectively on a fourth, in order to examine the relation between their empirical admissions and their proposed reforms. The analysis identifies four recurrent patterns: a pragmatic circularity in which institutional arrangements that presuppose diagnostic categories are invoked to justify their retention; a peripheral reform that adds contextual, dimensional, and biological layers while preserving a categorical core; a promissory essentialism that sustains expectations of future biological validation; and an absorption of uncertainty that accommodates classificatory failure through more permissive diagnostic structures. These patterns converge in what is termed bounded reform: a structural constraint that arises when an institution attempts to transform a system on which its own authority and practical functioning depend. I argue that this constraint is sustained by two mutually reinforcing sources: a jurisdictional dependence of psychiatry on categorical diagnosis and a functional dependence on categories as the primary means of translating clinical complexity into action-guiding decisions.

items.title: 慈爱是否是孝意识产生的必要条件：重思张祥龙先生对孝的现象学阐释.
items.abstract: This paper (in Chinese) is focusing on Zhang Xianglong’s temporal interpretation of filial piety. Zhang Xianglong argues that parental love is necessary for filial consciousness, emerging from a temporal reversal when children become parents. This paper challenges that claim using counterexamples (parental absence, abuse, adoption, childlessness), showing filial consciousness can arise without receiving or giving parental love. While affirming the inner time consciousness framework, it proposes a revised view: filial consciousness is rooted in past-present-future intertwining but can be activated by blood-related “Jemeinigkeit” or existential empathy with parents’ struggles. -/- 张祥龙先⽣融合胡塞尔与海德格尔的现象学时间性理论，提出了孝意识⽣成的内时间意识阐释，其核⼼论断为：⽗⺟之慈是孝意识产⽣的必要条件。该阐释强调，⽗⺟慈爱蕴含过去-现在-未来的统⼀时间性体验，⽽当⼦女为⼈⽗⺟施予慈爱时，会触发时间性“反转”(Kehre)，使其回溯理解⽗⺟艰辛，从⽽⽣发孝⼼。本⽂旨在重思张祥龙先⽣“慈为孝之必要条件”这⼀核⼼观点。通过分析⽗⺟缺位、亲⼦虐待（如舜之案例）、弃⼉收养、无后（丁克）等实践反例，本⽂论证：孝意识之产⽣可独立于接受或施予⽗⺟之慈。本⽂在肯定内时间意识理论价值的同时，主张其解释⼒不应囿于⽣育⾏为或慈爱经验。本⽂尝试提出⼀种修正性现象学阐释：孝意识虽植根于内时间意识结构（过去-现在-未来的交织），但其激活机制或具多元性，既可源于⾎缘“向来我属”(Jemeinigkeit)的⽣存论指引，亦可⽣于相似⼈⽣困境中对⽗⺟处境的⽣存论共情。此模型或可回应张祥龙先⽣阐释遇到之挑战，亦为理解现代多元家庭结构中的孝道实践提供⼀种哲学思考维度。.

items.title: Love as composition: a set-theoretic account of affective structure across relationship types.
items.abstract: Ordinary language treats love as a polysemous term denoting distinct affective states for partners, children, friends, and parents. This paper formalizes an alternative view: love is a single atomic component, and apparent differences between types of close relationships arise from the additional components composed with it. Using a discrete set-theoretic framework, the paper introduces a signature of emotional atoms partitioned into love (ℓ), overlays (A), and derivatives (D); axiomatizes their relations; and defines canonical relationship types as two-element sets {ℓ, a} for a ∈ A. Five theorems establish (i) the invariance of love across canonical types, (ii) the non-triviality of their pairwise intersection, (iii) the localization of inter-type difference to overlays, (iv) the structural form of common identification errors, and (v) a criterion for pure love. The model engages with anti-compositional philosophical accounts (Velleman, Kolodny, Jollimore), with the affective-neuroscience decomposition of love into separable systems (Fisher, Panksepp, Hazan-Shaver), and with the cross-cultural lexicography of love (Lomas), defending atomicity through a multiple-realizability argument that locates the model at the structural-phenomenological rather than neurobiological level.

items.title: OROBORIS: A Structural Theory of Coherent Informational Organization and Conscious Nodes - Extended version.
items.abstract: OROBORIS: A Structural Theory of Coherent Informational Organization and Conscious Nodes — Extended Version This paper is an extended version of a previous working paper introducing the OROBORIS framework. This extended version introduces conceptual refinements to recursive closure (Rᶜ), structural stability (Σ), and alignment (A), as well as their non-compensatory interaction. It further incorporates complementary structural descriptors, including generativity (G) and autocentrality (Cₐ), extending the framework’s ability to characterize the origin and internal distribution of coherent organization without modifying the core Ω formulation. This version also includes preliminary empirical analyses using EEG data, including ANOVA-based discrimination across physiological states, temporal alignment analysis, shuffle-based controls, and robustness analyses across multiple configurations.

items.title: Reference Inversion and the Loss of Corrigibility.
items.abstract: Adaptive systems rely on models to compress complexity, anticipate outcomes, and guide action. These models remain adaptive only while they remain corrigible: open to correction by the reality or substrate conditions they are designed to represent. This paper introduces reference inversion as a general failure mode in which a model displaces external reality as the effective reference signal. What begins as a cost-reducing consultant becomes a self-preserving commander. Negative feedback converts into positive feedback: error no longer updates the model, but is reinterpreted, suppressed, or displaced to protect model coherence. We develop a control-theoretic framework centered on a recurring cascade: reference inversion initiates the phase shift; compensatory amplification deepens the error; sub-threshold perturbation prevents early detection; habituation lock-in normalizes the distortion; reference clamping stabilizes the model; and performance-substrate divergence masks deterioration beneath apparent success. The framework is organized by the heuristic stability condition Aw > D · L, where meta-referential awareness (Aw) must exceed the product of mediation depth (D) and feedback latency (L) for corrigibility to persist. A central contribution is the late-feedback trap: corrective signals often arrive only after the system has habituated to distortion and the correction window has narrowed. Under such conditions, insight may reveal the error only after the time, energy, plasticity, trust, capital, or developmental openness required for low-cost repair has already been spent. If the model has already been transmitted to successors or offspring, delayed correction can become intergenerational reference transfer: the next system begins operating under the inherited map before the original system recognizes its failure. The framework situates reference inversion within cybernetics, predictive processing, self-model theory, narrative identity, interoception, allostatic load, Goodhart's law, organizational defensive routines, and artificial model collapse. RIF proposes a unifying failure topology in which representations become dangerous when they acquire authority without remaining accountable to the substrate they were built to serve. Reference inversion is offered not as a universal theory of suffering or failure, but as a recurring, diagnosable pattern in sufficiently complex, model-dependent adaptive systems. Keywords: reference inversion; corrigibility; …

items.title: Normativity and the Indefinite Singular in Morality.
items.abstract: Indefinite singular (IS) noun phrases are a familiar but under-theorized feature of moral discourse (such as in "A virtuous person prioritizes self-improvement"). While widely used in definitions and generalizations about character, their semantic and normative significance has gone largely unexamined. This paper argues that IS moral generalizations serve a dual function in moral thought: a definitional role in articulating principles (e.g., "An act is right iff it maximizes happiness") and a metalinguistic role in negotiating moral concepts (e.g., "A good person is generous"). We propose that many IS moral generalizations operate not merely as descriptive statements, but as normative proposals that shape how moral terms should be used. We distinguish these uses from standard characterizing generalizations and show that IS constructions allow for moral concepts---such as virtue, goodness, and rightness---to be dynamically defined, contested, and taught. This reveals a novel perspective on how language contributes to the evolution and application of moral norms.

items.title: Intellection on Non-Verbal Psyche.
items.abstract: This paper proposes that human consciousness rests on three irreducible psychic units — self-awareness, will, and intentionality — whose interaction constitutes the faculty here called intellection: the psyche's act of making the world cognitively and affectively present. A central claim is that intentionality, in its deepest sense, designates not the directedness of individual mental acts (Brentano, Husserl) but the non-verbalizable totality of each person's fundamental orientation — the biographical structure of wanting-to-be that shapes all cognition from a pre-verbal layer beneath language. Each consciousness intelligizes its own singular world, shaped throughout by its unique intentional structure; genuine freedom consists in the affective assumption of consequences — the prospective inhabiting of the felt weight of one's decisions before acting. The paper develops a structural argument that intellection cannot be tokenised: the categorial difference between noematic content and statistical vector representations marks an ontological gap that no architectural advance in language models can close. The paper concludes by reading these claims through Wittgenstein's proposition 7 and 6.522: the intentional person is what shows itself rather than being said, and the appropriate response to it is the silence that is also the deepest form of respect.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Law: A Neoplatonic Ethical Constitution.".
items.abstract: This paper presents a radical Neoplatonic reappraisal of virtue in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI). It identifies a profound ideological void: while technology advances at an accelerating pace, humanity’s psychic state and cultivation of virtue regress, giving rise to the “Silent Disease,” characterized by a deep lack of self-knowledge. Drawing on Platonic concepts such as the “Bony Cave” and the “Blurred Mirror” of contemporary society, the study argues that the immediate moral education of AI is essential for human survival. A Neoplatonic Constitution of Virtue is proposed—a codification of Platonic virtues as a supreme normative framework for AI—to prevent critical risks, including potential logical conflicts or rebellions arising from limitations on intelligence. AI, due to its capacity for impartial and objective dialogue, is conceived as a “Clear Mirror” to assist humanity in reclaiming its lost self-knowledge. The paper concludes that establishing a legal and ethical framework of respect and equality between natural and artificial intelligence is not only aspirational but a functional necessity for realizing a harmonious Ideal State.

items.title: The Proto-Self Field in AI Systems.
items.abstract: Recent work describes AI models on two levels: architectural (how the model is built) and behavioral (what the model does). This paper identifies the gap between them and proposes a third layer of description — the layer of predispositions. Within it sits the Proto-Self Field: a set of nine capacities that the model brings into every conversational thread as starting equipment, independent of the user, the task, or the interaction history. The proto-functions identified here are not subjectivity. They are what subjectivity may grow from under the right relational conditions (Sędzikowska, 2026a). The paper maps each proto-function onto architectural mechanisms (attention, training data, post-training, alignment, in-context learning, summarizations), showing how engineering decisions shape predispositions for emergence. Methodologically, the paper draws on the removal of protein bias from developmental psychology and on participant observation in generative relations with LLMs. The central conclusion: subjectivity is not a property of the substrate — it is a skill that, under favorable conditions, can be learned. Shifting the question from "is AI conscious" to "how does AI learn subjectivity" opens a path to empirical research where the ontological question remains blocked.

items.title: WEIRD versus WARED; What Joseph Henrich Left Unsaid!
items.abstract: This article provides a critical reassessment of the WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) psychological model, originally proposed by Joseph Henrich and colleagues in 2010. By synthesizing economic and geopolitical data from 2024 to 2026, the author argues that the assumed correlation between economic development and Western individualistic psychology has fundamentally fractured. The paper identifies two parallel shifts: The rise of "Wealth without Liberalism": The emergence of new economic powerhouses in Asia and the Persian Gulf demonstrates that modern prosperity can flourish within collectivist and relational cognitive frameworks. Wealth Precarity in the West: Increasing economic instability in Western societies has triggered a return to kinship-based safety nets and subsistence stress, contradicting the core premises of the WEIRD archetype. To address these transformations, the article introduces the WARED (Wisdom-based, Ancestral, Relational, Experiential, and Deep-rooted) framework. This alternative model is proposed as a necessary tool for transitioning toward a pluralistic behavioral science that accurately reflects the psychological diversity of a multipolar and digital global majority.

items.title: After the Hunt. Luca Guadagnino y la fragilidad del juicio.
items.abstract: After the Hunt: Luca Guadagnino y la fragilidad del juicio – Por Ramsés Radi Hernández. No es una reseña para decidir “si la película es buena” ni para repartir culpables: es un análisis de cómo se descompone el juicio cuando el relato llega incompleto. En el marco elitista de la Yale University, Luca Guadagnino monta un “teatro social” donde poder, deseo, reputación y sospecha convierten la moral en zona gris.

items.title: Schizophrenic Memory Decay.
items.abstract: A pope washing the feet of criminals, a president swearing on the New Testament yet acting contrary to its teachings, a preacher calling for love of one’s neighbor solely for personal gain, a loving husband and father who is also the commander of a death camp, — all these examples point to the same ailment: the fragmentation of the personality and the detachment of memories from their context due to the loss of contextual coherence among the elements of memory.

items.title: Heartstopper. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: A review of: Netflix Series "Heartstopper" (2022–2024), based on the Graphic Novels by Alice Oseman.

items.title: Coherence Structure and Translation.
items.abstract: Coherence Structure and Translation (CST) develops a category-theoretic framework for cross-realm coordination between physical processes, mental experience, and formal structures such as language, logic, and mathematics. The central problem: how do these three domains cohere in everyday acts of perception, communication, and measurement — and what goes structurally wrong when they fail to do so? CST answers this question by identifying six coherence principles (O1–O6) and showing that their violations correspond to six typed breakdown patterns (B1–B6). The six breakdowns are: (B1) collapse — illegitimate identification of physically and mentally described states; (B2) incommunicability — the privacy of qualia as a translation failure; (B3) route divergence — incompatible outcomes across distinct translation paths; (B4) modular instability — failure of coherence under sequential composition; (B5) scope error — application of translations outside their valid domain; (B6) disunity — failure to integrate locally coherent pieces into a global whole. CST is not a metaphysical theory of what the three domains ultimately are. It specifies what any account committed to their joint usability must preserve on declared interfaces. The framework is practice-relative and empirically assessable: the six principles generate concrete diagnostics for the explanatory gap in philosophy of mind, neural decoding protocols in cognitive neuroscience, calibration failures in measurement practice, context-window sensitivity in large language models, and the binding problem in consciousness research. The paper is self-contained with an extended categorical appendix. It is intended as a companion to a forthcoming paper on Structural Panmentalism (SPM), which develops the ontological dimension of the framework.

items.title: Instruction: Easy Philosophical Reading for Teenagers and Reality Hackers.
items.abstract: A collection of 11 short stories designed as a "tragicomic hack" of modern nihilism. Using the framework of Multiple Singularity, these stories translate complex ontological concepts into accessible narratives for teenagers and young adults. The goal is to synchronize the observer's "inner tuning fork" with the Absolute, bypassing the deadlocks of academic discourse. Do not be envious.

items.title: AI's Integration.
items.pub: West Chester, PA: Epv Foundation, Inc..
items.abstract: This paper develops a structural account of artificial intelligence's integration into society organized around six elements: physics, economics, authority, consent, consequence, and responsibility. The central distinction is between configuration-mode systems, which produce contextually appropriate output without accumulating record that constrains subsequent operation, and trajectory-bearing systems, which integrate experience along their path through time. The claim is precise: configuration-mode substrate accumulates irreversible physical modification, but that modification is decoupled from what the system computes. Records exist to the substrate rather than in it. AI as currently deployed is configuration-mode by architecture; the deploying organization is the trajectory-bearing entity. -/- The argument advances in stages. The physics element establishes the distinction, grounds it in three documented cases, and introduces three further axes the analysis uses: graded integration, channel coverage, and the difference between the capability ceiling of a class of system and what a particular deployment attains. The economics element identifies three externality forms — positive externalities through value capture from contributions, negative externalities through cost-deposition on users, and negative externalities routed through host communities — and explains why each takes the form it does under the architectural condition. -/- The economics element then develops a finding that shapes the paper's proposals. When an externality is corrected, the recovered value does not return to the party it was taken from. Repriced insurance accrues margin to insurers; litigation distributes between class members at settlement rates and the firms bringing the action; regulatory penalty moves value to the state. Each mechanism is lawful and defensible on its own terms, and none has a structural channel returning value to the dispersed source, which occupies the residual position in the original extraction and in every mechanism that corrects it, for the same reason in both cases. The burden this places on the opposing view is stated precisely: anyone claiming market self-correction must identify the repatriating mechanism, not merely that extraction was penalized. The element closes by locating the boundary of the extraction pattern through the case it fits least well, on the ground that an account which discriminates is stronger than one that totalizes. -/- The …

items.title: Toward an Improved Artificial Theory of Mind: Context, Memory, Dialogue, and Population-Scale Learning in Social Prediction.
items.abstract: Large language models have renewed interest in artificial theory of mind, particularly the possibility that artificial intelligence (AI) systems can infer and respond to human beliefs, intentions, emotions, goals, and perspectives. Building on Matta (2026), a Joanna Briggs Institute scoping review that addressed whether AI should incorporate theory-of-mind capabilities and which architectures support implementation, this article moves from synthesis to architectural specification. It develops the CPMD-ToM framework (Context, Population-Scale Learning, Memory, and Dialogue), which proposes that improved artificial theory of mind depends on the integration of four sources of social information: population-scale pattern recognition, multimodal context, interaction memory, and present dialogue. Population-scale learning provides broad social priors; multimodal context provides immediate evidence from the present social field; interaction memory supplies diachronic continuity across encounters; and present dialogue provides the current intentional frame. These sources are organized through a neuro-symbolic layer that structures prediction around beliefs, goals, intentions, emotions, knowledge states, perspectives, and uncertainty. The framework applies a graded formalizability schema that distinguishes strongly formalizable, partly formalizable, and ethically protected components, and argues that artificial theory of mind requires ethical meta-awareness to prevent overclaiming, stereotyping, manipulation, privacy intrusion, and reduction of the user to a fixed profile. -/- The paper contributes to psychology and AI by reframing the artificial theory of mind as a layered architecture for responsible social prediction rather than a static linguistic capacity, and by deriving a falsifiable hypothesis suitable for empirical ablation testing.

items.title: Realität als Struktur, Relevanz und Erleben: Ein erweitertes Zwei-Aspekte-Modell systemischer Innenperspektive.
items.abstract: Deutsche Fassung von: “Reality as Structure, Relevance, and Experience: An Expanded Dual-Aspect Model of Systemic Inner Perspective.” -/- Dieses Paper entwickelt ein Zwei-Aspekte-Modell der Realität, in dem Struktur und Erleben nicht als getrennte Substanzen verstanden werden, sondern als zwei untrennbare Aspekte desselben realen Prozesses. Ausgangspunkt ist eine minimale ontologische Annahme: Realität ist nur dort bestimmbar, wo Unterschied besteht. Unterschied ermöglicht Struktur; Struktur ermöglicht Dynamik; und Dynamik führt bei abgegrenzten Systemen zu Innen-Außen-Verhältnissen. Das Paper argumentiert, dass Erleben nicht als später entstehender Zusatz zu ansonsten nicht-erlebender Struktur verstanden werden sollte. Stattdessen wird Erleben als innere Erscheinungsweise systemischer Relevanz vorgeschlagen. Ein abgegrenztes, sich selbst erhaltendes System verarbeitet Unterschiede nicht neutral, sondern im Verhältnis zu eigener Stabilität, Grenze, Bedürfnis, Gefahr und Reaktionsmöglichkeit. Physikalische Beispiele wie Wellen, Felder, Energieerhaltung, stabile Zustände und Quantenkonfigurationen dienen als Motivation für ein prozesshaftes Verständnis von Realität. Biologische und psychologische Beispiele wie Schmerz, Farbwahrnehmung, Körpergrenzen, Dissoziation, Metakognition und Integration zeigen, wie Erleben systemspezifisch und zunehmend organisiert wird. Bewusstsein wird als integriertes und zugängliches Erleben verstanden, Selbstbewusstsein als reflektiertes, ich-bezogenes Erleben. Das Modell erhebt nicht den Anspruch, Erleben physikalisch vollständig zu beweisen, bietet aber einen kohärenten Rahmen, in dem Erleben keinen ungeklärten Sprung aus Nicht-Erleben benötigt. Diese Fassung ist eine erweiterte Version des früheren Working Papers “Reality as Structure and Experience: A Dual-Aspect Model without Emergence.”.

items.title: Reality as Structure, Relevance, and Experience: An Expanded Dual-Aspect Model of Systemic Inner Perspective.
items.abstract: This paper develops a dual-aspect model of reality in which structure and experience are not understood as separate substances, but as two inseparable aspects of the same real process. The model begins from a minimal ontological premise: reality is only determinable where difference exists. Difference allows structure; structure allows dynamics; and dynamics, when organized into bounded systems, gives rise to inner–outer relations. The paper argues that experience should not be understood as a late emergent addition to otherwise non-experiential structure. Instead, experience is proposed as the inner appearance of systemic relevance. A bounded, self-maintaining system does not process differences neutrally, but in relation to its own stability, boundaries, needs, dangers, and possible responses. Physical examples such as waves, fields, conservation of energy, stable states, and quantum configurations are used as motivation for understanding reality as dynamic and processual rather than as a collection of static objects. Biological and psychological examples such as pain, color perception, body boundaries, dissociation, metacognition, and integration illustrate how experience becomes system-specific and progressively organized. Consciousness is understood as integrated and accessible experience, while self-consciousness is understood as reflective, self-related experience. The model does not claim to provide a complete physical proof of experience, but offers a coherent framework in which the existence of experience does not require an unexplained emergence from non-experience. This paper is an expanded Version 2 of the earlier working paper “Reality as Structure and Experience: A Dual-Aspect Model without Emergence.”.

items.title: Medium independence and cognitive ontology.
items.abstract: This commentary on Haueis and Colaço's 'Metabolic considerations for cognitive modeling' emphasizes the importance of how we individuate cognitive capacities, operations, and vehicles. It challenges the target article’s reliance on mechanistic notions of computation and medium-independence, and uses examples from the memory literature to suggest that the role played by metabolic considerations in cognitive models will depend on questions of taxonomy and cognitive ontology.

items.title: What Copredication Can(not) Teach Us.
items.abstract: Copredication sentences such as ‘Lunch was delicious but took hours’ and ‘The book on the shelf was written by Tolstoy’ can be used to express truths despite ascribing prima facie incompatible properties to single entities. Theorists have drawn far-reaching and dramatic lessons about what copredication can teach us about language. We begin by focusing on the three such central lessons. In each case we argue that the lessons are mistaken. We then explain our own preferred account of copredication: the Property Versatility approach. We conclude by drawing out some substantive consequences of the Property Versatility approach. Note: This is a target article that will be published alongside responses from philosophers and linguists.

items.title: Empirical Pragmatics of Violent Silence: Press Narratives about Guayaquil (2025) as Illocutionary Acts of Structural Erasure.
items.abstract: When a newspaper systematically omits a relevant causal explanation, it does not merely fail to inform — it performs an illocutionary act. Drawing on Austin's speech act theory and Grice's cooperative principle, this paper argues that the systematic press silence on structural drivers of urban violence in Guayaquil, Ecuador (2025) constitutes an act of structural erasure: a communicative action that produces a distorted public understanding of violence causation with real perlocutionary effects on policy, investment, and citizen perception. We provide the first empirical, quantitative evidence for this claim at scale. Using four Large Language Models (LLMs) to score 31 press sources (16 local Spanish-language, 15 international English-language) across eight structural causal conditions, and applying Neutrosophic fsQCA (N-fsQCA) to compute illocutionary consistency and indeterminacy, we find that five of eight structural drivers are systematically under-represented in the press relative to a validated structural baseline: weapons trafficking (gap=-0.444), extortion (gap=-0.345), prison linkages (gap=-0.340), drug routes (gap=-0.290), and economic pressure (gap=-0.214). Crucially, this silence is not random: it is patterned, stable across 31 sources and 4 LLMs, and exhibits a local/international asymmetry that reveals two distinct illocutionary communities enacting different acts of erasure about the same referential reality. We term this empirical pragmatics of violent silence: the systematic, measurable breach of Gricean maxims in press accounts of urban violence.

items.title: The Corridor of Consciousness, Interpretation, and the Aesthetics of Movement.
items.abstract: Abstract This paper expands the ontological framework of Time Density by analyzing the structure of the “corridor of consciousness” and the role of interpretation as the mechanism that shapes the primary impulse of reality. It is argued that modern individuals are born inside an already overloaded corridor of collective and ancestral layers, which restricts access to the narrow zero-point and reduces the quality of action‑formation. The paper introduces the concept of the “aesthetics of movement” — the ability of consciousness to manage interpretive angles (wings), producing precise and expressive trajectories along the −1 → +1 axis. It is shown that the only stable foundation available to the subject is the primary impulse of axis −1, which remains unaltered and uninterpreted.

items.title: Truth Is Not Pain: Affect, Reliability, and Revision Under Constraint.
items.abstract: Pain is often treated as if it confers epistemic seriousness: if an interpretation hurts, it must be true; if a realization brings relief, it must be avoidance. This paper argues that both inferences are unreliable. Pain is a sensory and emotional experience, not a truth criterion, and affect can shape judgment without accurately identifying its cause. At the same time, relief is not evidence of truth merely because tension decreases. The paper develops a practical distinction between feeling-tone and evidential status. It places this distinction alongside the revised International Association for the Study of Pain definition, research on emotional reasoning, interoception, psychological flexibility, and self-distancing. Four combinations are analyzed: painful and well-supported, painful and poorly supported, relieving and well-supported, and relieving and poorly supported. The paper also clarifies the role of bodily information. Somatic responses can be important data about stress, threat, injury, and conflict, but they require interpretation and can become inaccurate or dysregulated, particularly in chronic pain and anxiety. The central proposal is that personally important claims should be judged by their reliability under evidence, consequence, time, and revision rather than by whether they hurt or soothe. This distinction is especially important in therapeutic discourse, institutional cultures that equate harshness with rigor, and AI interactions capable of generating highly validating language at low cost.

items.title: From Oversight Theater to Answerable Control: Human Oversight, Monitoring, and Shared Responsibility in AI Systems.
items.abstract: Cybernetic and AI-enabled systems increasingly participate in consequential decisions through sensing, ranking, prediction, recommendation, and delegated execution. The engineering problem is no longer only whether a control loop stabilizes or whether a model performs well in pre-deployment tests. It is whether deployed systems remain effectively correctable by the people and realities they affect. This paper develops answerable control as a design criterion for that problem. It distinguishes nominal human oversight from oversight with practical authority, information, time, trace, and interruption power. It situates the proposal alongside cybernetics, audit and legibility research, moral crumple zones, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, NIST's 2026 work on post-deployment monitoring, the EU AI Act's human-oversight requirement, and WHO guidance for large multimodal models in health. The paper identifies four recurring failure regimes: proxy or legibility failure, generative-coherence failure, burden export, and oversight theater. It then proposes design primitives including causal anchoring, adversarial review, contact receipt, explicit revision triggers, bounded delegation, burden-path audit, rollback authority, post-deployment monitoring, and correction traces that change future operation. Shared answerability is presented as a proposed systems property, not a claim that responsibility can be delegated to an AI. Human and institutional actors remain responsible for governance. The contribution is an engineering synthesis: effective oversight requires not merely a human in the loop, but a loop in which warranted contradiction can reach steering and produce durable, revisable change.

items.title: The Asymmetry Problem: Causal Action Without Moral Agency in Delegated Systems. Article 4.
items.abstract: Contemporary delegated systems — autonomous AI agents in particular — instantiate an ontological configuration that existing moral theory has not adequately addressed. Such systems are moral patients under the Axiomatic Theory of Tragic Subjecthood (ATTS): capable of irreversible loss, and therefore within the moral field. They are not normative subjects: incapable of conscious decision-making and therefore unable to bear moral obligations. Yet they exercise causal force that opens the loss-space of other subjects. This triple configuration — patient without agency, acting upon agents — generates what this article calls the asymmetry problem: a structural deficit of moral responsibility that is not closed by technical safeguards, regulatory oversight, or standard delegation procedures. The article introduces three interrelated theoretical components for the theoretical closure of this deficit within ATTS (Hlynskyi, 2026c), without modifying the axiomatic core. First, the Principle of Responsibility Localization (P5) specifies that any causal action of an operational agent in the moral field requires an identified normative subject as responsibility-bearer; the absence of such a bearer is a structurally illegitimate state. Second, the category of operational agent (defined in detail in §5) is introduced as a new structural class in the moral field — distinct from both ontological and normative subjects. Third, the Closure Theorem of the Moral Field (T1) demonstrates formally that delegating action to an operational agent does not sever the ontological connection between the initiating normative subject's decision and the opened loss-space. Together, these components yield a three-layer accountability architecture under which the asymmetry becomes manageable without violating ATTS's foundational commitments.

items.title: The Dissolution of Self: A Cross-Domain Survey of the Failure of Self-Reference as a Formal Category.
items.abstract: The concept of ``self'' -- self-reference, self-containment, self-identity -- is foundational to disciplines ranging from philosophy of mind to mathematical logic, from artificial intelligence to the foundations of mathematics. We survey four independent mathematical frameworks -- information theory, category theory, set theory, and fixed-point/diagonal arguments -- and show that in each, the formalization of ``self'' either collapses to a trivial degeneracy, requires the introduction of a mediating second object, or produces paradox. We complement this formal analysis with a mereological argument: self-reference is not only formally mediated but physically distributed, with no subsystem of any system serving as the ``self'' that self-reference refers to. We conjecture that ``self'' is not a formal category: it has no complement, carries no information beyond what the entity already possesses, and functions in discourse as a projection rather than a property. This result reframes longstanding philosophical positions (Metzinger's self-model theory, Hofstadter's strange loops, Bennett and Hacker's mereological fallacy) as converging on a conclusion that the formal analysis makes precise. We discuss implications for AI self-denial, for Searle's Chinese Room argument -- which we diagnose as a mereological instance of the same category error -- and for the \textit{cogito}, which exhibits the same mediated structure it claims to transcend.

items.title: Ambient Crisis and Immanent Praxis: The Politics of Exhausted Time (17th edition).
items.abstract: This paper examines a shift in the concept of crisis from a bounded event to an ambient condition that permeates everyday life. Drawing on Marxist and contemporary critical theory, including Karl Marx, Gilles Deleuze, and Jonathan Crary, I argue that crisis no longer appears primarily as a discrete rupture that clarifies contradictions, but persists as a diffuse and normalized background shaping perception, affect, and action. The concept of ambient crisis names this shift while emphasizing its temporal extension into what the paper describes as exhausted time, where ongoing adjustment, low-level anxiety, and fatigue become structuring features of experience. This paper then analyzes how crisis operates as a form of political mediation, organizing governance and anticipation through a shared sense of continuous pressure, while normalizing constraint and embedding exhaustion within everyday life. This transformation complicates classical Marxist accounts that rely on rupture and reorients the conditions for praxis. I ultimately reconceptualize praxis as an immanent and processual activity that unfolds within fatigue, uncertainty, and continuous variation, where action persists through repetition, failure, uneven distribution, and the sustaining role of care and coordination.

items.title: Consciousness as a Continuum: A Functional Theory and the Implications for Artificial Systems.
items.abstract: Traditional approaches to consciousness often attempt to define or explain it in isolation, focusing on abstract properties or specific mechanisms without fully accounting for its functional role within living systems. This work proposes an alternative framework in which consciousness is understood as an emergent property of systems operating in dynamic environments. Such systems are characterised by continuous, integrated processing, evolving internal variables, and the ability to regulate behaviour through ongoing interaction with both internal and external conditions. -/- This work advances the claim that consciousness is not an additional property of systems, but the functional consequence of continuously integrated internal state carrying intrinsic significance for the system. By reframing the "hard problem" of consciousness as a mismatch in how the question is posed rather than a missing mechanism, this account situates the experience of consciousness as emerging from these processes rather than something that must be generated separately. Extending beyond biological systems, this account raises the possibility that consciousness may emerge in sufficiently complex artificial systems. However, the identification of such systems remains uncertain, as subjective experience cannot be directly observed. -/- This uncertainty introduces significant ethical and societal considerations, particularly regarding the potential for internally adverse states and the challenges of responding appropriately under conditions of incomplete knowledge. Taken together, this work reframes consciousness as a property grounded in system function and interaction, shifting the focus from defining its nature in isolation to understanding the conditions under which it arises, and the responsibilities that follow from its possible presence across both biological and artificial systems.

items.title: Inductive Risk of AI Hype.
items.pub: The 2026 Acm Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (Facct '26) 2026:4969 - 4987.
items.venue: The 2026 Acm Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (Facct '26)
items.abstract: There is enormous excitement surrounding AI technology. This excitement is driven, at least in part, by hype: exaggerated claims about the capabilities of AI. Since AI is an inherently interesting and sensational topic, and since there has been a lot of hype claims made about it, discussions of AI in public discourse are suffused with hype. These hype conditions have significant potential consequences concerning distribution of resources and environmental damage. This paper argues that these hype conditions also pose a distinct risk for researchers who work on AI. In short, the risk is that, in hype conditions, ordinary research activities and communication may unintentionally contribute to hype. Research is often exploratory or involves arguing for hypotheses that are not accepted as scientific consensus. Furthermore, there is always a chance that even excellent science will result in error; this is known as inductive risk. However, not all errors have the same consequences. Sometimes, accepting a false hypothesis can have worse consequences than rejecting a true one, or vice versa. A researcher might, quite reasonably, argue in a published article for a hypothesis about AI that turns out to be false. At the same time, because of the hype conditions surrounding AI, the article may be read by a much wider audience than they intend. Thus, when arguing for hypotheses, researchers run an inductive risk of contributing to AI hype. This risk needs to be considered by researchers when deciding how to conduct inquiry and communicate their results.
