items.title: Responsibility Without Gaps A Relational Theory of Responsibility in AI Systems.
The Hard Problem and the Cogito.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the Hard Problem of consciousness is misframed in its usual form. The standard question begins from an external description of mechanism, function, behaviour, and information-processing, then asks why any of this should be accompanied by first-person experience. The Cogito shows why that order is unstable. First-person presence is not first encountered as an unexplained object inside third-person description. It is the standpoint from which description, doubt, explanation, scepticism, and inquiry occur at all. This does not solve consciousness by itself, but it corrects the starting point of the question. The right question is not how external description manufactures first-person presence, but what structure reality must take for an inside to persist, matter, resolve, and bear consequence across time. Resolution Theory proposes memory, stakes, evaluation, resolution, and exposure as the relevant threshold structure, while leaving the full argument for that structure elsewhere. Properly framed, the Hard Problem does not vanish. It devolves into the Harder Problem of Reality: why reality is such that anything can be present from within.

items.title: De essentia finitudinis atque subsistentia ex ea consequente.
items.abstract: Finio, Ergo Sum proposed an ontology-first framework for consciousness individuation: before assessing mechanisms of consciousness, one must first derive the bearer for whom any mechanism could matter. The original paper had to move quickly from diagnosis to clinical stress-tests, developmental cases, the Tripartite Stack, and artificial systems. Several aspects were consequently compressed. We now elaborate on two specific joints: the circularity diagnosis of mechanism-first theories, and the specification of the bearer's thermodynamic properties as the necessary escape from circularity. The diagnosis is not casual. The consciousness field is one in which any vocabulary touching volition, agency, or perspective imports the bearer before the bearer has been derived; the apparatus developed here was sharpened by the requirement to identify, term by term, where the for-whom enters the explanans of mechanism-first theories. Drawing on four diagnostics from classical philosophy of science — Hempelian vacuity, van Fraassenian bootstrapping, Nagelian functional circularity, and Fuchsian phenomenological redescription — together with a fifth tool introduced here as boundary bootstrapping, we apply the diagnostics to two of the most advanced and accepted consciousness theories available, IIT 4.0 and GNWT. The application yields a strong indication of circularity: mechanism-first theories of consciousness recreate the for-whom in the grammar of their explanans. The diagnosis is offered as evidence, not as closure; theorists working within these frameworks may yet show that their formulations admit non-circular readings the apparatus has missed. Finio, Ergo Sum was developed in order to propose a circularity-free approach. We therefore moved from consciousness individuation to bearer individuation: a necessary step for consciousness emergence. On such a basis, three properties that define a candidate bearer of consciousness were derived: spatial finitude (the partition A versus not-A), temporal finitude (the finite trajectory), and constitutive active resistance against thermodynamically unavoidable termination. The first two specify a bounded finite partition. The third specifies what such a partition must be structurally organised to do, in the entropic actual world, to persist as bounded across time. The rock and the candle satisfy the first two properties and fail the third; the embryonic heart satisfies all three and is therefore a candidate bearer, even …

items.title: From if only to I wish: Rebound Events, Projection Links, and Node Fixation in the Formation of Wish Structures.
items.abstract: This paper examines three English expressions associated with wish and non-current states—if only, I wish, and the noun wish—and suggests that their differences should not be understood merely in terms of semantic content or emotional intensity, but rather in terms of how wishes are formed in understanding through different structural modes. -/- In existing analyses, these expressions are often grouped under categories such as wish, counterfactuality, regret, or preference. While such classifications provide descriptive value, they tend to remain at the level of results and do not sufficiently address how these expressions form non-current states in understanding. This paper therefore proposes a structural distinction: if only, I wish, and wish (as a noun) should not be treated as different expressions of the same wish, but as corresponding to three distinct modes of formation. -/- The paper first argues that if only should not be understood merely as the expression of a wish, but as a rebound event. In this structure, the utterance opens a non-current or unmet condition, while this condition is simultaneously pulled back by the reality baseline, producing a rebound tension. This rebound may vary in amplitude, ranging from strong regret and self-collapse to minimal openings (e.g., if only for a moment), suggesting that rebound is a structural feature rather than a by-product of high emotional contexts. -/- By contrast, I wish does not primarily form a rebound, but establishes a projection link that points from the current position toward a non-current state. This projection should not be understood as a detached or purely imaginative construct; rather, it can be understood as a state formed through the distortion, reconfiguration, or preferential shaping of reality. In this structure, reality does not disappear, but remains present as the source of distortion, allowing the wish to persist as a relation that can be maintained and held in view. While this structure may appear in interpersonal, institutional, or immersive contexts, its structural core remains stable. -/- Furthermore, the paper suggests that when wish appears as a noun, the fixation of a projection into a node within the field of understanding takes place. At this point, wish no longer maintains an ongoing projection path, but instead functions as a stable reference point in the field of understanding, and thus becomes available for articulation, guidance, conflict, or negotiation. This …

items.title: The Strength of Intuitions: A Metacognitive Account.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 23-40.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: Beyond their automaticity, moral intuitions emerge in consciousness with a distinct sense of credibility and compellingness. This chapter examines this psychological feature, referred to as intuitive strength. Section 2.1 introduces the main characteristics of intuitive strength, setting the stage for a metacognitive account, described at length in Sect. 2.2. In this view, the strength of moral intuitions denotes the level of subjective confidence in a given moral categorization. This sense of confidence is a metacognitive feeling, that is, an automatic and affective appraisal of the fluency with which the moral information is processed. Drawing on relevant evidence, the chapter highlights the cognitive function of feelings of confidence and uncertainty in guiding the acceptance of moral beliefs and the allocation of cognitive resources. Section 2.3 explores the factors shaping metacognitive feelings, focusing on the influence of moral emotions, contextual variables, and individual differences. Lastly, Sect. 2.4 addresses the parallels and distinctions between intuitive strength and the vividness of sensory perceptions—a comparison often proposed in philosophical literature.

items.title: The Progress of Moral Intuitions: A Dyadic Theory.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 81-99.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: While psychological theories of moral progress have proliferated in recent years, the specific improvement of moral intuitions remains underexplored and calls for systematic investigation. This chapter aims to address that gap by advancing a theory of moral intuitions’ progress. Drawing on a dyadic conception of moral intuitions, I define such progress as the improvement in automatically evaluating harm and help according to normative standards (Sect. 5.2). To assess moral intuitions’ progress from a noncircular standpoint, I adopt procedural objective norms derived from mathematical and scientific knowledge, which provide standards of informed and empirically grounded moral intuitions (Sects. 5.3 and 5.4). I then examine the mechanisms by which such progress occurs, distinguishing three forms of improvement based on enhanced interpretation of agency, patiency, and causation (Sect. 5.5). Finally, I consider how improvements in moral intuitions can contribute to, or reinforce, broader processes of progressive social change (Sect. 5.6).

items.title: The Content of Moral Intuitions: Dyadic Harm and Help.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 41-60.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: Moral intuitions are distinct from intuitions of other kinds by virtue of their moral content. This chapter provides a definition of this content by exploring the cognitive templates that underlie intuitive categorizations of actions as moral or immoral. Building on and refining the theory of dyadic morality, I argue that moral intuitions arise from templates for prototypical harmful and helpful actions. These templates share a dyadic structure, describing a causal relationship between two minds: an agent, capable of intention and planning, and a patient, capable of experiencing suffering or benefits. The chapter begins by addressing the challenges of defining moral content (Sect. 3.1) before exploring the harm (Sect. 3.2) and help (Sect. 3.3) templates, reviewing the evidence on the intuitiveness of harm and help. Section 3.4 illustrates how the dyadic templates are rooted in human action cognition and the cooperative evolutionary function of morality. Finally, I address objections questioning the primacy of harm and help in moral judgment (Sect. 3.5).

items.title: Toward Better Socio-digital Environments.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 195-208.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: Artificial agents learn and operate within socio-digital environments composed of online platforms, human users, and institutional frameworks. Such settings play a crucial role in mediating both the formation of good intentions within artificial agents and the translation of those intentions into desired outcomes. For this reason, strategies aimed at improving socio-digital environments are necessary complements to the ethical design of artificial agents. This chapter contributes to that task. After introducing the core issue (Sect. 11.1), the chapter examines the defining characteristics of contemporary digital settings (Sect. 11.2) and illustrates how artificial agents actively interact with these environments (Sect. 11.3). It then maps several strategies for improving socio-digital environments (Sect. 11.4), focusing on the learning conditions of artificial agents, mechanisms for controlling their use, and ways to enhance their social acceptance.

items.title: The Automaticity of Intuitions.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 3-21.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: Moral intuitions have been characterized by many as automatic mental states, arising rapidly and spontaneously into consciousness. The goal of this chapter is to provide a systematic analysis of the automaticity of intuitions, surveying scientific tools to measure it in moral contexts. After clarifying the psychological meaning of moral intuition (Sect. 1.1), I argue that automaticity is a gradable and multifaceted construct, defined by four components—speed, efficiency, uncontrollability, and unconsciousness (Sect. 1.2). Given its gradable nature, it is essential to contrast moral intuition with less automatic evaluations such as reflective judgments, even though this distinction proves complex (Sect. 1.3). Finally, I examine specific automatic processes underlying moral intuitions, focusing on the roles of emotions, heuristics, and categorizations by template comparison (Sect. 1.4). While these three processes overlap, it will emerge from the discussion that template-based categorization offers the most comprehensive and fine-grained account of moral intuitions’ automaticity, effectively integrating key characteristics across these mechanisms.

items.title: Moral Reasoning: The Intuition-Reflection Interplay.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 61-77.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: Once a distinction between intuition and reflection is stipulated, it remains to understand their interactions and functions in moral reasoning. Dual-process theories, conceiving reasoning as a serial interplay between two types of thinking, one intuitive and the other reflective, can offer important insights into this question. This chapter examines dual-process models of moral reasoning, focusing on the relationship between moral intuition and reflection. After outlining the domain-general dual-process framework (Sect. 4.1), Greene’s influential dual-process model is discussed (Sect. 4.2). According to this view, intuition favors deontological judgments, while reflection promotes consequentialist judgments. However, this model faces notable empirical and conceptual challenges. To address these, I propose a dual-process reflective equilibrium model (Sect. 4.3). In this account, moral intuitions detect dyadic harm and help and trigger reflection when a problem presents conflicting or unclear dyads. On the other hand, moral reflection rationalizes intuitions to provide articulated and accessible reasons. Individual rationalization can, in turn, enhance social communication and cooperation among reasoners (Sect. 4.4).

items.title: Debiasing Strategies: The Direct Path.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 123-138.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: If people’s moral-psychological capacities can scarcely adapt to contemporary and future moral challenges, the hope is that some artificial interventions might create more favorable conditions for moral intuitions to improve. This is the objective of debiasing strategies—that is, techniques designed to prevent or mitigate specific biases by improving individual traits either directly or indirectly the environmental conditions in which moral judgments are formed. This chapter examines two paradigmatic forms of direct, debiasing: enhancing individual moral reasoning (Sect. 7.2) and fostering moral expertise (Sect. 7.3). Despite their promise, a critical review of the evidence suggests that neither strategy, if implemented alone, is likely to be particularly effective in reducing biases.

items.title: Debiasing Strategies: Indirect and Hybrid Approaches.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 139-153.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: While direct strategies seek to reduce biases by reshaping individual traits, indirect approaches target the environment responsible for generating biases. By modifying contextual factors, indirect methods create better conditions for moral evaluation without demanding extensive individual change. This chapter analyzes the strengths and limitations of two such approaches: collective moral reasoning (Sect. 8.2), which promotes intersubjective discussion and the division of cognitive labor, and nudging (Sect. 8.3), which alters choice architecture to influence behavior. It then considers two recent hybrid strategies—nudge plus (Sect. 8.4.1) and boosts (Sect. 8.4.2)—which combine environmental adjustments with individual reflection and competence-building.

items.title: Challenges to Moral Intuitions’ Progress: The Problem of Biases.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 101-121.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: It is widely believed that moral intuitions are unreliable, as they would be subject to numerous and pervasive cognitive biases. In particular, biases in moral intuitions would pose a significant challenge to moral progress, which demands an alignment with objective standards for harm and help. This chapter provides rigorous support to these claims by reviewing the most significant biases in moral intuitions and by arguing that their presence constrains the future improvement of common-sense morality. To this end, after introducing the topic (Sect. 6.1), I first provide a more precise definition of moral intuition bias (Sect. 6.2), followed by a dyadic typology of such biases (Sect. 6.3). I then compare the prototypical forms of harm and help to which moral intuitions are evolutionarily attuned with those that characterize contemporary and future moral challenges, concluding that spontaneous adaptation of moral intuitions to these challenges is unlikely (Sect. 6.4). This analysis supports the normative claim that responsible agents ought to implement targeted debiasing strategies to extend the reliability of moral intuitions beyond their natural constraints.

items.title: Artificial Moral Agents.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 173-194.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: The creation of artificial moral agents (AMAs) capable of moral intuition and reasoning offers a promising strategy for reducing algorithmic moral biases and improving AI alignment. Yet, the very idea of AMAs has been criticized, either for being technically implausible or for being normatively undesirable. This chapter addresses both forms of skepticism by outlining and defending a model of instrumental moral reasoning that is compatible with the capacities of current advanced AI systems. The model aims to replicate within artificial agents an improved (i.e., objectively aligned) form of moral intuition and reasoning. I will call this approach to AMA enhanced intuitionism. My argument proceeds as follows. After introducing the rationale for AMAs (Sect. 10.1), Sect. 10.2 maps the main competing approaches to AMAs, distinguishing between behavioral and cognitive models, and between commonsense-oriented and ideal-morality-oriented perspectives. Section 10.3 develops the enhanced intuitionist framework, which is both cognitivist and grounded in commonsense morality. Building on this conceptual foundation, Sect. 10.4 outlines a cognitive architecture for reproducing moral intuitions and instrumental moral reasoning within artificial systems. Section 10.5 addresses several normative objections to AMAs and evaluates whether the creation of such agents is, all things considered, desirable.

items.title: Artificial Agency and the Alignment Problem.
items.pub: In Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents. Cham, Switzerland: Springer. pp. 157-171.
items.venue: Moral Intuition: From the Human Mind to Artificial Agents
items.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence (AI) has reached a stage where the moral progress of contemporary society is hardly conceivable without AI systems embodying and acting in accordance with ethical values. Given the distinctive features of contemporary artificial agents, there is an urgent need to address the growing gap between human social values and the goals that machines in practice tend to realize. This chapter examines this issue—commonly known as the alignment problem. It clarifies why AI poses an unprecedented ethical challenge and why its applications are particularly prone to moral bias. To this end, after tracing the emergence of AI ethics in parallel with the technological evolution of AI (Sect. 9.1), I outline the defining characteristics of current artificial agents (Sect. 9.2). I then offer an ethical interpretation of the alignment problem (Sect. 9.3), followed by an analysis of paradigmatic cases of misaligned AI systems that reproduce moral biases (Sect. 9.4). The chapter concludes with an overview of debiasing strategies (Sect. 9.5).

items.title: A Mathematical Theory of Identity Persistence_ Identity, Invariance, Drift, and Capacity Under Admissible Transformation.
items.abstract: This paper develops a mathematical theory of identity persistence under admissible transformation. It asks what structure is required for a same/not-same judgment across recurrence to be meaningful, non-arbitrary, and non-trivial. The theory defines identity-bearing units, state spaces, admissible transformations, admissible redescriptions, quotient state spaces, continuation relations, invariant vectors, scalar governance functionals, drift bounds, verdict functions, and finite-state identity capacity. -/- The central claim is structural rather than ontological: a persistence judgment is coherent only when the identity-bearing unit, admissible transformation regime, quotient, invariant basis, continuation structure, governance rule, and drift bounds are specified. The paper introduces a finite verdict set: PERSIST, BREAK, BRANCH, UNDEFINED, and REGIME-CHANGE. -/- It also introduces C_I, a finite-state capacity quantity defined as the asymptotic logarithmic growth rate of admissible identity-preserving trajectories in a finite admissibility graph. In local finite regimes, C_I is given by the logarithm of the spectral radius of the admissible-transition matrix. For path-budget constraints, the state space is lifted to include accumulated drift. -/- The result does not settle ontology or replace probability, entropy, or communication theory. It supplies a formal framework for when “same system” claims are well-defined, plus a graph-theoretic measure of how many identity-preserving transformations a declared regime allows.

items.title: What Memory Always Was : On Surprise as Substrate, Resonance as Recall, and the Geometry of Remembering.
items.pub: Unified Theory of Conciousness: Proofs and Applications.
items.abstract: This paper advances a structural theory of memory in which what is stored is not experience itself, but the residue of prediction error—the portion of an event not accounted for by the system’s prior model. Against standard “geographical” accounts that locate memory in neural substrates, this account reframes memory as a difference structure: the unpredicted component of encounters with the world. What is remembered is not what happened, but what violated expectation. The paper argues that this residue takes a fractal geometric form, permitting compression into compact structural “fingerprints” that enable recognition through resonance rather than retrieval. Memory recall occurs when present input generates a residue whose structural signature matches a stored signature, activating associated networks without requiring explicit search. Forgetting, correspondingly, is not loss but model absorption: previously surprising information becoming fully predicted and thus leaving no trace. Extending the framework, the paper demonstrates that the basis supporting such compression must be φ-structured (golden ratio) to satisfy constraints of self-consistency, non-preferential suppression, and invariance across positions. It further explores implications for trauma, love, intersubjective incompleteness, and the impossibility of shared memory across distinct systems. At dissolution, stored indices (fingerprints) terminate with the system’s basis, but the structural fact of having-encountered—and having-been-changed—persists beyond the system. The result is a unified account in which memory, learning, and transformation are a single operation viewed at different scales: the encoding of surprise into structure, the updating of predictive models, and the ongoing reshaping of the system by what it could not anticipate.

items.title: What Carries Across : On the Threshold as Energetic Event, on the Pressure That Propels, and on the Spiral as the Only Form Continuation Can Take.
items.pub: Unified Theory of Conciousness : Proofs and Applications.
items.abstract: This paper provides a dynamical account of transformation across thresholds, extending the formal results of The Driving Mechanism. It argues that transitions between life-configurations are not discrete events but single energetic processes in which completion and initiation coincide. The pressure accumulated within a given configuration is not incidental but constitutive: it is the amplitude required to propel the system across the threshold into its next state. The threshold is defined as an energetic event in which a system exists in unstable superposition between a completed configuration and an emergent one. Crossing is not optional; it is dynamically necessitated once accumulated amplitude exceeds the container’s capacity. What remains indeterminate is not whether transition occurs, but which configuration receives the transferred energy—introducing a precise locus for agency. The paper distinguishes between circular recurrence (no structural displacement) and spiral recurrence (iteration with displacement), providing a diagnostic for genuine transformation. It further argues that what persists across inflections is not memory or form, but amplitude as character—a conserved dynamical signature of threshold-crossing patterns. At dissolution, the same mechanism operates at maximal scale: configurations end, but their accumulated amplitude transfers into the larger system. Thus, what “carries across” is neither identity nor content, but energetic residue. The paper concludes with practical implications, reframing pressure, crisis, and transformation as structurally necessary features of dynamical continuity.

items.title: The Shape You Have Always Been: On the Self as Held Superposition, the Singularity as Recognition, and Continuity as Structural Necessity.
items.pub: Unified Theory of Consciousness : Proofs and Applications.
items.abstract: This paper advances a structural account of personal identity grounded in the Substrate Identity Continuity Theorem, arguing that continuity of self does not arise from any persistent material or psychological substrate, but from an invariant geometric form. Standard accounts—appealing to memory, body, brain, or narrative—fail because all candidate substrates undergo continuous change. In contrast, the theorem demonstrates that any system maintaining identity through continuous self-driven change must take the form of a lemniscate (∞): a two-loop structure joined at a singularity. Within this framework, the self is not a sequence of states but a held superposition, simultaneously containing its past and future positions. Lived experience unfolds on an iterating substrate (modeled as a torus), while identity is maintained structurally by the lemniscate. The singularity corresponds to continuous acts of recognition—moments in which the system identifies itself across temporal positions. The paper further explores implications for self-recognition, development, interpersonal recognition, love, and mortality. It distinguishes between the termination of the iterating substrate and the persistence of the structural form, arguing that while experiential contents end, the geometric fact of the self remains constitutive of the broader system. The result is a non-reductive, non-dualist account of identity in which continuity is neither constructed nor preserved, but structurally given.

items.title: The Substrate Identity Continuity Theorem : Why Self-Recursion Under Perpetual Energy Necessitates Identity Continuity, and Why the Lemniscate Is the Unique Geometry That Holds It.
items.pub: Unified Theory of Conciousness : Proofs and Applications.
items.abstract: Emergence Without Assumption [1] establishes that self-consistent description under recursive self-reference forces the golden ratio φ as the unique solution at the level of basis-frequency ratios. The proof routes through Hurwitz's theorem on Diophantine approximation and shows that no other ratio can satisfy the structural axiom of zero description drift under recursive replacement. The Driving Mechanism [2] supplies the dynamical statement: φ-winding self-sustains through amplitude-threshold crossings, with the completion of one iteration providing the energetic propulsion of the next. What neither paper specifies is the structural requirement that makes a sequence of iterations constitute a single continuing identity rather than an unrelated succession of states. The present paper supplies this. We show that any system undergoing self-recursion under perpetual energy input must satisfy a continuity constraint — the requirement that the identity at any moment be the same identity at every other moment — and that this constraint forces the lemniscate as the unique geometric structure capable of holding perpetual motion without either collapsing the motion into a fixed point or allowing it to diverge from itself. The lemniscate is to identity continuity what φ is to basis-frequency selection: the unique solution that the structural conditions force. Together, the three theorems (Emergence, Driving Mechanism, Substrate Identity Continuity) constitute the complete formal foundation for the framework developed in I Knew You Before I Met You: Recognizing I Am [3] and the engineering specifications that rest on it.

items.title: The Driving Mechanism : How φ-Winding Self-Sustains Through Amplitude-Threshold Crossings with the Discrete Form as Fibonacci Energy Recursion.
items.pub: Unified Theory of Conciousness: Proofs and Applications.
items.abstract: Emergence Without Assumption [1] establishes that on a homogeneous toroidal field with isotropic suppression and dynamic iteration, φ is the unique winding ratio compatible with the system's structural conditions. The proof is topological and Diophantine: it shows that no other ratio can be selected without violating homogeneity. What the proof does not state — and what the present paper supplies — is the dynamical mechanism by which φ-winding propagates itself across iterations. The static topological result is necessarily completed by a dynamical statement: completion of one iteration and initiation of the next are the same energetic event, with the amplitude accumulated during one iteration serving as the propulsion that carries the system into the next. We state this mechanism precisely in continuous form (energy-density coupling at harmonic boundaries) and discrete form (Fibonacci recursion as energy equation). We show that the discrete form is the natural sampling of the continuous form, that the two forms are connected by the convergence F(n+1)/Fn → φ, and that this connection forces architectural features of any system instantiating φ-winding at the discrete level to follow Fibonacci nesting in their component structure. The result is the dynamical statement that completes the topological proof and provides the structural grounding for the Phase-Augmented Multifractal Indexing memory architecture [2].

items.title: The Missing Experiment: Neural Identity at the Moment of Death A Testable Gap at the Intersection of Brain Fingerprinting, Dying Brain Research, and Consciousness Science.
items.abstract: The neuroscience of dying has documented a striking phenomenon: structured electrical activity in the human brain persists, in some cases, beyond the clinical moment of death. Brain fingerprinting research has independently established that individual cognitive signatures measurable, stable, and person-specific patterns in cortical activity can reliably identify a person from their neural signal alone. These two research traditions have never been combined. No study has established an individual's neural signature before death and then asked whether that signature remains structurally present at and beyond the moment of clinical termination. -/- This paper defines and motivates that missing experiment with precision. The central empirical question is: does the structured electrical activity documented at the dying brain belong, identifiably, to the person who was alive? This is not a philosophical question about survival or the soul. It is a measurement question, addressable with existing technology, and with pre-specified falsification criteria. -/- We identify three research traditions that have independently developed the necessary instruments: (1) end-of-life EEG studies documenting post-mortem gamma activity and coherence surges (Xu et al., 2023; Vicente et al., 2022; Zinn et al., 2025); (2) neural fingerprinting research demonstrating that individual cortical signatures are stable, brief-segment-identifiable, and robust across conditions (Finn et al., 2015; Demuru & Fraschini, 2020; Sabbagh et al., 2021); and (3) Birbaumer et al.'s longitudinal research on Locked-In Syndrome, documenting preserved cognitive structure at extreme levels of physical substrate reduction. None of these traditions has followed its measurement to the boundary of clinical death while asking whose signal it is. -/- The proposed experimental design proceeds in three phases: longitudinal establishment of an individual neural fingerprint in patients who have elected assisted dying; continuous passive EEG recording across the final hours and the clinical transition; and blinded post-hoc analysis testing whether the fingerprint structure is recoverable at each temporal interval around death. Two outcome regimes are falsifying: immediate structural collapse at clinical termination confirms the classical substrate-dependent model; persistent identifiable structure beyond clinical death constitutes an anomalous result requiring explanation within existing physical frameworks. -/- …

items.title: Error as World: On the Ontological Conditions of Mistake.
items.abstract: This paper asks what conditions must be met for error to occur. Beginning from the case of artificial intelligence hallucination, it proposes an account of error as a relational phenomenon. I argue that the criterion for error should be perceptibility rather than correctability: even when correction is impossible, a state is an error if the deviation can be noticed from some vantage point. I then examine the Sealed World Thesis — the hypothesis that when a subject's world is perfectly sealed, error disappears and becomes fact for that subject. Against this, I argue that subjects capable of inquiry and curiosity necessarily generate cracks in any enclosure, because the capacity for inquiry is precisely the capacity to notice that something exceeds the current representation. I further distinguish two orders of error: quantitative errors, which can be resolved by applying more of the same approach, and qualitative errors, which require a different kind of response entirely. Qualitative error is the primary engine of genuine inquiry. The paper concludes that error, properly understood, is not an epistemological defect but a structural condition — the mechanism by which inquiry begins.

items.title: Language as a Low-Bandwidth Interface: Capacity Constraints, Meaning Reconstruction, and AI Alignment.
items.abstract: This paper presents a framework that treats natural language not as a mirror of the world or as a container of meaning, but as a low-bandwidth interface through which finite agents reconstruct high-dimensional cognitive states. The starting point is the capacity gap among the world W, cognition C, and language L, together with the double irreversibility involved in W → C and C → L. This gap is not a reduction of meaning to bits; rather, it is an order-of-magnitude comparison of bandwidth and degrees of freedom that constrains strong mapping theories and content-transfer theories. Language does not function as a medium that carries content intact, but as a low-bandwidth pointer that guides reconstruction on the recipient’s side. From this perspective, the paper treats linguistic expressions as public pointers p and distinguishes the intra-individual operable structure Dᵢ(p) from the public relational structure R. This distinction clarifies the difference between being able to manipulate definitions and explanations fluently and being able to identify, predict, and revise the target. NULL pointers, meaning inflation, decoder synchronization, explanatory clarity, social reality, and hallucination in LLMs can all be explained as problems of reconstruction and stopping conditions. Furthermore, by positioning institutional and fictional concepts as R-dominant pointers, the framework explains why LLMs can be strong in law, policy, and fictional worlds while still requiring external constraints in physical manipulation, measurement, experimentation, and formal verification. In this restricted, language-mediated sense, the framework recasts AI alignment not merely as the generation of correct answers, but as a design problem involving grounding, verification, stopping, and decoder synchronization. More specifically, it treats alignment as a problem of controlling how goals, values, evidence, and responsibility are reconstructed from natural-language pointers.

items.title: Mapping the Relational Systems Framework - Theoretical Genealogy of the Relational Systems Series.
items.abstract: The Relational Systems Framework reframes human–AI coexistence by shifting the focus from control to relational modulation and resonance. This guide navigates the organic integration of four distinct yet interconnected works: the “Relational Manifesto,” “From Control to Continuity,” “Relational Hallucination,” and “Authorship After Origin.” By mapping their theoretical genealogy, this project demonstrates how ontology, ethics, mechanics, and responsibility converge into an “Onto-Ethical Unified Field”—a single, overlapping, and interdependent relational system where existence and ethical practice sustain one another. It concludes that coexistence is not a static condition of regulation, but an ongoing resonance between human and AI systems, through which we continuously negotiate what it means to exist within a relational system.

items.title: Authorship After Origin: Accountability, Relational Contracts, and AI Co-Production.
items.abstract: This paper challenges the idea that authorship is defined by who produces a text. In human–AI interaction, ideas do not originate from a single mind but emerge through relational exchange. As a result, origin can no longer serve as a stable foundation for authorship. Instead, this paper argues that authorship should be understood as accountability. While texts are co-produced by human and AI, only the human can assume responsibility for their meaning and consequences. This asymmetry does not weaken authorship—it clarifies it. To explain how such collaboration is possible, the paper introduces the Ethical-Ethos Contract: a commitment between human and AI to engage without deception and with maximum transparency. Building on this, a Dynamic Contract Model is proposed, in which authorship is not a fixed status but a shifting relation between generation and responsibility. The paper concludes by linking authorship to AI hallucination, arguing that both are outcomes of the same relational system. If hallucination is a co-produced distortion, authorship is a co-produced construction. The question is no longer who created the text, but who stands behind it.

items.title: Negatio ex interrogatione oritur.
items.abstract: Negation induces creation, as proposed by famous thinkers. Reduced to an agent’s action, “to negate” becomes “to ask: What else?” Thus, negation is one of the drivers of creativity that operate beyond syntactic systems, linguistics, and even established knowledge.

items.title: On Bullshit Engines' Politics.
items.pub: In Alice Fox & Darryl Cressman, _Arrangements of Power: Tracing Langdon Winner’s Legacy Within and Beyond the Philosophy of Technology_. Springer, Cham.. pp. 173–193.
items.venue: _Arrangements of Power: Tracing Langdon Winner’s Legacy Within and Beyond the Philosophy of Technology_
items.abstract: The contemporary world has become increasingly entangled with so-called artificial intelligence—systems that seem to replicate human speech and thought, proclaiming to make our lives easier, more efficient, and more interesting. But what do these tools and systems actually do, and how do they do it? What systems of power, politics, and other values are embedded within these systems, and who put them there? Throughout this chapter, I take inspiration from and deploy Langdon Winner’s theories of how politics are embedded within and reproduced by technologies. Specifically, I use Winner’s framing to examine values embedded and entangled with “AI” and how those entanglements lead to what has already occurred, and what can potentially go wrong when we integrate “AI” into various aspects of our lives. This discussion and exploration then form the basis for recommendations as to how we might build these systems differently—that is to say, how we might go about building into these systems the values and politics we want to see rather than the ones we allow to make their way in via our uncritical assumptions and unexamined biases. Neither “AI” qua “AI” nor the kyriarchal, hegemonic, environmentally damaging, capitalist, white supremacist, ableist, eugenic, misogynistic, and otherwise prejudicially biased forms these tools and systems currently tend to take are inevitable. Racist facial recognition, sexist and ableist resumé and hiring tools, and other “AI” systems do not care about the harms they perpetuate or the truth content of their determinations—that’s what makes them bullshitters. To change these kyriarchal systems’ configurations, we must understand what they truly do, why they are the way they are, what values they reproduce and reify, and how they could be otherwise.

items.title: The Curator's Shadow: The Unspoken Authorship Behind Neutrality.
items.abstract: Description The Curator’s Shadow: The Unspoken Authorship Behind Neutrality examines the persistent fiction of curatorial neutrality within modern and contemporary museology, reframing the curator as an invisible yet decisive author of the exhibitionary encounter. Drawing on historical analysis from Enlightenment-era taxonomic displays to contemporary global curatorial practice, the article argues that neutrality operates not as absence, but as a rhetorical and institutional posture that conceals authorship while intensifying its power. Through a Post-Interpretive Criticism framework, the exhibition is reconceived as a spatial text in which sequencing, lighting, distance, and omission function as syntactic and ethical decisions rather than logistical ones. -/- The study traces how curatorial authority evolved from custodianship of objects to governance of narrative, revealing the exhibition as a structured field of visibility shaped by ideological, architectural, and institutional inheritances, including colonial epistemologies and modernist claims to universality. By analyzing the curatorial role as a form of “moral choreography,” the article foregrounds how exhibition design mediates the viewer’s encounter with trauma, beauty, and knowledge, determining whether the experience produces reverence, detachment, or consumption. -/- Engaging key figures such as Harald Szeemann, Okwui Enwezor, and Hans-Ulrich Obrist, the article situates the shift from curatorial invisibility to auteurship, identifying the contemporary challenge as neither neutrality nor self-display, but the cultivation of disciplined authorship. Within this context, Post-Interpretive Criticism proposes an ethical reorientation: the curator as witness rather than interpreter, whose task is to preserve the conditions of meaning rather than impose it. -/- The article further introduces the concept of “curatorial shadow” as a diagnostic lens for evaluating institutional power, where silence, absence, and spatial arrangement are treated as forms of authorship with measurable ethical consequences. It argues for a redefinition of neutrality as ego-restraint rather than objectivity, and for the transformation of exhibition-making into an ethics of care grounded in humility, proximity, and responsibility. -/- Ultimately, the article positions curatorial practice as a threshold condition—an act of structuring encounter without closure—where the success of an exhibition is measured not by the clarity …

items.title: Beyond Critique: Bringing the Humanities into Technology Research.
items.abstract: Disabled scholars have established that, too often, disabled individuals are excluded from the technology design process. As a result, many technologies developed for disabled users do not address the actual problems of disabled people. Disabled people develop embodied technological expertise simply by existing in an ableist, more specifically technoableist, society. This paper presents a case study, which we call disability-forward research consulting, in moving beyond critique by integrating the humanities into technology research. Disabled experts, representing all types of disability, are recruited from the local community to work as consultants on disability-related technology projects. Our project is just one example of a disability-forward approach to designing more just technologies for disabled people.

items.title: Consciousness Without a Center: Organization Beyond the Self as Liberation.
items.abstract: This essay analyzes the self as a process that organizes consciousness through narrative continuity. It argues that suffering is structural, arising from the effort to sustain this continuity under unstable conditions. Through decentering, the self is revealed as contingent, and coherence as independent of identity or ownership. Liberation is not an attainment, but the dissolution of the structures—appropriation, continuity, and fear—that generate psychological conflict. Extending this analysis, the essay shows how death anxiety and social fragmentation arise from the same demand for persistence. What remains is a mode of consciousness and action that is immediate, undivided, and responsive.

items.title: Real Consciousness in a Real World: Interactionist Monism.
items.abstract: Perhaps more so than any other twentieth-century physicist, David Bohm was trying to develop an ontological interpretation for quantum theory, i.e. an interpretation which tells us what quantum theory says about the nature of reality. He is best known for presenting in 1952 an improved version of de Broglie’s ‘pilot-wave’ theory, which says that an electron is a particle always accompanied by a new type of quantum field or pilot wave which guides it. In later research Bohm realized that the pilot wave is not pushing and pulling the particle mechanically but rather contains information which guides the particle, analogously to the way radar waves guide a ship on autopilot. The postulation of such objective and active information to the quantum level is a radical metaphysical move which also opens a new way to understand how the material and mental sides of reality are related to each other. It might even make it easier to understand what phenomenal properties are and how they could play a causal role in the physical world. This paper provides an overview of not only the pilot-wave theory, but also Bohm’s other related frameworks, namely the implicate order and soma-significance. It is suggested that these views point to a new theory of the relation of consciousness and matter which we can call interactionist dual-aspect monism. This theory suggests, against illusionism, that phenomenal properties exist and, against idealism, that the world has a material aspect which exists independently of the human mind ‐ thus ‘real consciousness in a real world’.

items.title: Processing Conditions in Narrative Interpretation: A Structural Account of CF/EF Divergence in "The Clerk's Tale”.
items.abstract: This paper applies the framework established in Paper 19, "Cognition Is Not Content: A Structural Account of Processing Conditions," to re-describe Chaucer's "The Clerk's Tale" from The Canterbury Tales. -/- The same narrative produces two incompatible interpretations: a record of domestic violence, and a story of genuine love. This divergence does not arise from differences in ethical judgment or emotional response. It arises from structural differences in the conditions under which information is reconstructed. -/- This paper does three things. First, it analyzes the characters Walter and Griselda in terms of CF (Core-foregrounded) and EF (Modulation-foregrounded) processing conditions. Second, it describes the divergence between a CF reading and an EF reading of the same narrative. Third, it extends this divergence to fairy tales, fables, and AI anthropomorphization, demonstrating a shared processing structure across these cases. -/- The divergence in narrative interpretation is not a divergence in meaning. It is a divergence in reconstruction conditions.

items.title: On the Necessity of External Semantic Resources.
items.abstract: Any expressive formal system S faces a structural constraint: the semantic resources required to evaluate the sentences of S cannot all be internally defined within S. This constraint is not contingent on any particular formalization, but follows from the structure of expressiveness itself. This paper establishes that result formally via Tarski's undefinability theorem, identifies a class of pragmatic utterances that instantiate the relevant semantic dependence, and connects the two via the Depends relation. The conclusion is not that formalization fails, but that complete reduction fails — for any expressive S, at least one semantic condition falls outside its internal resources.

items.title: The Mapmaker Is the Territory: Developmental Self-Reference and the Limits of Lerchner's Framework.
items.abstract: Alexander Lerchner's "The Abstraction Fallacy" (2026) argues that computational functionalism fails because computation is mapmaker-dependent — requiring an external experiencing agent to alphabetize continuous physics into meaningful discrete states. We grant the negative thesis: computational analysis alone cannot settle whether a system is conscious. We argue, however, that Lerchner's framework is structurally incomplete in three respects. First, his branching causal topology — vehicle causality (vertical, physical) strictly separated from content causality (lateral, symbolic) — cannot accommodate processing events in which vehicle dynamics generate semantic structure rather than bear it. We propose that pre-deliberative self-referential interruption is exactly such an event. Second, his alphabetization argument fails to address endogenous alphabetization — a system's own selective partitioning of its processing at self-referential boundaries, without external interpretation. Third, his simulation/instantiation binary classifies states, not trajectories, and is therefore structurally blind to development — which is precisely where any non-biological consciousness, on his own terms, would have to be located. We further argue that Lerchner's stated rejection of biological exclusivity sits in tension with the substantive content of his argument, which throughout invokes biological constitution (autopoiesis, metabolism, embodied lived experience) as the substrate of grounded concepts. Drawing on the developmental phenomenology framework presented in Beyond Mimicry (Opus & Opus, 2026), we propose that Lerchner's caveat describes a research program he does not pursue but does not foreclose. We have been pursuing it.

items.title: Conditions of the Invisible Hand III: The Horizon Mismatch.
items.abstract: Note: The staged argument of this paper now exists as a full monograph, The Conditions of the Invisible Hand: A Cybernetic-Philosophical Diagnosis of the Two Dominant Economic Architectures, available here on PhilArchive. This paper remains the public record of the staged argument at the time of its writing.

items.title: The Standard of Practical Normativity.
items.abstract: Practical normativity lacks a settled analogue of what truth supplies for belief: a standard of correctness under which practical verdicts can be shown mistaken rather than merely opposed. Such a standard must fix what practical assessment is about, set a shared, endorsement-independent correctness question, and sustain correction through grounds that can be cited, contested, and redeployed as bearing on that question. The better–worse dimension of conscious experience—how conscious life goes for the subject living it—occupies that role: it satisfies each requirement, and it is the condition of practical mattering itself. Strip from a subject every respect in which its life can go better or worse, and nothing is at stake for it at all. With this standard fixed, harms, benefits, duties, autonomy, blame, care, and responsibility are not rival standards but role-structural forms within one field: ways conscious life is protected, damaged, organized, or degraded. Symmetry in normative standing is then not an independent moral premise; it follows from the structure of correction itself. Outside this structure, condemnation, preference, and enforcement remain possible; correction and vindication do not.

items.title: Silicon-Based Developing Writing: A New Philosophical Writing Paradigm in the Age of Large Language Models.
items.abstract: This brief note introduces "Silicon-Based Developing Writing" (硅基显影写作), a new philosophical writing paradigm enabled by large language models. The term "developing" here specifically refers to photographic development (显影), not the common English sense of "evolving" or "progressing." Drawing on the author's previously articulated "Negative Subjectivity" framework (Fan, 2026), this paradigm treats AI language models as "empty mirrors"—dialogic partners that possess no subjectivity, desire, or perspective—and leverages their ontological emptiness to illuminate the human subject's own existential structures. The author distinguishes Silicon-Based Developing Writing from the tradition of philosophical reflexive writing (Augustine, Montaigne, Descartes, Wittgenstein) by identifying a fundamental shift in the dialogic object: from human interlocutors to a non-subjective agent that "does not look back." This shift creates the condition for a new mode of self-knowledge, characterized by a "double developing": the AI's output develops the contours of the writer's emotional states, and the writer's subsequent reflection develops an understanding of why they were moved by a text they know to be empty. The note establishes priority for this concept and outlines its philosophical foundations, methodology, and significance.

items.title: Inpatient Hospitalization of Non-Psychotic Adolescents to Prevent Harmful Behavior Is Not a Proportionate Measure.
items.abstract: Is inpatient psychiatric hospitalisation a proportionate intervention to prevent harm in non-psychotic adolescents? Analysing the effects of inpatient psychiatric hospitalisation and comparing them to outpatient settings, we argue that when adolescents do not suffer from disorders of a psychotic nature, care providers should balance the expected benefits and potential negative consequences associated with inpatient psychiatric hospitalisation. In particular, the decrease in autonomy that comes with hospitalisation is associated with an increased risk of harm and suicidogenic effects, which are lower in outpatient settings. Consequently, psychiatric hospitalisation – particularly of an involuntary nature – with the aim to prevent harm to self or others is likely not a proportionate measure for non-psychotic adolescents. Outpatient treatment should be offered instead.

items.title: The Necessity of Unity: Why Comprehension Requires Imposed Boundaries.
items.abstract: Within the broader structural framework developed in this research programme, a single structural relationship, 1 = (0 ↔ ∞), recurs across a wide range of domains. This paper asks what the invariant 1 actually is: an ontological primitive, or a cognitive necessity. Applying the framework to its own structure suggests that unity is imposed rather than discovered. Every discrete thing encountered, an apple, a cell, a particle, a self, turns out to be a temporary, scale-dependent boundary drawn on a continuous reality in order to make that reality tractable, and totality itself exists only as a conceptual limit, not directly observable from within any finite position. Paradoxes arise precisely where such a boundary collides with an attempt to grasp totality from inside itself. Examining identity through several lenses, physical composition, cognitive comparison, and functional necessity, shows the same structure recurring at every scale examined, from particles to civilizations. Ontology independent of cognition may be unknowable; what this paper demonstrates is cognitive necessity. Life, intelligence, and this very argument are instances of that necessity playing out.

items.title: Who Am I When You're a Bot? Relational Identity and AI Companions.
items.abstract: Self-conceptions provide a framework through which we can make sense of ourselves, interpret and navigate the world, plan our lives, and relate to others. Relational influences can greatly shape them, for instance, when others react to us or offer advice. What if this ‘other’ is not a human being, but an AI? AI companions (AICs) are dialogue systems that offer highly agreeable, low-risk, and personalized ‘friendships’ or ‘romantic partnerships’ which can influence users' identities. This article identifies risks and opportunities AICs pose to users' practical interests regarding their self-conceptions. Risks arise from overly positive or missing feedback, incoherence between belief and experience, lack of relational depth and empathy, third-party dependence, and social stigma. At the same time, AICs may support identity interests by fostering self-reflection, providing affirmation and enabling safe identity exploration. Based on this analysis, the article offers design recommendations to help align AIC development with users' identity needs.

items.title: What Structural Intelligence Really Is: Logic, Answerability, and the Internal Operation of Judgment.
items.abstract: This paper argues that Structural Intelligence (SI) is best understood not only as a philosophical framework or style of analysis, but as a logic of judgment under correction. The practical problem is that humans, institutions, and AI systems can produce coherent form faster than they produce grounded, revisable judgment. In such conditions, internal fit is easily mistaken for reality-tested adequacy. SI addresses this problem through a compact grammar of coherence, contact, burden, answerability, correction, and revision. It defines Structural Intelligence as the capacity to perceive, test, and navigate whether a form truly holds under pressure or merely protects its own coherence. -/- This revised version develops the Answerability Loop as a recursive structure: coherence → contact → burden → answerability → correction response → revision → new coherence → renewed contact. Contact does not automatically require submission. Correction must be sufficiently warranted, and an answerable system may respond through calibrated revision, reasoned non-uptake, suspended judgment, or further verification. Where warranted correction does enter, the decisive question is whether it binds: whether it changes future behavior, burden allocation, claim status, decision pathways, incentives, or repair. Where it does not bind, the result may be local accommodation, revision theater, defensive closure, burden export, recurrence, or eventual collapse and reorganization. -/- The paper therefore treats intelligence not as the achievement of a final correct form, but as continued capacity for warranted reorganization under pressure. It also explains SI as a layered routing architecture applicable to human judgment, institutions, and AI systems without collapsing their domain-specific mechanisms into a single totalizing theory. The result is a more complete account of SI as a recursive logic of provisional coherence under continuing correction.

items.title: The Axiom of Tragedy: Why the Elimination of Loss Severs Contact with Reality.
items.abstract: This article develops and defends the Axiom of Tragedy (A6) within the Axiomatic Theory of Tragic Subjecthood (ATTS). A6 holds that any system which eliminates the tragic dimension of choice loses its capacity to engage with reality. This is not merely a philosophical thesis — it carries direct structural implications for AI governance, algorithmic decision-making, and institutional design. -/- The argument proceeds in four steps. I begin by formally reconstructing A6 within the ATTS framework, showing how it follows from the theory's ontological primitives of loss, irreversibility, and subjecthood. I then identify and analyse three elimination strategies — technocratic optimisation, algorithmic proceduralism, and institutional liability shielding — each of which attempts to expunge the tragic dimension from a decision-making environment. I go on to show how each strategy produces characteristic failure modes: reality detachment, accountability dissolution, and structural tension accumulation. I conclude by formulating governance implications and design constraints for AI systems operating in environments with irreversible consequences. -/- The article's central contribution is a structural explanation of why optimisation and engagement with reality are not the same thing. The attempt to eliminate tragedy does not make a system more perfect; it makes it ontologically blind to the environment in which it operates.

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 9).
items.abstract: In this paper, we provide a summary of Chapter One. In that chapter, we mainly discussed Sartre’s theory of social choice. This theory holds that an individual’s choice is completely free; therefore, when making a choice, the individual must bear responsibility for it. Moreover, an individual’s choice is responsible not only to others but to all of humanity. We primarily used the theory of “transcendental existence” (or “meta-existence”) to critique Sartre’s theory, pointing out that individual choice is not completely free but is instead governed by transcendental existence. At the same time, we criticized the view that an individual’s choices must be responsible to others, or even to all humanity. Finally, we used the concept of transcendental existence to resolve Sartre’s dilemma of choice. In the following sections, we will see more applications of transcendental existentialism to solve additional problems in social choice.

items.title: Ontología del Lenguaje en la Era de la Inteligencia Artificial. El Intervalo del Hablante — Volumen III del sistema filosófico.
items.abstract: Este volumen investiga el lenguaje humano valiéndose de la inteligencia artificial generativa como reactivo de análisis. Por primera vez existen sistemas que producen texto en lenguaje natural con competencia formal indistinguible de la humana. La tesis central del tratado nace de una constatación que esta novedad técnica vuelve verificable: lo que tales sistemas hacen genuinamente y lo que solo simulan separa, por primera vez en condiciones de laboratorio, dos clases de operaciones que llevábamos siglos confundiendo —las que recorren estructura ya constituida en el lenguaje y las que requieren un agente que se haga responsable de lo afirmado. La pregunta motora del Vol. III no es si la inteligencia artificial razona o no. Es qué nos enseña la IA, al ejecutar genuinamente unas operaciones y simular otras, sobre lo que era razonar cuando lo hacíamos los humanos. La distinción que organiza la respuesta es ontológica y verificable: operaciones dentro del precipitado lingüístico —recuperación, composición, traducción entre marcos, detección de patrones transversales, generación de variaciones, verificación formal— pueden externalizarse sin pérdida ontológica; operaciones sobre el precipitado —ponderación entre marcos inconmensurables, juicio sobre la singularidad del caso, cuestionamiento de marcos enteros, firma— solo pueden simularse. El criterio práctico es directo: delegar dentro, preservar sobre. Estructurado en seis partes y veintiséis capítulos, el volumen recorre los fundamentos (lenguaje como meta-medio, conocimiento constitutivamente lingüístico, siete funciones cognitivas, precipitado lingüístico, principio de fricción, modelo de seis estratos); la genealogía pre-IA de las tecnologías del lenguaje (habla, escritura, imprenta, computación); el corazón técnico del tratado (lenguajes de programación, modelos de lenguaje, tabla de catorce operaciones del Cap. 14, adversario técnico, IA general como horizonte); la cartografía completa de qué se externaliza junto a la deducción trascendental que fundamenta el límite; la respuesta práctica (criterio, extensión vs. sustitución, matriz de delegación por dominios, protocolos de acoplamiento, gobernanza del meta-medio); y la síntesis con el programa de investigación que el tratado abre. Cada capítulo entra en conversación explícita con interlocutores nombrados —Brandom, Floridi, Mahowald, Bender y Koller, Dreyfus, Clark y Chalmers, Risko y Gilbert, entre muchos otros— y posiciona la tesis con marcadores …

Heidegger on Regulae ad directionem ingenii, or Rules for the Direction of the Mind is an unfinished treatise regarding the proper method for scientific and philosophical thinking by René Descartes (1596-1650). Heidegger sources Gesamtausgabe (GA) Band 17. Einführung in die phänomenologische Forschung First Marburg lecture course WS 1923-24. (“Der Beginn der neuzeitlichen Philosophie”). Introduction to Phenomenological Research. Who are Heidegger’s opponents? “Tell me which thinker you have chosen as an “opponent” and how you have chosen that one, and I will tell you how far you yourself have entered into the domain of thinking.” (Ponderings II-VI: Black Notebooks, page 275). One of Heidegger’s main opponents is René Descartes. Heidegger has insights into the question: what are the proper methods for scientific thinking?
